See Ibn Kathir's marginal note.]]: "Tell me about taqwa." He said: "Have you ever walked a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do?" He said: "I was careful and I gathered up my garments." Ka'b said: "That is taqwa." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "The God-fearing person is one who abandons what is not harmful out of fear of what is harmful." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: "Taqwa is abandoning what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has made obligatory. Whatever provision Allah grants after that is good upon good." It was said: "It is following the example of the Prophet ﷺ." A hadith says: "The essence of taqwa is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl 16:90]], and so on." Ibn ʿUmar said: "Taqwa is that you do not consider yourself better than anyone." Specifying the God-fearing by mention is an honouring of them, or because they are the ones who are truly guided by the guidance.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who believe﴾. The position of *alladhina* (who) is in the genitive as an adjective (*na't*) of *al-muttaqin* (the God-fearing). *Yu'minun* (they believe): *yusaddiqun* (they affirm as true). Abu ʿAmr and Warsh drop the hamzah, while the others pronounce it; and likewise both of them drop every silent hamzah that is the first radical of the verb, such as *yu'min* and *mu'min*, except for a few words that are counted [[Addition from manuscript B.]].

The reality of *iman* (faith) is affirmation with the heart. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You would not be believed by us﴾ [[Surah Yusuf 12:17]], meaning: 'You would not be affirmed by us' [[Addition from manuscript B.]]. In the sharia, it is: belief in the heart, verbal confession with the tongue, and action with the limbs. Confession and action are called *iman* for a reason of association, since they are among its branches.

*Islam* is submission and yielding. Every *iman* is *Islam*, but not every *Islam* is *iman*, if it is not accompanied by affirmation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say: "We believe." Say: "You have not believed, but say: 'We have submitted'"﴾ [[Surah al-Hujurat 49:14]]. This is because a man may be submissive outwardly while not affirming inwardly, and he may affirm inwardly while not yielding outwardly.

The answers of the Prophet ﷺ differed concerning both of these when Jibril, peace be upon him, asked him, and this is what Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Bawayh al-Zarrad al-Bukhari informed us: Abu al-Qasim ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Khuza'i told us, Abu Sa'id al-Haytham ibn Kulayb al-Shashi told us, Abu Ahmad ʿIsa ibn Ahmad al-ʿAsqalani [[The manuscript shows a page break here.]] told us, Yazid ibn Harun told us, Kahmas ibn al-Hasan told us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from Yahya ibn Yaʿmar, who said: "The first person who spoke about *qadar* (divine decree) in Basra was Ma'bad al-Juhani. Then I and Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman set out for Makkah, and we said: 'If we met any of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we would ask him about what these people are saying.' We met ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, so I and my companion surrounded him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I knew he would leave the speaking to me, so I said: 'O Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, there have appeared among us people who go deep into this knowledge and seek it, claiming that there is no qadar, and that the matter is *unuf* (newly created without decree).' He said: 'When you meet them, inform them that I am innocent of them and they are innocent of me. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uhud and spent it in the way of Allah, Allah would not accept anything from him until he believes in qadar, both its good and its evil.'" Then he said:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab told us, he said: "While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, there came a man with exceedingly white clothing and exceedingly black hair, showing no trace of travel, and none of us knew him. He came and sat before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [his knee touching his knee], and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about Islam.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, you establish the prayer, you give the zakat, you fast Ramadan, and you make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' We were amazed that he asked and then affirmed the answer. Then he said: 'Tell me about iman.' He said: 'That you believe in Allah alone, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire, and the qadar, its good and its evil.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about ihsan.' He said: 'That you worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about the Hour.' He said: 'The one asked about it does not know it better than the one asking.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' He said: 'Then tell me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, and that you see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in building tall structures.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he left. After three days, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'O ʿUmar, do you know who the man was?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That was Jibril. He came to you to teach you the matters of your religion, and he never came to me in any form except that I recognized him in it, except in this form of his.'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in *al-Iman*, chapter on Jibril's question about iman and Islam, 1/114; and by Muslim in *al-Iman*, chapter on iman, Islam and ihsan, nos. 8 and 9, 1/36–37. The author also cited it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 1/8–9.]]

The Prophet ﷺ, in this hadith, made *Islam* the name of what appears of actions, and *iman* the name of what is hidden of belief. This does not mean that actions are not part of *iman*, nor that the affirmation of the heart is not part of *Islam*. Rather, that is a detailed explanation of a single whole, all of which is one thing, whose comprehensive term is *al-din* (the religion). For this reason he said, "That was Jibril, who came to you to teach you the matters of your religion."

The evidence that deeds are part of faith is what we were informed by Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣāliḥī: Abu al-Qāsim Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Shāh narrated to us: Abū Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Quraysh ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: Bishr ibn Mūsā narrated to us: Khalaf ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, from Jarīr al-Rāzī, from Sahl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dīnār, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Faith has seventy-some branches. The best of them is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the least of them is removing harmful things from the road. Modesty (ḥayāʾ) is a branch of faith." [Narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Īmān, chapter "The matters of faith," 1/50. Also narrated by Muslim in al-Īmān, chapter "Explaining the number of the branches of faith and their best and least," no. (57), 1/63. The author also narrated it in Sharḥ al-Sunnah, 1/34.]

It is also said: faith (al-īmān) is derived from security (al-amān). Thus the believer (al-mu'min) is so called because he secures himself from the punishment of Allah, and Allah the Exalted is the Giver of Security (Mu'min) because He secures His servants from His punishment. [For a detailed discussion of the topics of faith, refer to the book "Al-Īmān" by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah.]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen). Al-ghayb is a verbal noun used in the place of a noun, so the absent one is called "ghayb," just as the just one is called "ʿadl" and the visitor is called "zawr." Al-ghayb is that which is hidden from the eyes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Al-ghayb here is everything you have been commanded to believe in that is out of your sight, such as the angels, the Resurrection, Paradise, Hellfire, the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), and the Scale (al-mīzān)." It is also said that al-ghayb here is Allah the Exalted; it is also said it is the Qur'an. Al-Ḥasan said: "It means the Hereafter." Ziрr ibn Ḥubaysh and Ibn Jurayj said: "It means revelation." A parallel is the verse: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ (35 – al-Najm). Ibn Kaysān said: "It means divine decree (al-qadar)." ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd said: "We were with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd and we mentioned the companions of Muḥammad (ﷺ) [and what they preceded us in], and ʿAbd Allāh said: 'The affair of Muḥammad was clear to those who saw him. By the One besides whom there is no god, no one has ever believed with a faith better than faith in the unseen.' Then he recited: 'Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book...' up to his words: '...the successful.'" [Addition from "B."]

Abū Jaʿfar, Abū ʿAmr, and Warsh recite ﴿yu'minūn﴾ without the hamzah (glottal stop). Likewise Abū Jaʿfar omits every silent hamzah except in the words anbi'hum, nabbi'hum, and nabbi'nā. Abū ʿAmr omits all of them except when the hamzah is a sign of the jussive (jazm), as in nabbi'hum, anbi'hum, and tasu'hum, and in in nash', wa-nansaʾhā, and similar, or when it is a shift from one dialect to another, as in mu'ṣadah and ri'iyyā. Warsh omits every silent hamzah that was the first radical of the verb (fāʾ al-fiʿl), except tu'wī and tu'wīhi. He does not omit a hamzah that is the middle radical of the verb (ʿayn al-fiʿl), except al-ru'yā and its like, provided it is not on the pattern of fiʿl, as in dhi'b.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they establish the prayer﴾. That is, they perpetuate it and guard it at its appointed times, with its limits, its pillars, and its forms. It is said: "He stood by the matter" and "He established the matter" when he carried it out, giving its rights. What is meant here is the five daily prayers, mentioned in the singular form (al-wuḥdān) [in B: "the singular"], as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾ (213 – al-Baqarah), meaning the books.

In the language, ṣalāh means supplication (duʿāʾ). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And pray for them﴾ (103 – al-Tawbah), that is, "supplicate for them." In the Sharīʿah (sacred law), it is the name for specific acts: standing, bowing, prostration, sitting, supplication, and praise. It has been said regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ (56 – al-Aḥzāb), and the rest of the verse, that the ṣalāh from Allah in this verse is mercy, from the angels is seeking forgiveness, and from the believers is supplication.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾: [(meaning)] "We have given them." Provision (al-rizq) is the name for everything from which one benefits, even a child or a slave. Its original meaning in the language is portion and share. ﴿They spend﴾: they give charity. Qatādah said: "They spend in the way of Allah and in His obedience." The root meaning of infāq (spending) is taking out from the hand and possession, and from it comes nifāq al-sūq (the slump of the market), because goods leave the hand in it. From it also: "The animal's soul departed (nafiqat al-dābbah)" when its spirit left it. This verse refers to believers from among the polytheist Arabs.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾: the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books sent down to the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn [and Abū ʿAmr], the people of Basra, and Yaʿqūb omit every elongation (madd) that falls between two words. The others elongate it. This verse refers to believers from the People of the Book.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, that is, in the Abode of the Hereafter. The world was called dunyā because it is near (danā) the Hereafter, and the Hereafter was called ākhirah because it comes later (ta'akhkhur) and is after the world. ﴿They are certain﴾, that is, they are certain that it will occur. From al-īqān, which is knowledge. It is said: īqān and yaqīn are knowledge derived from inference (istidlāl). Therefore Allah is not called "Mūqin" (one who is certain), nor is His knowledge called yaqīn, since His knowledge is not derived from inference.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the people of this description. Ulāʾika is a word meaning a reference to a group, like "hum" (they). The kāf is for addressing, as in the particle of that (dhālika). ﴿Upon guidance﴾, that is, right direction, clarity, and insight ﴿from their Lord. And those are the successful﴾, that is, the saved, who succeeded by entering Paradise and were rescued from the Fire. Al-falāḥ may also mean remaining, that is, they will remain in lasting bliss. The root meaning of al-falāḥ is cutting and splitting, and from it the farmer is called fallāḥ because he plows (yashuqq) the earth. There is a proverb: "Iron is cut (yufliḥ) by iron," meaning it is split. Thus they are assured (maqṭūʿ) of good in this world and the next.

**Al-Baghawi's *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 2 (al-Baqarah), verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Baqarah is Madani [[The number of its verses is 285, though it is said to be 286 or 287 (al-Itqan, vol. 1, p. 235).]]
It has 287 verses.
* *
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ Al-Sha'bi and a group of scholars said: "Alif Lam Mim, and all the other disjointed letters (huruf al-hijaʾ) at the beginnings of the surahs, belong to the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses) whose knowledge Allah the Exalted has reserved for Himself. They are the secret of the Qur'an. So we believe in their outward form and entrust their knowledge to Allah the Exalted. The benefit of mentioning them is to seek belief in them." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of Allah the Exalted in the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs." Ali said: "Every book has its choice part, and the choice part of this Book is the letters of hijaʾ [[In manuscript B: "al-hijaʾ."]]." Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "I used to ask al-Sha'bi about the openings of the surahs, and he said: 'O Dawud, every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs, so leave them and ask about anything else.'"

A group of scholars said: "Their meanings are known." It was said: "Each letter of them is the key to one of Allah's names, as Ibn Abbas said regarding Kaf Ha Ya ʿAyn Sad (Kaf-Ha-Ya-ʿAyn-Sad): the Kaf is from *Kafi* (the Sufficient), the Ha is from *Hadi* (the Guide), the Ya is from *Hakim* (the Wise), the ʿAyn is from *ʿAlim* (the All-Knowing), and the Sad is from *Sadiq* (the Truthful)." It was said regarding Alif Lam Mim Sad: "I am Allah, the King, the Truthful." Al-Rabi ibn Anas said regarding Alif Lam Mim: "The Alif is the key to His name Allah, the Lam is the key to His name al-Latif (the Subtle), and the Mim is the key to His name al-Majid (the Glorious)."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The Alif is the blessings (ala') of Allah, the Lam is His gentleness (lutf), and the Mim is His dominion (mulk)." Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The meaning of Alif Lam Mim is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing. The meaning of Alif Lam Sad is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing and the Most Excellent. The meaning of Alif Lam Ra is: I am Allah, who sees. The meaning of Alif Lam Mim Ra is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing and the All-Seeing." Al-Zajjaj said: "This is good, for the Arabs mention a letter of a word while meaning the whole word, as when they say: 'I said to her: Stop for us (qifi lana),' and she said: 'Qaf' [[This verse is by al-Walid ibn ʿUqba, and its completion is: "We do not reckon that we have forgotten the al-Ijaf." See: Tafsir al-Tabari 1/212; Tafsir al-Wahidi 1/26.]], meaning: 'I stopped.'"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: "They are the names of Allah the Exalted, *muqatta'ah* (separated) [[Note in manuscript A: "separated, not joined."]]. If people knew how to join them, they would know the Greatest Name of Allah. Do you not see that you say Ra, Ha Mim, Nun, and it becomes *al-Rahman* (the Most Gracious), and so on for the rest, except that we are not able to join them?" Qatadah said: "These letters are the names of the Qur'an." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "They are the names of the surahs [[In the original: "the surah."]]. Their explanation is that when a speaker says, 'I recited Ha Mim,' the listener understands that he recited the surah that begins with Ha Mim." It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are oaths. Al-Akhfash said: "Allah swore by these letters because of their nobility and excellence, since they are the foundations (*mabadi'*) [[In the printed edition: "mabani" (building blocks).]] of His revealed Books and the building blocks of His Most Beautiful Names." [[See these opinions in: Tafsir al-Tabari 1/205–224; Tafsir al-Wahidi 1/25–26.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is the Book﴾. That is, this Book, which is the Qur'an. It was said: "The word *dhalika* (that) contains an implied meaning, i.e., 'This is that Book.'" Al-Farra' said: "Allah had promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would send down to him a Book that water would not erase and that would not wear out from much repetition. When He sent down the Qur'an, He said, 'This is *dhalika* (that) Book which I promised to send down to you, in the Torah and the Gospel and on the tongues of the prophets before you.'" *Hadha* (this) is used for what is near, and *dhalika* (that) for what is far. Ibn Kaysan said: "Before Surat al-Baqarah, Allah the Exalted had sent down surahs which the polytheists denied. Then He sent down Surat al-Baqarah and said, *dhalika al-Kitab* (that Book), meaning the surahs that preceded al-Baqarah, 'there is no doubt in it.'"

*Al-Kitab* (the Book) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used with the meaning of *al-maktub* (the written). It is as one says of a created thing, *khalq* (creation), and of this dirham, *darb fulan* (the minted coin of so-and-so), meaning *madrub* (minted). The root of *kataba* is gathering and joining together. A military unit is called *katiba* because of its gathering together. A book is called *kitab* because it joins one letter to another.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, that is, there is no doubt that it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that it is the truth and the reality. It was said: "This is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., 'Do not doubt it,' like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so there shall be no obscenity or wickedness﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah 2:197]], meaning: 'Do not commit obscenity and do not commit wickedness.'"

Ibn Kathir read *fihi* (in it) with *ishba'* (prolonging the vowel) when joined, and likewise every pronoun *ha'* (ha of the pronoun) preceded by a sukun (silent letter) is prolonged when joined, provided it is not followed by a silent letter. If the silent letter before the *ha'* is a *ya'*, he prolongs it with a *kasrah* as a *ya'*; if it is other than *ya'*, he prolongs it with a *dammah* as a *waw*. Hafs agreed with him in His saying, ﴿therein humiliated﴾ [[Surah al-Furqan 25:69]], so he prolonged it (*fayushbi'uhu*) [[In manuscript B: "fa-ashbaʿahu."]].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i perform *idgham al-ghunnah* (assimilation with nasalization) before the *lam* and *ra'*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i add before the *ya'*, and Hamzah adds before the *waw*. The others do not assimilate them. Abu Ja'far conceals (*ikhfa'*) the *nun* and *tanwin* before the *kha'* and *ghayn*.

﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾: that is, it is guidance, meaning right direction and clarification, for the people of taqwa (God-consciousness). It was said: "It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning *hadiyan* (guiding), its implied sense being: there is no doubt in its guidance for the God-fearing." *Al-huda* (guidance) is that by which a person is guided. *Lil-muttaqin* (for the God-fearing) means for the believers. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "*Al-Muttaqi* (the God-fearing) is one who guards himself against shirk, the major sins, and the gross immoralities." It is derived from *al-ittiqa'* (guarding), whose root meaning is a barrier between two things. From this one says, *ittaqa bi-tursihi*, meaning he made his shield a barrier between himself and what he targeted.

It is said in a hadith: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would take cover behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" [[Narrated by Muslim in *al-Jihad wa al-Siyar*, chapter on the battle of Hunayn (1776), from al-Bara', vol. 3, p. 1401. The author also cited it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 4/33.]], meaning: when the war intensified, we made him a barrier between ourselves and the enemy. Thus the God-fearing person makes obedience to the command of Allah and abstention from what He forbade a barrier between himself and the punishment. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Ka'b al-Ahbar [[Ibn Kathir alone reports that the one questioned was Ubayy ibn Ka'b. See Ibn Kathir's marginal note.]]: "Tell me about taqwa." He said: "Have you ever walked a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do?" He said: "I was careful and I gathered up my garments." Ka'b said: "That is taqwa." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "The God-fearing person is one who abandons what is not harmful out of fear of what is harmful." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: "Taqwa is abandoning what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has made obligatory. Whatever provision Allah grants after that is good upon good." It was said: "It is following the example of the Prophet ﷺ." A hadith says: "The essence of taqwa is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl 16:90]], and so on." Ibn ʿUmar said: "Taqwa is that you do not consider yourself better than anyone." Specifying the God-fearing by mention is an honouring of them, or because they are the ones who are truly guided by the guidance.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who believe﴾. The position of *alladhina* (who) is in the genitive as an adjective (*na't*) of *al-muttaqin* (the God-fearing). *Yu'minun* (they believe): *yusaddiqun* (they affirm as true). Abu ʿAmr and Warsh drop the hamzah, while the others pronounce it; and likewise both of them drop every silent hamzah that is the first radical of the verb, such as *yu'min* and *mu'min*, except for a few words that are counted [[Addition from manuscript B.]].

The reality of *iman* (faith) is affirmation with the heart. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You would not be believed by us﴾ [[Surah Yusuf 12:17]], meaning: 'You would not be affirmed by us' [[Addition from manuscript B.]]. In the sharia, it is: belief in the heart, verbal confession with the tongue, and action with the limbs. Confession and action are called *iman* for a reason of association, since they are among its branches.

*Islam* is submission and yielding. Every *iman* is *Islam*, but not every *Islam* is *iman*, if it is not accompanied by affirmation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say: "We believe." Say: "You have not believed, but say: 'We have submitted'"﴾ [[Surah al-Hujurat 49:14]]. This is because a man may be submissive outwardly while not affirming inwardly, and he may affirm inwardly while not yielding outwardly.

The answers of the Prophet ﷺ differed concerning both of these when Jibril, peace be upon him, asked him, and this is what Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Bawayh al-Zarrad al-Bukhari informed us: Abu al-Qasim ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Khuza'i told us, Abu Sa'id al-Haytham ibn Kulayb al-Shashi told us, Abu Ahmad ʿIsa ibn Ahmad al-ʿAsqalani [[The manuscript shows a page break here.]] told us, Yazid ibn Harun told us, Kahmas ibn al-Hasan told us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from Yahya ibn Yaʿmar, who said: "The first person who spoke about *qadar* (divine decree) in Basra was Ma'bad al-Juhani. Then I and Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman set out for Makkah, and we said: 'If we met any of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we would ask him about what these people are saying.' We met ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, so I and my companion surrounded him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I knew he would leave the speaking to me, so I said: 'O Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, there have appeared among us people who go deep into this knowledge and seek it, claiming that there is no qadar, and that the matter is *unuf* (newly created without decree).' He said: 'When you meet them, inform them that I am innocent of them and they are innocent of me. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uhud and spent it in the way of Allah, Allah would not accept anything from him until he believes in qadar, both its good and its evil.'" Then he said:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab told us, he said: "While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, there came a man with exceedingly white clothing and exceedingly black hair, showing no trace of travel, and none of us knew him. He came and sat before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [his knee touching his knee], and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about Islam.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, you establish the prayer, you give the zakat, you fast Ramadan, and you make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' We were amazed that he asked and then affirmed the answer. Then he said: 'Tell me about iman.' He said: 'That you believe in Allah alone, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire, and the qadar, its good and its evil.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about ihsan.' He said: 'That you worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about the Hour.' He said: 'The one asked about it does not know it better than the one asking.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' He said: 'Then tell me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, and that you see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in building tall structures.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he left. After three days, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'O ʿUmar, do you know who the man was?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That was Jibril. He came to you to teach you the matters of your religion, and he never came to me in any form except that I recognized him in it, except in this form of his.'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in *al-Iman*, chapter on Jibril's question about iman and Islam, 1/114; and by Muslim in *al-Iman*, chapter on iman, Islam and ihsan, nos. 8 and 9, 1/36–37. The author also cited it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 1/8–9.]]

The Prophet ﷺ, in this hadith, made *Islam* the name of what appears of actions, and *iman* the name of what is hidden of belief. This does not mean that actions are not part of *iman*, nor that the affirmation of the heart is not part of *Islam*. Rather, that is a detailed explanation of a single whole, all of which is one thing, whose comprehensive term is *al-din* (the religion). For this reason he said, "That was Jibril, who came to you to teach you the matters of your religion."

The evidence that deeds are part of faith is what we were informed by Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣāliḥī: Abu al-Qāsim Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Shāh narrated to us: Abū Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Quraysh ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: Bishr ibn Mūsā narrated to us: Khalaf ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, from Jarīr al-Rāzī, from Sahl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dīnār, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Faith has seventy-some branches. The best of them is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the least of them is removing harmful things from the road. Modesty (ḥayāʾ) is a branch of faith." [Narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Īmān, chapter "The matters of faith," 1/50. Also narrated by Muslim in al-Īmān, chapter "Explaining the number of the branches of faith and their best and least," no. (57), 1/63. The author also narrated it in Sharḥ al-Sunnah, 1/34.]

It is also said: faith (al-īmān) is derived from security (al-amān). Thus the believer (al-mu'min) is so called because he secures himself from the punishment of Allah, and Allah the Exalted is the Giver of Security (Mu'min) because He secures His servants from His punishment. [For a detailed discussion of the topics of faith, refer to the book "Al-Īmān" by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah.]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen). Al-ghayb is a verbal noun used in the place of a noun, so the absent one is called "ghayb," just as the just one is called "ʿadl" and the visitor is called "zawr." Al-ghayb is that which is hidden from the eyes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Al-ghayb here is everything you have been commanded to believe in that is out of your sight, such as the angels, the Resurrection, Paradise, Hellfire, the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), and the Scale (al-mīzān)." It is also said that al-ghayb here is Allah the Exalted; it is also said it is the Qur'an. Al-Ḥasan said: "It means the Hereafter." Ziрr ibn Ḥubaysh and Ibn Jurayj said: "It means revelation." A parallel is the verse: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ (35 – al-Najm). Ibn Kaysān said: "It means divine decree (al-qadar)." ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd said: "We were with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd and we mentioned the companions of Muḥammad (ﷺ) [and what they preceded us in], and ʿAbd Allāh said: 'The affair of Muḥammad was clear to those who saw him. By the One besides whom there is no god, no one has ever believed with a faith better than faith in the unseen.' Then he recited: 'Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book...' up to his words: '...the successful.'" [Addition from "B."]

Abū Jaʿfar, Abū ʿAmr, and Warsh recite ﴿yu'minūn﴾ without the hamzah (glottal stop). Likewise Abū Jaʿfar omits every silent hamzah except in the words anbi'hum, nabbi'hum, and nabbi'nā. Abū ʿAmr omits all of them except when the hamzah is a sign of the jussive (jazm), as in nabbi'hum, anbi'hum, and tasu'hum, and in in nash', wa-nansaʾhā, and similar, or when it is a shift from one dialect to another, as in mu'ṣadah and ri'iyyā. Warsh omits every silent hamzah that was the first radical of the verb (fāʾ al-fiʿl), except tu'wī and tu'wīhi. He does not omit a hamzah that is the middle radical of the verb (ʿayn al-fiʿl), except al-ru'yā and its like, provided it is not on the pattern of fiʿl, as in dhi'b.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they establish the prayer﴾. That is, they perpetuate it and guard it at its appointed times, with its limits, its pillars, and its forms. It is said: "He stood by the matter" and "He established the matter" when he carried it out, giving its rights. What is meant here is the five daily prayers, mentioned in the singular form (al-wuḥdān) [in B: "the singular"], as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾ (213 – al-Baqarah), meaning the books.

In the language, ṣalāh means supplication (duʿāʾ). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And pray for them﴾ (103 – al-Tawbah), that is, "supplicate for them." In the Sharīʿah (sacred law), it is the name for specific acts: standing, bowing, prostration, sitting, supplication, and praise. It has been said regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ (56 – al-Aḥzāb), and the rest of the verse, that the ṣalāh from Allah in this verse is mercy, from the angels is seeking forgiveness, and from the believers is supplication.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾: [(meaning)] "We have given them." Provision (al-rizq) is the name for everything from which one benefits, even a child or a slave. Its original meaning in the language is portion and share. ﴿They spend﴾: they give charity. Qatādah said: "They spend in the way of Allah and in His obedience." The root meaning of infāq (spending) is taking out from the hand and possession, and from it comes nifāq al-sūq (the slump of the market), because goods leave the hand in it. From it also: "The animal's soul departed (nafiqat al-dābbah)" when its spirit left it. This verse refers to believers from among the polytheist Arabs.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾: the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books sent down to the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn [and Abū ʿAmr], the people of Basra, and Yaʿqūb omit every elongation (madd) that falls between two words. The others elongate it. This verse refers to believers from the People of the Book.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, that is, in the Abode of the Hereafter. The world was called dunyā because it is near (danā) the Hereafter, and the Hereafter was called ākhirah because it comes later (ta'akhkhur) and is after the world. ﴿They are certain﴾, that is, they are certain that it will occur. From al-īqān, which is knowledge. It is said: īqān and yaqīn are knowledge derived from inference (istidlāl). Therefore Allah is not called "Mūqin" (one who is certain), nor is His knowledge called yaqīn, since His knowledge is not derived from inference.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the people of this description. Ulāʾika is a word meaning a reference to a group, like "hum" (they). The kāf is for addressing, as in the particle of that (dhālika). ﴿Upon guidance﴾, that is, right direction, clarity, and insight ﴿from their Lord. And those are the successful﴾, that is, the saved, who succeeded by entering Paradise and were rescued from the Fire. Al-falāḥ may also mean remaining, that is, they will remain in lasting bliss. The root meaning of al-falāḥ is cutting and splitting, and from it the farmer is called fallāḥ because he plows (yashuqq) the earth. There is a proverb: "Iron is cut (yufliḥ) by iron," meaning it is split. Thus they are assured (maqṭūʿ) of good in this world and the next.

**Al-Baghawi's *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 2 (al-Baqarah), verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2)**

Surat al-Baqarah is Madani [[The number of its verses is 285, though it is said to be 286 or 287 (al-Itqan, vol. 1, p. 235).]]
It has 287 verses.
* *
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ Al-Sha'bi and a group of scholars said: "Alif Lam Mim, and all the other disjointed letters (huruf al-hijaʾ) at the beginnings of the surahs, belong to the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses) whose knowledge Allah the Exalted has reserved for Himself. They are the secret of the Qur'an. So we believe in their outward form and entrust their knowledge to Allah the Exalted. The benefit of mentioning them is to seek belief in them." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of Allah the Exalted in the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs." Ali said: "Every book has its choice part, and the choice part of this Book is the letters of hijaʾ [[In manuscript B: "al-hijaʾ."]]." Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "I used to ask al-Sha'bi about the openings of the surahs, and he said: 'O Dawud, every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs, so leave them and ask about anything else.'"

A group of scholars said: "Their meanings are known." It was said: "Each letter of them is the key to one of Allah's names, as Ibn Abbas said regarding Kaf Ha Ya ʿAyn Sad (Kaf-Ha-Ya-ʿAyn-Sad): the Kaf is from *Kafi* (the Sufficient), the Ha is from *Hadi* (the Guide), the Ya is from *Hakim* (the Wise), the ʿAyn is from *ʿAlim* (the All-Knowing), and the Sad is from *Sadiq* (the Truthful)." It was said regarding Alif Lam Mim Sad: "I am Allah, the King, the Truthful." Al-Rabi ibn Anas said regarding Alif Lam Mim: "The Alif is the key to His name Allah, the Lam is the key to His name al-Latif (the Subtle), and the Mim is the key to His name al-Majid (the Glorious)."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "The Alif is the blessings (ala') of Allah, the Lam is His gentleness (lutf), and the Mim is His dominion (mulk)." Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The meaning of Alif Lam Mim is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing. The meaning of Alif Lam Sad is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing and the Most Excellent. The meaning of Alif Lam Ra is: I am Allah, who sees. The meaning of Alif Lam Mim Ra is: I am Allah, the All-Knowing and the All-Seeing." Al-Zajjaj said: "This is good, for the Arabs mention a letter of a word while meaning the whole word, as when they say: 'I said to her: Stop for us (qifi lana),' and she said: 'Qaf' [[This verse is by al-Walid ibn ʿUqba, and its completion is: "We do not reckon that we have forgotten the al-Ijaf." See: Tafsir al-Tabari 1/212; Tafsir al-Wahidi 1/26.]], meaning: 'I stopped.'"

Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: "They are the names of Allah the Exalted, *muqatta'ah* (separated) [[Note in manuscript A: "separated, not joined."]]. If people knew how to join them, they would know the Greatest Name of Allah. Do you not see that you say Ra, Ha Mim, Nun, and it becomes *al-Rahman* (the Most Gracious), and so on for the rest, except that we are not able to join them?" Qatadah said: "These letters are the names of the Qur'an." Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "They are the names of the surahs [[In the original: "the surah."]]. Their explanation is that when a speaker says, 'I recited Ha Mim,' the listener understands that he recited the surah that begins with Ha Mim." It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are oaths. Al-Akhfash said: "Allah swore by these letters because of their nobility and excellence, since they are the foundations (*mabadi'*) [[In the printed edition: "mabani" (building blocks).]] of His revealed Books and the building blocks of His Most Beautiful Names." [[See these opinions in: Tafsir al-Tabari 1/205–224; Tafsir al-Wahidi 1/25–26.]]

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is the Book﴾. That is, this Book, which is the Qur'an. It was said: "The word *dhalika* (that) contains an implied meaning, i.e., 'This is that Book.'" Al-Farra' said: "Allah had promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would send down to him a Book that water would not erase and that would not wear out from much repetition. When He sent down the Qur'an, He said, 'This is *dhalika* (that) Book which I promised to send down to you, in the Torah and the Gospel and on the tongues of the prophets before you.'" *Hadha* (this) is used for what is near, and *dhalika* (that) for what is far. Ibn Kaysan said: "Before Surat al-Baqarah, Allah the Exalted had sent down surahs which the polytheists denied. Then He sent down Surat al-Baqarah and said, *dhalika al-Kitab* (that Book), meaning the surahs that preceded al-Baqarah, 'there is no doubt in it.'"

*Al-Kitab* (the Book) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used with the meaning of *al-maktub* (the written). It is as one says of a created thing, *khalq* (creation), and of this dirham, *darb fulan* (the minted coin of so-and-so), meaning *madrub* (minted). The root of *kataba* is gathering and joining together. A military unit is called *katiba* because of its gathering together. A book is called *kitab* because it joins one letter to another.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, that is, there is no doubt that it is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that it is the truth and the reality. It was said: "This is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., 'Do not doubt it,' like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so there shall be no obscenity or wickedness﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah 2:197]], meaning: 'Do not commit obscenity and do not commit wickedness.'"

Ibn Kathir read *fihi* (in it) with *ishba'* (prolonging the vowel) when joined, and likewise every pronoun *ha'* (ha of the pronoun) preceded by a sukun (silent letter) is prolonged when joined, provided it is not followed by a silent letter. If the silent letter before the *ha'* is a *ya'*, he prolongs it with a *kasrah* as a *ya'*; if it is other than *ya'*, he prolongs it with a *dammah* as a *waw*. Hafs agreed with him in His saying, ﴿therein humiliated﴾ [[Surah al-Furqan 25:69]], so he prolonged it (*fayushbi'uhu*) [[In manuscript B: "fa-ashbaʿahu."]].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i perform *idgham al-ghunnah* (assimilation with nasalization) before the *lam* and *ra'*. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i add before the *ya'*, and Hamzah adds before the *waw*. The others do not assimilate them. Abu Ja'far conceals (*ikhfa'*) the *nun* and *tanwin* before the *kha'* and *ghayn*.

﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾: that is, it is guidance, meaning right direction and clarification, for the people of taqwa (God-consciousness). It was said: "It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning *hadiyan* (guiding), its implied sense being: there is no doubt in its guidance for the God-fearing." *Al-huda* (guidance) is that by which a person is guided. *Lil-muttaqin* (for the God-fearing) means for the believers. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "*Al-Muttaqi* (the God-fearing) is one who guards himself against shirk, the major sins, and the gross immoralities." It is derived from *al-ittiqa'* (guarding), whose root meaning is a barrier between two things. From this one says, *ittaqa bi-tursihi*, meaning he made his shield a barrier between himself and what he targeted.

It is said in a hadith: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would take cover behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" [[Narrated by Muslim in *al-Jihad wa al-Siyar*, chapter on the battle of Hunayn (1776), from al-Bara', vol. 3, p. 1401. The author also cited it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 4/33.]], meaning: when the war intensified, we made him a barrier between ourselves and the enemy. Thus the God-fearing person makes obedience to the command of Allah and abstention from what He forbade a barrier between himself and the punishment. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said to Ka'b al-Ahbar [[Ibn Kathir alone reports that the one questioned was Ubayy ibn Ka'b. See Ibn Kathir's marginal note.]]: "Tell me about taqwa." He said: "Have you ever walked a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What did you do?" He said: "I was careful and I gathered up my garments." Ka'b said: "That is taqwa." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "The God-fearing person is one who abandons what is not harmful out of fear of what is harmful." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: "Taqwa is abandoning what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has made obligatory. Whatever provision Allah grants after that is good upon good." It was said: "It is following the example of the Prophet ﷺ." A hadith says: "The essence of taqwa is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾ [[Surah al-Nahl 16:90]], and so on." Ibn ʿUmar said: "Taqwa is that you do not consider yourself better than anyone." Specifying the God-fearing by mention is an honouring of them, or because they are the ones who are truly guided by the guidance.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿who believe﴾. The position of *alladhina* (who) is in the genitive as an adjective (*na't*) of *al-muttaqin* (the God-fearing). *Yu'minun* (they believe): *yusaddiqun* (they affirm as true). Abu ʿAmr and Warsh drop the hamzah, while the others pronounce it; and likewise both of them drop every silent hamzah that is the first radical of the verb, such as *yu'min* and *mu'min*, except for a few words that are counted [[Addition from manuscript B.]].

The reality of *iman* (faith) is affirmation with the heart. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You would not be believed by us﴾ [[Surah Yusuf 12:17]], meaning: 'You would not be affirmed by us' [[Addition from manuscript B.]]. In the sharia, it is: belief in the heart, verbal confession with the tongue, and action with the limbs. Confession and action are called *iman* for a reason of association, since they are among its branches.

*Islam* is submission and yielding. Every *iman* is *Islam*, but not every *Islam* is *iman*, if it is not accompanied by affirmation. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins say: "We believe." Say: "You have not believed, but say: 'We have submitted'"﴾ [[Surah al-Hujurat 49:14]]. This is because a man may be submissive outwardly while not affirming inwardly, and he may affirm inwardly while not yielding outwardly.

The answers of the Prophet ﷺ differed concerning both of these when Jibril, peace be upon him, asked him, and this is what Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Bawayh al-Zarrad al-Bukhari informed us: Abu al-Qasim ʿAli ibn Ahmad al-Khuza'i told us, Abu Sa'id al-Haytham ibn Kulayb al-Shashi told us, Abu Ahmad ʿIsa ibn Ahmad al-ʿAsqalani [[The manuscript shows a page break here.]] told us, Yazid ibn Harun told us, Kahmas ibn al-Hasan told us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from Yahya ibn Yaʿmar, who said: "The first person who spoke about *qadar* (divine decree) in Basra was Ma'bad al-Juhani. Then I and Humayd ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman set out for Makkah, and we said: 'If we met any of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we would ask him about what these people are saying.' We met ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, so I and my companion surrounded him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I knew he would leave the speaking to me, so I said: 'O Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, there have appeared among us people who go deep into this knowledge and seek it, claiming that there is no qadar, and that the matter is *unuf* (newly created without decree).' He said: 'When you meet them, inform them that I am innocent of them and they are innocent of me. By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uhud and spent it in the way of Allah, Allah would not accept anything from him until he believes in qadar, both its good and its evil.'" Then he said:

ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab told us, he said: "While we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, there came a man with exceedingly white clothing and exceedingly black hair, showing no trace of travel, and none of us knew him. He came and sat before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [his knee touching his knee], and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about Islam.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'You testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, you establish the prayer, you give the zakat, you fast Ramadan, and you make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to find a way to it.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' We were amazed that he asked and then affirmed the answer. Then he said: 'Tell me about iman.' He said: 'That you believe in Allah alone, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire, and the qadar, its good and its evil.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about ihsan.' He said: 'That you worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he said: 'Tell me about the Hour.' He said: 'The one asked about it does not know it better than the one asking.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' He said: 'Then tell me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, and that you see barefoot, naked, destitute shepherds competing in building tall structures.' He said: 'You have spoken truly.' Then he left. After three days, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'O ʿUmar, do you know who the man was?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'That was Jibril. He came to you to teach you the matters of your religion, and he never came to me in any form except that I recognized him in it, except in this form of his.'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in *al-Iman*, chapter on Jibril's question about iman and Islam, 1/114; and by Muslim in *al-Iman*, chapter on iman, Islam and ihsan, nos. 8 and 9, 1/36–37. The author also cited it in *Sharh al-Sunnah* 1/8–9.]]

The Prophet ﷺ, in this hadith, made *Islam* the name of what appears of actions, and *iman* the name of what is hidden of belief. This does not mean that actions are not part of *iman*, nor that the affirmation of the heart is not part of *Islam*. Rather, that is a detailed explanation of a single whole, all of which is one thing, whose comprehensive term is *al-din* (the religion). For this reason he said, "That was Jibril, who came to you to teach you the matters of your religion."

The evidence that deeds are part of faith is what we were informed by Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ṣāliḥī: Abu al-Qāsim Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Shāh narrated to us: Abū Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Quraysh ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: Bishr ibn Mūsā narrated to us: Khalaf ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, from Jarīr al-Rāzī, from Sahl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dīnār, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Faith has seventy-some branches. The best of them is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the least of them is removing harmful things from the road. Modesty (ḥayāʾ) is a branch of faith." [Narrated by al-Bukhārī in al-Īmān, chapter "The matters of faith," 1/50. Also narrated by Muslim in al-Īmān, chapter "Explaining the number of the branches of faith and their best and least," no. (57), 1/63. The author also narrated it in Sharḥ al-Sunnah, 1/34.]

It is also said: faith (al-īmān) is derived from security (al-amān). Thus the believer (al-mu'min) is so called because he secures himself from the punishment of Allah, and Allah the Exalted is the Giver of Security (Mu'min) because He secures His servants from His punishment. [For a detailed discussion of the topics of faith, refer to the book "Al-Īmān" by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah.]

The words of the Exalted: ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen). Al-ghayb is a verbal noun used in the place of a noun, so the absent one is called "ghayb," just as the just one is called "ʿadl" and the visitor is called "zawr." Al-ghayb is that which is hidden from the eyes. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Al-ghayb here is everything you have been commanded to believe in that is out of your sight, such as the angels, the Resurrection, Paradise, Hellfire, the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), and the Scale (al-mīzān)." It is also said that al-ghayb here is Allah the Exalted; it is also said it is the Qur'an. Al-Ḥasan said: "It means the Hereafter." Ziрr ibn Ḥubaysh and Ibn Jurayj said: "It means revelation." A parallel is the verse: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ (35 – al-Najm). Ibn Kaysān said: "It means divine decree (al-qadar)." ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd said: "We were with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd and we mentioned the companions of Muḥammad (ﷺ) [and what they preceded us in], and ʿAbd Allāh said: 'The affair of Muḥammad was clear to those who saw him. By the One besides whom there is no god, no one has ever believed with a faith better than faith in the unseen.' Then he recited: 'Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book...' up to his words: '...the successful.'" [Addition from "B."]

Abū Jaʿfar, Abū ʿAmr, and Warsh recite ﴿yu'minūn﴾ without the hamzah (glottal stop). Likewise Abū Jaʿfar omits every silent hamzah except in the words anbi'hum, nabbi'hum, and nabbi'nā. Abū ʿAmr omits all of them except when the hamzah is a sign of the jussive (jazm), as in nabbi'hum, anbi'hum, and tasu'hum, and in in nash', wa-nansaʾhā, and similar, or when it is a shift from one dialect to another, as in mu'ṣadah and ri'iyyā. Warsh omits every silent hamzah that was the first radical of the verb (fāʾ al-fiʿl), except tu'wī and tu'wīhi. He does not omit a hamzah that is the middle radical of the verb (ʿayn al-fiʿl), except al-ru'yā and its like, provided it is not on the pattern of fiʿl, as in dhi'b.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And they establish the prayer﴾. That is, they perpetuate it and guard it at its appointed times, with its limits, its pillars, and its forms. It is said: "He stood by the matter" and "He established the matter" when he carried it out, giving its rights. What is meant here is the five daily prayers, mentioned in the singular form (al-wuḥdān) [in B: "the singular"], as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth﴾ (213 – al-Baqarah), meaning the books.

In the language, ṣalāh means supplication (duʿāʾ). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And pray for them﴾ (103 – al-Tawbah), that is, "supplicate for them." In the Sharīʿah (sacred law), it is the name for specific acts: standing, bowing, prostration, sitting, supplication, and praise. It has been said regarding the words of the Exalted ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ (56 – al-Aḥzāb), and the rest of the verse, that the ṣalāh from Allah in this verse is mercy, from the angels is seeking forgiveness, and from the believers is supplication.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from what We have provided them﴾: [(meaning)] "We have given them." Provision (al-rizq) is the name for everything from which one benefits, even a child or a slave. Its original meaning in the language is portion and share. ﴿They spend﴾: they give charity. Qatādah said: "They spend in the way of Allah and in His obedience." The root meaning of infāq (spending) is taking out from the hand and possession, and from it comes nifāq al-sūq (the slump of the market), because goods leave the hand in it. From it also: "The animal's soul departed (nafiqat al-dābbah)" when its spirit left it. This verse refers to believers from among the polytheist Arabs.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was revealed before you﴾: the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books sent down to the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Kathīr, Qālūn [and Abū ʿAmr], the people of Basra, and Yaʿqūb omit every elongation (madd) that falls between two words. The others elongate it. This verse refers to believers from the People of the Book.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, that is, in the Abode of the Hereafter. The world was called dunyā because it is near (danā) the Hereafter, and the Hereafter was called ākhirah because it comes later (ta'akhkhur) and is after the world. ﴿They are certain﴾, that is, they are certain that it will occur. From al-īqān, which is knowledge. It is said: īqān and yaqīn are knowledge derived from inference (istidlāl). Therefore Allah is not called "Mūqin" (one who is certain), nor is His knowledge called yaqīn, since His knowledge is not derived from inference.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the people of this description. Ulāʾika is a word meaning a reference to a group, like "hum" (they). The kāf is for addressing, as in the particle of that (dhālika). ﴿Upon guidance﴾, that is, right direction, clarity, and insight ﴿from their Lord. And those are the successful﴾, that is, the saved, who succeeded by entering Paradise and were rescued from the Fire. Al-falāḥ may also mean remaining, that is, they will remain in lasting bliss. The root meaning of al-falāḥ is cutting and splitting, and from it the farmer is called fallāḥ because he plows (yashuqq) the earth. There is a proverb: "Iron is cut (yufliḥ) by iron," meaning it is split. Thus they are assured (maqṭūʿ) of good in this world and the next.

**Al-Baghawi, *Ma'alim al-Tanzil*, on 2:6–10**

His words, ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾: he means the polytheists of the Arabs. Al-Kalbi said: he means the Jews.

Kufr (disbelief) is denial (al-juhud), and its root is from *kufr*, which means concealment. From this, the night is called *kafir* because it conceals things with its darkness, and the farmer is called *kafir* because he covers the seed with soil. The disbeliever conceals the truth by his denial.

Disbelief has four types: disbelief of denial (kufr inkar), disbelief of rejection (kufr juhud), disbelief of obstinacy (kufr 'inad), and disbelief of hypocrisy (kufr nifaq). Disbelief of denial is that a person does not know God at all and does not acknowledge Him. Disbelief of rejection is that a person knows God with his heart but does not affirm Him with his tongue, like the disbelief of Iblis and the disbelief of the Jews. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ (2:89). Disbelief of obstinacy is that a person knows God with his heart and acknowledges Him with his tongue, but does not adopt the religion, like the disbelief of Abu Talib, when he says:

*"And indeed I know that the religion of Muhammad*
*is among the best religions of mankind in religion,*

*Were it not for blame, or fear of insult,*
*you would find me generous in declaring it clearly."*

As for disbelief of hypocrisy, it is that a person affirms with his tongue but does not believe in his heart. All these types are equal in that whoever meets God, exalted is He, with any one of them, will not be forgiven.

His words, ﴿It is the same for them﴾: that is, equal in their sight. ﴿Whether you warn them﴾: that is, frighten them and caution them. Warning (inzar) is informing together with frightening and cautioning. Every warner is a teacher, but not every teacher is a warner. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pronounced the two hamzahs in ﴿a'anzarta-hum﴾ as two full hamzahs, and likewise every two hamzahs occurring at the beginning of a word. The others softened the second hamzah. ﴿Am﴾ is a conjunctive particle following the interrogative. ﴿Lam﴾ is a particle of jussive (jazm), which only precedes the verb, because jussive mood is specific to verbs. ﴿You warn them or not, they will not believe﴾. This verse concerns peoples upon whom the word of wretchedness had been decreed in God's prior knowledge. Then He mentioned the cause of their abandonment of faith.

He said: ﴿God has sealed﴾, that is, God has stamped ﴿upon their hearts﴾, so they do not comprehend any good and do not understand it.

The reality of sealing (khatm) is making something secure so that what is outside does not enter it and what is inside does not leave it. From this comes sealing upon a door. The people of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) said: that is, He judged their hearts to be disbelieving, because of what preceded from His eternal knowledge concerning them. The Mu'tazilah said: He placed upon their hearts a sign by which the angels would recognise them.

﴿And upon their hearing﴾: that is, upon the place of their hearing, so they do not hear the truth and do not benefit from it. He intended "upon their ears," as He said ﴿upon their hearts﴾. He used the singular only because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and a verbal noun is neither dualised nor pluralised.

﴿And upon their sight is a veil﴾: this is the beginning of a new statement. Ghishawah means a covering, so they do not see the truth. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read *absarihim* with imalah (inclination of the vowel, pronouncing the alif toward the i-sound). Likewise, every alif after which comes a genitive ra' in nouns, where the ra' is the lam of the verb, they incline. Hamzah inclines from these those in which the ra' recurs, such as *al-qarar* and similar. Al-Kisa'i added the imalah of *jabbarin*, *al-jawar*, *al-jar*, *bari'ikum*, *man ansari*, *nusari'u* and its pattern. Likewise, these (readers) incline every alif that stands in the position of the lam of the verb, or that is a marker of feminine gender, when a ra' precedes it. The marker of feminine gender is like *al-kubra* and *al-ukhra*. The lam of the verb is like *tara* and *iftara*, where they pronounce the ra' with a kasrah.

﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾: that is, in the Hereafter. It has been said: killing and captivity in this world, and lasting punishment in the next. Punishment (adhab) is anything that troubles a person and is hard upon him. Al-Khalil said: punishment is that which prevents a person from his desire, and from it comes *sweet water* (al-ma' al-'adhb), because it prevents thirst.

His words: ﴿And among the people are those who say: "We believe in God"﴾. It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, Jadd ibn Qays and their companions, when they displayed the word of Islam in order to be safe from the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, while believing the opposite of it. Most of them were Jews. *Al-nas* (the people) is the plural of *insan* (human), who was named so because he was entrusted with a covenant and then forgot, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We had certainly taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾ (20:115). It has been said: it is because of his manifestness, from their saying *anastu*, meaning I saw. It has also been said: because he is made to feel at ease (yustanas) with it. ﴿And the Last Day﴾: that is, the Day of Resurrection.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they are not believers. They deceive God﴾: that is, they oppose God. The root of *khad'* (deception) in the language is concealment, and from it comes *makhda'* (a private chamber), for the room in which goods are hidden. So the deceiver shows the opposite of what he conceals. Deception from God, in His saying ﴿And He is their deceiver﴾ (4:142), means that He shows them and hastens to them from the bounty of this world what is contrary to what is hidden from them of the punishment of the Hereafter. It has been said: the origin of *khad'* is corruption; its meaning is that they corrupt the faith they displayed by the disbelief they concealed.

His words, ﴿And He is their deceiver﴾: that is, He corrupts their bounty in this world by what leads them to the punishment of the Hereafter. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿they deceive God﴾, when *mufa'alah* (the pattern of mutual action) implies participation, and God, exalted is He, is far above participation in deception? It is answered: *mufa'alah* may occur without the sense of participation, as when you say "God pardon you" (*afakallah*), "I punished so-and-so" (*'aqabtu*), and "I stepped on the sandal" (*tara'qtu al-na'l*). Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that they deceive the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who harm God﴾ (33:57), meaning the friends of God. It has been said: the mention of God here is for embellishment, and the intended object of the deception is those who believe, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So to God belongs one-fifth and to the Messenger﴾ (8:41). It has also been said: its meaning is that they do in the religion of God what is deception in their own religion. ﴿And those who believe﴾: that is, they also deceive the believers by their saying, when they meet them, "We believe," while they are not believers.

﴿And they deceive not﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read *wa ma yakhda'un* like the first word, and they took it as *mufa'alah* that is specific to one party. The rest read *wa ma yakhda'una* according to the original form.

﴿Except themselves﴾: because the evil consequence of their deception returns to them, since God, exalted is He, informs His Prophet (ﷺ) of their hypocrisy, so they are exposed in this world and merit punishment in the next. ﴿And they do not perceive﴾: that is, they do not know that they are deceiving themselves and that the evil consequence of their deception returns upon them.

﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾: doubt and hypocrisy. The origin of *marad* (disease) is weakness. Doubt in religion is called a disease because it weakens religion, as disease weakens the body.

﴿So God increased them in disease﴾: because the verses used to descend one after another, verse after verse, and whenever they disbelieved in a verse they increased in disbelief and hypocrisy. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them filth upon their filth﴾ (9:125). Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read *fa zadahum* with imalah, and Hamzah extended the imalah to *zad* wherever it occurs, and to *zaagh*, *khaab*, *taab*, *haaq* and *daaq*. The others do not incline them.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾: *alim* (painful), which causes its pain to reach their hearts. ﴿Because they used to lie﴾: *ma* here is the verbal (masdar) particle, meaning because of their denial of God and His Messenger in secret. The Kufans read *yakdhibun* with lightening (takhfif), meaning because of their lying, ﴿when﴾ (*idh*) ﴿they said "We believe" while they were not believers.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 11–13:

﴿And when it is said﴾ al-Kisa'i recited "qila" (it was said), "ghiḍa" (it was reduced), "jiʼa" (it was brought), "hila" (it was prevented), "siqa" (it was driven), and "siʼat" (it was evil) by giving their initial letters a sound of ḍamma (rawm). He agreed with Ibn ʻAmir on "siqa," "hila," "siʼa," and "siʼat," and he agreed with the people of Madina on "siʼa" and "siʼat," because their original form is "quila," with a ḍamma on the qaf and a kasra on the waw, like "qutila." Likewise with its counterparts, so a ḍamma was indicated to signal the waw that had been converted. The rest recited with a kasra on their initial letters: they found the movement on the waw heavy, so they transferred its kasra to the fa' of the verb and the waw was converted into a ya' because of the kasra before it. 7/a ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, meaning to the hypocrites; it was also said to the Jews, i.e., the believers said to them, ﴿"Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ by disbelief and by hindering people from faith in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. It is also said the meaning is: do not disbelieve, for disbelief is the greatest corruption in religion. ﴿They say, "We are only reformers."﴾ They say this statement falsely, like their saying "We believe" while they are liars.

﴿Unquestionably﴾ is a word of alerting by which the addressee is made attentive. ﴿Indeed, they are the corrupters﴾ of themselves by disbelief and of people by hindering them from faith. ﴿But they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they do not know that they are corrupters, because they think that what they hold of concealing disbelief is righteousness. It is also said: they do not know what Allah has prepared for them of punishment.

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, i.e., to the hypocrites; it was also said to the Jews, ﴿"Believe as the people have believed"﴾ such as ʻAbd Allah ibn Salam and others among the believers of the People of the Book. It is also said: "as the Emigrants and the Helpers have believed." ﴿They say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ i.e., the ignorant. If it is asked how hypocrisy is valid alongside (the openness) [[In the original: al-muhajara.]] in their saying "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" it is said that they used to express this statement among themselves, not in front of the believers. Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ and the believers of that, and Allah responded to them, saying: ﴿"Unquestionably, they are the foolish, but they do not know"﴾ that they are such. The safih (foolish one) is one of light intellect and thin forbearance, from their saying: "a safih garment," i.e., thin. It is also said the safih is the liar who deliberately speaks ﴿the falsehood﴾ [[Addition from manuscript B.]] contrary to what he knows.

The people of Kufa and Syria recited ﴿"al-sufaha' ala"﴾ with both hamzas realized, and likewise every two hamzas occurring in two words, whether alike or different. The others realize the first and soften the second in the differing cases, seeking lightness. If they are alike, as in: ha'ula'i, awliya'i, ula'ika, and ja'a amru rabbika, Abu ʻAmr and al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir recited them with one hamza. Abu Ja'far, Warsh, al-Qawwas and Ya'qub recited with realization of the first and softening of the second. Qalun recited with softening of the first and realization of the second, because what is begun is more deserving of the hamza than what is pausing.

﴿And when it is said﴾ al-Kisa'i recited "qila" (it was said), "ghiḍa" (it was reduced), "jiʼa" (it was brought), "hila" (it was prevented), "siqa" (it was driven), and "siʼat" (it was evil) by giving their initial letters a sound of ḍamma (rawm). He agreed with Ibn ʻAmir on "siqa," "hila," "siʼa," and "siʼat," and he agreed with the people of Madina on "siʼa" and "siʼat," because their original form is "quila," with a ḍamma on the qaf and a kasra on the waw, like "qutila." Likewise with its counterparts, so a ḍamma was indicated to signal the waw that had been converted. The rest recited with a kasra on their initial letters: they found the movement on the waw heavy, so they transferred its kasra to the fa' of the verb and the waw was converted into a ya' because of the kasra before it. 7/a ﴿And when it is said to them﴾, meaning to the hypocrites; it was also said to the Jews, i.e., the believers said to them, ﴿"Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ by disbelief and by hindering people from faith in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. It is also said the meaning is: do not disbelieve, for disbelief is the greatest corruption in religion. ﴿They say, "We are only reformers."﴾ They say this statement falsely, like their saying "We believe" while they are liars.

﴿Unquestionably﴾ is a word of alerting by which the addressee is made attentive. ﴿Indeed, they are the corrupters﴾ of themselves by disbelief and of people by hindering them from faith. ﴿But they do not perceive﴾, i.e., they do not know that they are corrupters, because they think that what they hold of concealing disbelief is righteousness. It is also said: they do not know what Allah has prepared for them of punishment.

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, i.e., to the hypocrites; it was also said to the Jews, ﴿"Believe as the people have believed"﴾ such as ʻAbd Allah ibn Salam and others among the believers of the People of the Book. It is also said: "as the Emigrants and the Helpers have believed." ﴿They say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ i.e., the ignorant. If it is asked how hypocrisy is valid alongside (the openness) [[In the original: al-muhajara.]] in their saying "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" it is said that they used to express this statement among themselves, not in front of the believers. Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ and the believers of that, and Allah responded to them, saying: ﴿"Unquestionably, they are the foolish, but they do not know"﴾ that they are such. The safih (foolish one) is one of light intellect and thin forbearance, from their saying: "a safih garment," i.e., thin. It is also said the safih is the liar who deliberately speaks ﴿the falsehood﴾ [[Addition from manuscript B.]] contrary to what he knows.

The people of Kufa and Syria recited ﴿"al-sufaha' ala"﴾ with both hamzas realized, and likewise every two hamzas occurring in two words, whether alike or different. The others realize the first and soften the second in the differing cases, seeking lightness. If they are alike, as in: ha'ula'i, awliya'i, ula'ika, and ja'a amru rabbika, Abu ʻAmr and al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir recited them with one hamza. Abu Ja'far, Warsh, al-Qawwas and Ya'qub recited with realization of the first and softening of the second. Qalun recited with softening of the first and realization of the second, because what is begun is more deserving of the hamza than what is pausing.

Qalun recited with softening of the first and realization of the second, because what is begun is more deserving of the hamza than what is pausing.

﴿And when they meet those who believe﴾, meaning these hypocrites, when they meet the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar), ﴿they say, "We believe"﴾ like your belief. ﴿And when they are alone﴾ they return. It is possible that it is from seclusion (al-khalwa), with ﴿ila﴾ meaning "with," i.e., with their devils (shayatin). It was also said that ﴿ila﴾ here means "ma'a" (with), as Allah the Exalted said [addition from manuscript B]: ﴿and do not consume their wealth along with your wealth﴾ (2 – An-Nisa'), meaning, along with your wealth.

﴿Shayatinihim﴾ means their chiefs and their soothsayers (kahana). Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: they were five men from the Jews: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf in Medina; Abu Burda in the tribe of Aslam; 'Abd al-Dar in Juhayna; 'Awf ibn 'Amir in the tribe of Asad; and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sawda' in Syria. A soothsayer does not exist without a devil (shaytan) who follows him.

Al-shaytan is the rebellious, obstinate one among the jinn and mankind, and among every thing. Its root meaning is distance; it is said "bi'r shuttun," meaning a well of great depth. The devil is called "shaytan" because of its extension (imtidad) in evil and its distance from good.

Mujahid said: "to their companions among the hypocrites and the polytheists." ﴿They say, "We are with you"﴾, meaning: in your religion. ﴿"We are only mockers"﴾ of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, by what we show of Islam.

Abu Ja'far read ﴿mustahzi'un﴾ and ﴿yastahzi'un﴾, ﴿qul ista'hzu﴾, ﴿li-yutfu'u﴾, ﴿li-yuwatu'u﴾, ﴿yastanbi'unaka﴾, ﴿khatin﴾ and ﴿khatun﴾, ﴿mutakin﴾ and ﴿mutakkun﴾, ﴿fama'lun﴾ and ﴿al-munshi'un﴾, with the omission of the hamza (hamza, the glottal stop) in all of them.

﴿Allah mocks them﴾, meaning He requites them for their mockery. The requital is named by the same name because it corresponds to it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and the requital for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ (40 – Ash-Shura). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is that a gate of Paradise is opened for them, and when they reach it, it is shut against them, and they are returned to the Fire. It was also said: it is that a light is struck for the believers, by which they walk over the Sirat (bridge), and when the hypocrites reach it, a barrier is placed between them and the believers, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and a barrier is placed between them and what they desire﴾ (54 – Saba'), and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be struck between them﴾ (13 – Al-Hadid), up to the end of the verse.

Al-Hasan said its meaning is: Allah reveals the believers' knowledge of their hypocrisy. ﴿And He extends them﴾, i.e., leaves them and grants them respite. (Al-madd) and (al-imdad) are the same, and their root meaning is increase, except that (al-madd) is mostly used for evil and (al-imdad) for good. Allah the Exalted said regarding (al-madd): ﴿and We extend for him the punishment, an extension﴾ (79 – Maryam), and regarding (al-imdad) He said: ﴿and We supported you with wealth and sons﴾ (6 – Al-Isra'), and ﴿and We supplied them with fruit﴾ (22 – At-Tur).

﴿In their transgression﴾, meaning in their misguidance, and its root meaning is exceeding the limit, from which comes "the water overflowed" (taghā al-mā'). ﴿Wandering blindly﴾, meaning they hesitate in misguidance, bewildered.

﴿Those are the ones who have purchased misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾, meaning they have substituted disbelief for faith. ﴿So their trade has not profited﴾, meaning they did not gain in their trade. He attributed the profit to the trade because profit occurs in it, as the Arabs say: "your sale profited and your deal lost." ﴿And they were not guided﴾ (from misguidance). It was also said: they were not correct in their trade.

﴿Their likeness﴾ (mathaluhum): their resemblance; it was also said: their description. Al-mathal is a saying widely circulated among people, by which the meaning of a thing is known, and it is one of the seven categories of the Qur'an. ﴿Like the likeness of the one who﴾, meaning those who, as indicated by the context of the verse. A parallel to it is: ﴿And he who brought the truth and confirmed it, those are the God-fearing﴾ (33 – Az-Zumar). ﴿Kindled﴾ means lit ﴿a fire, and when it illuminated﴾ the fire ﴿what was around him﴾, i.e., around the one who kindled it. (Adā'a) is both intransitive and transitive: it is said "al-shay' ada'a bi-nafsihi" (the thing shone by itself) and "ada'ahu ghayruhu" (another made it shine); here it is transitive. ﴿Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

He says: their likeness in their hypocrisy is like the likeness of a man who kindled a fire on a dark night in a desert, and warmed himself and saw what was around him, and protected himself from what he feared. While he was in that state, his fire went out, and he remained in darkness, wandering and bewildered. Likewise the hypocrites: by displaying the word of faith, they felt safe regarding their wealth and children, they married believing women, inherited from them, and shared the spoils with them; that is their light. When they die, they return to darkness and fear. It was also said: the removal of their light is in the grave. It was also said: on the Day of Resurrection, when they say to the believers: "Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light." It was also said: the removal of their light is by the exposure of their beliefs upon the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). He struck the fire as a parable, then did not say "Allah extinguished their fire," but expressed it as the removal of the light, because light is both light and heat; their light is removed and the heat remains upon them.

'Ata' and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, and their waiting for the coming out of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their seeking victory through him over the polytheists of the Arabs; when he came out, they disbelieved in him.

Then Allah described them, saying:
