Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 19–20:

﴿Or like a downpour﴾: that is, like the companions of a downpour (ṣayyib, heavy rain). This is another parable, which God, exalted is He, struck for the hypocrites, with a different meaning. If you wish, liken them to the one who kindles a fire, and if you wish, liken them to the people of the downpour. It was also said that the particle *aw* (ﺃَوْ, "or") here carries the sense of *wa* (ﻭَ, "and"), meaning "and like a downpour," as in God's saying ﴿or they increase﴾ (ﺃَوْ يَزِيدُونَ), meaning "and they increase." *Ṣayyib* is the rain, and everything that descends from above to below is a *ṣayyib*. It is on the pattern *fa'īl* from *ṣāba, yaṣūbu*, meaning it descended from the sky, that is, from the cloud. It was said that it is the sky itself, and *al-samā'* ("the sky") is everything that is above you and shades you. It is a noun of genus that can be singular or plural. ﴿In it﴾: that is, in the *ṣayyib*. It was also said: in the sky, that is, in the cloud, and for this reason it is masculine. It was also said that *al-samā'* can be masculine or feminine. God, exalted is He, said ﴿the sky splitting asunder thereby﴾ (73:18), and He said ﴿when the sky is split open﴾ (82:1). ﴿Darkness﴾: the plural of *ẓulmah* (darkness). ﴿And thunder﴾: the sound heard from the cloud. ﴿And lightning﴾: the fire that comes out of it.

ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and most of the exegetes, may God be pleased with them, said: *al-raʿd* (thunder) is the name of an angel who drives the clouds, and *al-barq* (lightning) is the gleam of a whip of light with which the angel drives the cloud. It was said that the sound is the driving of the cloud; it was said that it is the glorification (tasbīḥ) of the angel; it was said that thunder is the angel's speech and lightning is his laughter. Mujāhid said: *al-raʿd* is the name of the angel, and its sound is also called *raʿd*.[[The reports mentioned here were not cited by Ibn Kathir or al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur; some of them were mentioned by al-Qurtubi, and most of them are open to objection, as in the commentary of Ustadh Maḥmūd Shākir on al-Ṭabarī at the exegesis of God's saying (or like a downpour from the sky, in it are darknesses, thunder and lightning), the verse. Al-Ṭabarī's Tafsir: as long as no evidence has been reported for what was mentioned, one should suspend judgment on it, because these cosmic phenomena and what follows them are linked to laws and norms, some of which have become explained by the scholars of this field. See also: al-Isrā'īliyyāt wal-Mawḍū'āt fī Kutub al-Tafsīr by Shaykh Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Abū Shahba, pp. 414–417.]] *Al-barq* is *maṣaʿ*,[[In al-Nihayah by Ibn al-Athir, who also quoted Mujahid's words, meaning he strikes the cloud with a blow and the lightning is seen gleaming. Al-Nihayah fi Gharib al-Hadith wal-Athar: 4/337.]] an angel who drives the clouds. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said: thunder is an angel who drives the cloud; when it disperses, he gathers it together, and when his anger intensifies, fire flies out of his mouth, and that is the thunderbolts (ṣawāʿiq). It was also said that thunder is the sound of the wind veering between the clouds, and the first view is more sound.

﴿They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts﴾: the plural of *ṣāʿiqah* (thunderbolt), which is the shout by which whoever hears it dies or is struck senseless. Every destroying punishment is called *ṣāʿiqah*. It was said that the thunderbolt is a piece of punishment that God, exalted is He, sends down upon whom He wills.

It is related from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from his father, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whenever he heard the sound of thunder and thunderbolts, would say: "O God, do not kill us by Your anger, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Da'awat, chapter on what one says when hearing thunder, no. 3514: 9/412, and he said: this is a strange (gharīb) hadith, which we only know from this route; and Aḥmad: 2/100; and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, p. 212; and Ibn al-Sunni in ʿAmal al-Yawm wal-Layla, no. 298; and al-Dulabi in al-Kuna: 2/117, all from the hadith of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Arṭāh, from Abū Muṭr, from Sālim... Abū Muṭr: none declared him trustworthy except Ibn Ḥibbān, yet al-Ḥākim authenticated it: 2/286, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him. It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i in ʿAmal al-Yawm wal-Layla (p. 518). See also: Sharh al-Sunnah: 4/393, with the annotation of Ustadh al-Arna'ut; and al-Kalim al-Ṭayyib with the takhrij of al-Albani, p. 88.]]

God's saying ﴿in dread of death﴾: that is, for fear of destruction. ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾: that is, He is knowing of them. It was said: He gathers them. Mujāhid said: He gathers them and then punishes them. It was also said: He destroys them. The evidence is God's saying ﴿unless you are encompassed (by destruction)﴾ (12:66), meaning that you are all destroyed. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī incline (imālah) *al-kāfirīn* (ﺍﻟْﻜَﺎﻓِﺮِﻳﻦَ) in the accusative and genitive positions, but they do not incline ﴿first disbeliever in it﴾ (ﺃَوَّلَ ﻛَﺎﻓِﺮٍ ﺑِﻪِ, 2:41).

﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾: that is, it draws near. One says *kāda yafʿalu* ("he nearly did") when something has come close to happening but did not happen. ﴿Snatches away their sight﴾: it seizes them. *Al-khaṭf* is taking away by force with speed. ﴿Whenever﴾ (ﻛُﻠَّﻤَﺎ): a particle of a whole sentence joined to *mā* of conditional function, so it becomes a particle of repetition, and their meaning is "whenever." ﴿It lights up for them, they walk in it; and when it darkens upon them, they stand still﴾: that is, they halt, bewildered. God likened them, in their disbelief and hypocrisy, to people who were in a desert on a dark night, and a rain fell upon them containing darkness, of which the characteristic is that the traveller cannot walk in it; and thunder, of which the characteristic is that the listeners put their fingers into their ears from its terror; and lightning, of which the characteristic is that it nearly snatches their sight and blinds it from its intense flash. This is a parable God struck for the Qur'an and for the conduct of the disbelievers and hypocrites with it. The rain is the Qur'an, because it is the life of hearts just as rain is the life of bodies. The darknesses are what the Qur'an contains of mention of disbelief and polytheism. The thunder is what they were warned with of threats and the mention of the Fire. The lightning is what it contains of guidance, clarity, promise and the mention of Paradise.

The disbelievers stop their ears when the Qur'an is recited, for fear that the heart might incline towards it, because faith in their view is disbelief, and disbelief is death. ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾: that is, the Qur'an overwhelms their hearts. It was said: this is a parable God struck for Islam. The rain is Islam; the darknesses are the trials and tribulations in it; the thunder is the threats and fears in it in the Hereafter; and the lightning is the promise and threat in it. ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾: meaning that when the hypocrites see trial and hardship in Islam, they flee out of fear of destruction. ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾, that is, gathers them: meaning their flight does not benefit them, because God, exalted is He, is behind them and gathers them and punishes them. ﴿The lightning nearly﴾: meaning the signs of Islam unsettle them towards reflection, were it not for the wretchedness that preceded for them.

﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾: meaning that when the hypocrites manifest the word of faith, they believe; and when they die, they return to the darkness. It was also said that its meaning is: whenever they gain booty and ease in Islam, they remain steadfast and say, "We are with you." ﴿And when it darkens upon them﴾: meaning when they see hardship and trial, they draw back and stand, that is, halt, as God, exalted is He, said ﴿and among the people is one who worships God on an edge﴾ (22:11). ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing﴾: that is, their ears ﴿and their sight﴾, the outward ones, just as He took away their inward hearing and sight. It was also said: He would have taken away what they gained of honour and security, which for them is in the position of hearing and sight.

﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾: capable. Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah recited *shāʾa* (ﺷَﺎﺀَ) and *jāʾa* (ﺟَﺎﺀَ) wherever they occur with imālah (the vocalic inclination of the final alif toward the i-sound).

See also: al-Isrā'īliyyāt wal-Mawḍū'āt fī Kutub al-Tafsīr by Shaykh Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Abū Shahba, pp. 414–417.]] *Al-barq* is *maṣaʿ*,[[In al-Nihayah by Ibn al-Athir, who also quoted Mujahid's words, meaning he strikes the cloud with a blow and the lightning is seen gleaming. Al-Nihayah fi Gharib al-Hadith wal-Athar: 4/337.]] an angel who drives the clouds. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said: thunder is an angel who drives the cloud; when it disperses, he gathers it together, and when his anger intensifies, fire flies out of his mouth, and that is the thunderbolts (ṣawāʿiq). It was also said that thunder is the sound of the wind veering between the clouds, and the first view is more sound.

﴿They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts﴾: the plural of *ṣāʿiqah* (thunderbolt), which is the shout by which whoever hears it dies or is struck senseless. Every destroying punishment is called *ṣāʿiqah*. It was said that the thunderbolt is a piece of punishment that God, exalted is He, sends down upon whom He wills.

It is related from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from his father, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whenever he heard the sound of thunder and thunderbolts, would say: "O God, do not kill us by Your anger, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Da'awat, chapter on what one says when hearing thunder, no. 3514: 9/412, and he said: this is a strange (gharīb) hadith, which we only know from this route; and Aḥmad: 2/100; and al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, p. 212; and Ibn al-Sunni in ʿAmal al-Yawm wal-Layla, no. 298; and al-Dulabi in al-Kuna: 2/117, all from the hadith of al-Ḥajjāj ibn Arṭāh, from Abū Muṭr, from Sālim... Abū Muṭr: none declared him trustworthy except Ibn Ḥibbān, yet al-Ḥākim authenticated it: 2/286, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him. It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i in ʿAmal al-Yawm wal-Layla (p. 518). See also: Sharh al-Sunnah: 4/393, with the annotation of Ustadh al-Arna'ut; and al-Kalim al-Ṭayyib with the takhrij of al-Albani, p. 88.]]

God's saying ﴿in dread of death﴾: that is, for fear of destruction. ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾: that is, He is knowing of them. It was said: He gathers them. Mujāhid said: He gathers them and then punishes them. It was also said: He destroys them. The evidence is God's saying ﴿unless you are encompassed (by destruction)﴾ (12:66), meaning that you are all destroyed. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī incline (imālah) *al-kāfirīn* (ﺍﻟْﻜَﺎﻓِﺮِﻳﻦَ) in the accusative and genitive positions, but they do not incline ﴿first disbeliever in it﴾ (ﺃَوَّلَ ﻛَﺎﻓِﺮٍ ﺑِﻪِ, 2:41).

﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾: that is, it draws near. One says *kāda yafʿalu* ("he nearly did") when something has come close to happening but did not happen. ﴿Snatches away their sight﴾: it seizes them. *Al-khaṭf* is taking away by force with speed. ﴿Whenever﴾ (ﻛُﻠَّﻤَﺎ): a particle of a whole sentence joined to *mā* of conditional function, so it becomes a particle of repetition, and their meaning is "whenever." ﴿It lights up for them, they walk in it; and when it darkens upon them, they stand still﴾: that is, they halt, bewildered. God likened them, in their disbelief and hypocrisy, to people who were in a desert on a dark night, and a rain fell upon them containing darkness, of which the characteristic is that the traveller cannot walk in it; and thunder, of which the characteristic is that the listeners put their fingers into their ears from its terror; and lightning, of which the characteristic is that it nearly snatches their sight and blinds it from its intense flash. This is a parable God struck for the Qur'an and for the conduct of the disbelievers and hypocrites with it. The rain is the Qur'an, because it is the life of hearts just as rain is the life of bodies. The darknesses are what the Qur'an contains of mention of disbelief and polytheism. The thunder is what they were warned with of threats and the mention of the Fire. The lightning is what it contains of guidance, clarity, promise and the mention of Paradise.

The disbelievers stop their ears when the Qur'an is recited, for fear that the heart might incline towards it, because faith in their view is disbelief, and disbelief is death. ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾: that is, the Qur'an overwhelms their hearts. It was said: this is a parable God struck for Islam. The rain is Islam; the darknesses are the trials and tribulations in it; the thunder is the threats and fears in it in the Hereafter; and the lightning is the promise and threat in it. ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾: meaning that when the hypocrites see trial and hardship in Islam, they flee out of fear of destruction. ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾, that is, gathers them: meaning their flight does not benefit them, because God, exalted is He, is behind them and gathers them and punishes them. ﴿The lightning nearly﴾: meaning the signs of Islam unsettle them towards reflection, were it not for the wretchedness that preceded for them.

﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾: meaning that when the hypocrites manifest the word of faith, they believe; and when they die, they return to the darkness. It was also said that its meaning is: whenever they gain booty and ease in Islam, they remain steadfast and say, "We are with you." ﴿And when it darkens upon them﴾: meaning when they see hardship and trial, they draw back and stand, that is, halt, as God, exalted is He, said ﴿and among the people is one who worships God on an edge﴾ (22:11). ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing﴾: that is, their ears ﴿and their sight﴾, the outward ones, just as He took away their inward hearing and sight. It was also said: He would have taken away what they gained of honour and security, which for them is in the position of hearing and sight.

﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾: capable. Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamzah recited *shāʾa* (ﺷَﺎﺀَ) and *jāʾa* (ﺟَﺎﺀَ) wherever they occur with imālah (the vocalic inclination of the final alif toward the i-sound).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 21–24:

His words, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "O mankind" is an address to the people of Makkah, and "O you who have believed" is an address to the people of Madinah [[See: al-Kafi al-Shaf by Ibn Hajar (p. 5).]]. Here it is general, except that it does not include children and the insane.

﴿Worship﴾ means affirm the oneness (tawhid) of. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Every instance of worship ('ibadah) mentioned in the Qur'an means tawhid. ﴿your Lord who created you﴾. Khalq (creation) is the bringing of a thing into existence without a prior pattern. ﴿and those before you﴾, that is, and He created those before you. ﴿so that you may be mindful (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾, so that you may be saved from the punishment. It has also been said that the meaning is: be hoping for taqwa (God-consciousness), by becoming in cover and protection from the punishment of Allah. The command of Allah is behind you, He does whatever He wills, as He said: ﴿So speak to him gently; perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ (20:44), meaning: call him to the truth and be hoping for him to remember, while the command of Allah is behind him, He does what He wills. Sibawayh said: la'alla (perhaps) and 'asa (it may be) are two particles of hope, and from Allah they are obligatory.

﴿Who made for you the earth a bed﴾, that is, a carpet. It has also been said: a place of sleep. It has been said: a spread, that is, He made it smooth and did not make it a rough place where one cannot settle. Al-Bukhari said: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Wa'il, from 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, from 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which sin is the greatest in the sight of Allah?" He said: "That you make a rival to Allah while He created you." I said: "Indeed that is great. Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that it will eat with you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tawhid, chapter on the saying of Allah "So do not set up rivals to Allah" (13/491). And by Muslim in Iman, chapter on shirk being the worst of sins, no. (86), 1/90. And the author narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 1/82.]]. Here al-ja'l (making) means khalq (creation). ﴿and the sky a structure﴾, and a raised ceiling.

﴿And He sent down from the sky﴾, that is, from the clouds, ﴿water﴾, the rain. ﴿And brought forth thereby fruits﴾, the various colours of fruits and kinds of plants, ﴿as provision for you﴾, food for you and fodder for your animals. ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah﴾, that is, equals that you worship as you worship Allah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-nidd is the opposite (didd), and it is among the words that have opposite meanings. Allah the Exalted is free of any equal or opposite.

﴿While you know﴾ that He is the One, the Creator of these things.

﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, that is, ﴿and if﴾ [[Addition from "b".]] you are in doubt, because Allah the Exalted knew that they were doubters, ﴿concerning what We have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿upon Our servant﴾, Muhammad, ﴿then produce﴾, an imperative of incapacitation (amr ta'jiz), ﴿a surah﴾. A surah is a portion of the Qur'an with a known beginning and end, from as'artu, meaning I gave abundance; the hamza was dropped. It has also been said: surah is a name for an elevated rank, and from it comes sur (wall) of a building, because of its height. It was named surah because the reader attains through its recitation an elevated rank, until he completes the ranks by completing the surahs of the Qur'an. ﴿of its like﴾, that is, like the Qur'an. "Min" here is extra (sillah), as in His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze﴾ (24:30). It has also been said: the pronoun in "mithlihi" refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: of the like of Muhammad (ﷺ), who was unlettered and did not write or read well.
[Mahmud said: Here it is "min mithlihi" rather than in the other surahs, because min indicates partiality, and this surah is the first of the Qur'an after al-Fatihah. So he included "min" so that it would be known that the challenge applies to all the surahs of the Qur'an. Had he included "min" in the other surahs, the challenge would have applied to all surahs of the Qur'an, and had he not included it in the other surahs, the challenge would have applied to some surahs only.] [[Omitted from the printed edition, in the margin of Ibn Kathir and others.]].

﴿And call your witnesses﴾, that is, seek help from your gods that you worship ﴿besides Allah﴾. Mujahid said: men who will bear witness for you ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that Muhammad (ﷺ) says it from his own self. When He challenged them, they were unable.

So He said: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾ (the first refers to what has passed, and the second to what remains). He only said this to show the inimitability (i'jaz) and that the Qur'an was a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ), since they were unable to produce its like.

﴿So fear the Fire﴾, that is, believe, and guard yourselves by faith against the Fire.

﴿Whose fuel is men and stones﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said, and most of the exegetes: it means the stones of sulphur, because they burn most fiercely. It has also been said: all stones. This is evidence of the greatness of that Fire. It has also been said: He meant by them the idols, because most of their idols were carved from stone, as He said: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ (21:98). ﴿Prepared﴾, made ready ﴿for the disbelievers﴾.

It has been said: a spread, that is, He made it smooth and did not make it a rough place where one cannot settle. He said: "That you make a rival to Allah while He created you." I said: "Indeed that is great. Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that it will eat with you." I said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tawhid, chapter on the saying of Allah "So do not set up rivals to Allah" (13/491). And by Muslim in Iman, chapter on shirk being the worst of sins, no. (86), 1/90. And the author narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 1/82.]]. Here al-ja'l (making) means khalq (creation). ﴿and the sky a structure﴾, and a raised ceiling.

﴿And He sent down from the sky﴾, that is, from the clouds, ﴿water﴾, the rain. ﴿And brought forth thereby fruits﴾, the various colours of fruits and kinds of plants, ﴿as provision for you﴾, food for you and fodder for your animals. ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah﴾, that is, equals that you worship as you worship Allah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-nidd is the opposite (didd), and it is among the words that have opposite meanings. Allah the Exalted is free of any equal or opposite.

﴿While you know﴾ that He is the One, the Creator of these things.

﴿And if you are in doubt﴾, that is, ﴿and if﴾ [[Addition from "b".]] you are in doubt, because Allah the Exalted knew that they were doubters, ﴿concerning what We have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿upon Our servant﴾, Muhammad, ﴿then produce﴾, an imperative of incapacitation (amr ta'jiz), ﴿a surah﴾. A surah is a portion of the Qur'an with a known beginning and end, from as'artu, meaning I gave abundance; the hamza was dropped. It has also been said: surah is a name for an elevated rank, and from it comes sur (wall) of a building, because of its height. It was named surah because the reader attains through its recitation an elevated rank, until he completes the ranks by completing the surahs of the Qur'an. ﴿of its like﴾, that is, like the Qur'an. "Min" here is extra (sillah), as in His saying: ﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze﴾ (24:30). It has also been said: the pronoun in "mithlihi" refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: of the like of Muhammad (ﷺ), who was unlettered and did not write or read well.
[Mahmud said: Here it is "min mithlihi" rather than in the other surahs, because min indicates partiality, and this surah is the first of the Qur'an after al-Fatihah. So he included "min" so that it would be known that the challenge applies to all the surahs of the Qur'an. Had he included "min" in the other surahs, the challenge would have applied to all surahs of the Qur'an, and had he not included it in the other surahs, the challenge would have applied to some surahs only.] [[Omitted from the printed edition, in the margin of Ibn Kathir and others.]].

﴿And call your witnesses﴾, that is, seek help from your gods that you worship ﴿besides Allah﴾. Mujahid said: men who will bear witness for you ﴿if you are truthful﴾ that Muhammad (ﷺ) says it from his own self. When He challenged them, they were unable.

So He said: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do﴾ (the first refers to what has passed, and the second to what remains). He only said this to show the inimitability (i'jaz) and that the Qur'an was a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ), since they were unable to produce its like.

﴿So fear the Fire﴾, that is, believe, and guard yourselves by faith against the Fire.

﴿Whose fuel is men and stones﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said, and most of the exegetes: it means the stones of sulphur, because they burn most fiercely. It has also been said: all stones. This is evidence of the greatness of that Fire. It has also been said: He meant by them the idols, because most of their idols were carved from stone, as He said: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ (21:98). ﴿Prepared﴾, made ready ﴿for the disbelievers﴾.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 25:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾, meaning, inform them. Bushra (good tidings) is every true report by which the skin of the face changes (from joy or grief). It is used for good and for bad, but it is used for good more often. ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning good actions, that is, the believers who are among the people of obedience. ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾ means: they made their deeds sincere, as He said, ﴿So let him who hopes for the meeting with his Lord do righteous deeds﴾ (18:110), meaning free of showing off (riya'). Muʿadh said: The righteous deed is one that contains four things: knowledge, intention, patience, and sincerity.

﴿That for them are gardens﴾: the plural of jannah (garden). The jannah is an orchard containing fruit-bearing trees, and it was so named because it is concealed (yajtann) and covered by its trees. Al-Farra' said: the jannah is that which contains palm trees, and the Firdaws is that which contains vines.

﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, meaning beneath their trees and their dwellings. ﴿The rivers﴾, meaning the waters in the rivers, because a river does not flow [by itself]. It was also said that ﴿beneath them﴾ means by their command, based on His words, exalted is He, quoting Pharaoh: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ (43:51), meaning by my command. Al-anhar is the plural of nahr (river), and it was so named for its breadth and brightness, and from the same root comes al-nahar (daytime).

In a hadith: "The rivers of Paradise flow in a channel that is not dug."[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf 13/96; Hannad in al-Zuhd 1/171; al-Tabari in al-Tafsir 1/384; and al-Marwazi in Zawa'id al-Zuhd p. 524. al-Suyuti also attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th, and declared it sound, from Ibn Mas'ud. See al-Durr al-Manthur 1/94; Tafsir Ibn Kathir 4/177; and Fath al-Samawi 1/148.]]

﴿Whenever﴾, meaning whenever ﴿they are provided﴾, that is, are fed, ﴿with fruit therefrom﴾, meaning from the Garden, a fruit of whatever kind; ﴿min﴾ here is extra (silah). ﴿Provision﴾ means food. ﴿They will say, "This is what we were provided with before,"﴾ and "qabl" is in the nominative case as an adverbial of place/time (al-ghayah). Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾ (30:4). It was said: "before" refers to the world. It was also said: the fruits in Paradise are similar in color but different in taste; so when they are given one fruit after another, they think it is the first. ﴿And they will be given it in semblance﴾, that is, the provision is similar. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and al-Rabiʿ said: similar in color and different in taste. al-Hasan and Qatadah said: similar, meaning some of it resembles the rest in excellence; all of it is choice, with no inferior part in it. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it resembles the fruits of this world, except that it is better. It was also said: similar in name but different in taste. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in Paradise except the names."

Abu Huraybah narrated: Ana Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Salihi informed us; Abu Saʿid Muhammad ibn Musa al-Sayrafi informed us; Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Saffar informed us; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿIsa al-Bartiyy informed us; Muhammad ibn Kathir informed us; Sufyan al-Thawri informed us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise eat and drink, but they do not urinate, defecate, blow their noses, or spit. They are inspired to praise and glorify (Allah) as you are inspired to breathe. Their food is belching, and their sweat is musk."[[Narrated by Muslim in al-Jannah wa Sifat Naʿimiha wa Ahliha, bab fi sifat al-jannah wa ahliha, no. 2835, 4/2180. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/212.]]

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And for them therein﴾, in the gardens, ﴿are spouses﴾, meaning women and female servants, that is, of the wide-eyed houris (hur al-ʿin), ﴿purified﴾, from excrement, urine, menstruation, postnatal bleeding, spittle, mucus, semen, children, and every impurity. Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi said: In Paradise there is intercourse as you wish, but no children. al-Hasan said: They are your old women, bleary-eyed and blind, purified from the impurities of this world. It was also said: purified from bad character.
﴿And they therein will abide forever﴾, meaning they will remain eternally, not dying there and not leaving it.

Abu ʿAmr ʿAbd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi informed us; Abu Hamid Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us; Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Farabri informed us; Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari informed us; Qutaybah ibn Saʿid informed us; Jarir informed us, from ʿUmarah, from Abu Zurʿah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first group to enter Paradise will be in the form of the moon on the night of the full moon. Then those who follow them will be like the brightest star in the sky in its brilliance. They will not urinate or defecate, nor spit or blow their noses. Their combs are gold, their sweat is musk, their censers are aloeswood [i.e., their incense is pure oud wood, not perfumed][[Meaning their incense is pure aloeswood, not mixed. See al-Nihayah 1/63.]], their spouses are the wide-eyed houris, and they are all of one form, in the image of their father Adam, sixty cubits tall."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Khalq, bab ma ja'a fi sifat al-jannah wa annaha makhluqah, 6/318; and Muslim in al-Jannah wa Sifat Ahliha, bab awwal zumrah tadkhul al-jannah, no. 2834, 4/2178. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/211.]]

ʿAbd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us; ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us; Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi informed us; ʿAli ibn al-Jaʿd informed us; Fudayl, that is Ibn Marzuq, informed us, from ʿAtiyyah, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first group to enter Paradise on the Day of Resurrection will have faces like the moon on the night of the full moon. The second group will be in the color of the brightest star in the sky. Each man among them will have two wives, and each wife will have seventy garments, and the marrow of their shins will be visible through them, beyond their flesh, blood, and garments."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Sifat al-Jannah, bab ma ja'a fi sifat nisa' ahl al-jannah, 7/239-241, and he said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi is weak, and the rest of its narrators are trustworthy. See Mizan al-I'tidal 3/79. al-Haythami mentioned it from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Saʿid and said: al-Tirmidhi narrated it in abridged form; al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat, and the chain of Ibn Mas'ud is sound; in the chain of Abu Saʿid is ʿAtiyyah, and most scholars consider him weak. al-Bazzar narrated only the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. Majma' al-Zawa'id 10/411-412. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/212.]]

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Kharaqi al-Marwazi informed us; Abu al-Hasan ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tayasfuni informed us; ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us; ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar al-Jawhari informed us; Ahmad ibn ʿAli al-Kushmihani informed us; ʿAli ibn Hujr informed us; Isma'il ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Kathir al-Madani informed us, from Humayd al-Tawil, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a woman of the women of the people of Paradise looked upon the earth, she would light up everything between them, and fill everything between them with fragrance, and her headdress upon her head would be better than this world and all that is in it."[[al-Haythami said: al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat, and its chain is good. Majma' al-Zawa'id 10/418.]] [Sahih. Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad narrated it from Muʿawiyah ibn ʿUmar, from Abu Ishaq, from Humayd.][[Addition from manuscript B.]]

Abu al-Hasan ʿAli ibn Yusuf al-Juwayni informed us; Abu Muhammad Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Muhammad ibn Shurayk al-Shafiʿi informed us; ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Muslim informed us; Abu Bakr al-Jurbadhi informed us; Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Himsi informed us; ʿUthman ibn Saʿid ibn Kathir ibn Dinar informed us; Muhammad ibn al-Muhajir informed us, from al-Dahhak al-Maʿafiri, from Sulayman ibn Musa, who said: Kurayb told me that he heard Usamah ibn Zayd say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anyone who will strive for Paradise? Paradise has no equal. By the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is a light that shines, a basil plant that sways, a lofty palace, a flowing river, a ripe fruit, a beautiful and lovely wife, many garments, an eternal abode in a safe home, fresh fruit, luxury, and blessing in a lofty, splendid place." They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, we are those who strive for it." He said: "Say, if Allah wills." The people said: "If Allah wills."[[Narrated by Ibn Majah in al-Zuhd, bab sifat al-jannah, no. 4332, 2/1448. Ibn Hibban declared it sound in Sifat al-Jannah (651), from Mawarid al-Zam'an. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/223, and its editor said: al-Dahhak al-Maʿafiri: only Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy, and his teacher Sulayman ibn Musa al-Umawi al-Dimashqi is disputed.]]

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise are beardless, with kohl-darkened eyes, and their youth never fades and their garments never wear out."[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Saghir and al-Awsat, and its chain is hasan. Ahmad narrated it from Abu Hurayrah, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat from Anas, and its chain is good. Part of it is in the Sahih. Majma' al-Zawa'id 10/398-399.]]

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Samad al-Turabi informed us; al-Hakim Abu al-Fadl al-Haddadi informed us; Abu Yazid Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Khalid informed us; Ishaq al-Hanzali informed us; Abu Muʿawiyah informed us; ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq informed us, from al-Nuʿman ibn Saʿid, from ʿAli, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in Paradise there is a market where there is no buying or selling, except for images of men and women. When a man desires an image, he enters it. In it is the gathering of the wide-eyed houris, who call out with a voice that no created being has ever heard like it: 'We are the eternal ones, so we will never perish. We are the bountiful ones, so we will never be miserable. We are the content ones, so we will never be angry. Blessed is the one who belongs to us and whom we belong to, or who is ours.'"[[Narrated by Ahmad as a marfuʿ hadith 1/156 from ʿAli; al-Tirmidhi in abridged form in Sifat al-Jannah, bab ma ja'a fi suq al-jannah, 7/264, and said: This is a hasan gharib hadith. Hannad in al-Zuhd 1/92; and Ibn Abi Shaybah 13/100. In its chain is ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq al-Wasiti: Ahmad said: "He is nothing; munkar al-hadith." Yahya said: "Matruk (abandoned)." Ibn Hajar said: "Weak, of the seventh rank" (Taqrib). al-Mundhiri declared it weak, and Ibn al-Jawzi included it among the fabricated reports (Fayd al-Qadir by al-Manawi 2/468). The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/226.]] Abu ʿIsa narrated it from Hannad and Ahmad ibn Mani' from Abu Muʿawiyah, as a marfuʿ hadith, and said: This is a gharib hadith.

Isma'il ibn ʿAbd al-Qahir al-Jurjani informed us; ʿAbd al-Ghafir ibn Muhammad al-Farisi informed us; Muhammad ibn ʿIsa al-Juludi informed us; Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan informed us; Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj informed us; Abu ʿUthman Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbar al-Basri informed us; Hammad ibn Salamah informed us, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in Paradise there is a market which they visit every Friday. The north wind blows and sweeps dust onto their faces and garments, and they grow in beauty and loveliness. They return to their families, having grown in beauty and loveliness. Their families say to them: 'By Allah, you have grown in beauty and loveliness after us!' They reply: 'And by Allah, you too have grown in beauty and loveliness after us!'"[[Narrated by Muslim in al-Jannah, bab fi suq al-jannah wa ma yanaluna fiha min al-naʿim, no. 2833, 4/2178. The author also narrated it in Sharh al-Sunnah 15/227 and said: This is a sahih hadith.]]

The exegesis of the Almighty's words: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it.﴾ The occasion of revelation of this verse is that when Allah, exalted is He, cited the examples of the fly and the spider, saying: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ (22:73), and He said: ﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider, which takes a home﴾ (29:41), the Jews said: "What did Allah intend by mentioning these lowly things?" [[See: al-Tabari: 1/400; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi, p. 59; al-Wasit of al-Wahidi: 1/64.]] It is also said that the polytheists said: "We do not worship a god who mentions such things," so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾ [[Ibid.]], meaning He does not refrain, and shame does not prevent Him, ﴿to present an example﴾, meaning to mention a likeness. ﴿[Even] of a mosquito﴾: "ma" is extra (silah), meaning an example of a mosquito, and "mosquito" is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "example."

The baqq is the small bug, and the mosquito (ba'ud) was so named as if it were a part (ba'd) of the baqq. ﴿Or what is above it﴾ means the fly and the spider. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it means "or what is below it," as one says, "So-and-so is ignorant," and it is said, "and above that," meaning, "and more ignorant."

﴿As for those who believe﴾ in Muhammad and the Qur'an, ﴿they know that it﴾, meaning the example, ﴿is the truth﴾, the sincere reality, ﴿from their Lord. As for those who disbelieve, they say: "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾, meaning by this example. When he omitted the alif and lam (of "hadha"), he put it in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) and a detached (qat') term. Then He answered them, saying: ﴿By it He leads many astray﴾, meaning by this example, ﴿many﴾ of the disbelievers, because they deny it, so they increase in misguidance. ﴿And by it He guides many﴾, meaning by this example, ﴿many﴾ of the believers, so they affirm it.

Al-Idlal (leading astray) is diverting from the truth to falsehood. It is also said that it means destruction; it is said, "The water perished (dalla) in the milk" when it is destroyed. ﴿And none leads astray by it except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾, meaning the disbelievers. The root of fisq is departure; it is said, "The date (rutbah) departed (fasaqat)" when it came out of its skin. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he departed from the command of his Lord﴾ (18:50), meaning he went out. Then He described them, saying:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 27–29:

Then He said: ﴿Those who break﴾ (yunqudun), meaning they oppose and abandon. The root meaning of naqd (breaking) is to break. ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾: the command of Allah which He imposed upon them on the Day of the Covenant (al-mithaq), by His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [7:172]. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which He took from the prophets and all the nations, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [3:81], and the rest of the verse. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which was imposed upon them in the Torah, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and make known his description. ﴿After its confirmation﴾ (mithaqihi), its affirmation. And al-mithaq is the firmly affirmed covenant. ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, meaning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in all the messengers, peace be upon them, because they said: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others." And the believers said: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [2:285]. It is also said that He meant by it the ties of kinship (al-arham). ﴿And they cause corruption on the earth﴾ by sins, and by hindering people from believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in the Qur'an. ﴿Those are the losers﴾, the ones who are cheated. Then He addressed the polytheists of the Arabs, in a manner of wonder:

﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah﴾ after the establishment of the proofs and the clarity of the evidences. Then He mentioned the proofs, saying: ﴿While you were dead﴾, as sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers, ﴿then He gave you life﴾ in the wombs and in this world, ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ at the end of your terms, ﴿then He will bring you to life﴾ for the resurrection, ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning you will be sent back in the Hereafter, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

Ya'qub recited "turja'un" (tarji'un) throughout the Qur'an with a fatha on the ya' and the ta', treating it as the active voice (tasmiyat al-fa'il).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾, so that you may take heed and reflect. It is also said: so that you may benefit. ﴿Then He rose over to the heaven﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes of the early generations said: meaning He ascended to the heaven. Ibn Kaysan, al-Farra' and a group of grammarians said: meaning He turned toward the creation of the heaven. It is also said: He intended, because He first created the earth, then He turned to the creation of the heaven. ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾, creating them level, without flaw or crack. ﴿And He is Knower of all things.﴾ Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qalun recited "huwa" and "hiya" with a sukun on the ha' when it is preceded by a waw, a fa', or a lam; al-Kisa'i and Qalun added: "thumma huwa" and "Qalun" in ﴿let him dictate, he [huwa]﴾ [2:282].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 27–29:

Then He said: ﴿Those who break﴾ (yunqudun), meaning they oppose and abandon. The root meaning of naqd (breaking) is to break. ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾: the command of Allah which He imposed upon them on the Day of the Covenant (al-mithaq), by His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [7:172]. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which He took from the prophets and all the nations, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [3:81], and the rest of the verse. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which was imposed upon them in the Torah, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and make known his description. ﴿After its confirmation﴾ (mithaqihi), its affirmation. And al-mithaq is the firmly affirmed covenant. ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, meaning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in all the messengers, peace be upon them, because they said: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others." And the believers said: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [2:285]. It is also said that He meant by it the ties of kinship (al-arham). ﴿And they cause corruption on the earth﴾ by sins, and by hindering people from believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in the Qur'an. ﴿Those are the losers﴾, the ones who are cheated. Then He addressed the polytheists of the Arabs, in a manner of wonder:

﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah﴾ after the establishment of the proofs and the clarity of the evidences. Then He mentioned the proofs, saying: ﴿While you were dead﴾, as sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers, ﴿then He gave you life﴾ in the wombs and in this world, ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ at the end of your terms, ﴿then He will bring you to life﴾ for the resurrection, ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning you will be sent back in the Hereafter, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

Ya'qub recited "turja'un" (tarji'un) throughout the Qur'an with a fatha on the ya' and the ta', treating it as the active voice (tasmiyat al-fa'il).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾, so that you may take heed and reflect. It is also said: so that you may benefit. ﴿Then He rose over to the heaven﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes of the early generations said: meaning He ascended to the heaven. Ibn Kaysan, al-Farra' and a group of grammarians said: meaning He turned toward the creation of the heaven. It is also said: He intended, because He first created the earth, then He turned to the creation of the heaven. ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾, creating them level, without flaw or crack. ﴿And He is Knower of all things.﴾ Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qalun recited "huwa" and "hiya" with a sukun on the ha' when it is preceded by a waw, a fa', or a lam; al-Kisa'i and Qalun added: "thumma huwa" and "Qalun" in ﴿let him dictate, he [huwa]﴾ [2:282].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 27–29:

Then He said: ﴿Those who break﴾ (yunqudun), meaning they oppose and abandon. The root meaning of naqd (breaking) is to break. ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾: the command of Allah which He imposed upon them on the Day of the Covenant (al-mithaq), by His saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [7:172]. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which He took from the prophets and all the nations, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ [3:81], and the rest of the verse. It is also said that He meant by it the covenant which was imposed upon them in the Torah, that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and make known his description. ﴿After its confirmation﴾ (mithaqihi), its affirmation. And al-mithaq is the firmly affirmed covenant. ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, meaning belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in all the messengers, peace be upon them, because they said: "We believe in some and disbelieve in others." And the believers said: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [2:285]. It is also said that He meant by it the ties of kinship (al-arham). ﴿And they cause corruption on the earth﴾ by sins, and by hindering people from believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in the Qur'an. ﴿Those are the losers﴾, the ones who are cheated. Then He addressed the polytheists of the Arabs, in a manner of wonder:

﴿How do you disbelieve in Allah﴾ after the establishment of the proofs and the clarity of the evidences. Then He mentioned the proofs, saying: ﴿While you were dead﴾, as sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers, ﴿then He gave you life﴾ in the wombs and in this world, ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ at the end of your terms, ﴿then He will bring you to life﴾ for the resurrection, ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning you will be sent back in the Hereafter, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

Ya'qub recited "turja'un" (tarji'un) throughout the Qur'an with a fatha on the ya' and the ta', treating it as the active voice (tasmiyat al-fa'il).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾, so that you may take heed and reflect. It is also said: so that you may benefit. ﴿Then He rose over to the heaven﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes of the early generations said: meaning He ascended to the heaven. Ibn Kaysan, al-Farra' and a group of grammarians said: meaning He turned toward the creation of the heaven. It is also said: He intended, because He first created the earth, then He turned to the creation of the heaven. ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾, creating them level, without flaw or crack. ﴿And He is Knower of all things.﴾ Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qalun recited "huwa" and "hiya" with a sukun on the ha' when it is preceded by a waw, a fa', or a lam; al-Kisa'i and Qalun added: "thumma huwa" and "Qalun" in ﴿let him dictate, he [huwa]﴾ [2:282].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 30:

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And when your Lord said﴾, meaning: "And your Lord said." The "idh" (when) is extra (zā'idah). It is also said that its meaning is: "Remember when your Lord said." The same applies to everything similar to this that occurs in the Qur'an; this is its way. "Idh" (إذ) and "idha" (إذا) are both particles of time, except that "idh" refers to the past and "idha" refers to the future. Each may be placed in the position of the other. Al-Mubarrad said: When "idh" is used with the future, its meaning is past, as in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And when those who disbelieve plot against you﴾ (8:30), meaning: "And when they plotted." And when "idha" is used with the past, its meaning is future, as in His saying: ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes﴾ (79:34), and ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾ (110:1), meaning: "will come."

﴿to the angels﴾: the plural of malak (angel). Its original form was ma'lak, from al-ma'lakah, al-alūkah and al-alūk, which mean risalah (message). It was transposed (qulibat) so it became mala'k, then the hamzah was dropped to seek lightness because of its frequent use, and its vowel was transferred to the lam, so it became malak.

By "them" he means the angels who were on the earth. That is because Allah, the Exalted, created the heavens and the earth, and created the angels and the jinn. He housed the angels in the heaven and housed the jinn on the earth. They remained and worshipped for a long time on the earth. Then envy and oppression appeared among them, and they caused corruption and killed. So Allah sent to them an army of angels called the Jinn, who were the guardians of the Gardens (al-jinan). He took their chief, Iblis, from the Garden (al-jannah); he was their leader, their guide, and the most knowledgeable of them. They descended to the earth and drove the jinn to the mountain ridges, the valley depths (and the depths of the valleys) and the islands of the seas, and they inhabited the earth. Allah lightened their worship. Allah gave Iblis the dominion of the earth, the dominion of the lowest heaven, and the treasury of the Garden. He would worship Allah sometimes on the earth, sometimes in the heaven, and sometimes in the Garden. Then self-admiration entered him, and he said to himself: "Allah has given me this dominion only because I am the most honoured of the angels in His sight." [Al-Wahidi mentioned this too in his Tafsir: 1/74. See also Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/131-133 and 138-141, where there are some narrations, which Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, declared weak. Shaykh Ahmad Shakir also cited this from him in his commentary on al-Tabari: 1/505.] So Allah, the Exalted, said to Himself and to His army: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place﴾

[Creator.]

﴿upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)﴾: meaning, a replacement for you, and one who will raise you up to Me. They disliked this because they were the least worshipful of the angels.

The khalifah here refers to Adam. He was called khalifah because he succeeded the jinn, meaning he came after them. It is also said that he was called so because others would succeed him. The correct view is that he is the khalifah of Allah on His earth, to establish His rulings and carry out His commands. [Ibn al-Qayyim, in his book "Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah" 1/151, has useful discussion and sound detail concerning the caliphate of Allah on His earth, which should be consulted for its benefit.] ﴿They said: Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein﴾ through sins.

﴿and sheds blood﴾ unjustly, meaning as the sons of the jinn did. They judged the unseen by the seen, and in reality they did not know the unseen. ﴿while we exalt You with Your praise﴾. Al-Hasan said: we say "Subhan Allah wa bihamdih" (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him), and this is the prayer of creation ﴿and the prayer of animals and others﴾ [Omitted in the original.] besides the children of Adam, and by it they are provided for.

Ismail ibn Abd al-Qahir informed us: Abd al-Ghafir ibn Muhammad informed us: Muhammad ibn Isa informed us: Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan informed us: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj informed us: Zuhayr ibn Harb informed us: Hibban ibn Hilal informed us: Wuhayb informed us: Sa'id al-Jurayri informed us, from Abu Abd Allah al-Jasri, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, from Abu Dharr, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Which speech is best?" He said: "What Allah has chosen for His angels, or for His servants: Subhan Allah wa bihamdih (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him)." [Narrated by Muslim in al-Dhikr wa al-Du'a, chapter on the virtue of Subhan Allah wa bihamdih, no. (2731): 4/2093; and al-Tirmidhi in al-Da'awat, chapter on which speech is most beloved to Allah, 10/52, and he said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.]

It is also said: "and we pray by Your command." Ibn Abbas said: everything in the Qur'an concerning tasbih refers to prayer. ﴿and we sanctify You﴾, meaning we extol You with holiness and purity. It is also said: "and we purify ourselves for Your obedience." It is also said: "and we declare You far above imperfection." The lam is connective (silah). It is also said: this was not from the angels by way of objection or self-admiration in their deeds, but out of wonder and seeking the wisdom behind it. ﴿He said﴾: Allah ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾: the benefit in it. It is also said: "Indeed, I know that among his descendants are those who will obey Me and worship Me, from among the prophets, the saints and the scholars." It is also said: "Indeed, I know that among you is one who will disobey Me, and that is Iblis." It is also said: "Indeed, I know that they will sin, and I will forgive them."

The people of the Hijaz and Basra read inni a'lamu with a fatha on the ya' (إِنِّيَ), and likewise every ya' of possession (idafah) that is followed by an open alif, except in a number of specified places. In some places they read with a fatha before a damma or kasra alif, and before other than alif. The reciters differ in the details of this.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 31:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾: Adam was named "Adam" because he was created from the adim (surface, skin) of the earth. It was also said: he was named so because he was of adam (wheat-coloured, brown) complexion. His kunyah (patronymic) was Abu Muhammad, and Abu al-Bashar (father of mankind). When Allah the Exalted created him, He taught him the names of things. That was because the angels said, when Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a khalifah (successor)﴾: "Let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create a creation more honoured by Him than us. And if He does, we are more knowledgeable than him, because we were created before him and have seen what he has not seen." So Allah the Exalted manifested His superiority over them through knowledge. In this is evidence that the prophets are superior to the angels, even though they are messengers, as the Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah have held. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: He taught him the name of every thing, even the qasʿah (bowl) and the quṣayʿah (small bowl). It was also said: the names of what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the names of the angels. It was also said: the names of his offspring, and it was said: the craft of every thing. The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, taught Adam all the languages, then each of his children spoke a language, so they dispersed in the lands, and each group was specific to one language. [[See: Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/485; al-Wasit of al-Wahidi: 1/77.]]

﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾: He said "presented them" (ʿaradahum) and not "presented them" (ʿaradahā) because when the named things include those who reason and those who do not, the reference is made with the form for those who reason, just as males and females are referred to with the masculine form. Muqatil said: Allah created every thing, the animal and the inanimate, then presented those forms to the angels, so the pronoun refers to the forms, which is why He said "presented them." ﴿He said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾ — "inform Me" (anbi'uni) means "tell Me" — ﴿of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾ regarding My statement that I do not create a creation except that you are more excellent and more knowledgeable than it. So the angels said, acknowledging their incapacity:

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 32–33:

﴿They said: "Glory be to You"﴾, exalting You above any imperfection, ﴿"We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."﴾ Its meaning is: You are far too exalted for us to encompass any part of Your knowledge except what You have taught us. ﴿"Indeed, You are the All-Knowing"﴾ of Your creation, ﴿"the All-Wise"﴾ in Your command. Al-Hakim (the All-Wise) has two meanings. The first is al-Hakim (the Judge), who is the just Judge. The second is al-Muhkim lil-amr (the One who makes the matter firm), so that corruption cannot reach it. The root of hikmah (wisdom) in the language is al-man' (prevention), for it prevents its possessor from falsehood. From this comes hikmat al-dabba (the bridle of the animal), because it prevents the animal from veering. When their inability became evident, ﴿Allah, the Exalted, said﴾:

﴿"O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ That is, tell them their names. So Adam named every thing by its name, and he mentioned the wisdom for which it was created. ﴿So when he had informed them of their names, He said﴾, Allah, the Exalted, ﴿"Did I not tell you"﴾, O My angels, ﴿"that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth"﴾, what was in them and what will be in them, because He had already said to them, ﴿"Indeed, I know that which you do not know"﴾ (2:30). ﴿"And I know what you reveal"﴾. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: this refers to their saying, ﴿"Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ ﴿"And what you conceal"﴾ refers to their saying: "Allah will never create a creature more honored by Him than us." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It is that Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which was lying between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a soul in it. He said: "This was created for a purpose." Then he entered through its mouth and exited through its rear, and said: "This is a creature that cannot hold together, for it is hollow." Then he said to the angels who were with him: "Tell me, if this one is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey him, what will you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said to himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over him, I will destroy him, and if he is empowered over me, I will disobey him." Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿"And I know what you reveal"﴾, meaning the obedience that the angels display, ﴿"and what you conceal"﴾, meaning Iblis's disobedience.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 32–33:

﴿They said: "Glory be to You"﴾, exalting You above any imperfection, ﴿"We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."﴾ Its meaning is: You are far too exalted for us to encompass any part of Your knowledge except what You have taught us. ﴿"Indeed, You are the All-Knowing"﴾ of Your creation, ﴿"the All-Wise"﴾ in Your command. Al-Hakim (the All-Wise) has two meanings. The first is al-Hakim (the Judge), who is the just Judge. The second is al-Muhkim lil-amr (the One who makes the matter firm), so that corruption cannot reach it. The root of hikmah (wisdom) in the language is al-man' (prevention), for it prevents its possessor from falsehood. From this comes hikmat al-dabba (the bridle of the animal), because it prevents the animal from veering. When their inability became evident, ﴿Allah, the Exalted, said﴾:

﴿"O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ That is, tell them their names. So Adam named every thing by its name, and he mentioned the wisdom for which it was created. ﴿So when he had informed them of their names, He said﴾, Allah, the Exalted, ﴿"Did I not tell you"﴾, O My angels, ﴿"that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth"﴾, what was in them and what will be in them, because He had already said to them, ﴿"Indeed, I know that which you do not know"﴾ (2:30). ﴿"And I know what you reveal"﴾. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: this refers to their saying, ﴿"Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ ﴿"And what you conceal"﴾ refers to their saying: "Allah will never create a creature more honored by Him than us." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It is that Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which was lying between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a soul in it. He said: "This was created for a purpose." Then he entered through its mouth and exited through its rear, and said: "This is a creature that cannot hold together, for it is hollow." Then he said to the angels who were with him: "Tell me, if this one is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey him, what will you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said to himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over him, I will destroy him, and if he is empowered over me, I will disobey him." Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿"And I know what you reveal"﴾, meaning the obedience that the angels display, ﴿"and what you conceal"﴾, meaning Iblis's disobedience.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 34–37 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. Abu Ja'far recited "lilmala'ikatu usjudu" with a *damma* on the *ta'* (*li-l-mala'ikatu*), by way of *jiwar* (assimilation to the adjacent alif of *usjudu*). He also recited ﴿Say: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (21:112) with a *damma* on the *ba'*. The grammarians (*nuhat*, the grammarians of Arabic) considered this very weak and attributed it to an error.

They differed as to which angels this address was directed. Some said it was addressed to those who were the inhabitants of the earth. The more sound view is that it was addressed to all the angels, based on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ (15:30).

As for His saying "usjudu" (prostrate), there are two views. The more sound view is that the prostration was truly to Adam, and it included the meaning of obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His command. This was a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of worship, like the prostration of Joseph's brothers to him in His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ (12:100). It did not involve placing the face on the ground; it was only bowing. When Islam came, it abrogated that with the greeting (*salam*).

It has also been said that the meaning of His saying ﴿prostrate to Adam﴾ is "towards Adam," so Adam was a *qibla* (direction of prostration), and the prostration was to Allah, the Exalted, just as the Ka'ba was made a *qibla* for prayer, while the prayer is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So they prostrated﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿except Iblis﴾. His name was 'Azazil in Syriac, and in Arabic al-Harith. When he disobeyed, his name and form were changed, and he was called Iblis, because he *ablasa* (despaired) of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, meaning he despaired.

They differed concerning him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: Iblis was one of the angels. Al-Hasan said: he was one of the jinn and was not one of the angels, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn, and so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ (18:50). Therefore he is the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind. Also, he was created from fire, whereas the angels were created from light. And also, he has offspring, whereas the angels have no offspring. The first view is more sound, because the address of prostration was to the angels. His saying "he was of the jinn" means he was of the angels who were the guardians of the Garden. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was of those who work in the Garden. He also said: he was of a people of the angels who fashion the ornaments of the people of the Garden.

It has also been said that a group of the angels were created from fire and were named jinn because they are hidden from the eyes, and Iblis was one of them. The evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ (37:158), which is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. When Allah removed him from the angels, he was given offspring.

His saying: ﴿abā﴾, meaning he refused and so did not prostrate. ﴿And he was arrogant﴾, meaning he acted proudly, refusing to prostrate ﴿to Adam﴾.* ﴿And he became﴾, meaning he came to be, ﴿of the disbelievers﴾. Most of the exegetes said: he was, in Allah's prior knowledge, of the disbelievers who were destined for wretchedness.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Turabi informed us: Ibn al-Hakim Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Haddadi informed us: Abu Yazid Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Khalid informed us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Hanzali informed us: Jarir, Waki' and Abu Mu'awiya informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping and saying: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is the Garden; and I was commanded to prostrate and I disobeyed, so for me is the Fire.'"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾. The reason for this is that there was no one in the Garden to be of his kind, so he slept a sleep, and Allah created his wife Hawwa' (Eve) from the short rib of his left side. She was named Hawwa' because she was created from a living thing (*hayy*). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created her without Adam perceiving it or feeling any pain. Had he felt pain, no man would ever have shown affection to a woman. When he awoke from his sleep, he saw her sitting at his head, in the most beautiful of Allah's creation.* He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "Your wife, whom Allah created for you, that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you."*

﴿And eat freely﴾, meaning abundantly and widely, ﴿from it wherever you wish﴾, meaning how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish. ﴿But do not approach this tree﴾, meaning for eating. Some scholars said the prohibition applied to a kind of tree. Others said it applied to a specific tree, and they differed about which tree it was. Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it was the ear of grain (*sunbula*). Ibn Mas'ud said: it was the grapevine. Ibn Jurayj said: the fig tree. Qatada said: the tree of knowledge, which contains everything. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the camphor tree.*

﴿So you would become﴾, meaning you would be, ﴿of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who harm themselves through disobedience. The root of *zulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾: *istazalla* (to cause to slip). ﴿Satan﴾ caused Adam and Hawwa' to slip, meaning he invited them to the slip. Hamza recited "fa-azalahuma" (he made them slip away), meaning he removed them ("al-shaytan") from it (the tree). *Shaytan* is on the pattern *fay'al*, from *shatana*, meaning he went far away. He was named so for his distance from good and from mercy. ﴿From it﴾, meaning from the Garden, ﴿and removed them from that in which they had been﴾, meaning the bliss. That was because Iblis wanted to enter to whisper to Adam and Hawwa', but the guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was a friend of Iblis, and was one of the most beautiful of animals. It had four legs like those of a camel, and it was among the guardians of the Garden. Iblis asked it to carry him into its mouth, so it did, and it passed by the guardians while they did not know, and it entered him into the Garden. Al-Hasan said: he saw them at the gate of the Garden because they were leaving it. When Adam entered the Garden and saw the bliss in it, he said: "If only there were an eternity." Satan seized that opportunity, and came to him through the notion of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wept and wailed a wailing that saddened them both, and he was the first to wail. They said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I weep for you both, because you will die and leave the bliss you are in." That affected them both, and they were grieved. Iblis departed, then came to them again after that and said: "O Adam, shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" He refused to accept it from him. Then Iblis swore to them by Allah that he was truly one of their sincere advisers. So they were deceived, not thinking that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then she gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to swear by Allah that Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his right mind, but that Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate.*

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "That meal left us with long grief." Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Adam: "Was there not among what I permitted you in the Garden a wide choice apart from the tree?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, by Your might, but I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I shall certainly cause you to descend to the earth, and you will not attain sustenance except with toil." So they were brought down from the Garden, and they had been eating in it "freely." Adam was taught the craft of iron, and was commanded to till the land. He tilled and sowed, then irrigated, until it ripened and he harvested it, then threshed it, then winnowed it, then ground it, then kneaded it, then baked it, then ate it, and he did not reach it until he had attained from it what he wished. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: when Adam ate from the tree which he had been forbidden, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "What made you do what you did?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' adorned it for me." He said: "I shall make it her lot that she will carry only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I shall make her bleed twice a month." Hawwa' then cried out, and it was said: "Upon you is the cry, and upon your daughters."*

When they both ate, their garments fell from them and their private parts were exposed, and they were removed from the Garden. That is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "Go down"﴾, meaning descend to the earth, namely Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent. ﴿Adam descended at Sarandib in the land of India, upon a mountain called Nud; Hawwa' at Jedda; Iblis at Ayla; and the serpent at Isfahan.*﴾ ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾: he intended the enmity that exists between the descendants of Adam and the serpent, and between the believers among the descendants of Adam and Iblis.
