**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 34–37 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. Abu Ja'far recited "lilmala'ikatu usjudu" with a *damma* on the *ta'* (*li-l-mala'ikatu*), by way of *jiwar* (assimilation to the adjacent alif of *usjudu*). He also recited ﴿Say: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (21:112) with a *damma* on the *ba'*. The grammarians (*nuhat*, the grammarians of Arabic) considered this very weak and attributed it to an error.

They differed as to which angels this address was directed. Some said it was addressed to those who were the inhabitants of the earth. The more sound view is that it was addressed to all the angels, based on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ (15:30).

As for His saying "usjudu" (prostrate), there are two views. The more sound view is that the prostration was truly to Adam, and it included the meaning of obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His command. This was a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of worship, like the prostration of Joseph's brothers to him in His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ (12:100). It did not involve placing the face on the ground; it was only bowing. When Islam came, it abrogated that with the greeting (*salam*).

It has also been said that the meaning of His saying ﴿prostrate to Adam﴾ is "towards Adam," so Adam was a *qibla* (direction of prostration), and the prostration was to Allah, the Exalted, just as the Ka'ba was made a *qibla* for prayer, while the prayer is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So they prostrated﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿except Iblis﴾. His name was 'Azazil in Syriac, and in Arabic al-Harith. When he disobeyed, his name and form were changed, and he was called Iblis, because he *ablasa* (despaired) of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, meaning he despaired.

They differed concerning him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: Iblis was one of the angels. Al-Hasan said: he was one of the jinn and was not one of the angels, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn, and so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ (18:50). Therefore he is the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind. Also, he was created from fire, whereas the angels were created from light. And also, he has offspring, whereas the angels have no offspring. The first view is more sound, because the address of prostration was to the angels. His saying "he was of the jinn" means he was of the angels who were the guardians of the Garden. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was of those who work in the Garden. He also said: he was of a people of the angels who fashion the ornaments of the people of the Garden.

It has also been said that a group of the angels were created from fire and were named jinn because they are hidden from the eyes, and Iblis was one of them. The evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ (37:158), which is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. When Allah removed him from the angels, he was given offspring.

His saying: ﴿abā﴾, meaning he refused and so did not prostrate. ﴿And he was arrogant﴾, meaning he acted proudly, refusing to prostrate ﴿to Adam﴾.* ﴿And he became﴾, meaning he came to be, ﴿of the disbelievers﴾. Most of the exegetes said: he was, in Allah's prior knowledge, of the disbelievers who were destined for wretchedness.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Turabi informed us: Ibn al-Hakim Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Haddadi informed us: Abu Yazid Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Khalid informed us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Hanzali informed us: Jarir, Waki' and Abu Mu'awiya informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping and saying: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is the Garden; and I was commanded to prostrate and I disobeyed, so for me is the Fire.'"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾. The reason for this is that there was no one in the Garden to be of his kind, so he slept a sleep, and Allah created his wife Hawwa' (Eve) from the short rib of his left side. She was named Hawwa' because she was created from a living thing (*hayy*). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created her without Adam perceiving it or feeling any pain. Had he felt pain, no man would ever have shown affection to a woman. When he awoke from his sleep, he saw her sitting at his head, in the most beautiful of Allah's creation.* He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "Your wife, whom Allah created for you, that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you."*

﴿And eat freely﴾, meaning abundantly and widely, ﴿from it wherever you wish﴾, meaning how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish. ﴿But do not approach this tree﴾, meaning for eating. Some scholars said the prohibition applied to a kind of tree. Others said it applied to a specific tree, and they differed about which tree it was. Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it was the ear of grain (*sunbula*). Ibn Mas'ud said: it was the grapevine. Ibn Jurayj said: the fig tree. Qatada said: the tree of knowledge, which contains everything. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the camphor tree.*

﴿So you would become﴾, meaning you would be, ﴿of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who harm themselves through disobedience. The root of *zulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾: *istazalla* (to cause to slip). ﴿Satan﴾ caused Adam and Hawwa' to slip, meaning he invited them to the slip. Hamza recited "fa-azalahuma" (he made them slip away), meaning he removed them ("al-shaytan") from it (the tree). *Shaytan* is on the pattern *fay'al*, from *shatana*, meaning he went far away. He was named so for his distance from good and from mercy. ﴿From it﴾, meaning from the Garden, ﴿and removed them from that in which they had been﴾, meaning the bliss. That was because Iblis wanted to enter to whisper to Adam and Hawwa', but the guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was a friend of Iblis, and was one of the most beautiful of animals. It had four legs like those of a camel, and it was among the guardians of the Garden. Iblis asked it to carry him into its mouth, so it did, and it passed by the guardians while they did not know, and it entered him into the Garden. Al-Hasan said: he saw them at the gate of the Garden because they were leaving it. When Adam entered the Garden and saw the bliss in it, he said: "If only there were an eternity." Satan seized that opportunity, and came to him through the notion of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wept and wailed a wailing that saddened them both, and he was the first to wail. They said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I weep for you both, because you will die and leave the bliss you are in." That affected them both, and they were grieved. Iblis departed, then came to them again after that and said: "O Adam, shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" He refused to accept it from him. Then Iblis swore to them by Allah that he was truly one of their sincere advisers. So they were deceived, not thinking that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then she gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to swear by Allah that Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his right mind, but that Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate.*

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "That meal left us with long grief." Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Adam: "Was there not among what I permitted you in the Garden a wide choice apart from the tree?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, by Your might, but I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I shall certainly cause you to descend to the earth, and you will not attain sustenance except with toil." So they were brought down from the Garden, and they had been eating in it "freely." Adam was taught the craft of iron, and was commanded to till the land. He tilled and sowed, then irrigated, until it ripened and he harvested it, then threshed it, then winnowed it, then ground it, then kneaded it, then baked it, then ate it, and he did not reach it until he had attained from it what he wished. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: when Adam ate from the tree which he had been forbidden, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "What made you do what you did?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' adorned it for me." He said: "I shall make it her lot that she will carry only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I shall make her bleed twice a month." Hawwa' then cried out, and it was said: "Upon you is the cry, and upon your daughters."*

When they both ate, their garments fell from them and their private parts were exposed, and they were removed from the Garden. That is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "Go down"﴾, meaning descend to the earth, namely Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent. ﴿Adam descended at Sarandib in the land of India, upon a mountain called Nud; Hawwa' at Jedda; Iblis at Ayla; and the serpent at Isfahan.*﴾ ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾: he intended the enmity that exists between the descendants of Adam and the serpent, and between the believers among the descendants of Adam and Iblis. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an open enemy to you both﴾ (7:22).

Allah, exalted, said: "No, rather it is something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, then as You decreed it before You created me, forgive me." [[See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1/149; al-Tabari 1/545; al-Wasit of al-Wahidi 1/87.]]

It was also said: they are three things: modesty, supplication and weeping. Ibn 'Abbas said: Adam and Eve wept over what they had lost of the bliss of Paradise for two hundred years, and neither ate nor drank for forty days, and Adam did not approach Eve for a hundred years. Al-Mas'udi related from Yunus ibn Khabbab and 'Alqamah ibn Martad, who said: "If the tears of all the people of the earth were gathered, the tears of Dawud would be more, when he committed the sin; and if the tears of Dawud and the people of the earth were gathered, the tears of Adam would be more, when Allah expelled him from Paradise." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: It has reached me that when Adam was sent down (habata) to the earth, he remained for three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah, exalted.

His saying: ﴿Then He turned to him in forgiveness﴾, meaning He overlooked it for him. ﴿Indeed, He is the One who turns (in acceptance), the Most Merciful﴾: He accepts the repentance of His servants, ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 34–37 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. Abu Ja'far recited "lilmala'ikatu usjudu" with a *damma* on the *ta'* (*li-l-mala'ikatu*), by way of *jiwar* (assimilation to the adjacent alif of *usjudu*). He also recited ﴿Say: "My Lord, judge with truth"﴾ (21:112) with a *damma* on the *ba'*. The grammarians (*nuhat*, the grammarians of Arabic) considered this very weak and attributed it to an error.

They differed as to which angels this address was directed. Some said it was addressed to those who were the inhabitants of the earth. The more sound view is that it was addressed to all the angels, based on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ (15:30).

As for His saying "usjudu" (prostrate), there are two views. The more sound view is that the prostration was truly to Adam, and it included the meaning of obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by carrying out His command. This was a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of worship, like the prostration of Joseph's brothers to him in His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾ (12:100). It did not involve placing the face on the ground; it was only bowing. When Islam came, it abrogated that with the greeting (*salam*).

It has also been said that the meaning of His saying ﴿prostrate to Adam﴾ is "towards Adam," so Adam was a *qibla* (direction of prostration), and the prostration was to Allah, the Exalted, just as the Ka'ba was made a *qibla* for prayer, while the prayer is to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So they prostrated﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿except Iblis﴾. His name was 'Azazil in Syriac, and in Arabic al-Harith. When he disobeyed, his name and form were changed, and he was called Iblis, because he *ablasa* (despaired) of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, meaning he despaired.

They differed concerning him. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and most of the exegetes (*mufassirun*) said: Iblis was one of the angels. Al-Hasan said: he was one of the jinn and was not one of the angels, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn, and so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ (18:50). Therefore he is the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind. Also, he was created from fire, whereas the angels were created from light. And also, he has offspring, whereas the angels have no offspring. The first view is more sound, because the address of prostration was to the angels. His saying "he was of the jinn" means he was of the angels who were the guardians of the Garden. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was of those who work in the Garden. He also said: he was of a people of the angels who fashion the ornaments of the people of the Garden.

It has also been said that a group of the angels were created from fire and were named jinn because they are hidden from the eyes, and Iblis was one of them. The evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ (37:158), which is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. When Allah removed him from the angels, he was given offspring.

His saying: ﴿abā﴾, meaning he refused and so did not prostrate. ﴿And he was arrogant﴾, meaning he acted proudly, refusing to prostrate ﴿to Adam﴾.* ﴿And he became﴾, meaning he came to be, ﴿of the disbelievers﴾. Most of the exegetes said: he was, in Allah's prior knowledge, of the disbelievers who were destined for wretchedness.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Turabi informed us: Ibn al-Hakim Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Haddadi informed us: Abu Yazid Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Khalid informed us: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim al-Hanzali informed us: Jarir, Waki' and Abu Mu'awiya informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping and saying: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is the Garden; and I was commanded to prostrate and I disobeyed, so for me is the Fire.'"

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾. The reason for this is that there was no one in the Garden to be of his kind, so he slept a sleep, and Allah created his wife Hawwa' (Eve) from the short rib of his left side. She was named Hawwa' because she was created from a living thing (*hayy*). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, created her without Adam perceiving it or feeling any pain. Had he felt pain, no man would ever have shown affection to a woman. When he awoke from his sleep, he saw her sitting at his head, in the most beautiful of Allah's creation.* He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "Your wife, whom Allah created for you, that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you."*

﴿And eat freely﴾, meaning abundantly and widely, ﴿from it wherever you wish﴾, meaning how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish. ﴿But do not approach this tree﴾, meaning for eating. Some scholars said the prohibition applied to a kind of tree. Others said it applied to a specific tree, and they differed about which tree it was. Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it was the ear of grain (*sunbula*). Ibn Mas'ud said: it was the grapevine. Ibn Jurayj said: the fig tree. Qatada said: the tree of knowledge, which contains everything. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: the camphor tree.*

﴿So you would become﴾, meaning you would be, ﴿of the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who harm themselves through disobedience. The root of *zulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾: *istazalla* (to cause to slip). ﴿Satan﴾ caused Adam and Hawwa' to slip, meaning he invited them to the slip. Hamza recited "fa-azalahuma" (he made them slip away), meaning he removed them ("al-shaytan") from it (the tree). *Shaytan* is on the pattern *fay'al*, from *shatana*, meaning he went far away. He was named so for his distance from good and from mercy. ﴿From it﴾, meaning from the Garden, ﴿and removed them from that in which they had been﴾, meaning the bliss. That was because Iblis wanted to enter to whisper to Adam and Hawwa', but the guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was a friend of Iblis, and was one of the most beautiful of animals. It had four legs like those of a camel, and it was among the guardians of the Garden. Iblis asked it to carry him into its mouth, so it did, and it passed by the guardians while they did not know, and it entered him into the Garden. Al-Hasan said: he saw them at the gate of the Garden because they were leaving it. When Adam entered the Garden and saw the bliss in it, he said: "If only there were an eternity." Satan seized that opportunity, and came to him through the notion of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wept and wailed a wailing that saddened them both, and he was the first to wail. They said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I weep for you both, because you will die and leave the bliss you are in." That affected them both, and they were grieved. Iblis departed, then came to them again after that and said: "O Adam, shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" He refused to accept it from him. Then Iblis swore to them by Allah that he was truly one of their sincere advisers. So they were deceived, not thinking that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then she gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to swear by Allah that Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his right mind, but that Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate.*

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "That meal left us with long grief." Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Adam: "Was there not among what I permitted you in the Garden a wide choice apart from the tree?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, by Your might, but I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I shall certainly cause you to descend to the earth, and you will not attain sustenance except with toil." So they were brought down from the Garden, and they had been eating in it "freely." Adam was taught the craft of iron, and was commanded to till the land. He tilled and sowed, then irrigated, until it ripened and he harvested it, then threshed it, then winnowed it, then ground it, then kneaded it, then baked it, then ate it, and he did not reach it until he had attained from it what he wished. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: when Adam ate from the tree which he had been forbidden, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "What made you do what you did?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' adorned it for me." He said: "I shall make it her lot that she will carry only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I shall make her bleed twice a month." Hawwa' then cried out, and it was said: "Upon you is the cry, and upon your daughters."*

When they both ate, their garments fell from them and their private parts were exposed, and they were removed from the Garden. That is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "Go down"﴾, meaning descend to the earth, namely Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent. ﴿Adam descended at Sarandib in the land of India, upon a mountain called Nud; Hawwa' at Jedda; Iblis at Ayla; and the serpent at Isfahan.*﴾ ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾: he intended the enmity that exists between the descendants of Adam and the serpent, and between the believers among the descendants of Adam and Iblis. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an open enemy to you both﴾ (7:22).

*Editorial footnotes in the original text:*

- On the verse of the prostration of Joseph's brothers and the abrogation of prostration by the greeting: the source notes these are Baghawi's own statements.
- Regarding the narrative of Adam and Hawwa' (Eve), the footnote in the source states that most tafsir books mention this story when interpreting this verse, and that Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (1/156) says: "In this story there are additions mentioned by the exegetes, which we will not prolong by mentioning, because they are not among the things on which the meaning or interpretation of the verse depends." The footnote further observes that the unseen matters that Allah has reserved the knowledge of, and withheld from us, have no sound authentic texts indicating them; that most of the reports around them are open to objection or derive from *Isra'iliyyat* (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources); that it is enough for us what the texts contain; and that we leave knowledge of them to Allah, the Exalted. See *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* (1/59).
- Regarding the tree: the footnote quotes Ibn Jarir al-Tabari: "The correct position is to say that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade Adam and his wife from eating a specific tree among the trees of the Garden, apart from its other trees. They opposed what Allah forbade them and ate from it, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, described them. We have no knowledge of which tree it was specifically, because Allah did not set for His servants any evidence of it in the Qur'an or in authentic Sunna. How could it be known? It has been said it was the wheat tree, it has been said the grapevine, it has been said the fig tree, and it is possible it was one of them; that is knowledge, which if known does not benefit the one who knows it, and if someone is ignorant of it, his ignorance does not harm him." The footnote adds that al-Razi and other exegetes likewise preferred leaving it undetermined, which is the correct view. See Tabari, ed. Mahmud Shakir (1/520–521), and Ibn Kathir (1/146).
- Regarding the story of Adam eating from the tree: the footnote states that this difference over how and why Adam ate from the forbidden tree, on which exegetes have elaborated many tales, has no authentic report behind it. It belongs to the unseen, requiring a firm transmission, and these tales are likely drawn from *Isra'iliyyat*. The claim that Adam drank wine and was therefore not in his right senses is not correct, since the wine of Paradise has no intoxicating effect. The sound view is that he forgot and ate, as Allah the Exalted reported. See Ibn al-'Arabi, *Ahkam al-Qur'an* (1/19), Ibn 'Atiyya, *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz* (1/254–256), Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (1/161). Shaykh Muhammad Abu Shahba also refuted the Isra'iliyyat narrations in the exegesis of this verse, in his book *al-Isra'iliyyat wa-l-Mawdu'at fi Kutub al-Tafsir* (pp. 250–251).
- Regarding the report of Ibn 'Abbas about Hawwa' and the cry: the footnote states that Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* (2/381) narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, Wahidi mentioned it in *al-Wasit* with its chain (1/85–86), and Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (1/132) attributed it to others. The source also notes that there are reports from al-Suddi and al-Hasan with chains that are not established. See Ibn Kathir (1/147), ed. al-Wada'i.

Al-Hasan said: he saw them at the gate of the Garden because they were leaving it. When Adam entered the Garden and saw the bliss in it, he said: "If only there were an eternity." Satan seized that opportunity, and came to him through the notion of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wept and wailed a wailing that saddened them both, and he was the first to wail. They said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I weep for you both, because you will die and leave the bliss you are in." That affected them both, and they were grieved. Iblis departed, then came to them again after that and said: "O Adam, shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" He refused to accept it from him. Then Iblis swore to them by Allah that he was truly one of their sincere advisers. So they were deceived, not thinking that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then she gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab used to swear by Allah that Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his right mind, but that Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate.*

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "That meal left us with long grief." Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Adam: "Was there not among what I permitted you in the Garden a wide choice apart from the tree?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, by Your might, but I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely." He said: "By My might, I shall certainly cause you to descend to the earth, and you will not attain sustenance except with toil." So they were brought down from the Garden, and they had been eating in it "freely." Adam was taught the craft of iron, and was commanded to till the land. He tilled and sowed, then irrigated, until it ripened and he harvested it, then threshed it, then winnowed it, then ground it, then kneaded it, then baked it, then ate it, and he did not reach it until he had attained from it what he wished. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn 'Abbas: when Adam ate from the tree which he had been forbidden, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "What made you do what you did?" He said: "My Lord, Hawwa' adorned it for me." He said: "I shall make it her lot that she will carry only with hardship and give birth only with hardship, and I shall make her bleed twice a month." Hawwa' then cried out, and it was said: "Upon you is the cry, and upon your daughters."*

When they both ate, their garments fell from them and their private parts were exposed, and they were removed from the Garden. That is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We said, "Go down"﴾, meaning descend to the earth, namely Adam, Hawwa', Iblis and the serpent. ﴿Adam descended at Sarandib in the land of India, upon a mountain called Nud; Hawwa' at Jedda; Iblis at Ayla; and the serpent at Isfahan.*﴾ ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾: he intended the enmity that exists between the descendants of Adam and the serpent, and between the believers among the descendants of Adam and Iblis. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an open enemy to you both﴾ (7:22).

*Editorial footnotes in the original text:*

- On the verse of the prostration of Joseph's brothers and the abrogation of prostration by the greeting: the source notes these are Baghawi's own statements.
- Regarding the narrative of Adam and Hawwa' (Eve), the footnote in the source states that most tafsir books mention this story when interpreting this verse, and that Abu Hayyan in *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (1/156) says: "In this story there are additions mentioned by the exegetes, which we will not prolong by mentioning, because they are not among the things on which the meaning or interpretation of the verse depends." The footnote further observes that the unseen matters that Allah has reserved the knowledge of, and withheld from us, have no sound authentic texts indicating them; that most of the reports around them are open to objection or derive from *Isra'iliyyat* (narratives from Jewish and Christian sources); that it is enough for us what the texts contain; and that we leave knowledge of them to Allah, the Exalted. See *Fi Zilal al-Qur'an* (1/59).
- Regarding the tree: the footnote quotes Ibn Jarir al-Tabari: "The correct position is to say that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade Adam and his wife from eating a specific tree among the trees of the Garden, apart from its other trees. They opposed what Allah forbade them and ate from it, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, described them. We have no knowledge of which tree it was specifically, because Allah did not set for His servants any evidence of it in the Qur'an or in authentic Sunna. How could it be known? It has been said it was the wheat tree, it has been said the grapevine, it has been said the fig tree, and it is possible it was one of them; that is knowledge, which if known does not benefit the one who knows it, and if someone is ignorant of it, his ignorance does not harm him." The footnote adds that al-Razi and other exegetes likewise preferred leaving it undetermined, which is the correct view. See Tabari, ed. Mahmud Shakir (1/520–521), and Ibn Kathir (1/146).
- Regarding the story of Adam eating from the tree: the footnote states that this difference over how and why Adam ate from the forbidden tree, on which exegetes have elaborated many tales, has no authentic report behind it. It belongs to the unseen, requiring a firm transmission, and these tales are likely drawn from *Isra'iliyyat*. The claim that Adam drank wine and was therefore not in his right senses is not correct, since the wine of Paradise has no intoxicating effect. The sound view is that he forgot and ate, as Allah the Exalted reported. See Ibn al-'Arabi, *Ahkam al-Qur'an* (1/19), Ibn 'Atiyya, *al-Muharrar al-Wajiz* (1/254–256), Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit* (1/161). Shaykh Muhammad Abu Shahba also refuted the Isra'iliyyat narrations in the exegesis of this verse, in his book *al-Isra'iliyyat wa-l-Mawdu'at fi Kutub al-Tafsir* (pp. 250–251).
- Regarding the report of Ibn 'Abbas about Hawwa' and the cry: the footnote states that Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* (2/381) narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, Wahidi mentioned it in *al-Wasit* with its chain (1/85–86), and Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (1/132) attributed it to others. The source also notes that there are reports from al-Suddi and al-Hasan with chains that are not established. See Ibn Kathir (1/147), ed. al-Wada'i.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for you on the earth there is a dwelling place﴾, a place of settling; ﴿and provision﴾, sustenance and enjoyment; ﴿for a time﴾, until the end of your appointed terms.

﴿Then Adam received﴾: taliqqa means to receive with insight and understanding. It is said that tala??a (receiving) means learning. ﴿From his Lord, words﴾. The common reading (qira'at al-'ammah) is "Adamu" with a raised mim, and "kalimatin" with a lowered ta'. Ibn Kathir read "Adama" with a fatha, and "kalimatun" with a raised ta', meaning the words came to Adam from his Lord and were the cause of his repentance. The scholars differed concerning those words. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Hasan said: they are his saying, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves," to the end of the verse.

Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are his saying: "There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise. My Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the ﴿Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾." [[In (b): "the Most Forgiving."]] "There is no god but You, glory be to You and praise. My Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the most merciful of the merciful."

[[Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, after citing the views and attributing them to those who said them, said: "These views that we have related from those from whom we related them, although their wordings differ, their meanings agree that Allah, exalted is His praise, gave Adam words, and Adam received them from his Lord, accepted them and acted upon them, and repented to Allah from his sin, acknowledging his wrongdoing and disavowing his sin before his Lord, regretting what had passed from him of opposing His command. So Allah turned to him in acceptance of the words he received from Him and his remorse over the sin that had passed from him. What the Book of Allah indicates is that the words Adam received from his Lord are the words which Allah informed were spoken by him, disavowing before his Lord and acknowledging his sin, and that is His saying, 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves.' What the one who opposes our view has said, among the views we have related, is not refuted by its speaker, but it is a view for which there is no supporting proof that must be accepted; so it is permissible for us to attribute it to Adam, and that it is among what he received from his Lord when he turned to Him from his sin." Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/546. See also al-Wasit by al-Wahidi 1/87; Ibn Kathir 1/149. Al-Isra'iliyyat wa'l-Mawdu'at by Shaykh Muhammad Abu Shahba, p. 254.]]

It was said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: they are that Adam said: "O Lord, tell me: is what I did something I invented of my own accord, or something You decreed upon me before You created me?" Allah, exalted, said: "No, rather it is something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, then as You decreed it before You created me, forgive me." [[See: Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1/149; al-Tabari 1/545; al-Wasit of al-Wahidi 1/87.]]

It was also said: they are three things: modesty, supplication and weeping. Ibn 'Abbas said: Adam and Eve wept over what they had lost of the bliss of Paradise for two hundred years, and neither ate nor drank for forty days, and Adam did not approach Eve for a hundred years. Al-Mas'udi related from Yunus ibn Khabbab and 'Alqamah ibn Martad, who said: "If the tears of all the people of the earth were gathered, the tears of Dawud would be more, when he committed the sin; and if the tears of Dawud and the people of the earth were gathered, the tears of Adam would be more, when Allah expelled him from Paradise." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: It has reached me that when Adam was sent down (habata) to the earth, he remained for three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah, exalted.

[[See: al-Durr al-Manthur 1/141–142.]]

His saying: ﴿Then He turned to him in forgiveness﴾, meaning He overlooked it for him. ﴿Indeed, He is the One who turns (in acceptance), the Most Merciful﴾: He accepts the repentance of His servants, ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 38–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We said: Go down from it, all of you﴾. He means these four (Adam, Eve, the serpent and Iblis). It was also said: the first descent was from the Garden to the lowest heaven, and the second descent (in the other copy: "the second") was from the lowest heaven to the earth. ﴿Then, when there comes to you﴾, meaning: if there comes to you, O children of Adam, ﴿from Me guidance﴾, meaning right guidance and an explanation of the law. It was also said: a Book and a Messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾. Ya'qub recited "fa-la khawfa" with a fatha in the whole Qur'an, while the others recited it with a damma and tanwin, "fa-la khawfun 'alayhim", concerning what they will face ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over what they left behind. It was also said: there shall be no fear for them in this world, nor shall they grieve in the Hereafter.

﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾ (meaning: deny) ﴿and deny Our signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾, not leaving it and not dying therein.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾, meaning O descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob). The meaning of Isra'il is "servant of God"; "Il" is God, exalted is He. It was also said: the chosen one of God. Abu Ja'far recited "Isra'il" without hamza. ﴿Remember﴾, meaning: preserve (in memory). Remembrance may be in the heart and may be by the tongue. It was also said: by it is meant gratitude, and it is expressed with the word "remembrance" because in gratitude there is remembrance and in ingratitude there is forgetfulness. Al-Hasan said: remembering a blessing is being grateful for it. ﴿My blessing﴾, meaning: My blessings. Its form is singular but its meaning is plural, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ (14:34). ﴿Which I bestowed upon you﴾, meaning upon your forefathers and ancestors. Qatadah said: these are the blessings specific to the Children of Israel: the splitting of the sea and their deliverance from Pharaoh by his drowning, the shading of the clouds over them in the wilderness, the sending down of manna and quails, and the sending down of the Torah, among many blessings that cannot be counted. Others said: these are all the blessings God, mighty and majestic, has bestowed upon His servants. ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾, meaning: by complying with My command, ﴿I will fulfil your covenant﴾, by acceptance and reward.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: by this covenant is meant what is mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿And God had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from them twelve chieftains... He said: I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾ (5:12). This is His saying "I will fulfil your covenant." Al-Hasan said it is His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mountain: take what We have given you with strength﴾ (2:63), which is the law of the Torah. Muqatil said it is His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: you shall not worship except God﴾ (2:83). Al-Kalbi said: God made a covenant with the Children of Israel through Musa: "I will raise up from the children of Isma'il an unlettered Prophet; whoever follows him and believes in the light that he brings, I will forgive his sin, admit him to Paradise, and give him two rewards." This is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those given the Book: you shall make it clear to the people﴾ (3:187), meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And fear Me alone﴾, meaning: fear Me in breaking the covenant. Ya'qub retained the yas (ya' letters) that are omitted in the orthography, such as "fa-rhabuni", "fa-ttaquni", and "akhshawni", while the others omit them according to the orthography.

﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, meaning: agreeing with what is with you, namely the Torah, in monotheism, prophethood, reports, and the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions from the scholars and leaders of the Jews. ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, meaning in the Qur'an, intending among the People of the Book, because the Quraysh disbelieved before the Jews in Makkah. The meaning is: do not be the first to reject the Qur'an, lest the Jews follow you in that, and so you bear your sins and their sins. ﴿And do not exchange My signs﴾, meaning: do not substitute ﴿My signs﴾, by explaining the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿for a small price﴾, meaning a meagre worldly gain. This was because the leaders and scholars of the Jews had sources of income which they obtained from their common people and ignorant ones, who gave them each year a fixed portion of their crops, livestock and money. They feared that if they explained the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and followed him, those sources of income would be lost to them. So they altered his description and concealed his name, preferring the world to the Hereafter. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾, meaning: fear Me.

﴿And do not mix truth with falsehood﴾, meaning: do not confuse. It is said: "labisa al-thawb yalbasu lubsan" (he wore the garment), and "labisa 'alayhi al-amr yalbisu labsan" (the matter confused him), meaning he mixed it up. The meaning is: do not mix the truth that I have revealed to you concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the falsehood that you write with your own hands by altering the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Most scholars hold that the intended meaning is: do not clothe Islam in Judaism and Christianity. [Qatadah said: do not clothe Judaism and Christianity in Islam while you know that the religion of God is Islam, and that Judaism and Christianity are innovations that are not from God. See: al-Durr al-Manthur 1/155, and read the study entitled "Inna al-din 'inda Allah al-Islam" in issue (16) of the journal al-Buhuth al-Islamiyyah, published by the General Presidency of Scientific Research Administrations, Iftaa, Call and Guidance, Riyadh.]

Muqatil said: the Jews acknowledged some of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed some of it, so that they would be believed in that. He said: "do not mix the truth that you acknowledge with falsehood", meaning with what you conceal. So the truth is their statement (of what they acknowledge), and the falsehood is their concealment. "And do not conceal the truth", meaning do not hide it, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿While you know﴾ that he is a prophet sent (by God).

﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning the five prayers at their proper times and limits, ﴿and give zakat﴾, meaning: pay the obligatory zakat on your wealth. Zakat is derived from "zaka al-zar'u", when the crop grew and increased; it was also said it derives from "tazakka", meaning to purify oneself. Both meanings exist in zakat, since it contains purification and the growth of wealth. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, meaning: pray with those who pray, Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions. It was expressed with the word "bowing" because it is a pillar of the prayer, and because the prayer of the Jews had no bowing in it; it is as if He said: pray a prayer that includes bowing. It was said: its repetition after His saying "and establish prayer" is for this reason, meaning: pray with those whose prayer includes bowing. The first is general in regard to everyone, and this is specific to particular people. It was also said: this is an exhortation to establish prayer in congregation, as if He said to them: pray with the worshippers who preceded you in faith.

It was also said: the first descent was from the Garden to the lowest heaven, and the second descent (in the other copy: "the second") was from the lowest heaven to the earth. ﴿Then, when there comes to you﴾, meaning: if there comes to you, O children of Adam, ﴿from Me guidance﴾, meaning right guidance and an explanation of the law. It was also said: a Book and a Messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾. Ya'qub recited "fa-la khawfa" with a fatha in the whole Qur'an, while the others recited it with a damma and tanwin, "fa-la khawfun 'alayhim", concerning what they will face ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over what they left behind. It was also said: there shall be no fear for them in this world, nor shall they grieve in the Hereafter.

﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾ (meaning: deny) ﴿and deny Our signs﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾, not leaving it and not dying therein.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾, meaning O descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob). The meaning of Isra'il is "servant of God"; "Il" is God, exalted is He. It was also said: the chosen one of God. Abu Ja'far recited "Isra'il" without hamza. ﴿Remember﴾, meaning: preserve (in memory). Remembrance may be in the heart and may be by the tongue. It was also said: by it is meant gratitude, and it is expressed with the word "remembrance" because in gratitude there is remembrance and in ingratitude there is forgetfulness. Al-Hasan said: remembering a blessing is being grateful for it. ﴿My blessing﴾, meaning: My blessings. Its form is singular but its meaning is plural, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you should count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ (14:34). ﴿Which I bestowed upon you﴾, meaning upon your forefathers and ancestors. Qatadah said: these are the blessings specific to the Children of Israel: the splitting of the sea and their deliverance from Pharaoh by his drowning, the shading of the clouds over them in the wilderness, the sending down of manna and quails, and the sending down of the Torah, among many blessings that cannot be counted. Others said: these are all the blessings God, mighty and majestic, has bestowed upon His servants. ﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾, meaning: by complying with My command, ﴿I will fulfil your covenant﴾, by acceptance and reward.

Qatadah and Mujahid said: by this covenant is meant what is mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿And God had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised from them twelve chieftains... He said: I will surely remove from you your misdeeds﴾ (5:12). This is His saying "I will fulfil your covenant." Al-Hasan said it is His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mountain: take what We have given you with strength﴾ (2:63), which is the law of the Torah. Muqatil said it is His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: you shall not worship except God﴾ (2:83). Al-Kalbi said: God made a covenant with the Children of Israel through Musa: "I will raise up from the children of Isma'il an unlettered Prophet; whoever follows him and believes in the light that he brings, I will forgive his sin, admit him to Paradise, and give him two rewards." This is His saying: ﴿And when God took the covenant of those given the Book: you shall make it clear to the people﴾ (3:187), meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And fear Me alone﴾, meaning: fear Me in breaking the covenant. Ya'qub retained the yas (ya' letters) that are omitted in the orthography, such as "fa-rhabuni", "fa-ttaquni", and "akhshawni", while the others omit them according to the orthography.

﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, meaning: agreeing with what is with you, namely the Torah, in monotheism, prophethood, reports, and the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions from the scholars and leaders of the Jews. ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾, meaning in the Qur'an, intending among the People of the Book, because the Quraysh disbelieved before the Jews in Makkah. The meaning is: do not be the first to reject the Qur'an, lest the Jews follow you in that, and so you bear your sins and their sins. ﴿And do not exchange My signs﴾, meaning: do not substitute ﴿My signs﴾, by explaining the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿for a small price﴾, meaning a meagre worldly gain. This was because the leaders and scholars of the Jews had sources of income which they obtained from their common people and ignorant ones, who gave them each year a fixed portion of their crops, livestock and money. They feared that if they explained the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and followed him, those sources of income would be lost to them. So they altered his description and concealed his name, preferring the world to the Hereafter. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾, meaning: fear Me.

﴿And do not mix truth with falsehood﴾, meaning: do not confuse. It is said: "labisa al-thawb yalbasu lubsan" (he wore the garment), and "labisa 'alayhi al-amr yalbisu labsan" (the matter confused him), meaning he mixed it up. The meaning is: do not mix the truth that I have revealed to you concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the falsehood that you write with your own hands by altering the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Most scholars hold that the intended meaning is: do not clothe Islam in Judaism and Christianity. [Qatadah said: do not clothe Judaism and Christianity in Islam while you know that the religion of God is Islam, and that Judaism and Christianity are innovations that are not from God. See: al-Durr al-Manthur 1/155, and read the study entitled "Inna al-din 'inda Allah al-Islam" in issue (16) of the journal al-Buhuth al-Islamiyyah, published by the General Presidency of Scientific Research Administrations, Iftaa, Call and Guidance, Riyadh.]

Muqatil said: the Jews acknowledged some of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed some of it, so that they would be believed in that. He said: "do not mix the truth that you acknowledge with falsehood", meaning with what you conceal. So the truth is their statement (of what they acknowledge), and the falsehood is their concealment. "And do not conceal the truth", meaning do not hide it, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿While you know﴾ that he is a prophet sent (by God).

﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning the five prayers at their proper times and limits, ﴿and give zakat﴾, meaning: pay the obligatory zakat on your wealth. Zakat is derived from "zaka al-zar'u", when the crop grew and increased; it was also said it derives from "tazakka", meaning to purify oneself. Both meanings exist in zakat, since it contains purification and the growth of wealth. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, meaning: pray with those who pray, Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions. It was expressed with the word "bowing" because it is a pillar of the prayer, and because the prayer of the Jews had no bowing in it; it is as if He said: pray a prayer that includes bowing. It was said: its repetition after His saying "and establish prayer" is for this reason, meaning: pray with those whose prayer includes bowing. The first is general in regard to everyone, and this is specific to particular people. It was also said: this is an exhortation to establish prayer in congregation, as if He said to them: pray with the worshippers who preceded you in faith.

Most scholars hold that the intended meaning is: do not clothe Islam in Judaism and Christianity. [Qatadah said: do not clothe Judaism and Christianity in Islam while you know that the religion of God is Islam, and that Judaism and Christianity are innovations that are not from God. See: al-Durr al-Manthur 1/155, and read the study entitled "Inna al-din 'inda Allah al-Islam" in issue (16) of the journal al-Buhuth al-Islamiyyah, published by the General Presidency of Scientific Research Administrations, Iftaa, Call and Guidance, Riyadh.]

Muqatil said: the Jews acknowledged some of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed some of it, so that they would be believed in that. He said: "do not mix the truth that you acknowledge with falsehood", meaning with what you conceal. So the truth is their statement (of what they acknowledge), and the falsehood is their concealment. "And do not conceal the truth", meaning do not hide it, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿While you know﴾ that he is a prophet sent (by God).

﴿And establish prayer﴾, meaning the five prayers at their proper times and limits, ﴿and give zakat﴾, meaning: pay the obligatory zakat on your wealth. Zakat is derived from "zaka al-zar'u", when the crop grew and increased; it was also said it derives from "tazakka", meaning to purify oneself. Both meanings exist in zakat, since it contains purification and the growth of wealth. ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, meaning: pray with those who pray, Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions. It was expressed with the word "bowing" because it is a pillar of the prayer, and because the prayer of the Jews had no bowing in it; it is as if He said: pray a prayer that includes bowing. It was said: its repetition after His saying "and establish prayer" is for this reason, meaning: pray with those whose prayer includes bowing. The first is general in regard to everyone, and this is specific to particular people. It was also said: this is an exhortation to establish prayer in congregation, as if He said to them: pray with the worshippers who preceded you in faith.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 2, verses 44–48:**

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾ That is, obedience. It was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews. A man among them would say to his relative and ally from among the Muslims, when he asked him about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ): "Hold fast to his religion, for his affair is true and his word is truthful." It is also said: this is an address to their rabbis, when they commanded their followers to adhere to the Torah, and then they opposed it and altered the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And you forget yourselves﴾ that is, you leave yourselves, so you do not follow him. ﴿while you recite the Scripture﴾ you read the Torah, in which is his description and attributes. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ [that it is true, so that you would follow him?]

The word "ʿaql" (intellect, reason) is derived from ʿiqal (the hobble) of the animal, which is what is tied around the knee of a camel to prevent it from straying. Likewise, the intellect prevents its possessor from disbelief and denial.

Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Salihi informed us: Abu ʿAmr Bakr ibn Muhammad al-Muzani informed us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, grandson of al-ʿAbbas ibn Hamzah, informed us: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali informed us: ʿAffan informed us: Hammad ibn Salamah informed us: ʿAli ibn Zayd informed us, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw men whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. I said: 'Who are these, O Jibril?' He said: 'These are preachers from your Ummah who enjoined righteousness upon the people and forgot themselves, while they recited the Book.'" [[Narrated by Ahmad from Anas ibn Malik: 3/120, 231, and 239. Also Ibn Hibban, no. (35) from Mawarid al-Zaman, and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 14/353, where he said: "This is a hasan hadith." In its chain is ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Jadʿan, who is weak (al-Taqrib: 2/37; Mizan al-Iʿtidal: 3/128), but the rest of its narrators are trustworthy. Ibn Hibban narrated it through another path that is not objectionable, so the hadith is strengthened by it. Al-Wahidi also narrated it in al-Tafsir al-Wasit: 1/96, with slight variation, from Anas as well.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Maylahi [folio 10b] informed us: Ahmad ʿAbd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah informed us: Sufyan informed us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Wa'il, who said: Usamah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out in the Fire (that is, his bowels will be cut), and he will go around as a donkey goes around its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is your condition? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good but I did not do it myself, and I used to forbid you from evil but I did it myself.'" And Shuʿbah said, from al-Aʿmash: "He will grind therein as the donkey grinds with its millstone." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter on the description of the Fire and that it is created: 6/331. And Muslim in al-Zuhd, chapter on the punishment of one who commands good but does not do it, and forbids evil but does it, no. (2989), 4/2290–2291. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 14/352.]]

﴿And seek help﴾ against what confronts you of various kinds of trials. It is also said: in seeking the Hereafter. ﴿through patience and prayer﴾; he means restraining the self from sins. It is also said: he means patience in performing the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: "Patience" is fasting, and for this reason the month of Ramadan was called "the month of patience," because fasting makes one averse to the world, and prayer makes one desirous of the Hereafter. It is also said: the "wa" (and) is in the sense of "ʿala" (upon), meaning: seek help through patience upon the prayer, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it﴾ (Ta-Ha: 132). ﴿And indeed it﴾ — it does not say "and indeed they both" — returns the pronoun to each of them individually, meaning: indeed each of these two qualities. Just as He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾ (al-Kahf: 33), meaning each one of them. It is also said: the meaning is: ﴿seek help through patience﴾ and indeed it is heavy, and through prayer and indeed it is heavy, so one of them was omitted for brevity. Al-Mu'arrij [[Mu'arrij al-Sadusi: Mu'arrij ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Harith of the Banu Sadus ibn Shaybān, Abu Fayd, a scholar of the Arabic language and genealogies, from the eminent companions of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, from the people of Basra. He had contact with the ʿAbbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and travelled with him to Khurasan, residing for a time in Marw and then moving to Nishapur. Among his works: Jamahir al-Qaba'il, Hadhf Nasab Quraysh, Gharib al-Qur'an, Kitab al-Amthal, and al-Maʿani (al-Aʿlam: 7/318).]] said: he returned the pronoun to the prayer, because it is more general, like His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 34), where the pronoun returns to the silver, because it is more general. It is also said: he returned the pronoun to the prayer because patience is included within it. Just as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 62), and He did not say "that they should please them both," because the Messenger's pleasure is included within the pleasure of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: he returned the pronoun to the act of seeking help. ﴿It is indeed heavy﴾, that is: it is burdensome, ﴿except for the humble﴾.

That is: the believers. Al-Hasan said: "the fearful." It is also said: "the obedient." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "the humble." The origin of khushu' (humility) is stillness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾ (Ta-Ha: 108). So the one who is khashi' is still and calm toward the obedience of Allah the Exalted.

﴿Those who are certain﴾ [who are sure] that they will be resurrected, that they will be called to account, and that they will return to Allah the Exalted; that is, they affirm the resurrection, and they made their return after death to the gathering place a return to Him. [[Omitted from B.]]

The word zann (assumption, supposition) is one of the words with opposite meanings; it may mean doubt, certainty, or hope, just as raja' (hope) may mean fear, hope, or security. ﴿That they will meet their Lord﴾ — seeing their Lord in the Hereafter, which is the sight of Allah the Exalted. It is also said: what is meant by "meeting" is arriving at Him. ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾, so He will recompense them for their deeds.

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾, that is, the worlds of your time. Although this preference was with regard to the forefathers, it brings honor to the descendants as well.

﴿And fear a Day﴾, and fear the punishment of a Day ﴿on which no soul will avail another soul at all﴾, that is, no soul will settle for another soul any right that is due to it. It is also said: it will not suffice; it is also said: it will not suffice for any of the hardships. ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub read it with a "ta'" because the word shafa'ah (intercession) is feminine. The rest read it with a "ya'" because shafʿ and shafaʿah have the same meaning, like waʿz and mawʿizah. So the masculine form is according to the meaning, and the feminine form is according to the wording, as in His saying: ﴿There has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ (Yunus: 57), and He said in another place: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 275). That is: no intercession will be accepted from it if it is a disbeliever. ﴿Nor will ransom be taken from it﴾, that is, compensation; it is called ʿadl because it is like the one being ransomed. The word ʿadl means "equal." ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of Allah.

So the masculine form is according to the meaning, and the feminine form is according to the wording, as in His saying: ﴿There has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾ (Yunus: 57), and He said in another place: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ (al-Baqarah: 275). That is: no intercession will be accepted from it if it is a disbeliever. ﴿Nor will ransom be taken from it﴾, that is, compensation; it is called ʿadl because it is like the one being ransomed. The word ʿadl means "equal." ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾, that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of Allah.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 2, verses 44–48:**

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾ That is, obedience. It was revealed concerning the scholars of the Jews. A man among them would say to his relative and ally from among the Muslims, when he asked him about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ): "Hold fast to his religion, for his affair is true and his word is truthful." It is also said: this is an address to their rabbis, when they commanded their followers to adhere to the Torah, and then they opposed it and altered the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And you forget yourselves﴾ that is, you leave yourselves, so you do not follow him. ﴿while you recite the Scripture﴾ you read the Torah, in which is his description and attributes. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾ [that it is true, so that you would follow him?]

The word "ʿaql" (intellect, reason) is derived from ʿiqal (the hobble) of the animal, which is what is tied around the knee of a camel to prevent it from straying. Likewise, the intellect prevents its possessor from disbelief and denial.

Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Salihi informed us: Abu ʿAmr Bakr ibn Muhammad al-Muzani informed us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, grandson of al-ʿAbbas ibn Hamzah, informed us: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl al-Bajali informed us: ʿAffan informed us: Hammad ibn Salamah informed us: ʿAli ibn Zayd informed us, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw men whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. I said: 'Who are these, O Jibril?' He said: 'These are preachers from your Ummah who enjoined righteousness upon the people and forgot themselves, while they recited the Book.'" [[Narrated by Ahmad from Anas ibn Malik: 3/120, 231, and 239. Also Ibn Hibban, no. (35) from Mawarid al-Zaman, and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 14/353, where he said: "This is a hasan hadith." In its chain is ʿAli ibn Zayd ibn Jadʿan, who is weak (al-Taqrib: 2/37; Mizan al-Iʿtidal: 3/128), but the rest of its narrators are trustworthy. Ibn Hibban narrated it through another path that is not objectionable, so the hadith is strengthened by it. Al-Wahidi also narrated it in al-Tafsir al-Wasit: 1/96, with slight variation, from Anas as well.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Maylahi [folio 10b] informed us: Ahmad ʿAbd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah informed us: Sufyan informed us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Wa'il, who said: Usamah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown into the Fire, and his intestines will spill out in the Fire (that is, his bowels will be cut), and he will go around as a donkey goes around its millstone. The people of the Fire will gather around him and say: 'O so-and-so, what is your condition? Did you not used to command us to do good and forbid us from evil?' He will say: 'I used to command you to do good but I did not do it myself, and I used to forbid you from evil but I did it myself.'" And Shuʿbah said, from al-Aʿmash: "He will grind therein as the donkey grinds with its millstone." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter on the description of the Fire and that it is created: 6/331. And Muslim in al-Zuhd, chapter on the punishment of one who commands good but does not do it, and forbids evil but does it, no. (2989), 4/2290–2291. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 14/352.]]

﴿And seek help﴾ against what confronts you of various kinds of trials. It is also said: in seeking the Hereafter. ﴿through patience and prayer﴾; he means restraining the self from sins. It is also said: he means patience in performing the obligatory duties. Mujahid said: "Patience" is fasting, and for this reason the month of Ramadan was called "the month of patience," because fasting makes one averse to the world, and prayer makes one desirous of the Hereafter. It is also said: the "wa" (and) is in the sense of "ʿala" (upon), meaning: seek help through patience upon the prayer, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it﴾ (Ta-Ha: 132). ﴿And indeed it﴾ — it does not say "and indeed they both" — returns the pronoun to each of them individually, meaning: indeed each of these two qualities. Just as He said: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce﴾ (al-Kahf: 33), meaning each one of them. It is also said: the meaning is: ﴿seek help through patience﴾ and indeed it is heavy, and through prayer and indeed it is heavy, so one of them was omitted for brevity. Al-Mu'arrij [[Mu'arrij al-Sadusi: Mu'arrij ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Harith of the Banu Sadus ibn Shaybān, Abu Fayd, a scholar of the Arabic language and genealogies, from the eminent companions of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, from the people of Basra. He had contact with the ʿAbbasid caliph al-Ma'mun and travelled with him to Khurasan, residing for a time in Marw and then moving to Nishapur. Among his works: Jamahir al-Qaba'il, Hadhf Nasab Quraysh, Gharib al-Qur'an, Kitab al-Amthal, and al-Maʿani (al-Aʿlam: 7/318).]] said: he returned the pronoun to the prayer, because it is more general, like His saying: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 34), where the pronoun returns to the silver, because it is more general. It is also said: he returned the pronoun to the prayer because patience is included within it. Just as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 62), and He did not say "that they should please them both," because the Messenger's pleasure is included within the pleasure of Allah the Exalted.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: he returned the pronoun to the act of seeking help. ﴿It is indeed heavy﴾, that is: it is burdensome, ﴿except for the humble﴾.

That is: the believers. Al-Hasan said: "the fearful." It is also said: "the obedient." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "the humble." The origin of khushu' (humility) is stillness. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾ (Ta-Ha: 108). So the one who is khashi' is still and calm toward the obedience of Allah the Exalted.

﴿Those who are certain﴾ [who are sure] that they will be resurrected, that they will be called to account, and that they will return to Allah the Exalted; that is, they affirm the resurrection, and they made their return after death to the gathering place a return to Him. [[Omitted from B.]]

The word zann (assumption, supposition) is one of the words with opposite meanings; it may mean doubt, certainty, or hope, just as raja' (hope) may mean fear, hope, or security. ﴿That they will meet their Lord﴾ — seeing their Lord in the Hereafter, which is the sight of Allah the Exalted. It is also said: what is meant by "meeting" is arriving at Him. ﴿And that they will return to Him﴾, so He will recompense them for their deeds.

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾, that is, the worlds of your time. Although this preference was with regard to the forefathers, it brings honor to the descendants as well.

﴿And fear a Day﴾, and fear the punishment of a Day ﴿on which no soul will avail another soul at all﴾, that is, no soul will settle for another soul any right that is due to it. It is also said: it will not suffice; it is also said: it will not suffice for any of the hardships. ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾.
