**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 2, verses 170–171:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾. It is said that this is a new narrative (qissah mustani'ah), and the *ha'* and *mim* in *lahum* (to them) refer to an unmentioned party (kinayah 'an ghayr madhkur).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam. Rafi' ibn Kharijah and Malik ibn 'Awf said: "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon," meaning, what we found our fathers following. "They were better and more knowledgeable than us." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. [See Tafsir al-Tabari 3/305.]

It is also said that the verse is connected to what precedes it, and that it was revealed concerning the polytheist Arabs and the disbelievers of Quraysh. The *ha'* and *mim* refer to the words of Allah: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (andad)﴾ (2:165). ﴿They say, "Rather, we will follow what we found" [al-alfayna]﴾, meaning what we found, ﴿upon it our fathers﴾, [i.e., in] the worship of idols.

It is also said that its meaning is: "And when it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has sent down,' [regarding] the permitting of what they had forbidden for themselves of the tilth (al-harth) and the livestock (al-an'am), the bahirah and the sa'ibah." The *ha'* and *mim* refer to the people in the words of Allah: ﴿O mankind, eat﴾ (2:168). ﴿They say, "Rather, we will follow"﴾.

Al-Kisa'i recited *bal nattabi'u* with the assimilation (idgham) of the *lam* into the *nun*. Likewise, he assimilates the *lam* of *hal* and *bal* into *ta'*, *tha'*, *za'*, *sin*, *sad*, *ta'* and *za'* (ظ). Hamzah agreed with him in *ta'*, *tha'* and *sin*. ﴿What we found﴾ means what we found ﴿upon it our fathers﴾ in forbidding and permitting.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Even though their fathers﴾, meaning: how can they follow their fathers when their fathers ﴿did not understand anything﴾? The *waw* in *awa-law* (أَوَلَوْ) is the *waw* of conjunction, and it is also called the *waw* of wonder (wawu al-ta'ajjub). The interrogative alif (alif al-istifham) has entered upon it for rebuke. The meaning is: "Would they follow their fathers even though they were ignorant and did not understand anything?" Its wording is general but its meaning is specific: they did not understand anything of the matters of religion, because they understood the affairs of this world. ﴿And were not guided﴾.

Then Allah struck a parable, and He, great is His remembrance, said:

﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calls and cries﴾. *Al-na'iq* and *al-na'q* are the shouting of the shepherd to the sheep. The meaning is: your likeness, O Muhammad, and the likeness of the disbelievers in their admonition and their invitation to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is like the likeness of the shepherd who shouts to the sheep. It is also said: the likeness of the preacher of the disbelievers and their caller with them is like the shepherd shouting to the sheep, while they hear nothing ﴿but a call﴾, meaning a sound, ﴿and a cry﴾. He attributed the parable to those who disbelieve because the context indicates it, as in the words of Allah: ﴿And ask the town﴾ (12:82). The meaning is: just as the beasts hear the voice of the shepherd but do not understand or comprehend what is said to them, so the disbeliever gains nothing from your admonition; he only hears your voice.

It is also said: its meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their lack of intellect and their failure to understand Allah and His Messenger, is like the likeness of the one addressed among the beasts, who grasps nothing of the command and the prohibition except the sound. Thus the meaning falls on the one addressed, and the speech is directed away from the one shouting. This is common in Arabic speech, where they do this and accept such speech to clarify the meaning among themselves. They say: "So-and-so fears you like the fear of the lion," meaning like his fear of the lion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, its keys would burden a company of strong men﴾ (28:76), whereas it is actually the company that is burdened by the keys.

It is also said: its meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in calling upon idols, which neither understand nor comprehend, is like the likeness of one who shouts at sheep, so nothing benefits from his shouting except that he is occupied with calling and crying out. Likewise, the disbeliever has from calling upon the gods and worshipping them nothing but toil and affliction, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call; and even if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ (35:14).

It is also said that the meaning of the verse is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in calling upon idols is like the likeness of one who shouts in the hollows of the mountains and hears a sound called *al-sada* (echo), from which he understands nothing. So the meaning of the verse is: like one who shouts at what hears nothing from him except calling and crying out.

﴿Deaf﴾. The Arabs say of one who neither hears nor understands: "As if he were deaf." ﴿Dumb﴾ concerning good, they do not speak it. ﴿Blind﴾ to guidance, they do not see it. ﴿So they do not understand.﴾

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 172–173:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things (ḥalālāt) that We have provided for you﴾

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us: Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Baghawi informed us: Ali ibn al-Ja'd informed us: Fudayl ibn Marzuq informed us, from Adi ibn Thabit, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O people, Allah is Good and accepts only what is good. Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers. He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously﴾ [23:51]. And He said: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾ [2:172]." Then he mentioned a man who travels far, disheveled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying, "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful. How then could his supplication be answered?" [Narrated by Muslim in az-Zakat, chapter: Accepting charity from lawful earnings, no. 1015, 2/703. The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah 8/7-8.]

﴿And give thanks to Allah﴾ for His blessings ﴿if you are indeed those who worship Him﴾. Then He explained the prohibited things, saying: [23/b]

﴿He has forbidden you only carrion (al-maytah)﴾. Abu Ja'far read al-maytah with a doubled ta' (shaddah) throughout the Qur'an, while the others double it only in some places. Al-maytah is anything whose slaughter (dhakah) was not accomplished from among what is slaughtered. ﴿And blood﴾: by this is meant flowing blood, as indicated by His saying: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [6:145]. The Sharia made an exception from carrion: fish and locusts, and from blood: the liver and the spleen, so it made these lawful.

Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib informed us: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm informed us: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us: al-Shafi'i informed us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam informed us, from his father, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. The two carrions are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are the liver and the spleen." [Narrated by Ibn Majah in al-At'imah, chapter on the liver and spleen, no. 3314, 2/1102, through the chain of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who is weak (al-Taqrib; Mizan al-I'tidal). Also by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad 2/97 from Ibn Umar; al-Shafi'i in al-Musnad 2/173, and the wording is his; al-Bayhaqi 1/254 as a mawquf report, then he said: "This chain is sound." Al-Daraqutni 4/272. al-Zayla'i in Nasb al-Rayah 4/202 attributed it to al-Shafi'i, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Hibban in ad-Du'afa', and Ibn Adi, who said: "It has another route." The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah 11/244. The hadith, and Allah knows best, is mawquf upon Ibn Umar, but it has the status of a marfu' report. See al-Albani's Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Sahihah, hadith no. 1118.]

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾: by this is meant all its parts, and it was expressed by "flesh" because that is its main part.

﴿And that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: that is, what was slaughtered for idols and tawaghit (false deities, rebellious powers). The root of al-ihlal is raising the voice. When they slaughtered for their gods they would raise their voices in mentioning them, and this practice became so established that every slaughterer was called a "muhill," even if he did not pronounce the name aloud. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ means what has had the name of other than Allah pronounced over it.

﴿So whoever is compelled﴾: with a kasrah on the nun and its counterparts, read by Asim and Hamzah. Abu Amr agreed with them except in the lam and the waw, as in ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman﴾ [17:110]. Ya'qub agreed except in the waw, and Ibn Amir agreed in the tanwin. All the others read it with a dammah. Whoever reads with a kasrah says: because the jazm (final vowel) is moved to a kasrah. Whoever reads with a dammah says: because of the dammah on the first letter of the verb, he transferred its vowel to the letter before it. Abu Ja'far read with a kasrah on the ta', and its meaning is: whoever is compelled to eat carrion, that is, is driven and forced to it.

﴿Not desiring﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it was said that it is in the accusative as an exception (istithna'). When you see that ghayr can occupy its position with "la" (not), it is a circumstantial clause; when it can occupy its position with "illa" (except), it is an exception.

﴿Nor transgressing (bagh wa la 'ad)﴾: the root of al-baghy is intending corruption, as one says: "the wound baghā" when it progresses toward corruption. The root of al-'udwan is injustice and exceeding the limit, as one says: "'adā 'alayhi 'adwan and 'udwanan" when he wronged him.

They differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿not desiring and not transgressing﴾. Some of them said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means: one who rebels against the ruler, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means: one who sins by his journey, by setting out to commit highway robbery or to cause corruption on earth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. They said: it is not permissible for one who sins by his journey to eat carrion when compelled to it, nor to take the concessions of the traveler until he repents. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, held this view, because permitting him to do so would be helping him in his corruption.

A group held that "al-baghy" and "al-'udwan" refer to the eating itself, and they differed over its details. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means you do not eat it without compulsion, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means you do not exceed for the sake of satiety. It was said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means not seeking it while finding other food, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means not exceeding what is limited for him, so he does not eat until he is satisfied, but eats from it only the amount of sustenance that keeps his life. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means one who deems it lawful, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means one who takes provision from it. It was said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means not going beyond the measure permitted to him, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means not falling short in what is permitted to him so that he leaves it. Masruq said: whoever is compelled to eat carrion, blood or the flesh of swine, and does not eat or drink until he dies, enters the Fire.

The scholars differed concerning the amount of carrion that is lawful for the one compelled to eat. Some of them said: it is the amount that keeps his soul from departing. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him [see Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas 1/156-166, Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-Arabi 1/55-57]. The other opinion is that he may eat until he is satisfied, and this is the view of Malik, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means one who separates from the community, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means one who innovates, opposing the Sunnah. He did not grant the innovator a concession to consume the prohibited thing in case of necessity.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾: that is, there is no blame upon him for eating it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward one who ate in a state of necessity, ﴿Merciful﴾ in that He granted His servants this concession.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 172–173:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things (ḥalālāt) that We have provided for you﴾

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us: Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Baghawi informed us: Ali ibn al-Ja'd informed us: Fudayl ibn Marzuq informed us, from Adi ibn Thabit, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O people, Allah is Good and accepts only what is good. Allah has commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers. He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously﴾ [23:51]. And He said: ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things that We have provided for you﴾ [2:172]." Then he mentioned a man who travels far, disheveled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying, "O Lord, O Lord," while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful. How then could his supplication be answered?" [Narrated by Muslim in az-Zakat, chapter: Accepting charity from lawful earnings, no. 1015, 2/703. The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah 8/7-8.]

﴿And give thanks to Allah﴾ for His blessings ﴿if you are indeed those who worship Him﴾. Then He explained the prohibited things, saying: [23/b]

﴿He has forbidden you only carrion (al-maytah)﴾. Abu Ja'far read al-maytah with a doubled ta' (shaddah) throughout the Qur'an, while the others double it only in some places. Al-maytah is anything whose slaughter (dhakah) was not accomplished from among what is slaughtered. ﴿And blood﴾: by this is meant flowing blood, as indicated by His saying: ﴿or blood poured forth﴾ [6:145]. The Sharia made an exception from carrion: fish and locusts, and from blood: the liver and the spleen, so it made these lawful.

Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib informed us: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm informed us: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us: al-Shafi'i informed us: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam informed us, from his father, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two carrions and two bloods have been made lawful for us. The two carrions are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are the liver and the spleen." [Narrated by Ibn Majah in al-At'imah, chapter on the liver and spleen, no. 3314, 2/1102, through the chain of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who is weak (al-Taqrib; Mizan al-I'tidal). Also by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad 2/97 from Ibn Umar; al-Shafi'i in al-Musnad 2/173, and the wording is his; al-Bayhaqi 1/254 as a mawquf report, then he said: "This chain is sound." Al-Daraqutni 4/272. al-Zayla'i in Nasb al-Rayah 4/202 attributed it to al-Shafi'i, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Hibban in ad-Du'afa', and Ibn Adi, who said: "It has another route." The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah 11/244. The hadith, and Allah knows best, is mawquf upon Ibn Umar, but it has the status of a marfu' report. See al-Albani's Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Sahihah, hadith no. 1118.]

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾: by this is meant all its parts, and it was expressed by "flesh" because that is its main part.

﴿And that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: that is, what was slaughtered for idols and tawaghit (false deities, rebellious powers). The root of al-ihlal is raising the voice. When they slaughtered for their gods they would raise their voices in mentioning them, and this practice became so established that every slaughterer was called a "muhill," even if he did not pronounce the name aloud. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: ﴿and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾ means what has had the name of other than Allah pronounced over it.

﴿So whoever is compelled﴾: with a kasrah on the nun and its counterparts, read by Asim and Hamzah. Abu Amr agreed with them except in the lam and the waw, as in ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon al-Rahman﴾ [17:110]. Ya'qub agreed except in the waw, and Ibn Amir agreed in the tanwin. All the others read it with a dammah. Whoever reads with a kasrah says: because the jazm (final vowel) is moved to a kasrah. Whoever reads with a dammah says: because of the dammah on the first letter of the verb, he transferred its vowel to the letter before it. Abu Ja'far read with a kasrah on the ta', and its meaning is: whoever is compelled to eat carrion, that is, is driven and forced to it.

﴿Not desiring﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and it was said that it is in the accusative as an exception (istithna'). When you see that ghayr can occupy its position with "la" (not), it is a circumstantial clause; when it can occupy its position with "illa" (except), it is an exception.

﴿Nor transgressing (bagh wa la 'ad)﴾: the root of al-baghy is intending corruption, as one says: "the wound baghā" when it progresses toward corruption. The root of al-'udwan is injustice and exceeding the limit, as one says: "'adā 'alayhi 'adwan and 'udwanan" when he wronged him.

They differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿not desiring and not transgressing﴾. Some of them said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means: one who rebels against the ruler, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means: one who sins by his journey, by setting out to commit highway robbery or to cause corruption on earth. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. They said: it is not permissible for one who sins by his journey to eat carrion when compelled to it, nor to take the concessions of the traveler until he repents. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, held this view, because permitting him to do so would be helping him in his corruption.

A group held that "al-baghy" and "al-'udwan" refer to the eating itself, and they differed over its details. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means you do not eat it without compulsion, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means you do not exceed for the sake of satiety. It was said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means not seeking it while finding other food, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means not exceeding what is limited for him, so he does not eat until he is satisfied, but eats from it only the amount of sustenance that keeps his life. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means one who deems it lawful, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means one who takes provision from it. It was said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means not going beyond the measure permitted to him, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means not falling short in what is permitted to him so that he leaves it. Masruq said: whoever is compelled to eat carrion, blood or the flesh of swine, and does not eat or drink until he dies, enters the Fire.

The scholars differed concerning the amount of carrion that is lawful for the one compelled to eat. Some of them said: it is the amount that keeps his soul from departing. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, and one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him [see Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas 1/156-166, Ahkam al-Qur'an by Ibn al-Arabi 1/55-57]. The other opinion is that he may eat until he is satisfied, and this is the view of Malik, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: ﴿not desiring﴾ means one who separates from the community, ﴿nor transgressing﴾ means one who innovates, opposing the Sunnah. He did not grant the innovator a concession to consume the prohibited thing in case of necessity.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾: that is, there is no blame upon him for eating it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward one who ate in a state of necessity, ﴿Merciful﴾ in that He granted His servants this concession.

Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book" (Qur'an 2:174).

It was revealed concerning the leaders and scholars of the Jews, who used to receive gifts and food from their common folk, and they hoped that the Prophet who was to be sent would be from among them. When Muhammad ﷺ was sent from among others, they feared the loss of their food and the end of their leadership. So they deliberately went to the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, changed it, and then brought it out to their people. When the common folk looked at the altered description, they found it contrary to the description of Muhammad ﷺ, so they did not follow him.

Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book" [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi with a weak chain from Ibn 'Abbas; see al-Durr al-Manthur fi al-Tafsir bi'l-Ma'thur by al-Suyuti 1/409.]] meaning the description of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood. "And exchange it" (i.e., the concealed matter) "for a small price" (i.e., a meager compensation), meaning the food they receive from their common folk. "They eat into their bellies nothing but Fire" (i.e., nothing but that which leads them to the Fire), and this is bribery, the unlawful, and the price of the religion. Since that leads them to the Fire, it is as if they had eaten Fire. It was also said that its meaning is that it turns into fire in their bellies. "Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection" (i.e., He will not speak to them with mercy or with anything that pleases them; He will only speak to them with rebuke). It was also said: He intends by this that He will be angry with them, as one says, "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so" when he is angry with him. "Nor will He purify them" (i.e., He will not cleanse them from the defilement of sins). "And for them is a painful punishment."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 175–177:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. How patient they are over the Fire!﴾ Ata' and al-Suddi said: "ma" here is an interrogative, meaning: What is it that made them patient over the Fire? And what is it that makes them endure the Fire, to the point that they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood? Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "By Allah, they have no patience for it, but rather, how bold they are in doing the deeds that bring them closer to the Fire." Al-Kisa'i said: "How patient they are over the deeds of the people of the Fire," meaning: how persistent they are in them.

﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth.﴾ That is, that punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth, so they denied it and disbelieved in it. In this case, "dhalika" is in the nominative position (i'rab: raf', grammatical case). Some of them said its position is in the accusative (nasb), meaning: "We did that to them because Allah..." i.e., "because Allah sent down the Book with the truth, so they differed concerning it." It was also said that its meaning is: that (i.e., their deed), which is their disbelief, their disputing, and their audacity against Allah, is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth. This is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has sealed their hearts﴾ (2:6–7). And ﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾ (they believe in part of it and disbelieve in part of it) ﴿are in extreme dissension﴾, that is, in far-reaching opposition and error.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west.﴾ Hamzah and Hafs read "laysa al-birra" with a fatha on the ra' (nasb), while the rest read it with a damma (raf'). Whoever reads it with raf' makes ﴿al-birr﴾ the subject of "laysa" (ism laysa), and its predicate is His statement "an tawallu" (that you turn), its estimated form being: "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces..." like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Their argument was only that they said, "Bring..."﴾ (45:25). Al-birr is every act of goodness that leads its doer to Paradise. The commentators differed about who is addressed by this verse. One group said it refers to the Jews and the Christians, because the Jews used to pray facing toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the west, and the Christians facing east, and each group claimed that righteousness lay in that. So Allah informed them that righteousness is other than their religion and their deeds, but rather it is what He explains in this verse. Qatadah and Muqatil ibn Hayyan held this view. Others said it refers to the believers, because at the beginning of Islam, before the obligations were revealed, a man who pronounced the two testimonies and prayed toward whatever direction, and died in that state, was granted Paradise.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, the obligations were revealed, the limits were set, and the qiblah was turned toward the Ka'bah, Allah sent down this verse, saying: ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [See: al-Tabari: 3/337–338; al-Wahidi: 1/250], that is, the whole of it is not that you pray toward the east or the west and do not act otherwise. ﴿But righteousness is﴾ what is mentioned in this verse. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata' and al-Dahhak held this view.

﴿But righteousness is﴾: Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "wa-lakinna" with a light nun, and "al-birru" with a damma. The rest read it with a doubled nun and "al-birra" with a fatha.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿one who believes in Allah﴾: "man" here is the ism (subject) of the predicate "al-birr," which is a verb, and it is not said that "al-birr Zayd" (it is correct). They differed about its explanation. It was said: when "man" occupies the position of a verbal noun (masdar), he made it the predicate of "al-birr," as if he said: "But righteousness is belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb. Al-Farra' recited: "By your life, it is not youths that the beards grow, but rather, youths are every generous young man." So he made the growing of beards the predicate of "youth." It was also said there is an ellipsis, meaning: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah," so mention of the first made the second unnecessary, like the saying: "Generosity is Hatim" (meaning: generosity is the generosity of Hatim). It was also said its meaning is: "But the one possessing righteousness is one who believes in Allah," like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They are of different ranks with Allah﴾ (3:163), meaning: possessing ranks. It was also said its meaning is: "But the righteous one is one who believes in Allah," like His statement: ﴿And the good end is for piety﴾ (20:132), meaning: for the pious. The meaning of "birr" here is belief and piety.

﴿and the Last Day, and the angels, and the Book﴾ meaning the revealed books, ﴿and the prophets﴾ all of them, ﴿and gives wealth﴾ gives away wealth, ﴿in spite of love for it﴾. The commentators differed about this pronoun. Most of the people of tafsir said it refers back to the wealth, meaning: he gives wealth while he is healthy and loves wealth. Ibn Mas'ud said: "That you give it while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for riches and fearing poverty."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliheyi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Musa ibn Isma'il informed us: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us: Umarah ibn al-Qa'qa' narrated to us: Abu Zur'ah informed us: Abu Hurayrah said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, which charity is greatest in reward?" He said: "That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, fearing poverty and hoping for riches, and do not delay until, when it reaches the throat, you say, 'To so-and-so such-and-such, and to so-and-so such-and-such,' when it already belonged to so-and-so." [Related by al-Bukhari: in Zakat, chapter: the virtue of the charity of the healthy and miserly person: 3/284–285, and in Wasaya (bequests). Muslim: in Zakat, chapter: explaining that the best charity is the charity of the healthy and miserly, no. 1032, 2/716. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 6/172–173.]

It was also said that the pronoun refers back to Allah, exalted and mighty is He, meaning: out of love for Allah, exalted is He.

﴿to relatives﴾: the people of kinship.

Abu Uthman Sa'id ibn Isma'il al-Dabbi informed us: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Jabbar ibn Muhammad al-Jarrahi informed us: Abu al-Abbas al-Mahbubi informed us: Abu Isa al-Tirmidhi informed us: Qutaybah informed us: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah related to us from Asim al-Ahwal, from Hafsah bint Sirin, from al-Rabab, from her paternal uncle Salman ibn Amir, reaching the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Charity to the poor is one charity, and to a relative it is two: charity and maintaining the ties of kinship." [Related by al-Tirmidhi: in Zakat, chapter on what has come concerning charity to relatives: 3/324, and he said: "a hasan hadith." Al-Nasa'i: in Zakat, chapter: charity to relatives: 5/92. Ibn Majah: in Zakat, chapter: the virtue of charity: (1844) 1/591. Al-Darimi: in Zakat, chapter: charity to relatives: 1/397. Ahmad: 4/18, 214, from Salman ibn Amir. Ibn Hibban: in Mawarid al-Zam'an p. 112. Al-Hakim: 1/407, and he said: "sahih in its chain," and al-Dhahabi agreed (see Majma' al-Zawa'id: 3/117). And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 6/192. (Its narrators are trustworthy except al-Rabab, mother of al-Ra'ih. The hafiz said in al-Taqrib: "acceptable." And in al-Mizan: "al-Rabab bint Sulay' from her paternal uncle Salman ibn Amir is not known except through the narration of Hafsah bint Sirin from her.")]

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and the orphans, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾. Mujahid said: it means the traveler cut off from his family who passes by you; the traveler is called "ibn al-sabil" (son of the road) because of his staying on the road. It was also said: it refers to the guest who descends upon a person. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest." [Related by al-Bukhari: in Riqaq, chapter: guarding the tongue: 11/308, and in Nikah and Adab. Muslim: in Iman, chapter: urging the honoring of the neighbor, no. 47, 1/68. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 14/212.] ﴿and the beggars﴾: meaning those who ask.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Abu Bujayd al-Ansari, who is Abd al-Rahman ibn Bujayd, from his grandmother, who is Umm Bujayd, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Turn away the beggar, even with a burnt hoof." In another narration, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If you find nothing but a burnt hoof, then give it to him." [Related by Abu Dawud: in Zakat, chapter: the right of the beggar: 2/251. Al-Tirmidhi: in Zakat, chapter: what has come concerning the right of the beggar: 3/332, and he said: "hasan sahih." Al-Nasa'i: in Zakat, chapter: explaining the miskin: 5/86. Al-Hakim authenticated it: 1/417, and al-Dhahabi agreed. Ibn Hibban: 6/383 with the wording "turn away the beggar, even with a hoof." Ahmad: 6/382 with a strong chain. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 6/175.]

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and for the captives﴾, meaning those in bondage. Most of the mufassirun said this, and it was said: freeing a soul and releasing a neck, and it was also said: ransoming prisoners of war. ﴿and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾: and gives zakat. ﴿And those who fulfill their covenant﴾ between them and Allah, exalted and mighty is He, and between them and the people, ﴿when they make a pledge﴾, meaning when they promise, they fulfill it; when they swear oaths and make vows, they fulfill them; when they make a covenant, they keep it; when they speak, they tell the truth; and when they are entrusted, they return the trust. They differed about the case of "al-muwfun" (those who fulfill). It was said it is in the nominative as a coordination with the predicate, meaning: "But righteousness is that of the believers and those who fulfill their covenant." It was also said its estimated form is: "and they are those who fulfill," as if he enumerated categories and then said: "they are these, and those who fulfill..." It was also said it is nominative as a beginning and predicate, meaning: "and they are those who fulfill." Then He said: ﴿and the patient﴾. There are four opinions about its case:

Abu Ubaydah said: it is accusative because of the lengthening of the speech; it is among the habits of the Arabs to change the i'rab (grammatical inflection) when the speech and the sequence are lengthened. A similar case is in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ (4:162) and ﴿the Sabians and the Christians﴾ (5:69). It was also said its meaning is "I mean the patient." It was also said its accusative is a coordination with His statement "dhawi al-qurba" (relatives), meaning: "and gives to the patient."

Al-Khalil said: it is accusative by way of praise. The Arabs put speech in the accusative for praise and blame, as though they intend to single out the one praised or blamed, so they do not place it after the beginning of the speech, but put it in the accusative. Praise is like His statement: ﴿and those who establish prayer﴾ (4:162). Blame is like His statement: ﴿cursed, wherever they are found﴾ (33:61).

His statement: ﴿in the time of misfortune﴾, that is, hardship and poverty, ﴿and adversity﴾, illness and disability, ﴿and in the time of battle﴾, that is, fighting and war.

Al-Mutahhar ibn Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Farisi informed us: Abu Dhar Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Salihani informed us: Abu Muhammad Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Hibban informed us: Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Baghawi informed us: Ali ibn al-Ja'd informed us: Zuhayr related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Harithah ibn Mudarrib, from Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When the fighting grew fierce and the two sides met, we took refuge with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and no one was closer to the enemy than he was." [Related by Muslim in Jihad and Siyar, chapter: on the battle of Hunayn, from al-Bara', 3/1776. Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak: 2/143 with the wording: "when it grew hot."] That is, when the war became intense. ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾ in their faith, ﴿and those are the God-fearing﴾.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. How patient they are over the Fire!﴾ Ata' and al-Suddi said: "ma" here is an interrogative, meaning: What is it that made them patient over the Fire? And what is it that makes them endure the Fire, to the point that they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood? Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "By Allah, they have no patience for it, but rather, how bold they are in doing the deeds that bring them closer to the Fire." Al-Kisa'i said: "How patient they are over the deeds of the people of the Fire," meaning: how persistent they are in them.

﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth.﴾ That is, that punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with the truth, so they denied it and disbelieved in it. And ﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾ (they believe in part of it and disbelieve in part of it) ﴿are in extreme dissension﴾, that is, in far-reaching opposition and error.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west.﴾ Hamzah and Hafs read "laysa al-birra" with a fatha on the ra' (nasb), while the rest read it with a damma (raf'). Whoever reads it with raf' makes ﴿al-birr﴾ the subject of "laysa" (ism laysa), and its predicate is His statement "an tawallu" (that you turn), its estimated form being: "It is not righteousness that you turn your faces..." like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Their argument was only that they said, "Bring..."﴾ (45:25). Al-birr is every act of goodness that leads its doer to Paradise. The commentators differed about who is addressed by this verse. One group said it refers to the Jews and the Christians, because the Jews used to pray facing toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the west, and the Christians facing east, and each group claimed that righteousness lay in that. So Allah informed them that righteousness is other than their religion and their deeds, but rather it is what He explains in this verse. Qatadah and Muqatil ibn Hayyan held this view. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated, the obligations were revealed, the limits were set, and the qiblah was turned toward the Ka'bah, Allah sent down this verse, saying: ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ [See: al-Tabari: 3/337–338; al-Wahidi: 1/250], that is, the whole of it is not that you pray toward the east or the west and do not act otherwise. ﴿But righteousness is﴾ what is mentioned in this verse. ﴿But righteousness is﴾: Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "wa-lakinna" with a light nun, and "al-birru" with a damma. The rest read it with a doubled nun and "al-birra" with a fatha.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿one who believes in Allah﴾: "man" here is the ism (subject) of the predicate "al-birr," which is a verb, and it is not said that "al-birr Zayd" (it is correct). They differed about its explanation. It was said: when "man" occupies the position of a verbal noun (masdar), he made it the predicate of "al-birr," as if he said: "But righteousness is belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb. Al-Farra' recited: "By your life, it is not youths that the beards grow, but rather, youths are every generous young man." So he made the growing of beards the predicate of "youth." It was also said there is an ellipsis, meaning: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah," so mention of the first made the second unnecessary, like the saying: "Generosity is Hatim" (meaning: generosity is the generosity of Hatim). It was also said its meaning is: "But the one possessing righteousness is one who believes in Allah," like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They are of different ranks with Allah﴾ (3:163), meaning: possessing ranks. It was also said its meaning is: "But the righteous one is one who believes in Allah," like His statement: ﴿And the good end is for piety﴾ (20:132), meaning: for the pious. The meaning of "birr" here is belief and piety.

Ibn Mas'ud said: "That you give it while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for riches and fearing poverty."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 178:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation for the murdered﴾. Al-Sha'bi, al-Kalbi and Qatadah said: This verse was revealed concerning two of the tribes of the Arabs who fought one another in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam), shortly before Islam. Between them there were killings and wounds, for which some of them did not take retribution from others, until Islam came. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: It was between the Banu Qurayzah and the Nadir. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It was between the Aws and the Khazraj. They all said: One of the two tribes had superiority over the other in number and nobility, and they used to marry their women without bridal gifts (mahr). So they swore: "We will kill, for a slave of ours, their free man; for a woman of ours, their man; and for a man of ours, their two men." They also made their wounds double the wounds of those others. So they brought their matter to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah Exalted revealed this verse, commanding equality. So they agreed and submitted. [[See: al-Tabari: 3/359; al-Wasit of al-Wahidi: 1/254.]]

His saying ﴿prescribed for you is retaliation﴾, i.e., retaliation is enjoined upon you ﴿for the murdered﴾. Al-qisas (retaliation) is equality and parity in wounds and blood-money (diyah). Its root is from qassa al-athar (he traced the track), when one follows it; so the one who is done to follows what was done to him, and does the like of it.

Then He explained the parity, saying: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. The general ruling in this is that when the two lives are equal, among free Muslims, or among Muslim slaves, or among free non-Muslim covenanters (mu'ahidun), or among their slaves, then from each category the male is killed if he kills a male, and the female is killed if she kills a female or a male. A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever, nor a free person for a slave, nor a parent for a child, nor a Muslim for a dhimmi; but a dhimmi is killed for a Muslim, a slave for a free person, and a child for a parent. This is the view of most of the people of knowledge from the Companions and those after them.

We were informed by Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib, who said: We were informed by Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal, who said: We were informed by Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm, who said: We were informed by al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman, who said: al-Shafi'i informed us, who said: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah informed us, from Mutarrif, from al-Sha'bi, from Abu Juhayfah, who said: "I asked Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, 'Do you have anything from the Prophet ﷺ besides the Qur'an?' He said: 'No, by He who split the grain and created the soul, except that Allah gives a servant understanding in the Qur'an, and what is in this sheet.' I said: 'And what is in this sheet?' He said: 'The blood-money, the freeing of captives, and that a Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever.'" [[al-Bukhari: in Diyat, chapter: A Muslim is not killed for a disbeliever: 12/260. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 10/171.]] It is also related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Prescribed punishments are not carried out in the mosques, and a father is not retaliated against for his son." [[Related by Abu Dawud: in Hudud, chapter: On carrying out the hadd in the mosque: 6/292, from Hakim ibn Hizam, with the wording: (The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade retaliation in the mosque, reciting poetry in it, and carrying out prescribed punishments in it). Al-Mundhiri said: In its chain is Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Muhajir al-Sha'thi al-Nasri al-Dimashqi; more than one has deemed him trustworthy, while Abu Hatim al-Razi said: his hadith is written down but not used as evidence. Al-Tirmidhi: in Diyat, chapter: What has come concerning a man who kills his son, whether he is retaliated against or not: 4/656, and said: This is a hadith we do not know in this chain as marfu' except from the hadith of Isma'il ibn Muslim al-Makki, and Isma'il has been criticized by some scholars because of his memory. Also Ibn Majah in Diyat: 2/888; al-Darimi in Diyat: 2/190; al-Hakim authenticated it: 4/369; and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan: 8/39.]] Al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) held that a Muslim is killed for a dhimmi, and that a free person is killed for a slave. The hadith is a proof for those who did not require retaliation of a Muslim for killing a dhimmi. And a group is killed for one person. It is related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that Umar ibn al-Khattab killed seven or five men for one man whom they had killed by ambush, and he said: "If the people of San'a' had colluded against him, I would have killed them all for him." [[Related by al-Bukhari: in Diyat, chapter: If a group of people harm a man: 12/226-227. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 10/182-183.]]

Retaliation applies to limbs just as it applies to lives, except in one matter: a healthy sound person is killed for a sick, infirm one; and in limbs, if someone cuts off a paralysed hand or one lacking a finger, a complete healthy limb is not cut off in return. The people of opinion held that retaliation for limbs applies only between two free men or two free women, and does not apply between male and female, nor between slaves, nor between a free person and a slave. Others hold that a limb in retaliation is measured against a life.

We were informed by Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Malihi, who said: We were informed by Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi, who said: We were informed by Muhammad ibn Yusuf, who said: We were informed by Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who said: We were informed by Abd Allah ibn Munir that he heard Abd Allah ibn Bakr al-Sahmi, who said: We were informed by Humayd, from Anas ibn al-Nadr, that al-Rubayyi', his paternal aunt, broke the front tooth of a girl. They asked for pardon from her, but they refused. They offered the arsh [[al-Arsh: the blood-money for an injury.]], but they refused. So they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but they insisted only on retaliation. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered retaliation. Anas ibn al-Nadr said: "O Messenger of Allah, is the front tooth of al-Rubayyi' to be broken? No, by Him who sent you with the truth, her tooth shall not be broken!" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Anas, the Book of Allah is retaliation." So the people were content and pardoned. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the servants of Allah are those who, if they swear by Allah, He fulfils it for them." [[Related by al-Bukhari in Sulh, chapter: Settlement concerning blood-money: 5/306. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 10/166.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾, i.e., something is left for him and he is forgiven from what was obligatory upon him, which is retaliation for intentional killing, and he is content with the blood-money. This is the saying of most of the exegetes. They said: The pardon is that he accepts blood-money for intentional killing. His saying ﴿by his brother﴾, i.e., from the blood of his brother, and by "the brother" is meant the one slain. The two pronouns in His saying ﴿for him﴾ and ﴿his brother﴾ refer back to "whoever", who is the killer. His saying "something" is evidence that when some of the guardians pardon, the retaliation falls away, because some of the blood has been cancelled.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then the pursuit should be made in good manner﴾, i.e., the one claiming the blood-money must pursue it in a good manner, so he does not demand more than his right.

﴿And payment to him should be made with good conduct﴾, i.e., the one from whom it is demanded must pay the blood-money graciously, without procrastination. He commanded each of them to act well in what is theirs and what is due from them. The view of most scholars from the Companions and the Successors is that when the guardian of the blood pardons retaliation in return for blood-money, he may take the blood-money even if the killer does not agree. Others said: he has no blood-money except with the killer's consent; this is the view of al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i and the people of opinion. The proof of the first view is what we were informed by Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib, who said: We were informed by Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal, who said: We were informed by Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm, who said: We were informed by al-Rabi', who said: al-Shafi'i informed us, who said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Abi Fudayk informed us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Shurayh al-Ka'bi, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Then you, O Khuza'ah, have killed this victim from Hudhayl, and I, by Allah, am his guarantor for blood-money. Whoever kills a victim after him, his people have a choice between two things: if they wish, they may retaliate; and if they wish, they may take the blood-money." [[Related by al-Bukhari, at length, from Abu Hurayrah, in Diyat, chapter: Whoever has a slain person, he has the choice of the two options: 12/205; and al-Shafi'i in al-Musnad: 2/99.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾, i.e., that which I have mentioned, of pardoning retaliation and taking blood-money, is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. The reason is that retaliation for life and wounds was obligatory in the Torah upon the Jews, and they were not permitted to take blood-money; while in the law of the Christians there was blood-money and they had no retaliation. So Allah Exalted gave this community the choice between retaliation and pardon in exchange for blood-money, as an alleviation from Him and a mercy.

﴿Then whoever transgresses after that﴾, i.e., kills the killer after the pardon and acceptance of blood-money, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾, namely to be killed in retaliation. Ibn Jurayj said: his killing becomes mandatory, so that pardon is no longer accepted. There is also evidence in the verse that the killer does not become a disbeliever by killing, because Allah Exalted addressed him after the killing with the address of faith, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation﴾, and said at the end of the verse: ﴿But whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾, and by it He meant the brotherhood of faith; so the brotherhood between them was not severed by the killing.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 179:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in retaliation (qisas) there is life for you﴾, meaning survival. This is because the one intending to kill, if he knows that when he kills he will be killed, refrains from killing, so in it there is his survival and the survival of the one who intended to kill him. It is said in the proverb: "Killing puts an end to killing." It is also said in the proverb: "Killing is more effective in preventing killing." It is also said that the meaning of "life" is his being saved from retribution in the Hereafter, for when retaliation is carried out against him, he is brought to life in the Hereafter, and if retaliation is not carried out against him in this world, retaliation will be carried out against him in the Hereafter. ﴿O people of understanding, that you may be mindful of God﴾, meaning that you may refrain from killing for fear of retaliation (qawad).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 180:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is prescribed for you﴾, meaning it is enjoined upon you, ﴿when death approaches any one of you﴾, meaning there come to him the causes of death and its signs from illnesses and diseases, ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾, meaning property. Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾ (2:272). ﴿Bequest to parents and relatives﴾: bequest was an obligation at the beginning of Islam, for parents and relatives, upon whoever died leaving property. Then it was abrogated (naskh) by the verse of inheritance. [[See: al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh by Abu'l-Qasim ibn Salama, p. 16; Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas: 1/203-207.]]

Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Qadi informed us: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Mahmish al-Ziyadi informed us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Hafs al-Tajir informed us: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid informed us: al-Haytham ibn Jamil informed us: Hammad ibn Salama informed us, from Qatada, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Amr ibn Kharija, who said: I was holding the halter of the camel of the Prophet ﷺ when he said: "Indeed Allah has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." [[A sound hadith narrated by Abu Dawud: in Wasaya, chapter: on bequest to an heir: 4/150. And al-Tirmidhi: in Wasaya, chapter: what has come regarding "no bequest to an heir": 6/309, and he said it is a hasan sahih hadith. And al-Nasa'i: in Wasaya: 6/247. And Ibn Majah: in Wasaya: 2712 and 2714, 2/905-906. And Ahmad: 4/186 and 5/267, from Amr ibn Kharija, and part of a hadith from Abu Umama al-Bahili. And the author in Sharh al-Sunna: 5/288-289. And on the subject there are reports from Ibn Abbas, from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, from Jabir, from Zayd ibn Arqam, from Ali, from Kharija ibn Amr al-Jumahi, and from al-Bara'. See Nasb al-Raya 4/403, 405.]] Some scholars held that its obligation has been abrogated with regard to relatives who inherit, and that its obligation remains with regard to those who do not inherit from among parents and relatives. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Tawus, Qatada and al-Hasan. Tawus said: Whoever bequeaths to people he has named and leaves his needy close relatives, the bequest is taken from them and returned to his close relatives. Most scholars held that the obligation has been abrogated with regard to all, and that it remains a firm requirement with regard to those who do not inherit.

Abu'l-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Abu Tahir Ahmad ibn ... [sic] informed us: Tahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is not right for a Muslim man who has something to bequeath to spend two nights without his bequest being written and kept at his head." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Wasaya, chapter: the bequests and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ "a man's bequest should be written and kept near him": 5/355. And Muslim: in Wasiyya, no. (1627), 3/1249. And the author in Sharh al-Sunna: 5/277.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in accordance with what is reasonable﴾, meaning he bequeaths in a reasonable manner, does not exceed one-third, and does not bequeath to the wealthy while leaving the poor. Ibn Mas'ud said: the bequest is to the closest, then the closest, i.e., the most needy, then the most needy.

Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Hiri informed us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Ruhaym al-Shaybani informed us: Ahmad ibn Hazim ibn Abi Gharza [[In A: "Ibn Abi Awza"; the correction is from Sharh al-Sunna.]] informed us: Ubayd Allah ibn Musa and Abu Nu'aym informed us, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Sa'id ibn Ibrahim, from Amir ibn Sa'd, from Sa'd ibn Malik, who said: The Prophet ﷺ came to visit me, so I said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall I bequeath all my property?" He said: "No." I said: "Then half?" He said: "No." I said: "Then a third?" He said: "A third, and a third is much. It is better that you leave your heirs wealthy than that you leave them destitute, begging from people with their hands." 25/a [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Wasaya, chapter: that one leave his heirs wealthy is better...: 5/363. And Muslim: in Wasiyya, chapter: bequest of a third, no. (1628), 3/1250. And the author in Sharh al-Sunna: 5/282-283.]]

And from Ibn Abi Mulayka: a man said to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I wish to make a bequest." She said: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependants do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "Allah only said ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependants." [[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi (al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti, 1/423).]]

And Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "That I bequeath a fifth is more beloved to me than that I bequeath a quarter, and that I bequeath a quarter is more beloved to me than that I bequeath a third; whoever bequeaths a third has not left [anything]." And al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he bequeaths a sixth, or a fifth, or a quarter. And al-Sha'bi said: they used to bequeath only a fifth or a quarter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as an obligation﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and it was said it is in the accusative as an object, meaning He made the bequest an obligation ﴿upon the God-fearing﴾, i.e., the believers.

The Almighty's statement: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾, that is, changes the bequest concerning the executors (al-awsiya'), the guardians (al-awliya') or the witnesses, ﴿after he has heard it﴾, that is, after he has heard the statement of the testator. For this reason the pronoun (al-kinaya) is used in the masculine form ("it" referring to the bequest), even though the bequest (al-wasiyya) is feminine. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the act of bequeathing (al-iya'), as in His statement: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition (mawʿiza) from his Lord﴾ [2:275], where the pronoun is returned to the admonition (al-waʿz): ﴿Its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾, while the deceased is innocent of it. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing﴾ of what the testator bequeathed, ﴿Knowing﴾ of the alteration of the one who alters it. Or: Hearing of his bequest, Knowing of his intention.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 182–183:

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever fears﴾ mean: whoever knows (*khawf* here means *'ilm*, knowledge), as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ (2:229), meaning: if you know. ﴿From a testator﴾: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read it with a *fatha* on the *waw* and a *shaddah* on the *sad*, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿what He enjoined upon Noah﴾ (42:13) and ﴿We have enjoined upon man﴾ (29:8). The others read it with a *sukun* on the *waw* and a light *sad*, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾ (4:11) and ﴿after any bequest he has made or debt﴾ (4:12).

﴿Partiality﴾ (*janaf*) means injustice and deviation from the truth. *Al-janaf* is inclination. ﴿Or sin﴾ means wrongdoing. Al-Suddi, Ikrimah and al-Rabi' said: *al-janaf* is error and *al-ithm* is deliberate wrongdoing.

﴿Then if he brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him﴾. The scholars differed about the meaning of the verse. Mujahid said: its meaning is that when a man attends a sick person who is making his bequest, and he sees him inclining, either through excess or extravagance, or by placing the bequest in the wrong place, there is no blame upon the one who is present if he orders him to be just and forbids him from *janaf*, so that he considers the interests of the testator and of the heirs. Others said: it means that if the deceased errs in his bequest or deliberately acts unjustly, there is no blame upon his guardian, his executor, or the ruler of the Muslims for making reconciliation after his death between his heirs and the beneficiaries, and for returning the bequest to justice and truth. Then ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, that is, there is no blame upon him. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Tawus said: *janafa* is *tawlijah* (a covert transfer of inheritance through a bequest, disguised as a permitted gift). This is when a man bequeaths to "the sons of his sons" while intending his own son, or to "the children of his daughter" and "the husband of his daughter" while intending his daughter herself.

Al-Kalbi said: the guardians and executors used to carry out the bequest of the deceased after the revelation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿whoever alters it after having heard it﴾ (2:181), even if it consumed the entire wealth and nothing remained for the heirs. Then His words, Exalted is He: ﴿whoever fears partiality from a testator﴾ abrogated (*naskh*) that ruling. Ibn Zayd said: the testator was unable to bequeath to the parents and the relatives as Allah had commanded, and he was unable to act rightly, so Allah took that matter away from them and prescribed the fixed shares (*al-fara'id*).

It is related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, a man or a woman may work in obedience to Allah for sixty years, then death comes upon them and they cause harm (*yudarran*) in their bequest, so the Fire becomes obligatory for them." Then Abu Hurayrah recited: ﴿after any bequest he has made or debt, without causing harm﴾ up to His words ﴿not causing harm﴾.¹

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, that is, it has been made obligatory and required. *Al-sawm* and *al-siyam* in the language mean abstention. It is said: "the day stood still (*sama*)" when it reached its midpoint and the noon sun stood still, because when the sun reaches the middle of the sky it halts and stops moving for a short while. From this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast (*sawman*)﴾ (19:26), meaning silence, since it is abstention from speech. In the Shari'ah (sacred law), *sawm* is abstention from eating, drinking and sexual intercourse, with the intention, during a specified time. ﴿As it was prescribed for those before you﴾, that is, the prophets and the nations. The scholars differed about this comparison.² Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the fasting of those before us was from the *'atamah* (night prayer time) until the following night, just as it was at the beginning of Islam.

A group of the people of knowledge said: what is meant is that the fasting of Ramadan was obligatory upon the Christians just as it was prescribed for us. It would sometimes fall in intense heat or intense cold, and it would be hardship for them during their travels and would harm their livelihoods. So their scholars and leaders agreed to make their fasting fall in a season of the year between winter and summer, so they made it in spring and added ten days as expiation for what they had done, and it became forty days. Then their king fell ill in his mouth, so he vowed to Allah that if he recovered from his ailment he would add a week to their fast. He recovered and added a week. Then that king died and another king ruled over them and said: "Complete it to fifty days." Mujahid said: they suffered two deaths, so they said: "Increase your fasting," and they added ten days before and ten days after. Al-Sha'bi said: "If I fasted the whole year, I would break the fast on the day about which there is doubt, whether it is said to be from Sha'ban or from Ramadan." That is because the Christians had Ramadan prescribed upon them, so they fasted a day before the thirtieth and a day after it. Then the later generation continued to follow the practice of the generation before it, until they reached fifty days. That is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may become righteous﴾, meaning through fasting, because fasting is a means to righteousness, since it involves restraining the self and breaking the desires. It was also said: ﴿so that you may guard yourselves﴾ against the desires of eating, drinking and sexual intercourse.
