**Al-Baghawi's commentary (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 2, verse 184:**

﴿A certain number of days﴾. It was said: At the beginning of Islam, fasting three days of every month was obligatory, along with fasting the Day of 'Ashura'. So they fasted in this way from the spring until the month of Ramadan, seventeen months. Then it was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) by the fasting of Ramadan. Ibn 'Abbas said: The first thing abrogated after the Hijrah was the direction of prayer (*qiblah*) and the fast. It is also said that the fasting of the month of Ramadan was revealed a month and some days before Badr. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The Battle of Badr took place on Friday, on the seventeenth night that had passed of the month of Ramadan, at the end of eighteen months from the Hijrah.

Abu al-Hasan al-Shirazi narrated to us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'A'ishah, the Mother of the Believers, that she said: "The Day of 'Ashura' was a day that the Quraysh used to fast in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madinah, he fasted it and commanded the people to fast it. But when Ramadan was made obligatory, it became the obligatory fast, and the Day of 'Ashura' was left. Whoever wished could fast it, and whoever wished could leave it."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Fasting, chapter "The fast of the Day of 'Ashura'" (4/102), and in the Book of Hajj, the Book of the Virtues of the Companions, and the Book of Tafsir. Muslim in the Book of Fasting, chapter "The fast of the Day of 'Ashura'", no. 1125 (2/792). The author (al-Baghawi) in Sharh al-Sunnah (6/212).]]

It was also said that what is meant by His words ﴿a certain number of days﴾ is the month of Ramadan, and it is not abrogated. The word *ayyaman* (days) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning "during certain numbered days." It was also said that it is in the accusative as an explanation (*tafsir*) [of the subject], and it was said that it is the predicate of the passive construction (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*). ﴿So whoever among you is sick or on a journey, [then a number] of other days﴾, meaning: whoever breaks the fast, then for him is a number [of days] to make up. "*Al-'adad*" and "*al-'iddah*" have the same meaning. ﴿Of other days﴾, meaning days other than the days of his illness or journey. The word *ukhar* (other) is in the genitive position, but it does not take nunation (tanwin), which is why it is in the accusative.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And upon those who are able to fast [it]﴾. The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of this verse and its ruling. Most of them held that the verse is abrogated. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Salamah ibn al-Akwa', and others. The reason is that at the beginning of Islam they were given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast and paying a ransom (*fidyah*). Allah gave them this choice so that it would not be hard upon them, for they were not yet accustomed to fasting. Then the choice was abrogated, and the obligation was revealed by His words: ﴿So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. Qatadah said: It applies specifically to the old man who is able to fast but finds it difficult; he was granted a concession to break the fast and pay a ransom, and then this was abrogated. Al-Hasan said: This refers to the sick person who has an illness that is recognized as sickness, yet is able to fast; he was given the choice between fasting and breaking the fast and paying a ransom, and then this was abrogated by His words: ﴿So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾.

The concession remains for those who are not able [to fast]. A group [of scholars] held that the verse is fixed (*muhkamah*), not abrogated. Its meaning is: "And upon those who used to be able to fast it in the time of youth but became unable to do so after old age, for them is a ransom instead of fasting." Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿And upon those who [are] able to fast it﴾ with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fathah* on the *ta'*, with it being light (*takhfif*), and with a *fathah* on the *waw* and it being doubled (*tashdid*), meaning: they are charged with fasting [but] are not able to. This is interpreted as referring to the old man and the old woman who are not able to fast, and to the sick person whose illness is not expected to go away. They are charged with fasting but are not able to, so they may break the fast and feed a needy person (*miskin*) for each day. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and he considered the verse to be fixed.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿A ransom: feeding a needy person﴾. The people of Madinah and Syria read it with the noun in the construct state (*mudaf*), and likewise in al-Ma'idah: "*kaffarat ta'am*" (expiation: feeding). They attached the ransom to the food, even though they are one thing, because the two expressions differ, as in His words: ﴿And the grain of the harvest﴾ (50:9), and as in their saying "*masjid al-jami'*" (the congregational mosque) and "*rabi' al-awwal*" (the first spring). The others read *fidyatun* and *kaffaratun* with nunation, and *ta'amu* in the nominative. Here, the people of Madinah and Syria read *masakin* in the plural, and the others in the singular. Whoever reads it in the plural puts the *nun* in the accusative, and whoever reads it in the singular puts the *nun* in the genitive and with nunation. *Al-fidyah* means the recompense. It is obligatory to feed a needy person for each day one mudd of food by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is a ratl and a third of the staple food of the region. This is the view of the jurists of the Hijaz. Some jurists of Iraq said: For each needy person, half a sa' for each day of breaking the fast. Some of them said: Half a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of something else. Some jurists said: [It is] what the one breaking the fast usually eats on the day he breaks it. Ibn 'Abbas said: He gives each needy person his evening meal and his pre-dawn meal.

﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, meaning: he adds to one needy person, so that for each day he feeds two needy persons or more. This was said by Mujahid, 'Ata', and Tawus. It was also said: Whoever exceeds the obligatory amount upon him, so he gives a sa' when he is obligated only to give a mudd, it is better for him.

﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. He [the one who holds] the abrogation view said: Its meaning is that fasting is better for him than the ransom. It was also said: This applies to the old man, if he burdens himself with fasting, even though it is hard for him, it is better for him than that he breaks the fast and pays the ransom. ﴿If you only knew﴾.

Know that there is no concession for a responsible believer to break the fast of Ramadan except for three categories. The first is one who must make up the fast and also pay the expiation (*kaffarah*). The second must make up the fast but does not pay the expiation. The third must pay the expiation but does not make up the fast. (The word *kaffarah* is used here in the sense of *fidyah*, as it comes in the context; otherwise, expiation is obligatory upon one who invalidates his fast in Ramadan by sexual intercourse, which is a sin committed through the fast.)[[The word *kaffarah* is used here in the sense of *fidyah*, as it appears in the context; otherwise, expiation is obligatory upon the one who invalidates his fast in Ramadan by intercourse, which he commits sinfully during the fast.]]

As for the one who must make up the fast and pay the expiation: the pregnant woman and the nursing woman, if they fear for their children, then they break the fast and make it up, and along with making it up they must pay the ransom. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid also said so, and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, took this position. Another group said: There is no ransom upon them. This was the view of al-Hasan, 'Ata', Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, and al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and the people of opinion (*ashab al-ra'y*) also took this position.

As for the one who must make up the fast but does not pay the expiation: the sick person, the traveler, the menstruating woman, and the woman in post-natal bleeding.

As for the one who must pay the expiation but does not make up the fast: the old man, and the sick person whose illness is not expected to go away.[[See: Tafsir al-Qurtubi 2/288–289; Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas 1/218–228.]]

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the days of fasting, saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan﴾. It is in the nominative case, meaning: "It is the month of Ramadan." Al-Kisa'i said: "The phrase means: 'Fasting has been prescribed for you, the month of Ramadan.'" The month is called "shahr" (month) because of its fame (shuhrah). As for "Ramadan," Mujahid said: "It is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, and one says 'the month of Ramadan' just as one says 'the month of Allah.'" The correct view, however, is that it is the name of the month, named after "ar-ramda'" (the scorching ground), which means heated stones. They used to fast it in intense heat, so stones would be scorched (turammadu) by the heat in it.

Allah's saying: ﴿in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. The Qur'an (al-Qur'an, recitation) is so called because it gathers together the surahs, the verses and the letters, and in it are gathered the narratives, the commands, the prohibitions, the promises and the threats.

The root of "qar'" (qara'a) is gathering (al-jam'), and the hamza may be dropped from it, so one says: "qaraytu al-ma' fi al-hawd" (I gathered the water in the pool) when you collect it. Ibn Kathir read "al-Qur'an" with a fathah on the ra' and without hamza, and ash-Shafi'i used to recite it likewise, saying: "It is not derived from qira'ah (recitation); rather it is a name for this Book, like the Tawrah and the Injil." It is narrated from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he was asked about the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ and ﴿We sent it down on the Night of Decree﴾ (97:1), and His saying: ﴿We sent it down on a blessed night﴾ (44:3), while it was sent down in other months as well. He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And a Qur'an which We divided [into parts]﴾ (17:106). He explained: the Qur'an was sent down all at once from the Preserved Tablet on the Night of Decree in the month of Ramadan to the House of Honour (Bayt al-'Izzah) in the lowest heaven. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, brought it down upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in installments over twenty-three years. That is His saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ (56:75).

Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: "I said to ash-Sha'bi: '﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾ — was it not sent down in the other months?' He said: 'Yes, but Jibril used to review with Muhammad (ﷺ) in Ramadan what had been revealed to him, so Allah decrees what He wills, confirms what He wills, and causes him to forget what He wills.'"

It is narrated from Abu Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The Scrolls of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, were sent down on the first three nights of Ramadan, the Tawrah of Musa, peace be upon him, was sent down on six nights of Ramadan that had passed, the Injil was sent down upon 'Isa, peace be upon him, on the thirteenth night that had passed of Ramadan, the Zabur of Dawud was sent down on the eighteenth night that had passed of Ramadan, and the Furqan was sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) on the twenty-fourth night of the month of Ramadan, six nights before its end." [[Narrated by Ahmad, 4/107, from Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'. See Musnad ash-Shamiyyin from Musnad al-Imam Ahmad, edited by Ali Muhammad Jamaz, 1/201, where there is 'Imran ibn Dawwar (with fathah on the waw followed by a ra'), Abu al-'Awwam al-Qattan al-Basri, who is truthful but makes mistakes and was accused of holding Kharijite opinions, from the seventh tier (at-Taqrib). It was also narrated by at-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (see Fayd al-Qadir: 3/57). Ibn Hajar mentioned it in al-Matalib al-'Aliyah: 3/286 from the narration of Abu Ya'la from Jabir, and said: "This is inverted; it is from Wathilah, so verify it."]]

Allah's saying: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾, from misguidance. "Huda" (guidance) is in the accusative case as a circumstantial qualifier (al-qat'), because "al-Qur'an" is definite and "huda" is indefinite. ﴿And clear proofs of the guidance﴾, that is, clear indications concerning the lawful and the unlawful, the prescribed limits and the rulings. ﴿And the Criterion﴾, that is, that which distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

Allah's saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. That is: whoever is resident in his home and the month reaches him. The scholars differed concerning one who was resident when the month began and then travelled. It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "It is not permissible for him to break the fast." This was also the view of 'Ubaydah as-Salmani, citing Allah's saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, that is, the entire month. Most of the Companions and jurists, however, held that if one begins a journey during the month of Ramadan, it is permissible for him to break the fast. The meaning of the verse is: whoever witnesses the entire month, let him fast it, that is, the whole month; and whoever of you does not witness the entire month, let him fast what he witnessed of it. The evidence for this is what Abu al-Hasan as-Sarakhsi related to us, from Zahir ibn Ahmad, from Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi, from Abu Mus'ab, from Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from 'Ubaydullah ibn 'Utbah ibn Mas'ud, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Makkah in the year of the Conquest in Ramadan, and he fasted until he reached al-Kadid, then he broke the fast, and the people broke their fast with him. So they would take the latest of the commands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Fasting, chapter "If he fasts some days of Ramadan and then travels," 4/180, and in Jihad and Maghazi. Muslim: in Fasting, chapter on the permissibility of fasting and breaking the fast in Ramadan for the traveller, no. 1113, 2/784. Al-Musannif in Sharh as-Sunnah: 6/310.]]

Allah's saying: ﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. He permitted breaking the fast for the excuse of illness and travel, and repeated this statement so that it would be known that this ruling is established in the abrogating text just as it is established in the abrogated one. The scholars differed concerning the illness that permits breaking the fast. The people of the literal reading (ahl az-Zahir) held that anything to which the name "illness" applies permits breaking the fast, and this is the view of Ibn Sirin. Tarif ibn Tammam al-'Utaridi said: "I entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin in Ramadan while he was eating, and he said: 'This finger of mine has been afflicted.'" Al-Hasan and Ibrahim an-Nakha'i said it is the illness that makes one unable to pray standing, so one may pray sitting. Most scholars held that it is an illness with which fasting is feared to cause the increase of an intolerable ailment. In general, if fasting exhausts him, he breaks the fast; and if it does not exhaust him, he is like the healthy person.

As for travel, breaking the fast during it is permissible, and fasting is permissible according to the general body of scholars, except what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, 'Urwah ibn az-Zubayr and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, that they said fasting is not permissible during travel, and whoever fasts must make it up. They cited the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not righteousness to fast during travel." [[Will come on p. 189.]] According to the others, this applies to one whom fasting exhausts; for him it is better to break the fast. The evidence for this is what 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi related to us, from Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah an-Nu'aymi, from Muhammad ibn Yusuf, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Adam, from Shu'bah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd ar-Rahman al-Ansari, who said: I heard Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on a journey and he saw a crowd and a man over whom shade had been cast, and he said: "What is this?" They said: "This is a fasting man." He said: "It is not righteousness to fast during travel." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Fasting, chapter "The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to one over whom shade is cast when the heat is intense," 4/183. Muslim: in Fasting, chapter on the permissibility of fasting and breaking the fast in Ramadan for the traveller, no. 1115, 2/786. Al-Musannif in Sharh as-Sunnah: 6/308.]]

The evidence for the permissibility of fasting is what Ustadh Abu al-Qasim 'Abd al-Karim ibn Hawazin al-Qushayri related to us, from Abu Nu'aym al-Isfara'ini, from Abu 'Awanah, from Abu Umayyah, from 'Abd Allah al-Qawariri, from Hammad ibn Zayd, from al-Jariri, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "We used to travel with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Ramadan; some of us were fasting and some of us were not, and the fasting did not blame the one not fasting, nor the one not fasting the one fasting." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Fasting, chapter "The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) did not blame one another," 4/186. Muslim: in Fasting, chapter on the permissibility of fasting and breaking the fast in Ramadan for the traveller, nos. 1116, 1118, 2/786-787. Al-Musannif in Sharh as-Sunnah: 6/306-307.]]

They differed concerning which of the two is better. One group said: breaking the fast during travel is better than fasting. This was narrated from Ibn 'Umar, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and ash-Sha'bi followed this view. Another group held that fasting is better; this was narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Anas, and Ibrahim an-Nakha'i and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise. Another group said: the better of the two is the easier of them for him, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ (2:185). This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. As for one who begins the day as a resident and fasting, then travels in the course of the day, according to most scholars it is not permissible for him to break the fast that day. Another group said he may break the fast; this is the view of ash-Sha'bi, and Ahmad also held it. As for the traveller who begins the day fasting, it is by consensus permissible for him to break the fast. The evidence for this is what 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib related to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm, from ar-Rabi', from ash-Shafi'i, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Muhammad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Jabir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Makkah in the year of the Conquest in Ramadan, and he fasted until he reached Kura' al-Ghamim, and the people fasted with him. It was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, the people find the fast hard." So he called for a cup of water after the 'Asr prayer and drank while the people watched, and some of the people broke their fast while some continued fasting. It reached him that some people had continued fasting, and he said: "Those are the disobedient." [[Narrated by Muslim: in Fasting, chapter on the permissibility of fasting and breaking the fast in Ramadan for the traveller, no. 1114, 2/785. Al-Musannif in Sharh as-Sunnah: 6/311; and ash-Shafi'i in al-Musnad: 1/268-269.]]

They differed concerning the journey that permits breaking the fast. Some said: a day's journey. A group held: two days' journey, and this is the view of ash-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Another group held: three days' journey, and this is the view of Sufyan ath-Thawri and the people of opinion (ashab ar-ra'y).

Allah's saying: ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾, by permitting breaking the fast in illness and travel, ﴿and does not intend hardship for you﴾. Abu Ja'far read "al-'usr" and "al-yusr" and similar words with a damma on the sin, while the others read them with sukun. Ash-Sha'bi said: "No man was ever given a choice between two matters and chose the easier of them, but that was more beloved of the two to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." ﴿And that you may complete the period﴾. Abu Bakr read it with the shaddah on the mim, while the others read it with the lighter form, and this is the preferred reading, because of the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ (5:3). The waw in His saying "wa-litukmiluu al-'iddah" is the waw of conjunction, and the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay), its implied sense being: "and He intends that you complete the period," i.e., that you complete the number of days of the month by making up what you broke of the fast during your illness and your travel. 'Ata' said: "﴿And that you may complete the period﴾ means the number of days of the month."

Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib related to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm, from ar-Rabi', from ash-Shafi'i, from Malik, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The month is twenty-nine nights, so do not fast until you see the crescent, and do not break the fast until you see it. If it is hidden from you, then complete the count to thirty." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Fasting, chapter "The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): When you see the crescent, fast..." 4/119, and in Divorce. Muslim: in Fasting, chapter on the obligation of fasting Ramadan upon sighting the crescent, no. 1080, 2/759. Al-Musannif in Sharh as-Sunnah: 6/228; and ash-Shafi'i in al-Musnad: 1/272.]]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Husayn al-Hiri informed us: Hajib ibn Ahmad al-Tusi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yahya informed us: Yazid ibn Harun informed us: Muhammad ibn Amr informed us, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not precede Ramadan by fasting a day or two days, unless it coincides with a fast that one of you used to keep. Fast when you see the crescent, and break your fast when you see it. If it is obscured from you, then count thirty days and then break your fast." [[Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/237, and it is a combination of two hadiths in al-Bukhari and Muslim (see al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Sawm, 4/119, 127, 128, and Muslim, Kitab al-Siyam, nos. 1082, 1188, 2/762, 765).]]

﴿And that you may glorify Allah﴾ and that you may magnify Allah ﴿for having guided you﴾ to what He is pleased with, namely the fasting of the month of Ramadan, and singled you out for it apart from the rest of the adherents of the other religions.

Ibn Abbas said: It refers to the takbirat (the glorifying declarations of "Allahu akbar") on the night of Eid al-Fitr. It is narrated from al-Shafi'i, Ibn al-Musayyab, Urwa and Abu Salama that they used to recite the takbir on the night of Eid al-Fitr, pronouncing it aloud, and they likened the night of Eid al-Adha to it, except for one who is performing Hajj, whose remembrance is the talbiya.

﴿And that you may be grateful﴾ to Allah for His blessings. Reports have been transmitted concerning the virtue of the month of Ramadan and the reward of those who fast.

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Marwazi informed us: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Siraj al-Tahhan informed us: Abu Ahmad Muhammad ibn Quraysh ibn Sulayman informed us: Ali ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Makki informed us: Abu Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated to me: Ismail ibn Ja'far narrated to me, from Abu Suhayl Nafi' ibn Malik, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "When Ramadan begins, the devils are chained, the gates of Paradise are opened, and the gates of Hell are closed." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: Kitab al-Sawm, bab hal yuqal Ramadan..., 4/112, and in Bad' al-Khalq. Muslim: Kitab al-Siyam, bab fadl shahr Ramadan, no. 1079, 2/758. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/215.]]

Abu Uthman Sa'id ibn Isma'il al-Dabbi informed us: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Jabbar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Jarrah informed us: Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Mahbubi informed us: Abu Isa Muhammad ibn Isa al-Tirmidhi informed us: Abu Kurayb Muhammad ibn al-Ala informed us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Ayyash informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the first night of Ramadan comes, the devils and the rebellious jinn are chained, the gates of Hell are closed so that none of them is opened, the gates of Paradise are opened so that none of them is closed, and a caller calls out: 'O seeker of good, come forward! O seeker of evil, desist!' And for Allah there are those freed from the Fire, and this happens every night." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi: Kitab al-Sawm, bab ma ja'a fi fadl shahr Ramadan, 3/359-360. Ibn Majah: Kitab al-Siyam, bab ma ja'a fi fadl shahr Ramadan, no. 1642, 1/526. Al-Hakim: 1/421, and its narrators are trustworthy, except that Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash, when he grew old, his memory deteriorated, and it has a supporting report that strengthens it, from the hadith of Ata ibn al-Sa'ib from Arfaja. Ahmad: 4/311-312 and 5/411, from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Nasa'i: 4/130. Ibn Khuzayma: 3/188. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/215.]]

Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Abi Nasr ibn Ahmad al-Kufani al-Harawi informed us, with this chain: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Rahman ibn Umar ibn Muhammad al-Tujibi al-Misri, with this chain, known as Ibn al-Nahhas [[There are some errors in the chain, which have been corrected from Sharh al-Sunna.]] was asked: Did Abu Sa'id Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad al-Anazi al-Basri, known as Ibn al-A'rabi, inform you at Makka? He said: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah al-Za'farani informed us: Sufyan ibn Uyayna informed us, from al-Zuhri: Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman informed us, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven; and whoever stands in prayer during Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven; and whoever stands in prayer on the Night of Qadr out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: Kitab al-Tarawih, bab man sama Ramadan iman wa ihtisaban, 4/115, and in Kitab al-Ta'bir. Muslim: Kitab Salat al-Musafirin, bab al-targhib fi qiyam Ramadan, no. 760, 1/524. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/217.]]

Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Qadi, the imam, informed us: Abu Sa'id Khalaf ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nizar narrated to us: al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Asad al-Saffar informed us: Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Ishaq al-Anazi informed us: Ali ibn Hujr ibn Iyas al-Sa'di informed us: Yusuf ibn Ziyad informed us, from Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab [26/b], from Salman, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us on the last day of Sha'ban, saying: "O people, there has come upon you a great month, [and in another narration, 'has come near to you' with a ta', atalla: ashraf (it has overlooked you)], a great month, a blessed month, a month in which is the Night of Qadr, which is better than a thousand months, a month whose fasting Allah has made obligatory and whose night prayer He has made voluntary. Whoever draws near to Allah in it with one good quality is like one who performed an obligation in other months, and whoever performs an obligation in it is like one who performed seventy obligations in other months. It is the month of patience, and the reward of patience is Paradise; it is the month of consolation (al-muwasat, i.e., sharing), and a month in which provision is increased. Whoever gives iftar to a fasting person in it, it will be for him a forgiveness of his sins and freedom of his neck from the Fire, and he will have a reward like his, without anything being diminished from his reward." They said: O Messenger of Allah, not all of us have something with which to give iftar to the fasting person. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah gives this reward to whoever gives iftar to a fasting person with a mouthful of milk, or a date, or a sip of water. Whoever satisfies a fasting person, Allah will give him to drink from my Pool a drink after which he will never thirst until he enters Paradise. And whoever lightens the burden of his servant in it, Allah will forgive him and free him from the Fire until he enters Paradise. It is a month whose beginning is mercy, whose middle is forgiveness, and whose end is freedom from the Fire. So increase in it in four qualities: two by which you please your Lord, and two of which you have no independence from. As for the two by which you please your Lord: testifying that there is no god but Allah, and seeking His forgiveness. As for the two of which you have no independence: you ask Allah for Paradise, and seek refuge with Him from the Fire." [[Narrated by Ibn Khuzayma: 3/191-192, in Kitab al-Sawm, bab fadl shahr Ramadan, and he said in it: "If the report is sound," and in its chain is Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, who is weak (al-Taqrib; Mizan al-I'tidal). Al-Mundhiri mentioned it in al-Targhib, 2/94-95, and said: Ibn Khuzayma narrated it in his Sahih. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it from his route, and Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Hibban narrated it in abridged form from them in al-Thawab.]]

Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Qadi, the imam, informed us: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn Mahmash al-Ziyadi informed us: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Umar ibn Hafs al-Tajir informed us: Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Bukayr al-Kufi informed us: Waki' informed us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied: a good deed is rewarded tenfold up to seven hundredfold. Allah, the Exalted, said: Except fasting, for it is for Me, and I will reward it. He leaves his food, his drink and his desire for My sake. For the fasting person there are two joys: a joy when he breaks his fast, and a joy when he meets his Lord. The odour from the mouth of the fasting person is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk. Fasting is a shield, fasting is a shield." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: Kitab al-Sawm, bab fadl al-sawm, 4/103, and in Kitab al-Libas and Kitab al-Tawhid. Muslim: Kitab al-Siyam, bab fadl al-sawm, no. 1151, 2/806. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/221.]]

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Malihi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Sa'id ibn Abi Maryam informed us: Muhammad ibn Mutarrif narrated to me: Abu Hazim narrated to me, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "In Paradise there are eight gates, one of which is called al-Rayyan, which only those who fast will enter." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: Kitab al-Sawm, bab al-Rayyan lil-sa'imin, 4/111. Muslim: Kitab al-Siyam, bab fadl al-sawm, no. 1152, 2/808. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/219-220.]]

Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Tawba informed us: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Harith informed us: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kisa'i informed us: Abd Allah ibn Mahmud informed us: Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah al-Khallal informed us: Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Rashid ibn Sa'd, from Yahya ibn Abd Allah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, from Abd Allah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Fasting and the Qur'an will intercede for the servant. Fasting will say: 'O Lord, I prevented him from food, drink and desires during the day, so grant me intercession for him.' And the Qur'an will say: 'O Lord, I prevented him from sleep at night, so grant me intercession for him.' So both will be granted intercession." [[Narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak: 1/554. Al-Mundhiri said: Ahmad and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir narrated it, and its narrators are those relied upon in the Sahih. Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated it in Kitab al-Ju' and elsewhere with a good chain, and al-Hakim said: sound according to the condition of Muslim. See al-Mundhiri, al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib, 2/84.]]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾. Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Jews of Madinah said, "O Muhammad, how does our Lord hear our supplication when you claim that between us and the heaven is a distance of five hundred years, and that the thickness of each heaven is the same?" So this verse was revealed. Al-Dahhak said: Some of the Companions asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying, "Is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿When My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ [[We have not found the first narration, but its chain contains al-Kalbi, who is an liar (al-Taqrib). As for the second narration, Ibn Jarir, al-Baghawi in his Mu'jam, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through the route of al-Salt ibn Hakim, from a man of the Ansar, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: A man came... so Allah revealed (When My servants ask you about Me). Al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/469.]] There is an implied element in it, as if He said: "Say to them: indeed I am near to them by knowledge; nothing is hidden from Me," just as He said: ﴿And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ (50:16).

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliki informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, Abd al-Wahid informed us, from Asim, from Abu 'Uthman, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invaded Khaybar, or he said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out for Khaybar, the people came upon a valley and raised their voices with the takbir: "Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar, there is no god but Allah." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; rather you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near, and He is with you." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari, in Kitab al-Tawhid, Bab: "And Allah is ever All-Hearing, All-Seeing," 13/372. And Muslim, in Kitab al-Dhikr wa al-Du'a' wa al-Tawbah, Bab istihbab khafd al-sawt bi al-dhikr, no. (4704), 4/2076.]]

The Almighty's saying: ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me﴾. The readers of Madinah, except Qalun, and Abu 'Amr, read the yā' in both places with affirmation in connected speech, while the rest read it without the yā', both in connected speech and at pause. Likewise the readers differed over affirming the yā's that are omitted in the written text and omitting them in recitation. Ya'qub affirms all of them, both in connected speech and at pause, and they agreed on affirming what is written in the text, both in connected speech and at pause. ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾: it was said that al-istijabah (responding) has the meaning of al-ijabah (answering), i.e., let them answer Me with obedience. In the language, al-ijabah means obedience and giving what is asked; so the ijabah from Allah the Exalted is giving, and from the servant it is obedience. It was also said: "So let them respond to Me" means let them ask Me for the answer. Its real meaning is: let them obey Me. ﴿And let them believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾, so that they may be rightly guided. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿I answer the call of the caller﴾, and ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ (40:60), while a person often calls and is not answered? We say: they differed concerning the meaning of the two verses. It was said: the meaning of "call" here is obedience, and the meaning of "answer" is reward. It was also said: the meaning of the two verses is specific, though their wording is general; their implied meaning is: "I answer the call of the caller if I will," as He said: ﴿He will remove that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾ (6:41); or: "I answer the caller's call if it accords with the decree"; or: "I answer him if the answer is good for him"; or: "I answer him if he does not ask for the impossible."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliki informed us, Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sam'an informed us, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayani informed us, Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us, Abd Allah ibn Salih informed us, Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me that Rabi'ah ibn Yazid narrated to him, from Abu Idris, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Allah responds to one of you so long as he does not supplicate for sin or the severing of ties of kinship, or hasten." They said, "O Messenger of Allah, what is hastening?" He said: "He says, 'I have called upon You, O Lord; I have called upon You, O Lord, yet I do not see You responding to me,' and then he becomes weary and abandons supplication." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari briefly, in Kitab al-Da'awat, Bab: "A servant is answered so long as he does not hasten," 11/140. And Muslim, in Kitab al-Dhikr wa al-Du'a' wa al-Tawbah, Bab: bayan annahu yustajab li al-da'i ma lam ya'jal, no. (2735), 4/2095, and the wording is his. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 5/190.]]

It was also said: the verse is general, and the meaning of His saying ﴿I answer﴾ is "I hear." It is said: there is nothing in the verse beyond the answering of the call; as for granting the wish, it is not mentioned in it. A master may answer his servant, and a father his son, yet not give him his request; so the answer is certainly present when the supplication occurs. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that He does not disappoint His servant's supplication. If He has decreed for him what he asked, He gives it to him; if He has not decreed it for him, He stores up the reward for him in the Hereafter, or averts from him an evil by means of it. The evidence for this is what Abd al-Wahid al-Maliki informed us, Abu Mansur al-Sam'ani informed us, Abu Ja'far al-Rayani informed us, Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Ibn Thawban, who is Abd al-Rahman ibn Thabit ibn Thawban, informed us, from his father, from Makhul, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, who narrated to them that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is no Muslim man on the face of the earth who calls upon Allah the Exalted with a supplication except that Allah gives him it, or averts from him an evil equal to it, so long as he does not supplicate for sin or the severing of ties of kinship." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, in Kitab al-Da'awat, Bab: fi intizar al-faraj, from Jabir: 10/24, and he said: "This is a hasan gharib sahih hadith from this route." And al-Hakim: 1/493, and he authenticated it and al-Dhahabi agreed with him. And Ahmad: 3/18, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 5/186.]] It was also said: Allah the Exalted answers the believer's supplication immediately, but delays granting his desire so that he continues to call upon Him and His voice is heard; and He hastens granting it to one whom He does not love, because He dislikes his voice. It was also said: supplication has etiquettes and conditions, and these are the causes of being answered. Whoever fulfils them is among those who are answered, and whoever falls short in them is among those who transgress in supplication, and so does not deserve to be answered.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives (al-rafath ila nisa'ikum)﴾. Al-rafath is a metaphor (kinaya) for sexual intercourse (al-jima'). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah, may He be exalted, is Modest and Generous, and He uses euphemism for everything mentioned in the Qur'an concerning mubashara (physical contact), mulamasa (touching), ifda' (reaching), and dukhul (entering). Al-rafath refers only to intercourse." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-rafath is a comprehensive word for everything men desire from women." The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: "At the beginning of this ruling, when a man broke his fast, food, drink, and intercourse were permitted to him until he prayed the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhira) or slept before it. If he prayed 'isha' or slept before it, food and women became forbidden to him until the next night." Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, had intercourse with his wife after he had prayed 'isha'. When he performed ghusl, he began to weep and blame himself. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I apologize to Allah and to you for this sinful self of mine. I returned to my wife after I had prayed 'isha', and I smelled a pleasant fragrance, so my self tempted me, and I had intercourse with my wife. Is there any concession for me?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were not deserving of that, O 'Umar." Then some men stood up and confessed to the same thing. Concerning 'Umar and his companions, it was revealed: [[Narrated by Ibn Jarir in his tafsir: 3/498. Shaykh Shakir said: "This hadith, with its chain, is a chain of weak narrators." It is attributed by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim: 1/476.]].

﴿It is made lawful for you﴾, i.e., it is permitted for you. ﴿On the night of the fast﴾, i.e., during the night of the fast. ﴿The going in unto your wives: they are a garment for you﴾, i.e., a comfort for you, ﴿and you are a garment for them﴾, i.e., a comfort for them. Its proof is His saying: ﴿And He made from it its mate that he might find comfort in her﴾ (7:189). It was said: no comfort is like the comfort of one spouse with the other. It was also said: each of the spouses is called a garment because they are bare at sleep and gather in one garment, until each one becomes to the other like the garment that he wears. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "They are a bedding for you, and you are a covering for them." Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "A woman is said to be your garment, your bedding, and your wrapper." It was also said: "Libas" is a name for what covers a thing, so each of them may be a covering for the other against what is not lawful, as came in the hadith: "Whoever marries has secured two-thirds of his religion." [[The wording is: "Whoever marries has secured half his religion, so let him fear Allah regarding the other half." Ibn al-Jawzi narrated it in al-'Ilal from Anas, traced to the Prophet, and said: "It is not authentic from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It has defects, among them Yazid al-Raqqashi. Ahmad said: nothing is to be written from him; he was a denounced narrator (munkar al-hadith). Al-Nasa'i said: munkar al-hadith, and there is confusion in it. Ahmad said: abandoned in hadith. Yahya said: he is worthless. It also contains Malik ibn Sulayman, whom they criticized." Al-'Ilal al-Mutanahiya 2/122. See Kashf al-Khafa' and Muzil al-Ilbas 2/313. It was narrated by al-Hakim with the wording: "Whoever Allah grants a righteous wife, she has helped him with half his religion, so let him fear Allah regarding the second half." Al-Hakim said: "Its chain is sound," and al-Dhahabi agreed: 2/161.]]

﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾, i.e., you were wronging yourselves and being unjust to them by intercourse after 'isha'. Al-Bara' said: "When the fasting of Ramadan was revealed, they would not approach women the whole of Ramadan, and some men were betraying themselves. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. ﴿So He turned to you in forgiveness﴾, i.e., He overlooked you, ﴿and pardoned you﴾, i.e., He erased your sins. ﴿So now, have intercourse with them (bashiru-hunna)﴾, i.e., lie with them, lawfully. Intercourse was called mubashara because the skin of each partner touches the other's. ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾, i.e., seek what Allah has ordained for you. It was said: what Allah has written for you in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), meaning the child. This was said by most of the exegetes. Mujahid said: "Seek offspring; if this wife does not bear, then that one." Qatada said: "Seek the concession that Allah has written for you in the Preserved Tablet, namely the permission to eat, drink, and have intercourse." Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "And seek what Allah has written for you," meaning the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr).

His saying: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾. It was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar named Abu Sirma ibn Qays ibn Sirma. 'Ikrima said: Abu Qays ibn Sirma. al-Kalbi said: Abu Qays Sirma ibn Anas ibn Abi Sirma. The reason was that he spent his day working on his land while fasting. When evening came, he returned to his family with dates and said to his family: "Bring the food." His wife wanted to feed him something warm, so she began preparing a warm dish for him. At the beginning, whoever prayed 'isha' and slept became forbidden food and drink. When she finished the food, she found him asleep. He had become weary and exhausted, so she woke him. He disliked disobeying Allah and His Messenger, so he refused to eat. He woke up fasting and exhausted. Before midday he fainted. When he recovered, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him, he said: "O Abu Qays, what is wrong with you? You have become exhausted (talih)?" [[Al-talih: one who has fallen from exhaustion, hardship, and weakness.]] He told him what had happened, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saddened by that. Then Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿And eat and drink﴾ [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of Fasting, chapter on the saying of Allah: "It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast..." 4/129.]], meaning during the nights of the fast, ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, meaning the whiteness of day from the blackness of night. They were called two threads because each of them appears at first stretched out like a thread.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi told us, Zahir ibn Ahmad told us, Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi told us, Abu Mus'ab told us, from Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Bilal calls at night, so eat and drink until Ibn Umm Maktum calls." He said: "Ibn Umm Maktum was a blind man; he would not call until he was told: 'You have reached morning, you have reached morning.'" [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of Adhan, chapter: the call to prayer of the blind when he has someone to inform him, 2/99. And Muslim: in the Book of Fasting, chapter: the beginning of the fast occurs at the break of dawn, no. (1092), 2/768. And al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 2/298.]]

Know that there are two dawns: a false dawn and a true dawn. The false dawn rises first, extended like the tail of a wolf, rising toward the sky. With its rising, the night does not end and food and drink are not forbidden to the fasting person. Then it sets, and after it the true dawn rises, spreading quickly across the horizon. With its rising, the day begins, and food and drink become forbidden to the fasting person.

Abu 'Uthman Sa'id ibn Isma'il al-Dabbi told us, Abu Muhammad 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Muhammad al-Jirahi told us, Abu al-'Abbas al-Mahbubi told us, Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi told us, Hannad and Yusuf ibn 'Isa told us, both said: Waki' told us, from Abu Hilal, from Sawada ibn Handhala, from Samura ibn Jundub, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let not the adhan of Bilal prevent you from your suhur, nor the extended dawn (al-fajr al-mustatil), but the dawn that spreads across the horizon (al-fajr al-mustatir fi al-ufuq)." [[Narrated by Muslim: in the Book of Fasting, chapter on the beginning of the fast occurring at the break of dawn, no. (1094), 2/770. And al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 2/300.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. The fasting person is forbidden food and drink at the break of true dawn, and this continues until the sun sets. When it sets, the breaking of the fast takes place.

Abu 'Uthman... [The chain follows:] 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi told us, Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi told us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf told us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il told us, al-Humaydi told us, Sufyan told us, Hisham ibn 'Urwa told us, saying: I heard my father say: I heard 'Asim ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, from his father, may Allah be pleased with them both, say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the night approaches from here, and the day departs from here, and the sun has set, the fasting person has broken his fast." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of Fasting, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, chapter: fasting and breaking the fast while traveling, 4/179. Narrated by Muslim: in the Book of Fasting, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, chapter on the time when the fast ends and the day departs, no. (1101), 2/772. And al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna: 6/259.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques (wa-'akifun fi al-masajid)﴾ [And you intend i'tikaf (retreat for worship) in the mosques, and the meaning is not intercourse with them in the mosques, because that is forbidden outside of i'tikaf]. [[Omitted from (b) and from the printed edition.]] Al-'ukuf is staying upon a thing. I'tikaf in the Shari'a is remaining in the mosque for the worship of Allah. It is a sunna, and it is not permissible outside the mosque, but it is permissible in all mosques.

[27b] Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Abd Allah ibn Yusuf informed us: al-Layth informed us, from Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, from Aisha, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to observe i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque for worship) during the last ten nights of Ramadan until Allah took him, and then his wives observed i'tikaf after him." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of i'tikaf, chapter on i'tikaf in the last ten nights, 4/271. Also narrated by Muslim: in the Book of i'tikaf, chapter on i'tikaf in the last ten nights of Ramadan, no. (1172), 2/831. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 6/391.]] The verse was revealed concerning a group of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who used to observe i'tikaf in the mosque. Whenever one of them felt the need for his wife, he would go out to her, have intercourse with her, then perform ghusl (ritual bath) and return to the mosque. So they were forbidden from this, by night and by day, until they finished their i'tikaf. Thus intercourse is forbidden during i'tikaf, and i'tikaf is invalidated by it. As for what falls short of intercourse among the acts of physical contact, such as kissing and touching with desire, it is disliked (makruh) and does not invalidate the i'tikaf according to most scholars, and this is the stronger of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i, just as Hajj is not voided by it. Another group said that it voids his i'tikaf, and this is the view of Malik. It was also said: if he ejaculates, his i'tikaf is voided; if he does not ejaculate, then it is not, like fasting. As for touching that is not intended for pleasure, it does not invalidate the i'tikaf, based on what Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Ibn Shihab, from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, from Amra bint Abd al-Rahman, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) observed i'tikaf, he would bring his head close to me and I would comb it, and he would not enter the house except for a human need." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of i'tikaf, chapter on the one observing i'tikaf putting his head into the house for ghusl, 4/286. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 6/400.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the limits of Allah﴾, meaning: those rulings which He mentioned concerning fasting and i'tikaf. "Limits" (hudud) means what Allah has forbidden. Al-Suddi said: "the conditions of Allah." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "the obligations of Allah." The root meaning of hadd in the language is prohibition, and from it the doorkeeper is called haddad, because he prevents people from entering. So the limits of Allah are what prevent people from transgressing them. ﴿So do not approach them﴾, meaning do not commit them. ﴿Thus﴾, in this manner, ﴿Allah makes clear His signs to mankind, that they may become righteous﴾, meaning so that they may guard against them and thereby be saved from the punishment.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 188:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis al-Kindi, against whom Rabi'ah ibn 'Abdan al-Hadrami brought a claim before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding a piece of land, saying that he had seized it from him. The Prophet ﷺ said to al-Hadrami, "Do you have evidence?" He said, "No." He said, "Then his oath is required of him." So he set off to swear, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, whoever swears falsely over another's property in order to consume it unjustly will meet Allah while He is displeased with him." [Narrated by Muslim: in Kitab al-Iman, chapter: The warning against one who takes the right of a Muslim by a false oath, with the Fire, no. 139, 1/123.] Then Allah revealed this verse: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾, meaning: none of you should consume the property of another unjustly, that is, by a means other than that which Allah has permitted. The root of "batil" (falsehood, vanity) is that which is gone and lost. Consuming wealth unjustly takes various forms: it may be by way of usurpation and plunder, it may be by way of frivolity such as gambling and the fee of a singer and the like, and it may be by way of bribery and betrayal. ﴿And use it as a bait to the rulers﴾, meaning: do not bring the matters of those possessions between you and their owners before the rulers. The root of "idla'" is sending down a bucket and dropping it into a well; it is said, "adla dalwahu" when one lowers his bucket, and "dallahu yadlu-hu" when he draws it up. Ibn 'Abbas said: this refers to a man who owes money but has no evidence, so he denies the debt and contests it before the judge, while he knows the right is upon him and that he is sinful for withholding it. Mujahid said concerning this verse: do not dispute while you are a wrongdoer. Al-Kalbi said: it is to present false testimony. As for His words ﴿and use it as a bait﴾, it is in a place of jazm (apocopation) by the repetition of the particle of prohibition; its meaning is "and do not use it as a bait to the rulers." It is also said that its meaning is: "and do not consume by falsehood while attributing it to the rulers." Qatadah said: do not put forward your brother's property before the judge while you know you are a wrongdoer, for his judgment does not make the unlawful lawful. Shurayh the judge used to say: "Indeed I judge in your favour, though I suspect you are a wrongdoer, but I cannot do otherwise than to rule according to the evidence presented to me, and my judgment does not make unlawful to you what is unlawful."

We were informed by 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib: we were informed by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal: we were informed by Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm: we were informed by al-Rabi': we were informed by al-Shafi'i: we were informed by Malik ibn Anas, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from Zaynab bint Abi Salamah, from Umm Salamah, wife of the Prophet ﷺ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes to me, and perhaps some of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I rule for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I rule for him from the right of his brother, let him not take it, for I am only cutting for him a piece of the Fire." [Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Kitab al-Ahkam, chapter: The Imam's admonition to the litigants, 13/157, and in Kitab al-Shahadat. Also narrated by Muslim: in Kitab al-Aqdiyah, chapter: Judging by the apparent and the eloquence of argument, no. 1713, 3/1337. The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 10/110.]

His words ﴿so that you may consume a portion﴾, meaning a party, ﴿of the wealth of the people through sin﴾, meaning through injustice. Ibn 'Abbas said: through a false oath by which one cuts off his brother's property. ﴿while you know﴾ that you are the ones in falsehood.

Al-Baghawi, *Ma'alim al-Tanzil* (*Tafsir al-Baghawi*), commentary on Surah al-Baqarah 2:189:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾. It was revealed concerning Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanm, both from the Ansar. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the matter with the crescent? It appears thin, then it grows until it becomes full of light, then it returns thin as it began, and it is never in one state"[[Narrated by Ibn 'Asakir with a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas. See al-Suyuti, *al-Durr al-Manthur*, 1/490.]]. So Allah revealed: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾. *Ahillah* is the plural of *hilal*, like *rida'* and *ardiyah*. It was called *hilal* because people raise their voices with remembrance (*dhikr*) when they see it, from their saying *istahalla al-sabiyy* ("the child cried out") when he shouts at the moment of his birth, and *ahalla al-qawm bi'l-hajj* ("the people raised their voices for the pilgrimage") when they raise their voices with the *talbiyah*. ﴿Say: They are times marked out for the people and for the Hajj﴾. *Mawaqit* is the plural of *miqat*, meaning: We did this so that people would know the times of the Hajj, the 'Umrah, the fast, the breaking of the fast, the terms of debts, the waiting periods of women, and other things. For this reason He made it differ from the sun, which is always in one state. ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾.

The exegetes said: In the Jahiliyyah and at the beginning of Islam, when a man among them entered the state of *ihram* for the Hajj or the 'Umrah, he would not enter a garden wall, a house, or a dwelling through its door. If he was a settled person (*ahl al-madar*), he would break a hole in the back of his house to enter and leave by it, or he would make a ladder and climb up by it. If he was a nomad (*ahl al-wabar*), he would come out from behind the tent or the pavilion, and he would neither enter nor leave by the door until he came out of his *ihram*. They considered this righteousness, except for those who were of the *Hums*, namely Quraysh and Kinanah [and Khuza'ah, Thaqif, Khath'am, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, and the Banu Mudar ibn Mu'awiyah. They were called *Hums* because of their strictness in their religion; *al-hamasah* means severity and firmness][[Omitted in manuscript (b).]]. One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered a house belonging to one of the Ansar, and a man from the Ansar called Rifa'ah ibn al-Tabut entered after him through the door while he was in *ihram*. They disapproved of this. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Why did you enter through the door while you are in *ihram*?" He said: "I saw you enter, so I entered after you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am of the Hums." The man said: "If you are of the Hums, then I am of the Hums. I am pleased with your guidance, your conduct, and your religion." So Allah revealed this verse[[Narrated by 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Qays ibn Jubayr al-Nahshali. See al-Suyuti, *al-Durr al-Manthur*, 1/492, and *Tafsir al-Tabari*, 3/556.]]. Al-Zuhri said: Some of the Ansar, when they entered the state of *ihlal* for the 'Umrah, nothing would stand between them and the sky. A man would go out in the state of *ihlal* for the 'Umrah, then a need would arise for him after he had left his house, so he would return and not enter by the door of the room, because of the roof of the house which would come between him and the sky. Instead he would breach the wall behind him, and then he would enter his room and attend to his need. Then it reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the state of *ihlal* for the 'Umrah during the time of al-Hudaybiyah and entered a room. A man from the Ansar of Banu Salamah entered after him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why did you do that?" He said: "Because I saw you enter." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am of the Hums." The Ansari said: "I am of the Hums too, and I am upon your religion." So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾[[Narrated by Ibn Jarir from al-Zuhri. See *Tafsir al-Tabari*, 3/558.]].

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr read *al-ghuyub*, *al-judub*, *al-'uyun*, and *shuyukhan* with a kasra on their first letters, because of the following *ya'* (*li-makan al-ya'*). The rest read them with a damma, according to the original form (*'ala al-asl*). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *jiyubihinna* with a kasra on the *jim*. Abu Bakr and Hamzah read *al-ghuyub* with a kasra on the *ghayn*. ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾, meaning: the righteousness is the righteousness of one who fears Allah.

﴿And enter houses through their doors﴾, in the state of *ihram*. ﴿And fear Allah that you may succeed﴾.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., in obedience to Allah, ﴿those who fight you﴾. At the beginning of Islam, Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger ﷺ to refrain from fighting the polytheists. Then, when he migrated to Medina, He commanded him, through this verse, to fight those of them who fought him. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: This is the first verse revealed about fighting. Then He commanded him to fight the polytheists in general, whether they fought or did not fight, by His saying: ﴿So kill the polytheists﴾. Thus this verse was abrogated by it (naskh). It was also said that it was abrogated by His saying ﴿So kill the polytheists﴾ and by nearly seventy verses. And His saying ﴿but do not transgress﴾ means: do not begin the fighting.

It was also said: this verse is muhkam (clear, not abrogated). The Prophet ﷺ was commanded to fight those who fight. The meaning of His saying ﴿but do not transgress﴾ is: do not kill women, children, the aged old man, the monks, or whoever offers you peace. This is the saying of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us, Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu Bakr ibn Sahl al-Quhistani, known as Abu Turab, informed us, Muhammad ibn Isa al-Tarsusi informed us, Yahya ibn Bukayr informed us, al-Layth ibn Sa'd informed us, from Jarir ibn Hazim, from Shu'bah, from Alqamah ibn Yazid, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) sent out an army, he would say: "Go out in the name of Allah and in the way of Allah. Fight those who disbelieve in Allah. Do not commit excess (ghulul), do not mutilate, do not kill a woman, nor a child, nor an aged old man." [[Narrated by Muslim: in Jihad, chapter: The Imam appointing commanders over expeditions... no. (1731) 3/1357. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 11/11.]]

Al-Kalbi related from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas: This verse was revealed concerning the Treaty of Hudaybiyah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out with his companions for the 'umrah, and they were one thousand four hundred. They traveled until they halted at Hudaybiyah, and the polytheists prevented them from the Sacred House. He made a treaty with them that he would return that year, on condition that they would vacate Mecca for him for three days in the following year, so that he might circumambulate the House. When the following year came, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions prepared for the 'umrah of qada' (the making-up pilgrimage). They feared that Quraysh would not fulfill what they had agreed, and that they would prevent them from the Sacred House. The companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked fighting them in the sacred month and in the Sacred Precinct (haram). So Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, meaning while in the state of ihram, ﴿those who fight you﴾, meaning Quraysh, ﴿but do not transgress﴾, that is, by beginning the fighting in the Sacred Precinct while in ihram. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 191–193:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾. It was said: the earlier verse was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. The root of thaqafah (skill and keen perception in matters) is ḥidhq and baṣar bi-al-umur (skilled insight into affairs), and its meaning is: kill them wherever you perceive their fighting and are able to kill them. ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, for they had expelled the Muslims from Makkah, so He said: expel them from their homes as they expelled you from your homes. ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾, meaning their polytheism (shirk) with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is more severe and greater than your killing them in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and in the state of ihram. ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein. But if they fight you, then kill them.﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿and do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you﴾ without an alif in these words, from killing (al-qatl), meaning: do not kill any of them. The Arabs say: "We killed the sons of so-and-so," while only some of them were killed. The rest recited with an alif, from fighting (al-qital). This was at the beginning of Islam: it was not permitted to initiate fighting in the Sacred City. Then it became abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. This is the saying of Qatadah. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: His saying ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾ means: wherever you find them, in the non-sacred area and in the Sacred Precinct. This verse became abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. Then the verse of the sword in Bara'ah abrogated it, so it is both abrogating and abrogated (nasikh and mansukh). Mujahid and a group said: this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and it is not permitted to initiate fighting in the Sacred Precinct.

﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾.

﴿But if they desist﴾ from fighting and disbelief, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: Forgiving of what has passed, Merciful to the servants.

﴿And fight them﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾, meaning shirk. That is, fight them until they embrace Islam, for nothing is accepted from an idolater except Islam; if he refuses, he is to be killed. ﴿And religion is for Allah﴾, meaning obedience and worship are for ﴿Allah﴾ alone, so nothing is worshipped besides Him.

Nafi' said: A man came to Ibn Umar during the fitnah of Ibn al-Zubayr and said: "What prevents you from going out?" He said: "What prevents me is that Allah, Exalted is He, has forbidden the blood of my brother." He said: "Do you not hear what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ (49:9)?" He said: "O son of my brother, for me to be reproached with this verse and not fight is more beloved to me than to be reproached with the verse in which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally﴾ (4:93)." He said: "Did not Allah say: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾?" He said: "We did that during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when Islam was few, and a man would be tested in his religion: either they would kill him or torture him, until Islam became widespread and there was no fitnah, and the whole religion was for Allah. But you want to fight until there is fitnah and the religion is for other than Allah."

And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: A man said to Ibn Umar: "How do you view fighting in fitnah?" He said: "Do you know what fitnah is? Muhammad (ﷺ) used to fight the polytheists, and entering among them was a fitnah. Your fighting is not for kingship."

﴿But if they desist﴾ from disbelief and embrace Islam, ﴿then there is no hostility﴾, meaning no path (of aggression), ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Its support is His saying: ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me﴾ (28:28). The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: al-'udwan is injustice (zulm), meaning: if they embrace Islam, there is no plundering, no taking captive, and no killing, ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾ who remain upon polytheism. What is done to the people of polytheism of these things is not injustice, and it is called 'udwan by way of recompense and reciprocity, as He said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ (2:194), and as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40). The disbeliever is called a wrongdoer (zalim) because he places worship in other than its proper place.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 194–195:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾. It was revealed concerning the ʿUmrat al-Qadaʾ (the make-up ʿUmrah). That is because the Prophet ﷺ set out as a pilgrim (for ʿUmrah) in Dhu al-Qaʿdah, but the polytheists prevented him from the House at al-Hudaybiyah. So he made a treaty with the people of Makkah that he would return that year and come back the following year, and would then perform his ʿUmrah. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned that year, and he came back the following year in Dhu al-Qaʿdah and performed his ʿUmrah in the sixth year after the Hijrah... (rather, the seventh year of the Hijrah). That is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month﴾, meaning Dhu al-Qaʿdah in which you entered Makkah and performed your ʿUmrah in the seventh year, ﴿for the sacred month﴾, meaning Dhu al-Qaʿdah in which you were prevented from the House in the sixth year. ﴿And the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾. Ḥurumāt is the plural of ḥurmah. He used the plural because He meant the sanctity of the sacred month, the sacred land, and the sanctity of the state of ihram. Qiṣāṣ (retaliation) means equality and likeness, namely that the doer is treated as he treated others. It was also said that this refers to the matter of fighting, meaning: if they begin fighting you in the sacred month, then fight them in it, for it is retaliation for what they did in it. ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾, and fight them ﴿in the same way as they have transgressed against you﴾. The recompense is named with the name of the initial act for the sake of parallelism in speech, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (42:40). ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is with the God-fearing﴾. 28/b

﴿And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction; and do good. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾ (195)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾. By it He means jihad, and every good that is in the way of Allah, but its unqualified use is understood to refer to jihad. ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. It was said: the bāʾ in His saying ﴿with your own hands﴾ is superfluous, meaning: "and do not throw your hands", that is, your selves, ﴿into destruction﴾. He expressed the self by the hands, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ (42:30), meaning what you have earned. It was also said that the bāʾ is in its proper place, and there is an ellipsis, meaning: do not throw yourselves, with your hands, into destruction, that is, perdition. It was also said: tahlukah is everything whose outcome is perdition, meaning: do not undertake that. It was also said: tahlukah is what can be guarded against, while halak is what cannot be guarded against. The Arabs do not say of a person "alqā biyadihi" (he threw his hand) except in the case of polytheism.

They differed in the interpretation of this verse. Some of them said: this is about stinginess and abandoning spending. It means: ﴿do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ by abandoning spending in the way of Allah. This is the statement of Ḥudhayfah, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah, ʿIkrimah and ʿAṭāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbas said concerning this verse: Spend in the way of Allah even if you have nothing but an arrow or a feathered shaft, and let none of you say, "I do not find anything." Al-Suddi said concerning it: Spend in the way of Allah even if it is a rope-tie, and do not say, "I have nothing." Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil ibn Ḥayyan said: When Allah commanded spending, a man said, "We have been commanded to spend in the way of Allah, and if we spent our wealth we would remain poor." So Allah revealed this verse. Mujahid said concerning it: Let not the fear of poverty prevent you from spending in a right cause.

We were told by Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ṣāliḥī, who was told by Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ḥīrī, who was told by Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Duḥaym al-Shaybānī, who was told by Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim ibn Abī Gharzah, who was told by Abū Ghassān, who was told by Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Wāsiṭī, who was told by Wāṣil, mawlā of Abū ʿUyaynah, from Bashshār ibn Abī Sayf, from al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿIyāḍ ibn Ghuḍayf, who said: We came to Abū ʿUbaydah to visit him when he was ill, and he said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever spends a surplus expenditure in the way of Allah, it is seven hundred (times rewarded). And whoever spends on his family, the good deed is (rewarded) tenfold." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Fada'il al-Jihad, chapter: What has come concerning the virtue of spending in the way of Allah, 5/254, and he said: this is a ḥasan ḥadith, which we know only through the ḥadith of al-Rukayn ibn Rabiʿ. In al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasaʾi from Khuraym ibn Fatik, without the addition ("and whoever spends on his family..."). Narrated by al-Nasaʾi in al-Jihad, chapter: The virtue of spending in the way of Allah, 6/49. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah 10/359 from Khuraym, and its isnad is sahih.]

Zayd ibn Aslam said: Some men used to go out on expeditions without provision, so either they were cut off, or they were dependents. So Allah commanded them to spend on themselves in the way of Allah. Whoever has nothing to spend should not go out without provision or food, and thus throw himself with his own hands into destruction. So tahlukah is that one perishes from hunger and thirst or from walking. It was also said: the verse was revealed concerning abandoning jihad. Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī said: It was revealed concerning us, the group of the Anṣar. That is because when Allah exalted His religion and gave victory to His Messenger, we said among ourselves: "We have left our families and our wealth until Islam spread and Allah gave victory to His Prophet. So if we return to our families and our wealth, and remain there, and repair what has been lost of them..." Then Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. So tahlukah is remaining with family and property and abandoning jihad. Abū Ayyūb continued to fight in the way of Allah until his last campaign, which he undertook at Constantinople in the time of Muʿawiyah, where he died and was buried at the base of the walls of Constantinople, while they were seeking rain through him.

It is narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever dies without having fought and without having resolved in his soul to fight, dies upon a branch of hypocrisy." [Narrated by Muslim in al-Imarah, chapter: The blame of one who dies without fighting and without resolving to fight, no. 1910, 3/1517. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah 10/375.]

Muhammad ibn Sirin and ʿUbaydah al-Salmani said: Throwing oneself into destruction is despair of the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He. Abu Qilabah said: It is the man who commits a sin and says, "I am ruined, there is no repentance for me," so he despairs of the mercy of Allah and plunges into sins. So Allah, Exalted is He, forbade them from that. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ (12:87).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do good﴾ [meaning: do good in your deeds and your conduct, and be generous to the poor], ﴿indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾. [Dropped from (B).]
