Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 3):

His words, exalted is He, ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾. 'Alqamah and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited ﴿And establish the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾. The scholars differed concerning the completion (itmam, fulfilling in full) of the two. Some of them said: it is that one completes them with their rites (manasik, sing. mansak, acts of worship), their limits (hudud), and their recommended practices (sunan). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Alqamah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Mujahid. The pillars (arkan, sing. rukn, essential elements) of the Hajj are five: the ihram (the sacred state entered into for pilgrimage), standing at 'Arafah, the tawaf al-ziyarah (the circumambulation of visitation), the sa'i (going back and forth) between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and shaving the head or cutting the hair. The Hajj has two stages of exiting the state of ihram (tahallul, lifting the prohibitions). The causes of tahallul are three: throwing the pebbles at Jamrat al-'Aqabah on the Day of Sacrifice, the tawaf al-ziyarah, and shaving. When two of these three things have been done, the first tahallul is attained, and with all three the second tahallul is attained. After the first tahallul, one may do everything that is forbidden in ihram except women; after the second, one may do everything.

The pillars of the 'Umrah are four: the ihram, the tawaf around the House (the Ka'bah), the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and shaving. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Tawus said: the completion of the Hajj and the 'Umrah is that you enter into ihram for both separately, as independent acts, beginning from the outskirts (duwayrah) of your household. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, and he said: it is that you enter into ihram for them from the outskirts of your household. The same is related from Ibn Mas'ud. Qatadah said: the completion of the 'Umrah is that it be performed outside the months of Hajj. [If it was in the months of Hajj] [[Omitted in manuscript A.]] and then he stayed until he performed Hajj, then it is a tamattu' (combining 'Umrah and Hajj in one journey), and upon him in it is a sacrificial animal (hady) if he finds one, or fasting if he does not find a sacrificial animal. The completion of the Hajj is that all its rites are performed, so that he does not incur an obligation of a sacrifice (dam) because of qiran (combining Hajj and 'Umrah under one ihram) or tamattu'. Al-Dahhak said: its completion is that the expenses be lawful, and that one refrain from what Allah has forbidden. Sufyan al-Thawri said: its completion is that you set out from your household for the two alone, and do not set out for trade or for some other need.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "The delegations are many, and the pilgrims are few." The community (ummah) agreed on the obligation of the Hajj upon whoever is able to make his way to it. They differed concerning the obligation of the 'Umrah. Most of the people of knowledge held that it is obligatory, and this is the view of 'Umar, 'Ali and Ibn 'Umar. 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "By Allah, the 'Umrah is indeed the companion of the Hajj in the Book of Allah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾." This is also the view of 'Ata', Tawus, Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. al-Thawri and al-Shafi'i in his more sound of his two opinions adopted it. Others held that it is a sunnah (recommended practice), and this is the view of Jabir, and al-Shafi'i [[In (manuscript) B: al-Sha'bi.]] said likewise, and Malik and the people of Iraq also adopted it. They interpreted His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾ to mean: complete them once you have entered upon them; as for beginning them, it is voluntary. Those who did not make them obligatory argued by what is related from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the 'Umrah: "Is it obligatory?" He said: ﴿No, and that you perform 'Umrah is better for you﴾. [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi: in the Book of Hajj, chapter: What has come concerning whether the 'Umrah is obligatory or not, 3/679, and he said: this is a hasan sahih hadith. But there is a question about his authentication of it, for its chain includes al-Hajjaj ibn Arta'ah, who is weak, and perhaps al-Tirmidhi's authentication of this report is due to its coming through other routes. Ahmad related it: 3/316, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Sunan and said: what is preserved from Jabir is that it is mawquf (ending with a companion), as Ibn Jurayj related it; and it is related from Jabir with the opposite, marfu' (traced to the Prophet), from the hadith of Ibn Lahi'ah, and both are weak (see al-Talkhis al-Habir: 2/226).]] The first view is more sound. The meaning of His saying, ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾ is: begin them. Once you have entered upon them, then complete them. So it is a command to begin and to complete, i.e., establish them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ (2:187), meaning: begin it and complete it.

Abu Mansur al-Sam'ani informed us, Abu Ja'far al-Rayani informed us, Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us, Ibn Abi Shaybah informed us, Abu Khalid al-Ahmar informed us, from 'Amr ibn Qays, from 'Asim, from Shaqiq, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'Umrah, for they remove poverty and sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron, gold and silver; and the accepted Hajj has no reward but Paradise." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Hajj, chapter: What has come concerning the reward of Hajj and 'Umrah, 3/538-539, and he said: hasan sahih gharib. It is also related by al-Nasa'i in the Book of Hajj, chapter: The merit of following up Hajj with 'Umrah: 5/115-116. Ibn Majah related it in the Book of Rites, chapter: The merit of Hajj and 'Umrah: 2/964, no. (2887). Ibn Khuzaymah related it in the Book of Rites, chapter: The command to follow up Hajj with 'Umrah, 4/130. Ahmad related it: 1/387, 3/446-447, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah. The author (al-Baghawi) in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/7 from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. It is sahih through its corroborations.]] Ibn 'Umar said: "There is no one among the creatures of Allah but that upon him are two obligations, Hajj and 'Umrah, if he is able to make his way to them, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾." He added after that: "Whatever is beyond that is better as a voluntary act." The community agreed that the Hajj and the 'Umrah may be performed in three ways: ifrad (performing Hajj alone), tamattu' and qiran. The form of ifrad is that one performs the Hajj alone, then after finishing it performs 'Umrah. The form of tamattu' is that one performs 'Umrah in the months of Hajj, then after finishing the acts of 'Umrah, enters into ihram for Hajj from Mecca and performs Hajj in that same year. The form of qiran is that one enters into ihram for Hajj and 'Umrah together, or enters into ihram for 'Umrah and then adds Hajj to it before beginning the tawaf, thereby becoming a qarin (one who combines). They differed concerning which of these forms is the best. A group held that ifrad is the best, then tamattu', then qiran; this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i, based on what Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us, Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us, Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Abu al-Aswad Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal, from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. Some of us entered into ihram for 'Umrah, some for Hajj and 'Umrah together, and some for Hajj. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered into ihram for Hajj. As for those who entered into ihram for 'Umrah, they exited the state; but those who entered into ihram for Hajj, or combined Hajj and 'Umrah, did not exit it until the Day of Sacrifice." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of Hajj, chapter: Tamattu', qiran and ifrad in Hajj, 3/421, and the wording is his. Muslim related it: in the Book of Hajj, chapter: Explanation of the modes of entering into ihram, no. (1211), 2/870. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/63.]]

Abu al-Hasan 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib informed us, 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us, Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm informed us, al-Rabi' informed us, al-Shafi'i informed us, Muslim informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was narrating about the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "We set out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intending only the Hajj, and we did not know anything else, nor did we know of 'Umrah." [[Part of a hadith about the Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), narrated by Muslim in the Book of Hajj, chapter: The Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ), no. (1218), 2/886. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/65.]] It is related from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) performed ifrad for the Hajj. [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi: in the Book of Hajj, chapter: What has come concerning ifrad of Hajj, 2/552-553. Also al-Daraqutni, 2/239. In its chain is 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi' al-Sa'igh, who is very weak; see Sunan al-Daraqutni with its commentary, 2/38. Muslim in his Sahih in the Book of Hajj, chapter: On ifrad in Hajj, related from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We entered into ihram with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for Hajj alone, at al-Jam' (Muzdalifah)"; and in the narration of Ibn 'Awn: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered into ihram for Hajj alone," 2/905.]] Others held that qiran is the best; this is the view of al-Thawri and the Companions of opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y, the Hanafis). They argued by what Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Salihi informed us, Abu Sa'id Muhammad ibn Musa al-Sayrafi informed us, Abu al-'Abbas Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Asamm informed us, Muhammad ibn Hisham ibn Mulas al-Numayri informed us, Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari informed us, Humayd informed us, who said: Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered into ihram and said: 'Here I am, [O Allah], for Hajj and 'Umrah.'" [[Narrated by Muslim: in the Book of Hajj, chapter: On ifrad and qiran of Hajj and 'Umrah, no. (1232), 2/905.]]

Others held that tamattu' is the best; this is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and they argued by what 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Mulayhi informed us, Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, Yahya ibn Bukayr informed us, al-Layth informed us, from 'Uqayl, from Ibn Shihab, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed tamattu' in the Farewell Pilgrimage, combining 'Umrah with Hajj. He drove the sacrificial animal (hady) with him from Dhu al-Hulayfah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began by entering into ihram for 'Umrah, then entered into ihram for Hajj. So the people performed tamattu' with the Prophet (ﷺ), combining 'Umrah with Hajj. Among the people were those who brought a sacrificial animal and drove it with them, and among them were those who did not bring one. When the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Mecca, he said to the people: 'Whoever among you has brought a sacrificial animal, he may not exit from anything that has been forbidden to him until he completes his Hajj. And whoever among you has not brought one, let him perform the tawaf around the House, and perform the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and shorten his hair and exit the state; then let him enter into ihram for Hajj. Whoever does not find a sacrificial animal, let him fast three days during the Hajj, and seven when he returns to his family.' So he (the Prophet) performed the tawaf when he arrived in Mecca, and touched the Corner (al-Rukn) first, then did the ramal (quick pace) for three circuits and walked for four. Then, when he had finished his tawaf at the House, he prayed two rak'ahs at the Station (al-Maqam) of Abraham, then said the salam and turned away. He came to al-Safa and performed seven circuits between al-Safa and al-Marwah. Then he did not exit from anything that had been forbidden to him until he had completed his Hajj. He sacrificed his animal on the Day of Sacrifice, and went forth (ifadah) and performed the tawaf at the House, then exited from everything that had been forbidden to him. Whoever among the people brought a sacrificial animal and drove it did as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did."

It is related from 'Urwah that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, informed him about the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning his tamattu' with the 'Umrah to the Hajj, and that the people performed tamattu' with him in the same way as Salim told me, from Ibn 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[Part of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Hajj, chapter: Whoever drives the camels with him, 3/539. And Muslim in the Book of Hajj, chapter: The obligation of a sacrifice upon the one who performs tamattu', no. (1227), 2/901. The author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/66-68.]]

Our shaykh, the Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The reports have differed concerning the ihram of the Prophet (ﷺ), as we have mentioned. Al-Shafi'i, in his book Ikhtilaf al-Ahadith (Differences of the Hadiths), mentioned a concise statement: that among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there were those who performed ifrad, qiran and tamattu', and each of them took the command of his rite from him and acted upon his instruction. So all of it was attributed to him, in the sense that he commanded it and permitted it. In the Arabic language it is permissible to attribute an action to the one who commanded it, just as it is permissible to attribute it to the one who performed it, as one says: "So-and-so built a house," meaning that he commanded its building; and as it is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) stoned Ma'iz, while in fact he only commanded his stoning. Al-Shafi'i preferred ifrad on the basis of the reports of Jabir, 'A'ishah and Ibn 'Umar, and he gave them precedence over the reports of others, because of Jabir's early companionship with the Prophet (ﷺ), the excellent and complete transmission of his account from the beginning to the end of the story of the Farewell Pilgrimage, and because of the excellence of 'A'ishah's memorization, may Allah be pleased with her, and Ibn 'Umar's closeness to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Shafi'i, in "Ikhtilaf al-Hadith" (Differences in the Hadith), inclined toward tamattu' (the combined performance of 'umrah and hajj), and said: "Of all the differences [of opinion], none is easier than this one, although error in it is blameworthy, because it is permissible: the Book, then the Sunnah, then what I know of no disagreement on, [show] that tamattu' with 'umrah followed by hajj, ifrad (performing hajj alone), and qiran (combining hajj and 'umrah under one ihram) are all permissible." He said: "Whoever says that he performed ifrad of hajj is likely to have said so on the basis of what he does not know of the scholars whom he met, [but] not of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, [namely] that no one remains in the state of hajj except that he began his ihram with hajj." [[See: Ikhtilaf al-Hadith by al-Shafi'i, in the margin of al-Umm: 7/404-409.]]

The Shaykh, the Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Among the things that indicate that he (the Prophet ﷺ) performed tamattu' is that the reports from Ibn 'Umar and 'Aishah conflict. We have been related from Ibn Shihab, from Salim, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed tamattu' in the Farewell Pilgrimage, with 'umrah followed by hajj." [[Part of a hadith of Ibn 'Umar mentioned earlier, in the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).]] Ibn Shihab also said, from 'Urwah, that 'Aishah informed him about the Prophet ﷺ [[Omitted from "A".]] regarding his tamattu' with 'umrah followed by hajj, so the people performed tamattu' with him, in the same manner as Salim informed me from Ibn 'Umar. Ibn 'Abbas said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "This is an 'umrah by which we have enjoyed (istamta'na)."

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said regarding the mut'ah (tamattu'): "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did it, and we did it with him."

The Shaykh, the Imam, said: What is related from Jabir, that he said: "We set out intending only hajj" — does not contradict tamattu', because their departure was with the intention of hajj; then some of them advanced the 'umrah, and some of them began their talbiyah with hajj, until the Prophet ﷺ commanded him to make it a mut'ah (tamattu').

His Exalted saying: ﴿And if you are prevented﴾. The scholars differed concerning the ihsar (being prevented) which permits the muhrim to exit (tahallul) from his ihram. A group held that every obstacle that prevents him from reaching the Sacred House, and the intent of his ihram, whether an enemy, illness, injury, loss of provisions, or the straying of his mount, permits him to exit. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr. Sufyan al-Thawri and the people of Iraq also held this view, and they said: "Because ihsar in the speech of the Arabs means the detention (habs) of an illness or sickness."

Al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: Whatever results from illness or loss of provisions is said of as uhsira, so he is muhsar; and whatever results from the detention of an enemy or imprisonment is said of as hasara, so he is mahsur. They treated the detention by an enemy as ihsar here by analogy with illness, since it has the same meaning. They argued with what is related from 'Ikrimah, from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever is broken or lame has exited (ihram), and he must perform hajj in the following year." [[Related by Abu Dawud in al-Manasik, chapter on al-Ihsar, 2/368; al-Mundhiri reported its authentication (tahsin) from al-Tirmidhi and affirmed it, and attributed it to al-Nasa'i. Also al-Tirmidhi in al-Hajj, chapter: What has come concerning one who assumes ihram for hajj and then is broken or lame, 4/8, and he said: this is a hasan hadith. Also Ibn Majah in al-Manasik, chapter al-Muhsar, no. (3077), 2/1028; Ahmad, 3/450, from al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr al-Ansari; Ibn Hajar in al-Fath, 4/7, attributed it to Ibn al-Sakan in Kitab al-Sahabah and said: it is not far from being sound. Also al-Darimi in al-Manasik, chapter on the muhsar by an enemy, 2/61. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah, 7/288.]]

'Ikrimah said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah, and they both said: "It is true." Another group held that he is not permitted to exit except by the detention of an enemy. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is no ihsar except the ihsar of an enemy." Its meaning is also related from Ibn 'Umar and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and it is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq also held this view, and they said: "Hasr and ihsar have one meaning."

Tha'lab said: The Arabs say: "I hasartu the man from his need, so he is mahsur," and "al-'aduw ahsarahu" when he prevents him from travelling, so he is muhsar. They argued that the revelation of this verse was concerning the incident of al-Hudaybiyah, and that was a detention from the side of the enemy. This is indicated by His Exalted saying in the context of the verse: ﴿But when you are secure﴾, and security is from fear. They weakened the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr by what is established from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "There is no hasr except the hasr of the enemy." Some of them interpreted it to mean that he exits by breaking or lameness only if he had stipulated that at the contracting of the ihram, as it is related that Dubaʻah bint al-Zubayr was ill, and the Prophet ﷺ said to her: "Perform hajj, and stipulate, and say: O Allah, my release is wherever You detain me." [[Related by Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter: The permissibility of the muhrim stipulating release by an excuse such as illness and the like, no. (1208), 2/869.]]

Then the muhsar exits by slaughtering the hady (offering) and shaving the head. The hady is a sheep, and this is what is meant by His Exalted saying: ﴿then what is easy of the offering﴾.

The place of its slaughter is where he was prevented, according to most of the scholars, because the Prophet ﷺ slaughtered the offering there in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. A group held that the muhsar remains in his ihram and sends his offering to the Haram, and arranges with someone to slaughter it there, and then he exits; this is the view of the people of Iraq.

Opinion differed regarding the muhsar who does not find a hady. In one view, there is no substitute for it, so he exits, and the hady remains as a debt upon him until he finds one. The second view: there is a substitute. On this basis, opinion differed: in one view, he must fast the (three days of) tamattu'; in another view, the sheep is valued in dirhams, and the dirhams are turned into food which is given in charity; if he is unable to feed, he fasts one day for each mudd of food, as in the expiation (fidyah) for perfume and clothing. For when the muhrim needs to cover his head against heat or cold, or to wear a shirt, or is ill and needs to treat himself with a medicine containing perfume, he may do so, but he owes a fidyah. His fidyah is in graduated order: he must slaughter a sheep; if he does not find one, he values the sheep in dirhams, and buys food with the dirhams and gives it in charity; if he is unable, he fasts one day for each mudd.

Then, if the muhsar's ihram was for a purpose that had become fixed upon him, that purpose remains a debt upon him. If it was for a voluntary hajj, then is there a qada' (making up) upon him? They differed on this. A group held that there is no qada' upon him, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. A people held that he must make qada', and this is the view of Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i and the Ashab al-Ra'y (the Hanafis).

His Exalted saying: ﴿then what is easy of the offering﴾ [i.e., upon him is what is easy of the offering] and its position is in the nominative case (raf'). It was also said: "ma" is in the accusative position, meaning: "so offer what is easy." Al-hady is the plural of hadiyyah, and it is the name for everything that is brought as an offering to the House of Allah seeking nearness to Him. "What is easy of the offering" is a sheep. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, because it is closest to ease. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: its highest is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its lowest is a sheep.

His Exalted saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. They differed regarding the place (mahall) where the muhsar's offering reaches, so that he may exit. Some said: it is its slaughter at the place where he was prevented, whether it was in the hill (outside the Haram) or in the Haram, and the meaning of "its place" is: where its slaughter and eating are lawful.

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us, Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad informed us, 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, Ma'mar informed us, al-Zuhri informed me, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr informed me, from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, concerning the incident of al-Hudaybiyah, who said: When he finished the matter of the document, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his Companions: "Get up, sacrifice, then shave." By Allah, no man among them rose until he said that three times. When none of them rose, he entered upon Umm Salamah and mentioned to her what he had encountered from the people. Umm Salamah said: "O Prophet of Allah, do you wish for that? Go out, then do not speak to anyone of them with a word until you sacrifice your camel and call your barber, and he shaves you." So he went out and did not speak to any of them until he did that: he sacrificed his camel and called his barber, who shaved him. When they saw that, they rose and sacrificed, and some of them began shaving others, until some of them nearly killed others out of grief. [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Shurut, chapter: Conditions in jihad and reconciliation with the people of war, 5/329-333.]]

Others said: The place of the muhsar's offering is the Haram. If he is performing hajj, its place is the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr); and if he is performing 'umrah, its place is the day his offering reaches the Haram.

His Exalted saying: ﴿And whoever among you is ill, or has an injury of the head﴾: its meaning is: do not shave your heads during the state of ihram, except that you are compelled to shave them due to illness or an injury to the head from vermin or headache. ﴿then a ransom﴾: there is an implied element in it, meaning: so he shaves, then upon him is a ransom. It was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah.

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us, Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, al-Hasan ibn Khalaf informed us, Ishaq ibn Yusuf informed us, from Abu Bishr Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla related to me, from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw him while lice were falling onto his face, and he said: "Do your vermin harm you?" He said: "Yes." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded him to shave while he was at al-Hudaybiyah, and he did not make clear to them that they would exit (ihram) there while they were hoping to enter Makkah. Then Allah revealed the ransom, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded him to feed a faraq (measure) among six poor persons, or sacrifice a sheep, or fast three days. [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Muhsar, chapter on His saying (Whoever among you is ill), 4/12; and Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter on the permissibility of the muhrim shaving his head, no. (1201), 2/860.]]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿then a ransom of fasting﴾, that is, three days; ﴿or charity﴾, that is, three *sa'* (a measure of volume) for six poor people, half a *sa'* for each poor person; ﴿or a sacrifice﴾. Its singular is *nasikah* (a sacrificial animal), that is, a slaughtered animal. The best of these is a camel, the middle is a cow, and the least is a sheep, and he may slaughter whichever of them he wishes. This ransom is by choice within a fixed measure, so he may choose between slaughtering, fasting, or giving charity. Every offering or food that is obligatory upon the *muhrim* (one in the state of ihram) must be in Makkah and given in charity to the poor of the Haram, except for an offering obligatory upon the *muhsar* (one prevented from completing the pilgrimage), who slaughters it where he was prevented. As for fasting, he may fast wherever he wishes.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then when you are secure﴾, that is, from your fear and recovered from your illness, ﴿then whoever enjoys [the benefit of] umrah until hajj, [let him give] what is feasible of offering﴾. The scholars differed concerning this *tamattu'* (the combining of umrah and hajj in one journey, with release from ihram between them). Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr held that its meaning is: whoever is prevented until the hajj has passed him and he has not released himself from ihram, then he comes to Makkah, exits his ihram by performing an umrah, and enjoys this release through that umrah until the following year, then performs hajj. He is thus a *mutamatti'* (one who enjoys this release) until his second ihram in the coming year.

Some others said its meaning is: ﴿Then when you are secure﴾ and you have released yourselves from your ihram after being prevented, without having performed the umrah, and you postponed the umrah until the next year, so you performed umrah in the months of hajj, then you released yourselves and enjoyed your release until the hajj, then you entered ihram for hajj. Then ﴿what is feasible of offering﴾ is incumbent upon you. This is the view of Alqamah, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abbas, Ata', and a group said: it refers to the man who arrives as a pilgrim performing umrah from one of the horizons (distant lands) during the months of hajj, completes his umrah, and remains in a state of release in Makkah until he starts the hajj from there, and performs hajj in that same year. He is thus one who enjoys the release from umrah until his ihram for hajj. So the meaning of *tamattu'* is enjoying, after exiting the umrah, what had been forbidden to him in ihram, until his ihram for hajj.

There are four conditions for the obligation of the offering of *tamattu'*. The first is that he enters ihram for umrah in the months of hajj. The second is that he performs hajj after completing the umrah in the same year. The third is that he enters ihram for hajj in Makkah and does not return to the *miqat* (the boundary point for ihram) for his ihram. The fourth is that he is not a resident of al-Masjid al-Haram. Whenever these conditions are met, he must give what is feasible of offering, which is the offering of a sheep that he slaughters on the Day of Sacrifice. If he slaughters it before that, after entering ihram for hajj, this is permitted according to some scholars, like the offerings for violations. Some others held that it is not permitted before the Day of Sacrifice, like the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever does not find [an offering], then fasting three days during hajj﴾, that is, fast three days. He fasts one day before *Tarwiyah* (the 8th of Dhu al-Hijjah), the day of Tarwiyah, and the day of Arafah. If he fasts before that, after entering ihram for hajj, it is permitted. It is not permitted on the Day of Sacrifice or the days of Tashriq according to most scholars. Some held that it is permitted to fast the three days of Tashriq. This is reported from Aisha, Ibn Umar, and Ibn al-Zubayr, and it is the view of Malik, al-Awza'i, Ahmad, and Ishaq.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and seven when you return﴾, that is, fast seven days when you return to your families and your land. If he fasts the seven before returning to his family, it is not permitted, and this is the view of most scholars. This is reported from Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. It was said that it is permitted to fast them after finishing the rites of hajj, and this is the meaning of the "return" mentioned in the verse.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is ten complete﴾. He mentioned it for emphasis, because the Arabs did not know how to calculate, so they needed extra explanation and further clarification. It was said: there is an inversion in it, meaning the fasting of ten days, three during hajj and seven when you return, ﴿is ten complete﴾. It was said: complete in reward and recompense. It was said: complete in that it is intended to be fasting in place of the offering. It was said: complete with its conditions and limits. It was said that its wording is a statement but its meaning is a command, meaning: complete them and do not reduce them. ﴿That﴾, that is, this ruling, ﴿is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾. The scholars differed concerning "present at al-Masjid al-Haram". Some people held that they are the people of Makkah, and this is the view of Malik. It was said: they are the people of the Haram, and Tawus among the Successors said this. Ibn Jurayj said: they are the people of Arafah, al-Raji', Dajnan, and Nakhlatan. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: whoever's homeland is within less than the distance for shortening prayer from Makkah is one of those present at al-Masjid al-Haram. Ikrimah said: they are those within the *miqat*. It was said: they are the people of the *miqat* and what is within it, and this is the view of the people of opinion. The offering for *qiran* (combining hajj and umrah in one ihram) is like the offering for *tamattu'*, and a Makkan who performs *qiran* or *tamattu'* has no offering obligation. Ikrimah said: Ibn Abbas was asked about the *tamattu'* of hajj, and he said: The Muhajirun, the Ansar, and the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) entered ihram in the Farewell Pilgrimage, and we entered ihram too. When we came to Makkah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Make your ihlal for hajj into umrah, except for whoever has garlanded the offering." So we circumambulated the House and between al-Safa and al-Marwah, we had relations with our wives, and we wore clothes. Then on the evening of Tarwiyah he commanded us to enter ihram for hajj. When we finish, our hajj is complete, and we owe an offering. Thus they combined two rites in one year, hajj and umrah. Allah sent this down in His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet, and He permitted it for people other than the people of Makkah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [[Narrated by al-Bukhari: in the Book of Hajj, chapter on the words of Allah the Exalted "That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram," 3/433.]].

Whoever misses the hajj, and missing it occurs by missing the standing at Arafah until dawn on the Day of Sacrifice, then he releases himself by performing umrah. He must make up the hajj in a later year, and the ransom is due, arranged and measured like the ransom of *tamattu'* and *qiran*.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us, Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us, Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Nafi', from Sulayman ibn Yasar, that Hannad ibn al-Aswad came on the Day of Sacrifice while Umar ibn al-Khattab was slaughtering his offering, and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, we made a mistake in the count. We thought that this day was the Day of Arafah." Umar said to him: "Go to Makkah, and you and those with you circumambulate the House, run between al-Safa and al-Marwah, slaughter an offering if you have one with you, then shave or trim your hair, then return. When next year comes, perform hajj and give offerings. Whoever does not find [an offering], then fasting three days during hajj and seven when you return" [[See: al-Muwatta': 1/383, and al-Bayhaqi connected it: 5/175, and the author (al-Baghawi) recorded it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/292.]].

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in performing the commands, ﴿and know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for committing what is forbidden.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 197–198 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾, meaning: the time of the Hajj is in well-known months. They are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah until the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Each of the two expressions is sound and there is no contradiction between them. Whoever says "ten" refers to the nights, and whoever says "nine" refers to the days, since the last of its days is the Day of 'Arafah, which is the ninth day. He said "months" in the plural form, although they are two months and part of a third, because it is a period of time, and the Arabs call a period complete even by its little or its much. The Arabs say, "I came to you on Thursday," when he came only during an hour of it, and they say, "I visited you this year," when he visited only during part of it. It is also said that two or more is a group (jama'ah), because the meaning of plurality is the joining of one thing to another. If two may be called a group, then two and part of a third may be called a group. Allah, may He be exalted, has referred to two persons with the plural form, saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ (66:4), meaning: your two hearts. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and others said: He meant by "the months" Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah in their entirety, because there remain for the pilgrim matters after 'Arafah that he must perform, such as the stoning (al-Rami), the sacrifice (al-Dhabh), shaving (al-Halq), the Tawaf of Ziyarah (the visiting circumambulation), and staying overnight in Mina. So they were in the legal status of the plural.

﴿Whoever undertakes the Hajj therein﴾, meaning: whoever obligates the Hajj upon himself by entering the state of ihram (the sacred state of consecration) and by the talbiyah (the call "Labbayk"). In this is evidence that whoever enters ihram for Hajj outside the months of Hajj, his ihram for Hajj is not valid. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir, and 'Ata', Tawus and Mujahid also said so, and al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i held it. Others said that his ihram is valid for 'Umrah (the lesser pilgrimage), because Allah, may He be exalted, singled out these months for the purpose of Hajj, so if it were valid in other than them, there would be no benefit in this specification, just as He linked the prayers to their appointed times. Then whoever enters ihram for an obligatory prayer before its time has entered, his ihram is not valid for the obligatory prayer. A group held that his ihram for Hajj is valid, and this is the view of Malik, al-Thawri, and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with them. As for 'Umrah, all the days of the year are suitable for it, unless one is already engaged in Hajj. It is narrated from Anas that he was in Makkah, and when his head was shaved, he would go out and perform 'Umrah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity (rafath) nor transgression (fusuq)﴾. Ibn Kathir and the people of Basra recited ﴿fa-la rafathun wa la fusuqun﴾ with a nominative ending and tanwin (nunation) on both words. The others recited them with the accusative without tanwin, like His saying, ﴿nor disputing during the Hajj﴾. Abu Ja'far recited all of them with the nominative and tanwin.

They differed concerning rafath. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Umar said it is sexual intercourse (al-jima'). This is also the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Qatadah, Ikrimah, al-Rabi' and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: rafath is sexual intercourse with women, kissing, caressing, and alluding to them with obscene speech. Husayn ibn Qays said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, took hold of the tail of his camel and began to twist it while he was driving it and saying:

"And they walk with us in gentle murmuring,
If the birds speak truly, we will have intercourse."

I said to him: "Do you engage in rafath while you are in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is only what is said in the presence of women." Tawus said: [[Narrated by Ibn Jarir with a sound chain: 4/127.]] Rafath is alluding to women about intercourse and mentioning it in front of them. 'Ata' said: rafath is a man's saying to a woman while in the state of ihram, "When I come out of ihram, I will have intercourse with you." It is also said: rafath is obscenity and foul speech.

As for fusuq: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is all acts of disobedience. This is the view of Tawus, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Rabi', and al-Qurazi. Ibn 'Umar said: it is what the muhrim (one in ihram) is forbidden from doing during ihram, such as killing game, cutting the nails, removing hair, and what is similar to these. Ibrahim, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: it is cursing (al-sibab), based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Cursing a Muslim is transgression (fusuq), and fighting him is disbelief (kufr)." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Iman, chapter on the believer's fear that his deeds may be nullified, 1/110. Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Cursing a Muslim is transgression and fighting him is disbelief," no. (116), 1/81. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 1/76.]] Al-Dahhak said it is calling people by offensive nicknames, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames. How bad is the name of transgression after faith﴾ (49:11).

'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: Adam informed us, saying: Sayyar Abu al-Hakam informed us, saying: I heard Abu Hazim say: I heard Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, say: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Whoever performs Hajj for the sake of Allah, and does not engage in rafath nor commit fusuq, will return as on the day his mother bore him." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Hajj, chapter on the excellence of the accepted Hajj, 3/382. Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter on the excellence of Hajj and 'Umrah and the Day of 'Arafah, no. (1350), 2/983. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 7/4.]]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor disputing during the Hajj﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: jidal (disputing) is that a person contends with his companion and argues with him until he angers him. This is the view of 'Amr ibn Dinar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, 'Ata' and Qatadah. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: it is that some of them say, "Hajj is today," and others say, "Hajj is tomorrow." al-Qurazi said: When Quraysh gathered in Mina, these said, "Our Hajj is more complete than your Hajj," and those said, "Our Hajj is more complete than your Hajj." Muqatil said: it is that the Prophet ﷺ said to them during the Farewell Pilgrimage, when they had entered ihram for Hajj: "Make your intention for Hajj into 'Umrah, except for whoever has garlanded the sacrificial animal (hady)." They said: "How can we make it 'Umrah when we have already named it Hajj?" This was their disputing. Ibn Zayd said: They used to stand at different places, each one claiming that his place was the place of Ibrahim, and they disputed about it. It is also said: it is what the people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age) used to do. Some would stand at 'Arafah and some at Muzdalifah, and some would perform Hajj in Dhu al-Qa'dah and some in Dhu al-Hijjah, and each said, "What I did is the correct one." So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿nor disputing during the Hajj﴾, meaning: the matter of Hajj has been settled upon what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did, so there is no disagreement about it afterward. This is the meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed, time has returned to its original form as on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." [[A portion of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adahi, chapter on whoever said the Adha is on the Day of Sacrifice, 10/7. Muslim in al-Qasamah, chapter on the severity of the prohibition of blood, honor and property, no. (1679), 3/1305. And the author in Sharh al-Sunnah 7/216.]] Mujahid said: its meaning is that there is no doubt about Hajj being in Dhu al-Hijjah, so the nasi' (intercalation of months) was nullified. The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the apparent form of the verse is a negation, but its meaning is a prohibition, meaning: do not engage in rafath, do not commit fusuq, and do not dispute. It is like His saying: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, meaning: do not doubt. And ﴿whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾, meaning: nothing is hidden from Him, and He will reward you for it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And take provision, for indeed the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾. It was revealed concerning some people from Yemen who used to set out for Hajj without provisions and would say: "We rely upon Allah," and they would say: "We are going to the House of Allah, so will He not feed us?" When they arrived in Makkah they would ask people, and at times their situation would lead them to plunder and seizure. So Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And take provision﴾, meaning: that with which you will sustain yourselves and protect your faces (from asking). The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: it is cakes (al-ka'k), raisins, parched barley flour (sawiq), dates, and the like. ﴿For indeed the best provision is taqwa﴾, meaning: [protection] from asking and from plunder. ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, meaning: O people of intellects.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah informed us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: 'Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they regarded trading in them as sinful, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾, during the seasons of Hajj. Ibn 'Abbas recited it thus. [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Buyu': 4/321, and in al-Hajj 3/395, and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 8/3.]] It is also narrated from Abu Umamah al-Taymi who said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "We are a people who hire out animals on this route," meaning to Makkah, "and they claim that we have no Hajj." He said: "Do you not enter ihram as they enter ihram, circumambulate as they circumambulate, and stone (the pillars) as they stone?" I said: "Yes." He said: "You are a pilgrim (hajj)." A man came to the Prophet ﷺ asking him about what you asked me about, and he did not answer him with anything until Jibril descended with this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, meaning: no sin, ﴿in seeking bounty﴾, meaning: provision, ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: through trade in the seasons of Hajj. ﴿Then when you depart﴾, meaning: when you move on quickly. Al-Ifadah (departure) is moving on in large numbers, and its origin is from the Arabs' saying: afada al-rajulma', meaning: he poured out water. ﴿From 'Arafat﴾: it is the plural of 'Arafah, a plural that includes what is around it, even though it is a single place, like their saying: thawb akhlaq (a garment of many patches).

They differed about the reason the site was named 'Arafat and the day 'Arafah. 'Ata' said: Jibril, peace be upon him, used to show Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the rites and say: "Did you recognize (arafta)?" and he would say: "I recognized." So that place was named 'Arafat and the day 'Arafah. Al-Dahhak said: When Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to the earth, he landed in India and Hawwa' landed in Jeddah, and each of them began to seek the other. They met at 'Arafat on the Day of 'Arafah and recognized one another (ta'arafa), so the day was named the Day of 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat. Al-Suddi said: When Ibrahim proclaimed the Hajj among the people and they answered him with the talbiyah, and those who came to him came, Allah commanded him to go out to 'Arafat and described it to him, so he set out. When he reached the Jamrah [[In the two manuscripts it reads "al-shajarah" (the tree), and the correct reading is "al-jamrah" (the pillar), as occurs in most tafsir works such as Ibn Kathir.]] at 'Aqabah, Satan confronted him to turn him back, so he struck him with seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble, and (Satan) flew and landed at the second Jamrah. He struck it and said "Allahu akbar," and it flew and landed at the third Jamrah. He struck it and said "Allahu akbar." When Satan saw that he would not obey him, he departed. Ibrahim then went on until he came to Dhu al-Majaz. When he looked at it he did not recognize it, so he passed on, and it was named Dhu al-Majaz. Then he went on until he stood at 'Arafat and recognized it by its description, so the time was named 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat. When evening came, he drew near (izdalafa) to Jam', meaning he came close to Jam', so it was named Muzdalifah.

It is related from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw in his dream on the night of al-Tarwiyah that he was being commanded to slaughter his son. When he woke in the morning, he spent the whole day in deliberation (rawwā yawmahu ajmaʿa), meaning he pondered: is this vision from Allah the Exalted or from Satan? That day was therefore named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). Then he saw the same dream a second time, on the night of ʿArafah, and when he woke he knew that it was from Allah the Exalted, so that day was named the Day of ʿArafah. It is also said that it was named so because people acknowledge (yaʿtarifūn) their sins on that day. It is also said that it was named from al-ʿarf, which means fragrance (al-ṭīb). Mina was named so because blood is poured there (yumannā al-dam, i.e., yuṣabb), so there is dung and blood there, and the place is not pure, whereas ʿArafat is free of these and therefore pure.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So remember Allah﴾ through supplication and the talbiyah (the chant of "Labbayk"), ﴿at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram)﴾. This is the area between the two mountains of Muzdalifah, from the narrow passages (al-Ma'zimān) of ʿArafah to al-Maḥsar. The two narrow passages and al-Maḥsar are not part of the Mash'ar. It is called Mash'ar from al-shiʿār, which is the sign, because it is one of the markers of the Hajj. The root of ḥarām is from al-man' (prohibition): it is prohibited to do in it anything that has not been permitted. Muzdalifah is called Jam' because two prayers, the ʿIshā' and the Maghrib, are combined there, and the departure from ʿArafat takes place after sunset, while the departure from Jam' takes place before sunrise on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr).

Ṭāwūs said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to depart from ʿArafat before the sun set, and from Muzdalifah after the sun rose, and they would say: "Shine forth, Thabir!" [[A mountain between Makkah and Mina, on the right of one who enters Makkah from it.]] "so that we may raid." Allah delayed this and advanced that.

Abu al-Ḥasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Muṣʿab informed us, from Malik, from Musa ibn ʿUqbah, from Kurayb, the freed slave of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, from Usamah ibn Zayd, that he heard him say: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed from ʿArafah, and when he reached the mountain pass (al-Shiʿb) he dismounted and urinated, then performed ablution but did not complete it. I said to him: 'The prayer, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'The prayer is ahead of you.' So he mounted, and when he came to Muzdalifah he dismounted and performed ablution, completing it. Then the prayer was called, and he prayed the Maghrib. Then each person made his camel kneel at his own resting place. Then the ʿIshā' was called, and he prayed it, and he did not pray anything between them." [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Hajj, chapter "Dismounting between ʿArafah and Jamʿ," 3/519, and by Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "Departing from ʿArafat to Muzdalifah," no. (1280), 2/934.]]

Jabir said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed until he reached Muzdalifah, and there he prayed the Maghrib and the ʿIshā' with one adhan and two iqamahs, and he did not perform any voluntary prayer between them. Then he lay down until dawn broke, and he prayed the Fajr when the morning light had become clear, with one adhan and one iqamah. Then he rode al-Qaṣwāʾ until he came to al-Mash'ar al-Ḥarām, faced the qiblah, and supplicated, glorified (Allah), declared His greatness (takbīr), affirmed His oneness (tahlīl), and declared Him to be One (tawḥīd). He remained standing until the light had become very bright, then he departed before the sun rose." [[Related by Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "The Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ)," no. (1218), 2/886. The author (al-Baghawi) also mentions it in Sharh al-Sunnah, 7/65.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us: Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Zuhayr ibn Harb informed us: Wahb ibn Jarir informed us: my father informed us, from Yunus al-Aylī, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that Usamah ibn Zayd was riding behind the Prophet (ﷺ) from ʿArafah to Muzdalifah, and then he had al-Fadl ride behind him from Muzdalifah to Mina. He said: "Both of them said: The Prophet (ﷺ) continued to recite the talbiyah until he threw the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah." [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Hajj, chapter "Dismounting between ʿArafah and Jamʿ," 3/519. Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "The recommendation for a pilgrim to recite the talbiyah until he begins throwing the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah," no. (1281), 2/391, and the wording is his. The author also mentions it in Sharh al-Sunnah, 7/185.]]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: remember Him with monotheism and glorification, just as He has mentioned you with guidance, so He guided you to His religion and the rites of His Hajj. ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾. Meaning: indeed you were before that. It is also said: "You were not before it except among those astray." This is like His words: ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ (26:186), meaning: we do not think you are except among the liars. The pronoun in His words "before it" refers to the guidance. It is also said that it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an implicit reference to something not mentioned.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 197–198 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾, meaning: the time of the Hajj is in well-known months. They are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah until the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Each of the two expressions is sound and there is no contradiction between them. Whoever says "ten" refers to the nights, and whoever says "nine" refers to the days, since the last of its days is the Day of 'Arafah, which is the ninth day. He said "months" in the plural form, although they are two months and part of a third, because it is a period of time, and the Arabs call a period complete even by its little or its much. The Arabs say, "I came to you on Thursday," when he came only during an hour of it, and they say, "I visited you this year," when he visited only during part of it. It is also said that two or more is a group (jama'ah), because the meaning of plurality is the joining of one thing to another. If two may be called a group, then two and part of a third may be called a group. Allah, may He be exalted, has referred to two persons with the plural form, saying: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ (66:4), meaning: your two hearts. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and others said: He meant by "the months" Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and Dhu al-Hijjah in their entirety, because there remain for the pilgrim matters after 'Arafah that he must perform, such as the stoning (al-Rami), the sacrifice (al-Dhabh), shaving (al-Halq), the Tawaf of Ziyarah (the visiting circumambulation), and staying overnight in Mina. So they were in the legal status of the plural.

﴿Whoever undertakes the Hajj therein﴾, meaning: whoever obligates the Hajj upon himself by entering the state of ihram (the sacred state of consecration) and by the talbiyah (the call "Labbayk"). In this is evidence that whoever enters ihram for Hajj outside the months of Hajj, his ihram for Hajj is not valid. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir, and 'Ata', Tawus and Mujahid also said so, and al-Awza'i and al-Shafi'i held it. Others said that his ihram is valid for 'Umrah (the lesser pilgrimage), because Allah, may He be exalted, singled out these months for the purpose of Hajj, so if it were valid in other than them, there would be no benefit in this specification, just as He linked the prayers to their appointed times. Then whoever enters ihram for an obligatory prayer before its time has entered, his ihram is not valid for the obligatory prayer. A group held that his ihram for Hajj is valid, and this is the view of Malik, al-Thawri, and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with them. As for 'Umrah, all the days of the year are suitable for it, unless one is already engaged in Hajj. It is narrated from Anas that he was in Makkah, and when his head was shaved, he would go out and perform 'Umrah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity (rafath) nor transgression (fusuq)﴾. Ibn Kathir and the people of Basra recited ﴿fa-la rafathun wa la fusuqun﴾ with a nominative ending and tanwin (nunation) on both words. The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: it is cakes (al-ka'k), raisins, parched barley flour (sawiq), dates, and the like. ﴿For indeed the best provision is taqwa﴾, meaning: [protection] from asking and from plunder. ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, meaning: O people of intellects.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliḥi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah informed us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: 'Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they regarded trading in them as sinful, so Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾, during the seasons of Hajj. Ibn 'Abbas recited it thus. [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Buyu': 4/321, and in al-Hajj 3/395, and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 8/3.]] It is also narrated from Abu Umamah al-Taymi who said: I said to Ibn 'Umar: "We are a people who hire out animals on this route," meaning to Makkah, "and they claim that we have no Hajj." He said: "Do you not enter ihram as they enter ihram, circumambulate as they circumambulate, and stone (the pillars) as they stone?" I said: "Yes." He said: "You are a pilgrim (hajj)." A man came to the Prophet ﷺ asking him about what you asked me about, and he did not answer him with anything until Jibril descended with this verse: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, meaning: no sin, ﴿in seeking bounty﴾, meaning: provision, ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: through trade in the seasons of Hajj. ﴿Then when you depart﴾, meaning: when you move on quickly. Al-Ifadah (departure) is moving on in large numbers, and its origin is from the Arabs' saying: afada al-rajulma', meaning: he poured out water. ﴿From 'Arafat﴾: it is the plural of 'Arafah, a plural that includes what is around it, even though it is a single place, like their saying: thawb akhlaq (a garment of many patches).

They differed about the reason the site was named 'Arafat and the day 'Arafah. 'Ata' said: Jibril, peace be upon him, used to show Ibrahim, peace be upon him, the rites and say: "Did you recognize (arafta)?" and he would say: "I recognized." So that place was named 'Arafat and the day 'Arafah. Al-Dahhak said: When Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to the earth, he landed in India and Hawwa' landed in Jeddah, and each of them began to seek the other. They met at 'Arafat on the Day of 'Arafah and recognized one another (ta'arafa), so the day was named the Day of 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat. Al-Suddi said: When Ibrahim proclaimed the Hajj among the people and they answered him with the talbiyah, and those who came to him came, Allah commanded him to go out to 'Arafat and described it to him, so he set out. When he reached the Jamrah [[In the two manuscripts it reads "al-shajarah" (the tree), and the correct reading is "al-jamrah" (the pillar), as occurs in most tafsir works such as Ibn Kathir.]] at 'Aqabah, Satan confronted him to turn him back, so he struck him with seven pebbles, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble, and (Satan) flew and landed at the second Jamrah. He struck it and said "Allahu akbar," and it flew and landed at the third Jamrah. He struck it and said "Allahu akbar." When Satan saw that he would not obey him, he departed. Ibrahim then went on until he came to Dhu al-Majaz. When he looked at it he did not recognize it, so he passed on, and it was named Dhu al-Majaz. Then he went on until he stood at 'Arafat and recognized it by its description, so the time was named 'Arafah and the place 'Arafat. When evening came, he drew near (izdalafa) to Jam', meaning he came close to Jam', so it was named Muzdalifah.

It is related from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw in his dream on the night of al-Tarwiyah that he was being commanded to slaughter his son. When he woke in the morning, he spent the whole day in deliberation (rawwā yawmahu ajmaʿa), meaning he pondered: is this vision from Allah the Exalted or from Satan? That day was therefore named the Day of Tarwiyah (deliberation). Then he saw the same dream a second time, on the night of ʿArafah, and when he woke he knew that it was from Allah the Exalted, so that day was named the Day of ʿArafah. It is also said that it was named so because people acknowledge (yaʿtarifūn) their sins on that day. It is also said that it was named from al-ʿarf, which means fragrance (al-ṭīb). Mina was named so because blood is poured there (yumannā al-dam, i.e., yuṣabb), so there is dung and blood there, and the place is not pure, whereas ʿArafat is free of these and therefore pure.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So remember Allah﴾ through supplication and the talbiyah (the chant of "Labbayk"), ﴿at the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram)﴾. This is the area between the two mountains of Muzdalifah, from the narrow passages (al-Ma'zimān) of ʿArafah to al-Maḥsar. The two narrow passages and al-Maḥsar are not part of the Mash'ar. It is called Mash'ar from al-shiʿār, which is the sign, because it is one of the markers of the Hajj. The root of ḥarām is from al-man' (prohibition): it is prohibited to do in it anything that has not been permitted. Muzdalifah is called Jam' because two prayers, the ʿIshā' and the Maghrib, are combined there, and the departure from ʿArafat takes place after sunset, while the departure from Jam' takes place before sunrise on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr).

Ṭāwūs said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period) used to depart from ʿArafat before the sun set, and from Muzdalifah after the sun rose, and they would say: "Shine forth, Thabir!" [[A mountain between Makkah and Mina, on the right of one who enters Makkah from it.]] "so that we may raid." Allah delayed this and advanced that.

Abu al-Ḥasan al-Sarakhsi informed us: Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us: Abu Muṣʿab informed us, from Malik, from Musa ibn ʿUqbah, from Kurayb, the freed slave of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, from Usamah ibn Zayd, that he heard him say: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed from ʿArafah, and when he reached the mountain pass (al-Shiʿb) he dismounted and urinated, then performed ablution but did not complete it. I said to him: 'The prayer, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'The prayer is ahead of you.' So he mounted, and when he came to Muzdalifah he dismounted and performed ablution, completing it. Then the prayer was called, and he prayed the Maghrib. Then each person made his camel kneel at his own resting place. Then the ʿIshā' was called, and he prayed it, and he did not pray anything between them." [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Hajj, chapter "Dismounting between ʿArafah and Jamʿ," 3/519, and by Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "Departing from ʿArafat to Muzdalifah," no. (1280), 2/934.]]

Jabir said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) departed until he reached Muzdalifah, and there he prayed the Maghrib and the ʿIshā' with one adhan and two iqamahs, and he did not perform any voluntary prayer between them. Then he lay down until dawn broke, and he prayed the Fajr when the morning light had become clear, with one adhan and one iqamah. Then he rode al-Qaṣwāʾ until he came to al-Mash'ar al-Ḥarām, faced the qiblah, and supplicated, glorified (Allah), declared His greatness (takbīr), affirmed His oneness (tahlīl), and declared Him to be One (tawḥīd). He remained standing until the light had become very bright, then he departed before the sun rose." [[Related by Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "The Hajj of the Prophet (ﷺ)," no. (1218), 2/886. The author (al-Baghawi) also mentions it in Sharh al-Sunnah, 7/65.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us: Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Zuhayr ibn Harb informed us: Wahb ibn Jarir informed us: my father informed us, from Yunus al-Aylī, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that Usamah ibn Zayd was riding behind the Prophet (ﷺ) from ʿArafah to Muzdalifah, and then he had al-Fadl ride behind him from Muzdalifah to Mina. He said: "Both of them said: The Prophet (ﷺ) continued to recite the talbiyah until he threw the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah." [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Hajj, chapter "Dismounting between ʿArafah and Jamʿ," 3/519. Muslim in al-Hajj, chapter "The recommendation for a pilgrim to recite the talbiyah until he begins throwing the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah," no. (1281), 2/391, and the wording is his. The author also mentions it in Sharh al-Sunnah, 7/185.]]

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, meaning: remember Him with monotheism and glorification, just as He has mentioned you with guidance, so He guided you to His religion and the rites of His Hajj. ﴿And indeed, before it, you were among those astray﴾. Meaning: indeed you were before that. It is also said: "You were not before it except among those astray." This is like His words: ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ (26:186), meaning: we do not think you are except among the liars. The pronoun in His words "before it" refers to the guidance. It is also said that it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as an implicit reference to something not mentioned.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 199–202:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾. The people of tafsir said: Quraysh and their allies and those who followed their religion, namely the Hums (the Hums, a term for the Quraysh and those who adhered to their religion, who considered themselves set apart in the sanctity of the sacred precinct), used to stand at Muzdalifah and say: "We are the People of God and the inhabitants of His Sanctuary, so we do not leave the Sanctuary nor go out from it." They considered it beneath them to stand together with the rest of the Arabs at ʿArafat, while all other people used to stand at ʿArafat. So when the people departed from ʿArafat, the Hums departed from Muzdalifah. God therefore commanded them to stand at ʿArafat and depart from it to Jamʿ together with the rest of the people, and He informed them that this is the sunnah (sunnah, the prophetic or divinely established practice) of Ibrahim and Ismaʿil, peace be upon them both. Some of them said: He addressed by it all the Muslims.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from where the people depart﴾ means from Jamʿ, that is: Then depart from Jamʿ to Mina. They said: this is because the departure from ʿArafat is before the departure from Jamʿ, so how could it be permissible to say: "When you depart from ʿArafat, remember God at the Sacred Landmark, then depart from ʿArafat"? The first view is the view of most of the people of tafsir.

In the speech there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its meaning being: "Whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, then there is no obscenity, nor wickedness, nor disputing during the Hajj; then depart from where the people depart; and when you depart from ʿArafat, remember God at the Sacred Landmark."

It has also been said: thumma (thumma, "then") here has the sense of waw (waw, "and"), that is, "and depart," like His saying: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾ (90:17). As for "the people" (al-nas), they are all the Arabs other than the Hums.

Al-Kalbi said: they are the people of Yemen and Rabiʿa. Al-Dahhak said: "the people" here means Ibrahim alone, as in His saying: ﴿or do they envy the people﴾ (4:54), and it intends Muhammad (ﷺ) alone, and it is said: he is the one who is followed, and he is the tongue of his people. Al-Zuhri said: "the people" here means Adam alone, and its evidence is the reading of Saʿid ibn Jubayr: "Then depart from where the forgetful depart" (al-nasi, with a yaa), and it is said: he is Adam, who forgot God's covenant when he ate from the tree.

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Malik informed us, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, that he said: Usama was asked while I was sitting, "How did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) travel during the Farewell Pilgrimage when he set off?" He said: "He used to travel at an ʿanaq (ʿanaq, a fast pace), and when he found an open space, he went at a nass (nass, a faster pace)." Hisham said: "The nass is above the ʿanaq."

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliḥi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nuʿaymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: Saʿid ibn Abi Maryam informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Suwayd informed me, saying: Amr ibn Abi Amr, mawla of al-Muttalib, informed me, saying: Saʿid ibn Jubayr, mawla of Walibah al-Kufi, informed me, saying: Ibn ʿAbbas informed me that he set off with the Prophet (ﷺ) on the Day of ʿArafat, and the Prophet (ﷺ) heard behind him a severe shouting and the beating of camels. So he pointed at them with his whip and said: "O people, upon you is tranquility, for righteousness is not in hastening," ﴿and seek forgiveness from God; surely God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when you have completed your rites﴾, that is, when you have finished your Hajj and slaughtered your nusuk, that is, your sacrificial animals. It is said: a man nasaka yansuku nusukan when he slaughters his nasika, and that is after throwing the Jamrat al-ʿAqaba and settling in Mina. ﴿Then remember God﴾ with takbir, praise and glorification of Him, ﴿as you remember your fathers﴾. This is because the Arabs, when they finished the Hajj, would stand by the House and mention the glories of their fathers, so God Exalted commanded them to remember Him, and said: Remember Me, for I am the One who did that for you and your fathers, and I was good to you and to them.

Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAta said: its meaning is: remember God as small children remember their fathers, for the child, when he first begins to speak, cries out only the name of his father and no other, so God says: remember God alone, as the child remembers his father, or more intensely. Ibn ʿAbbas was asked about His saying ﴿remember God as you remember your fathers﴾, and it was said: a man may pass a day without mentioning his father in it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: That is not so; rather, that you be angered for God when He is disobeyed more than your anger for your parents when they are insulted. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿or a greater remembrance﴾ means: and greater remembrance, rather greater, that is, and more abundant remembrance. ﴿Among the people is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world﴾. He intended by it the polytheists, who during the Hajj asked God only for worldly things, saying: "O God, give us sheep, camels, cattle and slaves." A man would stand and say: "O Lord, my father was great in his dome-tent, large in his bowl, and abundant in wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him." Qatadah said: This is a servant whose intention is the world; for it he spends, for it he labors and toils. ﴿And he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no share or lot.

﴿And among them is one who says: Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. He means the believers. They differed concerning the meaning of the two goods. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said: "In this world a good" is a righteous wife, and "in the Hereafter a good" is Paradise.

Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Hanifi informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub al-Tusi informed us, saying: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Yusuf ibn Khallad informed us, saying: al-Harith ibn Abi Usama informed us, saying: Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri informed us, saying: Haywa and Ibn Lahiʿa informed us, the two of them saying: Shurahbil ibn Sharik informed us, that he heard Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli narrating from Abd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, may God be pleased with him, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: "The world entire is a provision, and the best of its provisions is the righteous woman."

Al-Hasan said: "In this world a good" is knowledge and worship, and "in the Hereafter a good" is Paradise. Al-Suddi and Ibn Hibban said: ﴿In this world a good﴾ is lawful provision and righteous deeds, ﴿and in the Hereafter a good﴾ is forgiveness and reward.

Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Tawba informed us, saying: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Harith informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Yaʿqub al-Kisa'i informed us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Mahmud informed us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah al-Khallal narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Ayyub, who said: Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr narrated to me, from Ali ibn Yazid, from al-Qasim Abi Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The most beloved of My friends to Me is a believer of light load (khafif al-hadh, i.e., light of condition and little wealth), who has a share of prayer, worships his Lord excellently, obeys Him in secret, and was obscure among the people, not pointed at with fingers, whose provision was sufficient, so he was patient with that; then he shook his hand and said: His death was hastened, few were those who wept for him, and few were his inheritances."

Qatadah said: "In this world a well-being and in the Hereafter a well-being." Awf said concerning this verse: whoever God has given Islam, the Qur'an, family and wealth has been given a good in this world and a good in the Hereafter.

Shaykh Abu al-Qasim Abd Allah ibn Ali al-Kurkani al-Tusi informed us, saying: Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn Mahmish al-Ziyadi informed us, saying: Abu al-Fadl Abdus ibn al-Husayn ibn Mansur al-Simsar informed us, saying: Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Idris al-Hanzali al-Razi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Ansari informed us, saying: Humayd al-Tawil informed us, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw a man who had become like a young bird (of emaciation), and said: "Did you use to supplicate God for something, or ask Him for it?" He said: "O Messenger of God, I used to say: 'O God, whatever You would punish me with in the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.'" He said: "Glory be to God! You cannot bear it and you cannot endure it. Why did you not say: 'Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire'?"

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Sarakhsi informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Ishaq al-Hajjaji informed us, saying: Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Dawili informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mishkan informed us, saying: Abu Dawud informed us, saying: Shu'ba informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say: 'Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'"

Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Kisa'i informed us, saying: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us, saying: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm informed us, saying: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: al-Shafi'i informed us, saying: Saʿid ibn Salim al-Qaddah informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Yahya ibn Ubayd, mawla of al-Sa'ib, from his father Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, between the Corner of the Banu Jumah and the Black Stone: "Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those there is a share﴾, that is, a portion, ﴿of what they have earned﴾ of good, supplication, reward and recompense. ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, meaning: when He reckons, His reckoning is swift, needing neither the counting of fingers, nor the memorizing of the breast, nor deliberation, nor thought.

Al-Hasan said: "Swifter than the blink of an eye." It was also said: its meaning is that the coming of the Resurrection is near, for what is certainly to come is near. God Exalted said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ (42:17).

You cannot bear it and you cannot endure it. Why did you not say: 'Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire'?"

Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Sarakhsi informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Ishaq al-Hajjaji informed us, saying: Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Dawili informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Mishkan informed us, saying: Abu Dawud informed us, saying: Shu'ba informed us, from Thabit, from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say: 'Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.'"

Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Kisa'i informed us, saying: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us, saying: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm informed us, saying: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: al-Shafi'i informed us, saying: Saʿid ibn Salim al-Qaddah informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Yahya ibn Ubayd, mawla of al-Sa'ib, from his father Abd Allah ibn al-Sa'ib, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, between the Corner of the Banu Jumah and the Black Stone: "Our Lord, give us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter a good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For those there is a share﴾, that is, a portion, ﴿of what they have earned﴾ of good, supplication, reward and recompense. ﴿And God is swift in reckoning﴾, meaning: when He reckons, His reckoning is swift, needing neither the counting of fingers, nor the memorizing of the breast, nor deliberation, nor thought.

Al-Hasan said: "Swifter than the blink of an eye." It was also said: its meaning is that the coming of the Resurrection is near, for what is certainly to come is near. God Exalted said: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ (42:17).

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 203:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And remember Allah﴾, meaning the takbirat (the proclamations of "Allahu Akbar") after the prayers, and at the jamarat (the stoning pillars), he says takbir with each pebble and at other times. ﴿During the appointed days﴾.
