The people were mentioning David, so David came to Talut and said: "Fulfil for me what you promised me." He said: "Do you want the king's daughter without a dowry?" David said: "You did not stipulate a dowry for me, and I have nothing." He said: "I will not burden you with anything you cannot bear. You are a bold man, and in our vicinity are enemies of ours who are uncircumcised (*ghulf*)[[Plural of *aghlaf*, one who has not been circumcised.]]. If you kill two hundred of them and bring me their foreskins, I will marry you to my daughter." So he went out to them, and every time he killed one of them he strung its foreskin on a thread, until he had strung together all their foreskins. He brought them to Talut and threw them before him, and said: "Hand over my wife to me." So he married him to his daughter and placed his seal over his kingdom. The people inclined towards David, loved him, and mentioned him often. Talut envied him and wanted to kill him. A man called Dhu al-'Aynayn informed Talut's daughter about this, so she said to David: "You are going to be killed this night." He said: "And who will kill me?" She said: "My father." He said: "Have I committed any crime?" She said: "Someone who does not lie told me. And there is no harm to you in staying away tonight until you see the truth of that." He said: "If Allah has willed that, I cannot go out. But bring me a skin of wine (*ziqq*)[[The *ziqq* (with a kasra on the zay) is the skin of a goat, stripped from one hind leg, from the head and neck, then treated until it becomes a water-skin. They used it most for wine.]]." She brought it to him, and he placed it in his bed on the couch and covered it with a cloth, then he hid under the couch. Talut came in at midnight and said to her: "Where is your husband?" She said: "He is sleeping on the couch." So he struck it with the sword, and the wine spilled. When he smelled the scent of the drink, he said: "May Allah have mercy on David! How much he drinks wine!" and he left.

When morning came, David knew that he had not done anything. Talut said: "A man whom I have sought to harm is certainly not going to leave me alone until he takes his revenge upon me." So he strengthened his guards and chamberlains and bolted his doors. Then David came to him one night when the eyes were at rest. Allah, glorified is He, blinded the guards and opened the doors for him, so he entered upon him while he was sleeping on his bed. He placed an arrow by his head, an arrow by his feet, an arrow on his right, and an arrow on his left, then he left. When Talut awoke, he saw the arrows and recognised them. He said: "May Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on David. He is better than me. I had the upper hand over him and intended to kill him, but he had the upper hand over me and held back from me. Had he wished, he could have placed this arrow in my throat, and I am not one to be trusted." When the next night came, he came to him again, and Allah blinded the chamberlains. He entered upon him while he was sleeping, took the ewer of Talut from which he used to perform ablution and his cup from which he used to drink, cut some hairs from his beard and some threads from the hem of his garments, then he left and fled and hid himself. When Talut awoke and saw that, he set spies upon David and searched for him most intensely, but he could not find him. Then Talut rode out one day and found David walking in the wilderness. He said: "Today I will kill him." He galloped after him. David ran, and whenever he was frightened he could not be caught. He entered a cave, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed to a spider, and it spun a web over him. When Talut reached the cave and saw the spider's web, he said: "If he had entered here, he would have torn the spider's web," so he left it and went on. David set off and came to the mountain with the worshippers and worshipped there. The scholars and the devout spoke ill of Talut regarding David's affair. Talut then did not allow anyone who forbade him from killing David to live; he killed them, and he incited the killing of the scholars. He could not overcome any scholar among the Children of Israel whom he was able to kill without killing him. Until a woman who knew the Greatest Name of Allah was brought to him, and he ordered his baker to kill her. The baker had mercy on her and said: "Perhaps we will need a scholar," so he left her. Then repentance entered Talut's heart, and he regretted what he had done. He began to weep until the people had mercy on him.

Al-Baghawi's commentary (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 250–252 (part 2 of 2)

He would go out to the graves every night, weeping, and call out: "I implore Allah, any servant who knows that there is repentance for me, to inform me of it!" When he pressed them, a caller called out to him from the graves: "O Talut! Are you not content that you killed us, so that you now harm us even in death?" He wept and grieved all the more. The baker took pity on him and said: "What is wrong with you, O king?" He said: "Do you know of any scholar on earth whom I could ask whether there is repentance for me?" The baker said: "Your case is like that of a king who came to a village at nightfall. A rooster crowed, and he took it as an omen and said: 'Do not leave a single rooster in the village without slaughtering it.' When he wanted to sleep, he said to his companions: 'When the rooster crows, wake us so that we may set out before dawn.' They said to him: 'Have you left a single rooster whose voice we could hear? Rather, have you left a scholar on earth?'" So he grieved and wept all the more. When the baker saw this, he said to him: "What do you think? If I point you to a scholar, will you kill him?" He said: "No." So the baker bound him by a firm pledge, and informed him that a learned woman was with him. He said: "Take me to her, so that I may ask her whether there is repentance for me." She was from a household that knew the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), and whenever their men died out, their women would hold this knowledge. When Talut reached the door, the baker said: "If she sees you, she will be terrified." So he left him behind him and entered alone to her, and said to her: "Am I not the one who has done you the greatest favour, having saved you from being killed and given you shelter?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then I have a request of you: this is Talut, who asks whether there is repentance for him." She fainted from fear. He said to her: "He does not intend to kill you, but he asks you whether there is repentance for him." She said: "No, by Allah, I do not know of any repentance for Talut. But do you know the location of the grave of a prophet?" So he took them both to the grave of Ishmawil (Samuel). She prayed and supplicated, then called out: "O occupant of the grave!" Ishmawil came out of the grave, shaking the dust from his head. When he looked at the three of them, he said: "What is the matter with you? Has the Resurrection come?" She said: "No, but Talut asks you whether there is repentance for him." Ishmawil said: "O Talut, what have you done since I left?" He said: "I have left no evil undone, and I have come seeking repentance." He said: "How many sons do you have?" He said: "Ten men." He said: "I know of no repentance for you except that you renounce your kingdom, and go forth with your sons in the way of Allah, then send your sons forward so that they are killed before your eyes, and then you fight until you are killed as the last of them?" Then Ishmawil returned to the grave and fell dead. Talut returned, more grieved than ever, fearing that his son would not follow him. He wept until the lids of his eyes fell away, and his body wasted away. His sons came in to him, and he said to them: "What do you think? If I were thrown into the Fire, would you ransom me?" They said: "Yes, we would ransom you with whatever we are able." He said: "Then it is the Fire, if you do not do what I tell you." They said: "Then set it before us." He related the story to them. They said: "And you are going to be killed?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then there is no good for us in life after you. Our souls are content with what you have asked." So he prepared himself with his wealth and his sons. His sons went forward first, and they were ten. They fought before him until they were killed. Then he himself charged after them until he was killed. The one who killed him came to Dawud to give him good news, saying: "I have killed your enemy." Dawud said: "You are not the one who will live after him." So he struck off his neck. The kingdom of Talut lasted forty years until he was killed. The Children of Israel came to Dawud, gave him the treasures of Talut, and made him king over themselves.

Al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: Dawud reigned for seven years after the killing of Talut, and the Children of Israel did not unite under one king except Dawud. This is the meaning of Allah's words: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾. "Wisdom" here means prophethood. Allah combined for Dawud both kingship and prophethood, which had not been combined before; rather, kingship was in one tribe and prophethood in another. It was also said: "kingdom and wisdom" means knowledge together with action. His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾. Al-Kalbi and others said: this means the craft of making coats of mail. He would make them and sell them, and he would eat only from the work of his hands. It was also said: it means the speech of birds, the speech of the hukl (that which has no audible sound) and of ants, and fine speech. It was also said: it refers to the Psalms (al-Zabur). It was also said: it refers to a beautiful voice and melodies. Allah did not give any of His creatures a voice like his. When he recited the Psalms, wild animals would draw near until he could take them by their necks, birds would shade him, listening attentively, the flowing water would become still, and the wind would be calm.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah, exalted is He, gave him a chain attached to the Milky Way, its top at his hermitage (mihrab). Its strength was the strength of iron, its colour the colour of fire, its links circular and adorned with jewels, set with moist pearls. Whenever any event occurred in the air, the chain would ring, and Dawud would know of that event. Whoever was afflicted with a disease and touched it would be cured. After Dawud, peace be upon him, they would bring their disputes to it until it was taken up. Whoever wronged another and denied him a right would come to the chain. If he was truthful, he would stretch out his hand and grasp it; if he was lying, he could not reach it. This continued until deceit and trickery appeared among them. It is reported to us that one of their kings had entrusted a man with a precious jewel. When he asked for it back, the man denied it, and they took their dispute to the chain. The one who had the jewel went to a staff, hollowed it out, placed the jewel in it, and leaned on it until he came to the chain. The owner of the jewel said: "Return my deposit to me." The other said: "I do not know of any deposit of yours with me. If you are truthful, then take hold of the chain." He reached for it with his hand. It was said to the denier: "Stand up and you take hold of it." He said to the owner of the jewel: "Take my staff here and keep it safe until I take hold of the chain." So he took it from him. Then the denier stood up towards the chain and grasped it. The man said: "O Allah, if You know that this deposit which he claims from me has reached him, then bring the chain near to me." He stretched out his hand and grasped it. The people were astonished and doubted it. In the morning they found that Allah had taken up the chain.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾. The people of Medina and Ya'qub read "difa'" (with an alif) here and in surah al-Hajj. The others read it without the alif, because no one can overpower Allah, and He alone is the Repeller. Whoever reads it with the alif says: repelling may come from one party, as in the Arabic saying: "May Allah repel from you the harm (ahsana Allahu 'anka al-difa')." Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: "Were it not for Allah's repelling by means of the armies of the Muslims, the polytheists would have prevailed over the earth, killing the believers, and destroying the mosques and the lands." The rest of the exegetes said: "Were it not for Allah's repelling of the disbelievers and the wicked by means of believers and the righteous, the earth would have been destroyed with its inhabitants. But Allah repels the disbeliever by means of the believer, and the wicked by means of the righteous."

Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shuraihi informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us: Abu Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed us: Abu Bakr ibn Kharja informed us: Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal informed us: Abu Humayd al-Himsi informed us: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar informed us: Hafs ibn Sulayman informed us, from Muhammad ibn Suqa, from Wabara, from Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, repels calamity from a hundred households among the neighbours of a righteous Muslim on his account." Then he recited: "And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others..." [[Narrated by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his Tafsir: 5/374. In its chain is Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar, whom Ibn Ma'in and others declared weak. Abu Dawud said: "acceptable in narration" (ja'iz al-hadith). Muhammad ibn Musaffa al-Himsi the hafiz said: "trustworthy." Al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir and mentioned no criticism of him. Ibn Kathir, after attributing the hadith to al-Tabari, said: "This chain is weak, for Yahya ibn Sa'id is very weak" (Tafsir 1/537, Dar al-Arqam). Al-Haythami attributed it to al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat and said: "In it is Yahya ibn Sa'id, who is weak." See Majma' al-Zawa'id 8/163–164; Fayd al-Qadir 2/261.]] ﴿the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾

And when they came out to face Jalut (Goliath) and his forces, they said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience and make firm our feet and help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ (Talut and his army, meaning the believers, went out to face Jalut and his army, meaning the polytheists.) The meaning of *baraza* is that they came out into the open (*al-biraz*) of the earth, which is the level, elevated ground. "Pour upon us" means "send down upon us" and "pour out upon us." "Firm our feet" means "firm our hearts."

﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and David killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom, and taught him of what He willed. And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾ (251) ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers.﴾ (252)

﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah﴾, that is, by the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And David killed Jalut﴾. As for the manner of his killing, the people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis)[[These reports, taken as a whole, are from the Isra'iliyyat (narratives transmitted from Jewish and Christian sources). We have no need of them, since we have in our hands the Book and the Sunnah. Nothing in the Book of Allah or in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) indicates what they mention, and we have no need of any of this in understanding and reflecting upon the Qur'an, so do not pay them any heed... Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that this is among the Isra'iliyyat. See Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1/537, Dar al-Arqam edition. Al-Isra'iliyyat wal-Mawdu'at by Shaykh Abu Shahba, pp. 248–249.]] said: He crossed the river with Talut, among those who crossed. Iysha (Jesse), the father of David, had thirteen sons, and David was the youngest of them. He used to shoot with a sling (*al-qadhdhafa*). One day he said to his father: "O father, I never throw my sling at anything without knocking it down." His father said: "Rejoice, my son, for Allah has made your provision in your sling." Then he came to him another time and said: "O father, I entered between the mountains and found a lion lying down, so I mounted it and took hold of its ears, and it did not harm me." He said: "Rejoice, my son, for this is a good thing that Allah intends for you." Then he came to him on another day and said: "O father, I walk between the mountains and glorify Allah, and no mountain remains but that it glorifies Allah along with me." He said: "Rejoice, my son, for this is a good thing that Allah, the Exalted, has given you."

Then Jalut sent to Talut: "Come out to me, or send out to me a man who will fight me. If he kills me, then you will have my kingdom, and if I kill him, then I will have your kingdom." This was difficult for Talut, so he called out in his army: "Whoever kills Jalut, I will marry him to my daughter and share my kingdom with him." The people were afraid of Jalut, and none of them answered him. So Talut asked their prophet to supplicate to Allah, the Exalted, about this, and he supplicated to Allah concerning it. Then a horn containing holy oil (*duhn al-qudus*) and a furnace of iron were brought. It was said: "Your companion who will kill Jalut is the one upon whose head this horn will be placed. The oil will boil until it anoints his head, without flowing onto his face, and it will sit on his head like a crown (*al-iklil*). He will enter this furnace and fill it, and he will not shift about in it." Then Talut summoned the Children of Israel and tested them, but none of them agreed with it. So Allah revealed to their prophet that among the sons of Iysha there is one by whom Allah will kill Jalut. Talut summoned Iysha and said: "Present your sons to me." He brought out to him twelve men, like pillars (*al-sawari*)[[Plural of *sariya*, a column of stone or baked brick. It is reported in a hadith that he forbade praying between the pillars (*al-sawari*) during congregational prayer, because it breaks the row.]]. He began presenting them to the horn, but it showed nothing. He said to Iysha: "Do you have any other son besides these?" He said: "No." So the prophet said: "O Lord, he claims he has no son other than these." He said: "He lied." The prophet said: "Indeed, my Lord has called you a liar." Iysha said: "Allah has spoken truly, O Prophet of Allah. I have a young son called Dawud. I was ashamed to let people see him because of his short stature and lowliness, so I left him (*fakhallaftuhu*)[[In one copy: *fa-ja'altuhu* (I made him).]] tending the sheep in such-and-such a valley." David was a short man, sickly (*misqam*), yellowish (*misfar*), blue-eyed (*azraq*)[[He means blue-eyed, and the Arabs used to consider blue eyes a bad omen.]], and thin-haired (*am'ar*)[[Having little hair.]]. Talut summoned him. It is also said: Talut himself went out to him and found that the valley had flooded between him and the pen to which he used to bring the flock. He found David carrying two sheep, carrying them across the flood without wading through the water with them. When Talut saw him, he said: "This is him, without doubt. This one has mercy on the animals, so he is even more merciful towards people." He called him, placed the horn on his head, and the oil overflowed. Talut said: "Would you like to kill Jalut, and I will marry you to my daughter and place your seal over my kingdom?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Have you sensed in yourself anything by which you could strengthen yourself to kill him?" He said: "Yes. I am a shepherd, and when a lion or a leopard or a wolf comes and takes a sheep, I rise up against it, open its jaws to free the sheep, and break its neck." So Talut sent him back to his army.

David, peace be upon him, passed on his way by a stone, which called out to him: "O David, take me up, for I am the stone of Harun (Aaron), with which he killed such-and-such a king." So he took it up in his satchel (*mikhlah*). Then he passed by another stone, which said: "Take me up, for I am the stone of Musa (Moses), with which he killed such-and-such a king," so he took it up in his satchel. Then he passed by another stone, which said: "Take me up, for I am your stone with which you will kill Jalut." So he placed it in his satchel.

When the two sides lined up for battle, Jalut came forward and asked for single combat. David was chosen for him. Talut gave him a horse, armour, and weapons. David put on the weapons and mounted the horse, went a short distance, then turned back to the king. Those around him thought the boy had become frightened. He came and stood before the king, and the king said: "What is your matter?" He said: "If Allah does not help me, these weapons will avail me nothing. So let me fight as I wish." He said: "Do as you please." David took his satchel, slung it over his shoulder, took up the sling, and set off towards Jalut. Jalut was among the strongest and most powerful of men, and he used to defeat armies single-handedly. He had a helmet (*bayda*)[[Headgear worn in war.]] containing three hundred ratls of iron. When he looked at David, terror was cast into his heart, and he said to him: "Are you coming out to me?" He said: "Yes."

Jalut was on a piebald horse (*abqa*)[[Black and white, with the white markings (*tahjil*) reaching up to the thighs.]], wearing full armour. He said: "Have you come to me with a sling and a stone, as one comes to a dog?" He said: "Yes, you are worse than a dog." He said: "Without doubt, I will cut your flesh and divide it among the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky." David said: "Or rather, Allah will divide your flesh." Then David said: "In the name of the God of Ibrahim (Abraham)," and took out a stone. Then he took out another and said: "In the name of the God of Ishaq (Isaac)," and placed it in his sling. Then he took out a third and said: "In the name of the God of Ya'qub (Jacob)," and placed it in his sling. Then they all became one stone. David whirled the sling and hurled it, and Allah subjected the wind to him until the stone struck the nose of the helmet, penetrated his brain, and came out from the back of his neck, and it killed thirty men behind him. Allah, the Exalted, routed the army, and Jalut fell dead. David dragged him until he threw him before Talut. The Muslims rejoiced greatly, and they returned to the city safe and laden with booty. The people were mentioning David, so David came to Talut and said: "Fulfil for me what you promised me." He said: "Do you want the king's daughter without a dowry?" David said: "You did not stipulate a dowry for me, and I have nothing." He said: "I will not burden you with anything you cannot bear. You are a bold man, and in our vicinity are enemies of ours who are uncircumcised (*ghulf*)[[Plural of *aghlaf*, one who has not been circumcised.]]. If you kill two hundred of them and bring me their foreskins, I will marry you to my daughter." So he went out to them, and every time he killed one of them he strung its foreskin on a thread, until he had strung together all their foreskins. He brought them to Talut and threw them before him, and said: "Hand over my wife to me." So he married him to his daughter and placed his seal over his kingdom. The people inclined towards David, loved him, and mentioned him often. Talut envied him and wanted to kill him. A man called Dhu al-'Aynayn informed Talut's daughter about this, so she said to David: "You are going to be killed this night." He said: "And who will kill me?" She said: "My father." He said: "Have I committed any crime?" She said: "Someone who does not lie told me. And there is no harm to you in staying away tonight until you see the truth of that." He said: "If Allah has willed that, I cannot go out. But bring me a skin of wine (*ziqq*)[[The *ziqq* (with a kasra on the zay) is the skin of a goat, stripped from one hind leg, from the head and neck, then treated until it becomes a water-skin. They used it most for wine.]]." She brought it to him, and he placed it in his bed on the couch and covered it with a cloth, then he hid under the couch. Talut came in at midnight and said to her: "Where is your husband?" She said: "He is sleeping on the couch." So he struck it with the sword, and the wine spilled. When he smelled the scent of the drink, he said: "May Allah have mercy on David! How much he drinks wine!" and he left.

When morning came, David knew that he had not done anything. Talut said: "A man whom I have sought to harm is certainly not going to leave me alone until he takes his revenge upon me." So he strengthened his guards and chamberlains and bolted his doors. Then David came to him one night when the eyes were at rest. Allah, glorified is He, blinded the guards and opened the doors for him, so he entered upon him while he was sleeping on his bed. He placed an arrow by his head, an arrow by his feet, an arrow on his right, and an arrow on his left, then he left. When Talut awoke, he saw the arrows and recognised them. He said: "May Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on David. He is better than me. I had the upper hand over him and intended to kill him, but he had the upper hand over me and held back from me. Had he wished, he could have placed this arrow in my throat, and I am not one to be trusted." When the next night came, he came to him again, and Allah blinded the chamberlains. He entered upon him while he was sleeping, took the ewer of Talut from which he used to perform ablution and his cup from which he used to drink, cut some hairs from his beard and some threads from the hem of his garments, then he left and fled and hid himself. When Talut awoke and saw that, he set spies upon David and searched for him most intensely, but he could not find him. Then Talut rode out one day and found David walking in the wilderness. He said: "Today I will kill him." He galloped after him. David ran, and whenever he was frightened he could not be caught. He entered a cave, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed to a spider, and it spun a web over him. When Talut reached the cave and saw the spider's web, he said: "If he had entered here, he would have torn the spider's web," so he left it and went on. David set off and came to the mountain with the worshippers and worshipped there. The scholars and the devout spoke ill of Talut regarding David's affair. Talut then did not allow anyone who forbade him from killing David to live; he killed them, and he incited the killing of the scholars. He could not overcome any scholar among the Children of Israel whom he was able to kill without killing him. Until a woman who knew the Greatest Name of Allah was brought to him, and he ordered his baker to kill her. The baker had mercy on her and said: "Perhaps we will need a scholar," so he left her. Then repentance entered Talut's heart, and he regretted what he had done. He began to weep until the people had mercy on him.

Al-Baghawi's commentary (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 250–252 (part 2 of 2)

He would go out to the graves every night, weeping, and call out: "I implore Allah, any servant who knows that there is repentance for me, to inform me of it!" When he pressed them, a caller called out to him from the graves: "O Talut! Are you not content that you killed us, so that you now harm us even in death?" He wept and grieved all the more. The baker took pity on him and said: "What is wrong with you, O king?" He said: "Do you know of any scholar on earth whom I could ask whether there is repentance for me?" The baker said: "Your case is like that of a king who came to a village at nightfall. A rooster crowed, and he took it as an omen and said: 'Do not leave a single rooster in the village without slaughtering it.' When he wanted to sleep, he said to his companions: 'When the rooster crows, wake us so that we may set out before dawn.' They said to him: 'Have you left a single rooster whose voice we could hear? Rather, have you left a scholar on earth?'" So he grieved and wept all the more. When the baker saw this, he said to him: "What do you think? If I point you to a scholar, will you kill him?" He said: "No." So the baker bound him by a firm pledge, and informed him that a learned woman was with him. He said: "Take me to her, so that I may ask her whether there is repentance for me." She was from a household that knew the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), and whenever their men died out, their women would hold this knowledge. When Talut reached the door, the baker said: "If she sees you, she will be terrified." So he left him behind him and entered alone to her, and said to her: "Am I not the one who has done you the greatest favour, having saved you from being killed and given you shelter?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then I have a request of you: this is Talut, who asks whether there is repentance for him." She fainted from fear. He said to her: "He does not intend to kill you, but he asks you whether there is repentance for him." She said: "No, by Allah, I do not know of any repentance for Talut. But do you know the location of the grave of a prophet?" So he took them both to the grave of Ishmawil (Samuel). She prayed and supplicated, then called out: "O occupant of the grave!" Ishmawil came out of the grave, shaking the dust from his head. When he looked at the three of them, he said: "What is the matter with you? Has the Resurrection come?" She said: "No, but Talut asks you whether there is repentance for him." Ishmawil said: "O Talut, what have you done since I left?" He said: "I have left no evil undone, and I have come seeking repentance." He said: "How many sons do you have?" He said: "Ten men." He said: "I know of no repentance for you except that you renounce your kingdom, and go forth with your sons in the way of Allah, then send your sons forward so that they are killed before your eyes, and then you fight until you are killed as the last of them?" Then Ishmawil returned to the grave and fell dead. Talut returned, more grieved than ever, fearing that his son would not follow him. He wept until the lids of his eyes fell away, and his body wasted away. His sons came in to him, and he said to them: "What do you think? If I were thrown into the Fire, would you ransom me?" They said: "Yes, we would ransom you with whatever we are able." He said: "Then it is the Fire, if you do not do what I tell you." They said: "Then set it before us." He related the story to them. They said: "And you are going to be killed?" He said: "Yes." They said: "Then there is no good for us in life after you. Our souls are content with what you have asked." So he prepared himself with his wealth and his sons. His sons went forward first, and they were ten. They fought before him until they were killed. Then he himself charged after them until he was killed. The one who killed him came to Dawud to give him good news, saying: "I have killed your enemy." Dawud said: "You are not the one who will live after him." So he struck off his neck. The kingdom of Talut lasted forty years until he was killed. The Children of Israel came to Dawud, gave him the treasures of Talut, and made him king over themselves.

Al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: Dawud reigned for seven years after the killing of Talut, and the Children of Israel did not unite under one king except Dawud. This is the meaning of Allah's words: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾. "Wisdom" here means prophethood. Allah combined for Dawud both kingship and prophethood, which had not been combined before; rather, kingship was in one tribe and prophethood in another. It was also said: "kingdom and wisdom" means knowledge together with action. His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾. Al-Kalbi and others said: this means the craft of making coats of mail. He would make them and sell them, and he would eat only from the work of his hands. It was also said: it means the speech of birds, the speech of the hukl (that which has no audible sound) and of ants, and fine speech. It was also said: it refers to the Psalms (al-Zabur). It was also said: it refers to a beautiful voice and melodies. Allah did not give any of His creatures a voice like his. When he recited the Psalms, wild animals would draw near until he could take them by their necks, birds would shade him, listening attentively, the flowing water would become still, and the wind would be calm.

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah, exalted is He, gave him a chain attached to the Milky Way, its top at his hermitage (mihrab). Its strength was the strength of iron, its colour the colour of fire, its links circular and adorned with jewels, set with moist pearls. Whenever any event occurred in the air, the chain would ring, and Dawud would know of that event. Whoever was afflicted with a disease and touched it would be cured. After Dawud, peace be upon him, they would bring their disputes to it until it was taken up. Whoever wronged another and denied him a right would come to the chain. If he was truthful, he would stretch out his hand and grasp it; if he was lying, he could not reach it. This continued until deceit and trickery appeared among them. It is reported to us that one of their kings had entrusted a man with a precious jewel. When he asked for it back, the man denied it, and they took their dispute to the chain. The one who had the jewel went to a staff, hollowed it out, placed the jewel in it, and leaned on it until he came to the chain. The owner of the jewel said: "Return my deposit to me." The other said: "I do not know of any deposit of yours with me. If you are truthful, then take hold of the chain." He reached for it with his hand. It was said to the denier: "Stand up and you take hold of it." He said to the owner of the jewel: "Take my staff here and keep it safe until I take hold of the chain." So he took it from him. Then the denier stood up towards the chain and grasped it. The man said: "O Allah, if You know that this deposit which he claims from me has reached him, then bring the chain near to me." He stretched out his hand and grasped it. The people were astonished and doubted it. In the morning they found that Allah had taken up the chain.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾. The people of Medina and Ya'qub read "difa'" (with an alif) here and in surah al-Hajj. The others read it without the alif, because no one can overpower Allah, and He alone is the Repeller. Whoever reads it with the alif says: repelling may come from one party, as in the Arabic saying: "May Allah repel from you the harm (ahsana Allahu 'anka al-difa')." Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: "Were it not for Allah's repelling by means of the armies of the Muslims, the polytheists would have prevailed over the earth, killing the believers, and destroying the mosques and the lands." The rest of the exegetes said: "Were it not for Allah's repelling of the disbelievers and the wicked by means of believers and the righteous, the earth would have been destroyed with its inhabitants. But Allah repels the disbeliever by means of the believer, and the wicked by means of the righteous."

Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shuraihi informed us: Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us: Abu Abd Allah ibn Fanjawayh informed us: Abu Bakr ibn Kharja informed us: Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal informed us: Abu Humayd al-Himsi informed us: Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar informed us: Hafs ibn Sulayman informed us, from Muhammad ibn Suqa, from Wabara, from Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, repels calamity from a hundred households among the neighbours of a righteous Muslim on his account." Then he recited: "And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others..." [[Narrated by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari in his Tafsir: 5/374. In its chain is Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar, whom Ibn Ma'in and others declared weak. Abu Dawud said: "acceptable in narration" (ja'iz al-hadith). Muhammad ibn Musaffa al-Himsi the hafiz said: "trustworthy." Al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir and mentioned no criticism of him. Ibn Kathir, after attributing the hadith to al-Tabari, said: "This chain is weak, for Yahya ibn Sa'id is very weak" (Tafsir 1/537, Dar al-Arqam). Al-Haythami attributed it to al-Tabarani in al-Kabir and al-Awsat and said: "In it is Yahya ibn Sa'id, who is weak." See Majma' al-Zawa'id 8/163–164; Fayd al-Qadir 2/261.]] ﴿the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 253–254:

﴿Those are the messengers; some of them We have favored above others. Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾: that is, Allah Most High spoke to him, meaning Musa (peace be upon him). ﴿And He raised some of them in degrees﴾: meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). The Shaykh, the Imam (may Allah have mercy on him) said: No prophet was given a sign except that our Prophet was given the like of that sign, and he was preferred over others with signs such as: the splitting of the moon at his gesture; the trunk of the palm tree yearning at being separated from him; stones and trees greeting him; the speech of animals and their testifying to his prophethood; water gushing from between his fingers; and other miracles and signs that cannot be counted, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, which the people of the heavens and the people of the earth were unable to produce the like of.

Abu Bakr Ya'qub ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sayrafi informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Makhaladi informed us, saying: Abu al-Abbas ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Thaqafi informed us, saying: Qutayba ibn Sa'id informed us, saying: al-Layth ibn Sa'd informed us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, from his father, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs such that mankind believed upon their like. What I was given was revelation which Allah Most High revealed to me, so I hope to be the most numerous of them in followers on the Day of Resurrection." [Narrated by al-Bukhari: in Al-I'tisam bil-Kitab was-Sunna - chapter: the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) "I was sent with comprehensive words", 13/247, and in Fada'il al-Qur'an. Muslim: in Iman - chapter: the obligation of belief in the prophethood of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), no. (239), 1/134. And the author in Sharh al-Sunna 13/195-196.]

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Malihi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Sinan informed us, saying: Hushaym informed us, saying: Sayyar informed us, saying: Yazid al-Faqir informed us, saying: Jabir ibn Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with both of them) informed us, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things which no one before me was given: I was made victorious through terror (cast into the hearts of enemies) for a distance of one month's journey; the earth was made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, so whichever man of my nation the time of prayer reaches, let him pray; spoils of war were made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; I was given intercession; and every prophet was sent only to his own people, whereas I was sent to all people." [Narrated by al-Bukhari: at the beginning of the Book of Tayammum - first chapter 1/436, and in the Book of Prayer, in Jihad, and in Bad' al-Khalq and the Prophets; and Muslim: in Masajid, no. (521) 1/370-371; and the author in Sharh al-Sunna 13/196.]

Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Fadl al-Kharaqi informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Taysafuni informed us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Umar al-Jawhari informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Kushmihani informed us, saying: Ali ibn Hujr informed us, saying: Isma'il ibn Ja'far informed us, saying: al-Ala' ibn Abd al-Rahman informed us, from his father, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been favored over the prophets in six ways: I was given comprehensive words; I was made victorious through terror; spoils were made lawful for me; the earth was made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, and I was sent to all creation; and the prophets were sealed with me." [Narrated by Muslim: in Masajid and Places of Prayer, no. (523) 1/371; in another narration, "I was sent with comprehensive words." And the author in Sharh al-Sunna 13/197.]

His saying, Most High: ﴿And We gave Isa, son of Maryam, the clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. And had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after clear proofs had come to them. But they differed: among them were those who believed, and among them those who disbelieved. And had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another; but Allah does what He wills﴾: that is, after the messengers. ﴿After clear proofs had come to them﴾ ... ﴿Among them were those who believed﴾: remained steadfast in their belief by the grace of Allah; ﴿and among them those who disbelieved﴾: through being forsaken by Him. ﴿And had Allah willed, they would not have fought﴾: He repeated it for emphasis. ﴿But Allah does what He wills﴾: He grants success to whom He wills by grace, and forsakes whom He wills by justice.

A man asked Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), saying: O Commander of the Faithful, inform me about qadar (divine decree). He said: "A dark path, so do not tread it." He asked again, and he said: "A deep sea, so do not plunge into it." He asked again, and he said: "The secret of Allah on the earth, which has been hidden from you, so do not probe it." [Narrated by al-Ajurri in al-Shari'a p. 202, and al-Lalaka'i in Sharh Usul I'tiqad 4/629.]

His saying, Most High: ﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided you before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, no friendship, and no intercession. And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers.﴾ Al-Suddi said: He meant by it the obligatory zakat. Others said: He meant voluntary charity and spending in good. ﴿In which there is no trade﴾: that is, no ransom in it; He called it trade because ransom is buying one's own self. ﴿Nor friendship﴾: no friendship. ﴿Nor intercession﴾ except by the permission of Allah. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and the people of Basra all read it in the accusative (la bay'a, la khilala, la lagha, la ta'thim) throughout, and likewise in Surat Ibrahim (verse 31) "la bay'a fihi wa la khilal" and in Surat al-Tur (verse 23) "la laghwa fiha wa la ta'thim." The others read all of them in the nominative with tanwin. ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾: because they placed worship in other than its proper place.
