Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 255–256 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. Abdul-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliħi informed us: Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Sam'an informed us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us: Ibn Abi Shayba informed us: Abd al-A'la informed us, from al-Jurayri, from Abu al-Salil [[Abu al-Salil: he is Durayb ibn Nuqayr, also said to be Nuqayl, Abu al-Salil al-Qaysi al-Jurayri al-Basri. Ishaq ibn Mansur said, from Yahya ibn Ma'in: "Trustworthy." Ibn Hibban also mentioned him among the trustworthy. Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, vol. 4, p. 401.]], from Abd Allah ibn Rabah al-Ansari, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu al-Mundhir, which verse of the Book of Allah is the greatest?" I said: ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. He said: He struck me on the chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you (layahnika al-'ilm)." Then he said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, this verse has a tongue and two lips by which it sanctifies the King at the foot of the Throne." [[Narrated by Muslim in Salat al-Musafirin wa Qasriha, no. 810, 1/156, with a different wording. Al-Musannif (al-Baghawi) in Sharh al-Sunna, 4/459. "Layahnika al-'ilm" means: may knowledge be wholesome and pleasant for you.]]

Abdul-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliħi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: [I was informed] by Muhammad ibn Yusuf, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who said: Uthman ibn al-Haytham Abu Amr said: Awf informed us, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan. A visitor came and began scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "I am in need, I have a dependent family, and I have a severe need." So I let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu Hurayra, what did your prisoner do last night?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he complained of a severe need and a family, so I had mercy on him and let him go." He said: "He has indeed lied to you, and he will return." So I knew he would return, because of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying that he would return. I watched for him, and he came scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "Leave me, for I am in need, I have a dependent family, and I will not return." So I had mercy on him and let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Abu Hurayra, what did your prisoner do?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he complained of a severe need and a family, so I had mercy on him and let him go." He said: "He has indeed lied to you, and he will return." I watched for him a third time, and he came scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the third time; you claim you will not return, yet you return." He said: "Leave me, and I will teach you words by which Allah will benefit you." I said: "What are they?" He said: "When you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne, ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, until you finish the verse, for a guardian from Allah will always be over you, and no devil will come near you until morning." So I let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "What did your prisoner do last night?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he claimed he would teach me words by which Allah will benefit me, so I let him go." He said: "What are they?" I said: "He told me: when you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne from its beginning until you finish the verse, ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, and he said: a guardian from Allah will always be over you, and no devil will come near you until morning." They were the most eager of people for good. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He has indeed told you the truth, though he is a liar. Do you know who you were addressing for three nights, Abu Hurayra?" I said: "No." He said: "That was a devil." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Wakala, chapter: if a man appoints an agent and the agent neglects something, 4/486–487; and in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter: the description of Iblis and his troops, 6/335–336; and in Fada'il al-Qur'an. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna, 4/460.]]

Abdul-Wahid al-Maliħi informed us: Abu Mansur al-Sam'ani informed us: Abu Ja'far al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us: Yahya ibn Yahya informed us: Abu Mu'awiya informed us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr—he is al-Maliki—from Zurara ibn Mus'ab, from Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites in the morning the Verse of the Throne and the first two verses of ﴿Ha-Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ (40:2), will be guarded throughout that day until evening; and whoever recites them in the evening will be guarded throughout that night until morning." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Fada'il al-Qur'an, chapter on Surat al-Baqara and the Verse of the Throne, 8/182, and he said: "This is a gharib (strange) hadith." Its chain includes Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Mulayka (diminutive form), as in al-Mughni, and he is weak, of the seventh generation, according to al-Taqrib. See also Mizan al-I'tidal, 2/550.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (raf' bi'l-ibtida'), and its predicate is in ﴿there is no god but Him, the Living﴾. [The Living] is the one who remains, enduring forever, and he is the one who possesses life; and life is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿The Self-Subsisting﴾: Umar and Ibn Mas'ud read "al-Qayyam," and Alqama read "al-Qayyim." All of these are dialectal forms with one meaning. Mujahid said: ﴿al-Qayyum﴾ is the one who stands over every ﴿thing﴾. [[The word "shay'" (thing) is missing from manuscript (b).]] Al-Kalbi said: the one who stands over every soul with what it has earned. It was also said: he is the one who manages affairs. Abu Ubayda said: the one who does not cease to exist.

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Al-Sina (drowsiness) is slumber, and it is light sleep; the one in between sleep and wakefulness is called wasnan, and from it one says: wasina yasna, wasnan and sinatan. Al-Nawm (sleep) is the heavy kind that removes strength and reason. Al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi said: drowsiness is in the head and sleep is in the heart, so drowsiness is the first stage of sleep, which is slumber. It was also said: drowsiness is in the head, slumber is in the eye, and sleep is in the heart; it is a heavy stupor that falls upon the heart and prevents knowledge of things. Allah, Exalted is He, negated sleep from Himself because it is a defect, and He is free from defects, and because it is a change, and change is not possible for Him.

Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shurayhi informed us: Abu Ishaq Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Tha'labi informed us: Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us: Ali ibn Harb informed us: Abu Mu'awiya informed us: al-A'mash informed us, from Amr ibn Murra, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us and spoke five words. He said: "Allah does not sleep, nor is it fitting for Him to sleep. Rather, He lowers the scale and raises up to Him the deeds of the night before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light; if He were to unveil it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever His sight reaches of His creation." [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on his saying (ﷺ) "Allah does not sleep," and on his saying "His veil is light; if He unveiled it..."; and al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna, 1/173.]] It was also narrated by al-Mas'udi, from Amr ibn Murra, who said: "His veil is fire."

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in dominion and in creation. ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission﴾, that is, by His command. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. Mujahid, Ata' and al-Suddi said: ﴿what is before them﴾ is the affair of this world, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is the affair of the Hereafter. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿what is before them﴾ means the Hereafter, because they will go forward to it, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ means this world, because they leave it behind their backs. Ibn Jurayj said: what is before them is what has passed before them, and what is behind them is what will be after them. Muqatil said: what is before them is what existed before the creation of the angels, and what is behind them is what existed after their creation. It was also said: what is before them is what they have sent ahead of good or evil, and what is behind them is what they will do.

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾, that is, of Allah's knowledge, ﴿except what He wills﴾ that He make them aware of. This means they do not encompass any of the knowledge of the unseen except what He wills, of what He has informed the messengers about, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ (72:26–27).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, it fills and encompasses them. They differed about the Kursi. Al-Hasan said: it is the Throne itself. Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the Kursi is placed in front of the Throne. The meaning of His saying "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth" is that its extent is like the extent of the heavens and the earth. It is related in reports that the heavens and the earth, compared to the Kursi, are like a ring thrown in a desert, and the Kursi, compared to the Throne, is like a ring thrown in a desert. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the seven heavens and the seven earths, in comparison to the Kursi, are like seven dirhams thrown onto a shield. [[Al-Tabari related it with another chain: "Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: my father told me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The seven heavens in relation to the Kursi are nothing but seven dirhams thrown onto a shield.'" 5/399. Muhammad ibn Abi Shayba related it in Kitab al-'Arsh; Ibn Kathir attributed it to Ibn Mardawayh; al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, 2/149, in which is Ibrahim ibn Hisham ibn Yahya al-Ghassani, who is abandoned (matruk), and Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'a called him a liar. All routes of this hadith are weak and do not strengthen one another because of their weakness. See al-Nahj al-Sadid, p. 283.]]

Ali and Muqatil said: each leg of the Kursi is as long as the seven heavens and the seven earths, and it is in front of the Throne. The Kursi is carried by four angels, each angel having four faces, and their feet are on the rock beneath the seventh, lowest earth, a distance of five hundred years. One angel is in the form of the lord of mankind, Adam (peace be upon him), and he asks for sustenance and rain for the children of Adam from year to year. Another is in the form of the lord of livestock, which is the bull, and he asks sustenance for the livestock from year to year, and there is a mark on his face since the calf was worshipped. Another is in the form of the lord of predators, which is the lion, and he asks sustenance for the predators from year to year. [And another is in the form of the lord of birds, which is the eagle, and he asks sustenance for the birds from year to year.] [[The bracketed sentence is missing from manuscript (b).]] Some reports say that between the bearers of the Throne and the bearers of the Kursi there are seventy veils of darkness and seventy veils of light, the thickness of each veil being a distance of five hundred years. Were it not for that, the bearers of the Kursi would be burned by the light of the bearers of the Throne.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: by the Kursi He meant His knowledge. [[Al-Tabari related this from him in al-Tafsir, 5/397–398. Al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, said: "We have related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said: 'His knowledge.'" Then he said: all other reports from Ibn Abbas and others indicate that what is meant is the well-known Kursi, mentioned together with the Throne. See al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, 2/134–135.]] This is also the view of Mujahid. From this usage, a sheet of knowledge is called kurrasa. It was also said: His Kursi is His dominion and authority, and the Arabs call ancient rule a kursi.

﴿And it does not tire Him﴾, that is, it does not burden Him and does not weigh on Him. One says: "adani al-shay'" meaning it burdened me. ﴿Their preservation﴾, that is, the preservation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And He is the Most High﴾, exalted above His creation and transcendent above things and rivals. It was also said: al-'Aliyy means the One of dominion and sovereignty. ﴿The Most Great﴾: the Great, the one greater than whom there is nothing.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 255–256 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: A woman among the Ansar would be a muqlah (the muqlah is a woman whose children do not survive) [[Omitted in (B).]], and she would vow that if a child of hers survived, she would make him a Jew. When her child survived, she would place him among the Jews. Then Islam came, and among them were some of them. When Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them a number of the sons of the Ansar, and the Ansar wanted to take them back, saying: "They are our sons and our brothers." So this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give your companions the choice. If they choose you, then they are of you; and if they choose them, then expel them along with them." [[Narrated by al-Tabari in al-Tafsir: 5/409-410, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr as a mursal report; and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan: 9/186. al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur to Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir. See also the Tafsir of al-Nasa'i 1/273, 276, and al-Nahhas in Ma'ani al-Quran 1/266. al-Shawkani has a useful discussion of this verse in Fath al-Qadir 1/275. al-Wahidi narrated a part of it with its chain, without the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) "Give your companions the choice..." Asbab al-Nuzul p. 77.]]

Mujahid said: Some people from the Aws who had been nursed among the Jews, when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, said, those who had been nursed among them: "We will certainly go with them and adopt their religion." Their families prevented them, so this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi p. 78; Tafsir al-Tabari 5/411. In Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi p. 77, Mujahid said: This verse was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar who had a black slave boy called Subayh, whom he would force to accept Islam.]]

Masruq said: A man of the Ansar from Banu Salim ibn 'Awf had two sons who had become Christians before the Prophet's mission (ﷺ). Then they came to Madinah with a group of Christians carrying food. Their father clung to them and said: "I will not leave you until you embrace Islam." So they brought their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, will part of me enter the Fire while I am watching?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and he released them. [[Ibn Hajar attributed it in al-Kafi al-Shaf p. 23 to al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, and likewise al-Baghawi; it is in al-Wahidi p. 78 without a chain.]]

Qatadah and 'Ata' said: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book when they accept the jizyah (poll tax). That is because the Arabs were an unlettered nation who had no scripture, so nothing was accepted from them except Islam. When they embraced Islam, willingly or unwillingly, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ Then He commanded fighting the People of the Book until they become Muslims or acknowledge the jizyah; whoever among them gives the jizyah is not compelled to embrace Islam. It is also said that this was at the beginning, before being commanded to fight, and it was abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾: that is, faith from disbelief, and truth from falsehood. ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾: meaning Satan. It is also said: everything worshipped besides Allah the Exalted is a taghut. It is also said: everything that causes a person to transgress (yatghi al-insan); it is fa'ul from al-tughyan (transgression), and the taa' was added to it in place of the lam of the verb, as in their saying hanut and tabut, so the taa' in them is substituted for the ta' marbutah of the feminine. ﴿And believes in Allah, then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾: that is, he has held fast and taken refuge in the firm, binding covenant in religion. Al-Wuthqa is the feminine of al-awthaq (most secure). It is also said: al-'urwah al-wuthqa is the means that leads to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. ﴿There is no breaking of it﴾: there is no cutting off of it. ﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾: it is said, of your calling them to Islam; ﴿Knowing﴾: of your eagerness for their faith.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 255–256 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. Abdul-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliħi informed us: Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Sam'an informed us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us: Ibn Abi Shayba informed us: Abd al-A'la informed us, from al-Jurayri, from Abu al-Salil [[Abu al-Salil: he is Durayb ibn Nuqayr, also said to be Nuqayl, Abu al-Salil al-Qaysi al-Jurayri al-Basri. Ishaq ibn Mansur said, from Yahya ibn Ma'in: "Trustworthy." Ibn Hibban also mentioned him among the trustworthy. Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, vol. 4, p. 401.]], from Abd Allah ibn Rabah al-Ansari, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu al-Mundhir, which verse of the Book of Allah is the greatest?" I said: ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. He said: He struck me on the chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you (layahnika al-'ilm)." Then he said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, this verse has a tongue and two lips by which it sanctifies the King at the foot of the Throne." [[Narrated by Muslim in Salat al-Musafirin wa Qasriha, no. 810, 1/156, with a different wording. Al-Musannif (al-Baghawi) in Sharh al-Sunna, 4/459. "Layahnika al-'ilm" means: may knowledge be wholesome and pleasant for you.]]

Abdul-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Maliħi informed us: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us: [I was informed] by Muhammad ibn Yusuf, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, who said: Uthman ibn al-Haytham Abu Amr said: Awf informed us, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entrusted me with guarding the zakat of Ramadan. A visitor came and began scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "I am in need, I have a dependent family, and I have a severe need." So I let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Abu Hurayra, what did your prisoner do last night?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he complained of a severe need and a family, so I had mercy on him and let him go." He said: "He has indeed lied to you, and he will return." So I knew he would return, because of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying that he would return. I watched for him, and he came scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "Leave me, for I am in need, I have a dependent family, and I will not return." So I had mercy on him and let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Abu Hurayra, what did your prisoner do?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he complained of a severe need and a family, so I had mercy on him and let him go." He said: "He has indeed lied to you, and he will return." I watched for him a third time, and he came scooping from the food, so I seized him and said: "I will surely take you to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the third time; you claim you will not return, yet you return." He said: "Leave me, and I will teach you words by which Allah will benefit you." I said: "What are they?" He said: "When you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne, ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, until you finish the verse, for a guardian from Allah will always be over you, and no devil will come near you until morning." So I let him go. In the morning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "What did your prisoner do last night?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, he claimed he would teach me words by which Allah will benefit me, so I let him go." He said: "What are they?" I said: "He told me: when you go to your bed, recite the Verse of the Throne from its beginning until you finish the verse, ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, and he said: a guardian from Allah will always be over you, and no devil will come near you until morning." They were the most eager of people for good. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He has indeed told you the truth, though he is a liar. Do you know who you were addressing for three nights, Abu Hurayra?" I said: "No." He said: "That was a devil." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Wakala, chapter: if a man appoints an agent and the agent neglects something, 4/486–487; and in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter: the description of Iblis and his troops, 6/335–336; and in Fada'il al-Qur'an. Al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna, 4/460.]]

Abdul-Wahid al-Maliħi informed us: Abu Mansur al-Sam'ani informed us: Abu Ja'far al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us: Yahya ibn Yahya informed us: Abu Mu'awiya informed us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr—he is al-Maliki—from Zurara ibn Mus'ab, from Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites in the morning the Verse of the Throne and the first two verses of ﴿Ha-Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ (40:2), will be guarded throughout that day until evening; and whoever recites them in the evening will be guarded throughout that night until morning." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Fada'il al-Qur'an, chapter on Surat al-Baqara and the Verse of the Throne, 8/182, and he said: "This is a gharib (strange) hadith." Its chain includes Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Mulayka (diminutive form), as in al-Mughni, and he is weak, of the seventh generation, according to al-Taqrib. See also Mizan al-I'tidal, 2/550.]]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (raf' bi'l-ibtida'), and its predicate is in ﴿there is no god but Him, the Living﴾. [The Living] is the one who remains, enduring forever, and he is the one who possesses life; and life is an attribute of Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿The Self-Subsisting﴾: Umar and Ibn Mas'ud read "al-Qayyam," and Alqama read "al-Qayyim." All of these are dialectal forms with one meaning. Mujahid said: ﴿al-Qayyum﴾ is the one who stands over every ﴿thing﴾. [[The word "shay'" (thing) is missing from manuscript (b).]] Al-Kalbi said: the one who stands over every soul with what it has earned. It was also said: he is the one who manages affairs. Abu Ubayda said: the one who does not cease to exist.

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Al-Sina (drowsiness) is slumber, and it is light sleep; the one in between sleep and wakefulness is called wasnan, and from it one says: wasina yasna, wasnan and sinatan. Al-Nawm (sleep) is the heavy kind that removes strength and reason. Al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi said: drowsiness is in the head and sleep is in the heart, so drowsiness is the first stage of sleep, which is slumber. It was also said: drowsiness is in the head, slumber is in the eye, and sleep is in the heart; it is a heavy stupor that falls upon the heart and prevents knowledge of things. Allah, Exalted is He, negated sleep from Himself because it is a defect, and He is free from defects, and because it is a change, and change is not possible for Him.

Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Shurayhi informed us: Abu Ishaq Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Tha'labi informed us: Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us: Muhammad ibn Ja'far informed us: Ali ibn Harb informed us: Abu Mu'awiya informed us: al-A'mash informed us, from Amr ibn Murra, from Abu Ubayda, from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us and spoke five words. He said: "Allah does not sleep, nor is it fitting for Him to sleep. Rather, He lowers the scale and raises up to Him the deeds of the night before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light; if He were to unveil it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever His sight reaches of His creation." [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on his saying (ﷺ) "Allah does not sleep," and on his saying "His veil is light; if He unveiled it..."; and al-Musannif in Sharh al-Sunna, 1/173.]] It was also narrated by al-Mas'udi, from Amr ibn Murra, who said: "His veil is fire."

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in dominion and in creation. ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission﴾, that is, by His command. ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. Mujahid, Ata' and al-Suddi said: ﴿what is before them﴾ is the affair of this world, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ is the affair of the Hereafter. Al-Kalbi said: ﴿what is before them﴾ means the Hereafter, because they will go forward to it, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ means this world, because they leave it behind their backs. Ibn Jurayj said: what is before them is what has passed before them, and what is behind them is what will be after them. Muqatil said: what is before them is what existed before the creation of the angels, and what is behind them is what existed after their creation. It was also said: what is before them is what they have sent ahead of good or evil, and what is behind them is what they will do.

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾, that is, of Allah's knowledge, ﴿except what He wills﴾ that He make them aware of. This means they do not encompass any of the knowledge of the unseen except what He wills, of what He has informed the messengers about, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ (72:26–27).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, it fills and encompasses them. They differed about the Kursi. Al-Hasan said: it is the Throne itself. Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the Kursi is placed in front of the Throne. The meaning of His saying "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth" is that its extent is like the extent of the heavens and the earth. It is related in reports that the heavens and the earth, compared to the Kursi, are like a ring thrown in a desert, and the Kursi, compared to the Throne, is like a ring thrown in a desert. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the seven heavens and the seven earths, in comparison to the Kursi, are like seven dirhams thrown onto a shield. [[Al-Tabari related it with another chain: "Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: my father told me: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The seven heavens in relation to the Kursi are nothing but seven dirhams thrown onto a shield.'" 5/399. Muhammad ibn Abi Shayba related it in Kitab al-'Arsh; Ibn Kathir attributed it to Ibn Mardawayh; al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, 2/149, in which is Ibrahim ibn Hisham ibn Yahya al-Ghassani, who is abandoned (matruk), and Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'a called him a liar. All routes of this hadith are weak and do not strengthen one another because of their weakness. See al-Nahj al-Sadid, p. 283.]]

Ali and Muqatil said: each leg of the Kursi is as long as the seven heavens and the seven earths, and it is in front of the Throne. The Kursi is carried by four angels, each angel having four faces, and their feet are on the rock beneath the seventh, lowest earth, a distance of five hundred years. One angel is in the form of the lord of mankind, Adam (peace be upon him), and he asks for sustenance and rain for the children of Adam from year to year. Another is in the form of the lord of livestock, which is the bull, and he asks sustenance for the livestock from year to year, and there is a mark on his face since the calf was worshipped. Another is in the form of the lord of predators, which is the lion, and he asks sustenance for the predators from year to year. [And another is in the form of the lord of birds, which is the eagle, and he asks sustenance for the birds from year to year.] [[The bracketed sentence is missing from manuscript (b).]] Some reports say that between the bearers of the Throne and the bearers of the Kursi there are seventy veils of darkness and seventy veils of light, the thickness of each veil being a distance of five hundred years. Were it not for that, the bearers of the Kursi would be burned by the light of the bearers of the Throne.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: by the Kursi He meant His knowledge. [[Al-Tabari related this from him in al-Tafsir, 5/397–398. Al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, said: "We have related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that he said: 'His knowledge.'" Then he said: all other reports from Ibn Abbas and others indicate that what is meant is the well-known Kursi, mentioned together with the Throne. See al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, 2/134–135.]] This is also the view of Mujahid. From this usage, a sheet of knowledge is called kurrasa. It was also said: His Kursi is His dominion and authority, and the Arabs call ancient rule a kursi.

﴿And it does not tire Him﴾, that is, it does not burden Him and does not weigh on Him. One says: "adani al-shay'" meaning it burdened me. ﴿Their preservation﴾, that is, the preservation of the heavens and the earth. ﴿And He is the Most High﴾, exalted above His creation and transcendent above things and rivals. It was also said: al-'Aliyy means the One of dominion and sovereignty. ﴿The Most Great﴾: the Great, the one greater than whom there is nothing.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 255–256 (part 2 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: A woman among the Ansar would be a muqlah (the muqlah is a woman whose children do not survive) [[Omitted in (B).]], and she would vow that if a child of hers survived, she would make him a Jew. When her child survived, she would place him among the Jews. Then Islam came, and among them were some of them. When Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them a number of the sons of the Ansar, and the Ansar wanted to take them back, saying: "They are our sons and our brothers." So this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give your companions the choice. If they choose you, then they are of you; and if they choose them, then expel them along with them." [[Narrated by al-Tabari in al-Tafsir: 5/409-410, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr as a mursal report; and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan: 9/186. al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur to Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir. See also the Tafsir of al-Nasa'i 1/273, 276, and al-Nahhas in Ma'ani al-Quran 1/266. al-Shawkani has a useful discussion of this verse in Fath al-Qadir 1/275. al-Wahidi narrated a part of it with its chain, without the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) "Give your companions the choice..." Asbab al-Nuzul p. 77.]]

Mujahid said: Some people from the Aws who had been nursed among the Jews, when the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, said, those who had been nursed among them: "We will certainly go with them and adopt their religion." Their families prevented them, so this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi p. 78; Tafsir al-Tabari 5/411. In Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi p. 77, Mujahid said: This verse was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar who had a black slave boy called Subayh, whom he would force to accept Islam.]]

Masruq said: A man of the Ansar from Banu Salim ibn 'Awf had two sons who had become Christians before the Prophet's mission (ﷺ). Then they came to Madinah with a group of Christians carrying food. Their father clung to them and said: "I will not leave you until you embrace Islam." So they brought their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, will part of me enter the Fire while I am watching?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and he released them. [[Ibn Hajar attributed it in al-Kafi al-Shaf p. 23 to al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, and likewise al-Baghawi; it is in al-Wahidi p. 78 without a chain.]]

Qatadah and 'Ata' said: It was revealed concerning the People of the Book when they accept the jizyah (poll tax). That is because the Arabs were an unlettered nation who had no scripture, so nothing was accepted from them except Islam. When they embraced Islam, willingly or unwillingly, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ Then He commanded fighting the People of the Book until they become Muslims or acknowledge the jizyah; whoever among them gives the jizyah is not compelled to embrace Islam. It is also said that this was at the beginning, before being commanded to fight, and it was abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.

﴿The right course has become distinct from error﴾: that is, faith from disbelief, and truth from falsehood. ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾: meaning Satan. It is also said: everything worshipped besides Allah the Exalted is a taghut. It is also said: everything that causes a person to transgress (yatghi al-insan); it is fa'ul from al-tughyan (transgression), and the taa' was added to it in place of the lam of the verb, as in their saying hanut and tabut, so the taa' in them is substituted for the ta' marbutah of the feminine. ﴿And believes in Allah, then he has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾: that is, he has held fast and taken refuge in the firm, binding covenant in religion. Al-Wuthqa is the feminine of al-awthaq (most secure). It is also said: al-'urwah al-wuthqa is the means that leads to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted. ﴿There is no breaking of it﴾: there is no cutting off of it. ﴿And Allah is Hearing﴾: it is said, of your calling them to Islam; ﴿Knowing﴾: of your eagerness for their faith.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 257–258:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾: their Helper and Supporter. It was also said: their Lover. It was also said: the One who takes charge of their affairs and does not leave them to another. Al-Hasan said: the Guardian of their guidance. ﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾, that is, from disbelief (kufr) to faith (iman). Al-Waqidi said: every mention of "darknesses" and "light" in the Qur'an refers to disbelief and faith, except the one in Surat al-An'am, "and He made the darknesses and the light," where it refers to the night and the day. Disbelief is called darkness because its path is confused, and Islam is called light because its path is clear. ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut﴾. Muqatil said: this means Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the rest of the leaders of misguidance. ﴿They bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾: they call them from the light into the darknesses. The word taghut (false deity, tyrant) may be masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Exalted is He said regarding the masculine and singular: ﴿They desire to have their disputes judged by the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ (4:60). He said regarding the feminine: ﴿And those who avoid the taghut, not worshipping it﴾ (39:17). He said regarding the plural: ﴿They bring them out of the light into the darknesses﴾.

If it is asked: He said "they bring them out of the light," but they were disbelievers who were never in light at all? It is answered: they were the Jews, who used to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent, because of the description of him that they found in their books. When he was sent, they disbelieved in him. It was also said: it is a general statement concerning all disbelievers. They said: their preventing them from entering it is a "bringing out," just as a man says to his father, "You have expelled me from your property," when it was never his property. Exalted is He also said, relating the words of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, I have abandoned the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah﴾ (12:37), though he had never been in their religion. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was confounded. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (2:258)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ Its meaning: has the report of the one who argued with Abraham reached you, O Muhammad? That is, disputed and debated with him. He was Nimrod, and he was the first to place a crown on his head, and he acted tyrannically on the earth and claimed lordship. ﴿Because Allah had given him kingship﴾: that is, because Allah had given him kingship, he became arrogant (tagha). That is, that argument came from the insolence and tyranny of the king. Mujahid said: four people ruled the earth, two believers and two disbelievers. The two believers were Sulayman and Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and the two disbelievers were Nimrod and Bukhtanassar.

They differed about the time of this debate. Muqatil said: when Abraham broke the idols, Nimrod imprisoned him, then brought him out in order to burn him with fire, and he said to him: "Who is your Lord whom you call us to?" He said: "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death." Others said: this happened after he was thrown into the fire. That is because the people suffered a famine during the time of Nimrod, and the people were obtaining food from him [[bring in food.]]. Whenever a man came to him seeking food, he would ask him: "Who is your Lord?" If he said, "You," he would sell him food. Abraham came among those who came to him, and Nimrod said to him: "Who is your Lord?" He said: "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death." So Nimrod became occupied with the debate and did not give him anything. Abraham returned and passed by a heap of reddish sand, and he took from it, to comfort the hearts of his family when he entered upon them. When he came to his family and set down his goods, he slept. His wife got up to his goods and opened them, and behold, it was the finest food anyone had ever seen. She took it and prepared some for him, then brought it to him. He said: "From where is this?" She said: "From the food you brought." So he knew that Allah had provided for him, and he praised Allah.

Allah Exalted said: ﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death"﴾ [This is the answer to an unmentioned question, its implied meaning being that he was asked: "Who is your Lord?" and Abraham said, ﴿"My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death"﴾ [[Omitted in (B).]]]. Hamzah recited ﴿رَبِّيَ﴾ in ﴿My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death﴾ with the yā' silent (sukun), and likewise in ﴿حَرَّمَ رَبِّيَ الْفَوَاحِشَ﴾ (7:33), ﴿عَنْ آيَاتِيَ الَّذِينَ يَتَكَبَّرُونَ﴾ (7:146), ﴿قُلْ لِعِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ﴾ (14:31), ﴿آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ (19:30), ﴿مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ﴾ (21:83), ﴿عِبَادِيَ الصَّالِحُونَ﴾ (21:105), ﴿عِبَادِيَ الشَّكُورُ﴾ (34:13), ﴿مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطَانُ﴾ (38:41), ﴿إِنْ أَرَادَنِيَ اللَّهُ﴾ (39:38), and ﴿إِنْ أَهْلَكَنِيَ اللَّهُ﴾ (67:28). Hamzah made the yā' silent in all of these. Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i agreed with him in ﴿لِعِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾, and Ibn 'Amir (also agreed) in ﴿آيَاتِيَ الَّذِينَ﴾. The others pronounced the yā' with a fatha. ﴿He said﴾: Nimrod said: ﴿"I give life and cause death."﴾

The people of Medina recited ﴿أَنَا﴾ with the alif affirmed and with the madd (lengthening) in connected speech when it is followed by an alif with fatha or damma, while the rest omitted the alif. They all stopped on the alif. Most of the exegetes said: Nimrod called two men, killed one of them, and spared the other, and he made the sparing of the one from being killed a giving of life to him. So Abraham moved on to another proof, not out of incapacity, for his first argument was binding, since he meant by "giving life" the restoring of life to the dead. He could have said: "Then bring back to life whom you have caused to die, if you are truthful." So he moved on to another proof, clearer than the first.

﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾: that is, he was bewildered, stunned, and his argument was cut off. If it is asked: how was he confounded, when he could have opposed Abraham by saying to him: "Ask your Lord to bring it from the west"? It is answered: he did not say this because he feared that if he asked for that, Abraham would supplicate to his Lord, and that would have been an increase in his own disgrace and defeat. The correct view is that Allah turned him away from that counter-argument, to manifest the proof against him, or as a miracle for Abraham (peace be upon him). ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾. This verse is linked to the previous verse. Its implied sense is: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham﴾, and [have you considered] the one who passed by a town? It is also said that the implied sense is: "Have you seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, and have you seen the one who passed by a town?" [45b] They differed about this passer-by. Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said he was 'Uzayr ibn Shar-khiya. Wahb ibn Munabbih said he was Irmiya ibn Halqiya, who was from the tribe of Aaron, and he is al-Khidr. Mujahid said he was an unbeliever who doubted the resurrection.

They also differed about that town. Wahb, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah said it was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Al-Dahhak said it was the Holy Land. Al-Kalbi said it was Dayr Sabir Abad. Al-Suddi said it was Muslim-Baadh, and it is also said it was Dayr Hiraql (the Monastery of Heraclius). It is also said it was the land in which God destroyed those who left their homes, and they were thousands. It is also said it was the Village of the Grapes, which is two farsakhs (about six miles) from Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿And it was fallen upon its roofs﴾: that is, collapsed. It is said: "khawa al-bayt" (with a kasra on the waw), yakhwi khawan, [a shortened form], meaning it collapsed; and "khawa al-bayt" (with a fatha on the waw), khawa'an, [a lengthened form], meaning it became empty. ﴿Upon its roofs﴾: its ceilings. Its singular is 'arsh. It is also said that every building is an 'arsh. The meaning is that the ceilings fell, and then the walls collapsed upon them.

﴿He said: "How will God bring this to life after its death?"﴾ The cause of this, as narrated by Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Munabbih, [[The story is in al-Tabari: 5/447–454. Wahb ibn Munabbih, may God have mercy on him, was born in the year 34 AH. He is well known for narrating Isra'iliyyat (narratives from the People of the Book). He had a great deal of knowledge from the People of the Book, for he devoted his attention to it and went to great lengths. His hadith is in the two Sahihs through his brother Hammam. And in both Sahihs there is a well-known collection from Abu Hurayrah, most of which is in the authentic collections, narrated from him by Ma'mar. He died in the year 114 AH. See Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1/100 and Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' 4/544.]] is that God, the Mighty and Majestic, sent Irmiya to Nashiya ibn Amus, the king of the Children of Israel, to support him in this matter and bring him news from God, the Mighty and Majestic. The transgressions among the Children of Israel grew great, and they committed sins. God, the Exalted, revealed to Irmiya: "Remind your people of My blessings, make them aware of their transgressions, and call them to Me." Irmiya said: "I am weak unless You strengthen me, incapable unless You enable me to deliver the message, and forsaken unless You support me." God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "I will inspire you." Irmiya stood among them and did not know what to say, so God inspired him at that moment with an eloquent and lengthy sermon, in which he explained to them the reward of obedience and the punishment of disobedience. At its end he said, on behalf of God, the Exalted: "I swear by My might that I will bring upon them a trial in which the wise will be bewildered, and I will set over them a tyrant from Persia, to whom I will give awe, and from whose heart I will remove mercy. Following him will be a host like the darkness of the black night." Then God inspired Irmiya: "I will destroy the Children of Israel through Yafith, and Yafith is from the people of Babylon. They are descendants of Yafith ibn Nuh, peace be upon him." When Irmiya heard this, he cried out, wept, tore his garments, and threw ash upon his head. When God heard his supplication and weeping, He called to him: "O Irmiya, is what I revealed to you grievous to you?" He said: "Yes, O Lord. Let me die before I see among the Children of Israel what will not gladden me." God, the Exalted, said: "By My might, I will not destroy the Children of Israel until the matter comes from your side." Irmiya rejoiced at this and his soul was content. He said: "No, by Him who sent Moses with the truth, I will not be content with the destruction of the Children of Israel." Then he went to the king and informed him of this. He was a righteous king, so he rejoiced and was glad, and said: "If our Lord punishes us, it is for many sins, and if He pardons us, it is by His mercy."

Then they remained for three years after the revelation, increasing in nothing but disobedience and persistence in evil, and this was when their destruction drew near. Revelation became rare, and the king called them to repentance, but they did not respond. So God set Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them, and he went out with six hundred thousand banners, heading for the people of Bayt al-Maqdis. When he set out on his march, news reached the king, who said to Irmiya: "Where is what you claimed God revealed to you?" Irmiya said: "God does not break His promise, and I am certain of Him." When the appointed time drew near, God sent to Irmiya an angel who had taken the form of a man from the Children of Israel. He said to him: "Who are you?" The angel said: "I am a man from the Children of Israel. I came to you to ask your opinion about the people of my family. I have joined their kin and have done nothing to them but good, yet my generosity to them only increases their anger toward me. So give me your ruling about them." He said: "Be good in what is between you and God, join them in kinship, and be glad of good tidings." The angel departed, stayed for some days, then came back to him in the form of that man, sat before him, and said: "I am the one who came to you about my family." Irmiya said to him: "Have their characters not yet been purified for you?" He said: "O Prophet of God, by Him who sent you with truth, I know of no kindness that anyone among the people has ever given except that I have given it to them first and more besides." The Prophet Irmiya, peace be upon him, said to him: "Go back and be good to them. Ask God, who sets right the righteous among His servants, to set them right." The man stood up and departed. Then some days passed, and Bukhtansar and his troops had encamped around Bayt al-Maqdis, more numerous than locusts. The Children of Israel were terrified of them, so their king said to Irmiya: "O Prophet of God, where is what God promised you?" He said: "I trust in my Lord." Then the king came to Irmiya, who was sitting on the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis, laughing and rejoicing in the victory of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, which He had promised him. The king sat before him and said: "I am the one who came to you about my family, twice." The Prophet said: "Has the time not yet come for them to wake from what they are in?" The king said: "O Prophet of God, every harm I suffered from them before today I endured patiently, but today I saw them engaged in an act that does not please God." The Prophet said: "What act did you see them doing?" He said: "An enormous act that draws God's wrath. So God became angry, and I came to inform you. I ask you, by God who sent you as a prophet with truth, only that you call upon God against them, that He may destroy them." Irmiya said: "O Master of the heavens and the earth, if they are upon truth and right, then preserve them, and if they are upon an act You do not approve, then destroy them." When these words left the mouth of Irmiya, God sent a thunderbolt from heaven upon Bayt al-Maqdis, and the place of the sacrificial offering burst into flames, and seven of its gates were swallowed up. When Irmiya saw this, he cried out, tore his garments, threw ash upon his head, and said: "O Master of the heavens, where is Your promise that You made to me?" Then it was called out to him: "Nothing has befallen them except through your fatwa and your supplication." The Prophet, peace be upon him, was certain that it was his fatwa, and that this questioner had been the Messenger of God ﷺ. Then Irmiya fled until he mingled with the wild beasts.

Bukhtansar and his troops entered Bayt al-Maqdis, trampled al-Sham, killed the Children of Israel until he had exterminated them, and destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis. Then he ordered his troops that each man should fill his shield with earth and hurl it into Bayt al-Maqdis, so they did until they had filled it. Then he ordered them to gather everyone who was in the towns around Bayt al-Maqdis, and there gathered before them the young and old of the Children of Israel. He selected from them seventy thousand boys and divided them among the kings who were with him, so that each man received four youths. Among those youths were Daniel and Hananiya. He divided the remaining Children of Israel into three groups: a third he killed, a third he took captive, and a third he left in al-Sham. This was the first calamity God sent upon the Children of Israel for their wrongdoing. When Bukhtansar turned away from them, returning to Babylon with the captives of the Children of Israel, Irmiya came riding his donkey, with a container of grape juice and a basket of figs, until he reached Iliya (Jerusalem). When he stood over it and saw its ruin, he said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾

The one who said that the passer-by was 'Uzayr said: When Bukhtansar destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis and brought the captives of the Children of Israel to Babylon, among them were 'Uzayr, Daniel, and seven thousand people from the family of David. When 'Uzayr escaped from Babylon, he set out on his donkey until he reached Dayr Hiraql on the bank of the Tigris. He went around the town and saw no one there, yet most of its trees were laden with fruit. He ate from the fruit, pressed grapes and drank their juice, and put the surplus fruit in a basket and the surplus juice in a leather skin. When he saw the ruin of the town and the death of its people, he said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ He said it in amazement, not in doubt about the resurrection. [46a]

Returning to the narration of Wahb, he said: Then Irmiya tied his donkey with a new rope. God cast sleep upon him, and when he slept, God took his soul for a hundred years and caused his donkey to die. His grape juice and figs were with him. God blinded people's eyes to him, so no one saw him, and this was at midday. God also prevented wild beasts and birds from touching his flesh. When seventy years had passed since his death, God sent an angel to a king of the kings of Persia called Nushik. He said: "God commands you to set out with your people and rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis and Iliya, until it returns to being the most prosperous it has ever been." The king set out with a thousand qahramans, [[Persian, Arabized; they were among the king's trusted officials.]] each with three hundred thousand workers, and they began to rebuild it. God destroyed Bukhtansar with a gnat that entered his brain. God rescued those of the Children of Israel who remained, and he did not die in Babylon. He returned them all to Bayt al-Maqdis and its surroundings, and they rebuilt it for thirty years. They multiplied until they returned to the best condition they had ever been in. When the hundred years had passed, God restored the eyes of Irmiya, while the rest of his body was still dead. Then God restored his body while he watched. Then he looked at his donkey, and its bones were scattered and white, shining. He heard a voice from heaven: "O bones that have decayed, God commands you to come together." Some of them joined others and connected to one another. Then it was called out: "God commands you to clothe yourselves with flesh and skin," and it was so. Then it was called out: "God commands you to live," and it stood up by God's permission and brayed. God gave Irmiya a long life, and so he is the one who is seen in the wilderness. This is the meaning of God's saying, the Exalted: ﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him﴾, that is, brought him back to life. ﴿He said: "How long did you remain?"﴾ That is, how long did you stay? It is said: When God brought him back to life, He sent an angel to him and asked him: "How long did you remain?" ﴿He said: "I remained a day"﴾. God had caused him to die at midday, at the beginning of the day, and brought him back to life after a hundred years, near the end of the day, before the sun set. So he said: "I remained a day," while he thought the sun had set. Then he turned and saw some of the sun remaining, so he said: ﴿Or part of a day﴾, rather, part of a day. ﴿He said﴾, the angel ﴿"Rather, you remained a hundred years. Look at your food﴾, meaning the figs, ﴿and your drink﴾, meaning the juice, ﴿they have not spoiled﴾, that is, they have not changed. The figs looked as though they had been picked that very hour, and the juice as though it had been pressed that very hour.

Al-Kisa'i said: "It is as if the years had not passed over it." Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿لَمْ يَتَسَنَّ﴾ (lam yatasanna) with the hā' dropped in continuous recitation (waṣl), and likewise ﴿فَبِهُدَاهُمُ اقْتَدِهْ﴾ (6:90). The others read the hā' in both waṣl and waqf (pausal recitation) in both places. Whoever drops the hā' in waṣl treats the hā' as an extra, supplementary letter (ṣila zā'ida), and says: its original form is yatasannā, so the yā' was dropped by jazm (apocopation), and a hā' was substituted for it at pause. Abu 'Amr said: it is from at-tasannun with two nūns, meaning change, as in His words ﴿مِنْ حَمَإٍ مَسْنُونٍ﴾ (22:26), i.e., changed. So a yā' was substituted for one of the two nūns, as in His words ﴿ثُمَّ ذَهَبَ إِلَى أَهْلِهِ يَتَمَطَّى﴾ (75:33), i.e., yatamaṭṭaṭ (stretches himself), and as in His words ﴿وَقَدْ خَابَ مَنْ دَسَّاهَا﴾ (91:10), whose original form is dassaytuhā. Whoever retains the hā' in both states treats the hā' as an original radical of the verb (lām al-fi'l). This is according to the view of those who hold that the root of sanah (year) is sanhah, its diminutive is sunayhah, and the verb is from as-sānihah. He said "lam yatasanneh" and "lam yuthinnih" even though he reported about two things, because he returned the change to the nearer of the two words, which is the drink (ash-sharab), and was content with mentioning one of the two mentioned things, because it has the meaning of the other. ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى حِمَارِكَ﴾ So he looked, and behold, there were white bones. Allah assembled the bones, one upon another, clothed them with flesh and skin, and brought him to life while he was watching. ﴿وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾ It was said the wāw is extra and inserted. Al-Farra' said: the wāw was introduced to indicate that it is a condition for a following verb, meaning "and that We may make you a sign," i.e., a lesson and a proof of resurrection after death. This is what most exegetes said. Ad-Dahhak and others said: he returned to his town as a young man, while his sons and grandsons were elderly shaykhs and old women, and he had black hair and beard.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُهَا﴾ The people of the Hijaz and Basra read *nanshuruhā* with the rā', meaning "We bring it to life." It is said: Allah revived (anshara) the dead, inshār and nashrah, nushūr. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ﴾ (80:22), and of the intransitive form: ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ﴾ (67:15). The others read with the zāy, i.e., We raise them from the earth and return them to their place in the body, and We assemble some of them upon others. The verb *inshāz* of a thing means raising it and moving it. It is said: "anshaztuhu fa-nashaza," i.e., I raised it and it rose.

They differed about the meaning of the verse. Most said: He meant the bones of his donkey. As-Suddi said: Allah, exalted is He, brought Uzayr to life, then said to him: "Look at your donkey, which has perished and whose bones have decayed." Then Allah sent a wind which brought the donkey's bones from every plain and mountain, after birds and beasts had carried them away. They gathered, and some were assembled upon others while he was watching, so it became a donkey made of bones with no flesh or blood in it. ﴿ثُمَّ نَكْسُوهَا لَحْمًا﴾ Then He clothed the bones with flesh and blood, and it became a donkey without a soul. Then an angel came walking until he took hold of the donkey's nostril and blew into it, and the donkey stood up and brayed, by Allah's permission.

Others said: He meant the bones of this man. That is because Allah did not cause his donkey to die; rather, He caused him to die, then Allah revived his two eyes and head, while the rest of his body was dead. Then He said: "Look at your donkey," and he looked and saw his donkey standing upright, in the same state as on the day he tied it, alive, having not eaten or drunk for a hundred years. He looked at the *rummah* (piece of rope) on its neck, new and unchanged. The verse's implied meaning: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى حِمَارِكَ﴾ and look at your bones, how We raise them. There is inversion (taqdīm wa ta'khīr) in the verse, and its arrangement is: "and look at your donkey," and "look at the bones, how We raise them," and "and that We may make you a sign for the people."

Qatadah reported from Ka'b, and ad-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and as-Suddi from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: When Allah brought Uzayr back to life after He had caused him to die for a hundred years, he rode his donkey until he came to his locality. The people did not recognize him, and he did not recognize the people or his dwellings. He set off in confusion until he came to his house, and there he found an old woman, blind and paralyzed, who was now a hundred and twenty years old. She had known him and remembered him. Uzayr said to her: "O woman, is this the house of Uzayr?" She said: "Yes, this is the house of Uzayr." And she wept and said: "I have not seen anyone for so-and-so many years mentioning Uzayr." He said: "I am Uzayr." She said: "Glory be to Allah! Uzayr has been missing from us for a hundred years; we have not heard any mention of him." He said: "I am Uzayr; Allah caused me to die for a hundred years, then raised me." She said: "Uzayr was a man whose supplication was answered, and he would pray for the sick and for the afflicted for their recovery. So pray to Allah that He returns my sight to me, so that I may see you; if you are Uzayr, I will recognize you." He prayed to his Lord and passed his hand over her eyes, and they were restored. He took her hand and said: "Rise, by Allah's permission." Allah released her legs and she stood up healthy. She looked at him and said: "I testify that you are Uzayr." She went to the Children of Israel while they were in their assemblies and gatherings. A son of Uzayr, a great old shaykh a hundred and eighteen years old, and his grandsons were elderly shaykhs in the assembly. She called out: "This is Uzayr; he has come to you." They denied her. She said: "I am so-and-so, your freedwoman. He prayed to his Lord for me, and He returned my sight to me and released my legs, and he claimed that Allah had caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him." The people rose and came to him. His son said: "My father had a black birthmark like the crescent moon between his shoulders." He uncovered his shoulders, and behold, it was Uzayr.

As-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: When Uzayr returned to his people, Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) had burned the Torah, and there was no covenant from Allah among the creatures. Uzayr wept over the Torah, and an angel came to him with a vessel containing water and gave him to drink from that water, and the Torah took shape in his chest. He returned to the Children of Israel, Allah having taught him the Torah and sent him as a prophet. He said: "I am Uzayr," but they did not believe him. He said: "I am Uzayr, whom Allah has sent to you to renew your Torah for you." They said: "Dictate it to us." So he dictated it to them from memory. They said: "Allah has not placed the Torah in the chest of a man after it had gone, except that he is His son." So they said: "Uzayr is the son of Allah." The story will come in Surah Bara'ah, if Allah wills, exalted is He. [See: ad-Durr al-Manthur, 2/27-28.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَلَمَّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ﴾ that is, he saw it directly. ﴿قَالَ أَعْلَمُ﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it jussed (apocopated) and connected (mawṣūl), as an imperative, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "Know!" The others read "a'lamu" with a hamzat qaṭ' (cut alif) and a raised mīm, as a report about Uzayr that he said when he saw that: "I know ﴿أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ﴾ that Allah is powerful over all things."

**The exegesis of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾** Al-Hasan, Qatadah, ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and Ibn Jurayj said: The reason for this question from Abraham, peace be upon him, was that he passed by a dead animal. Ibn Jurayj said: It was the carcass of a donkey on the seashore. ʿAtaʾ said: In the lake of Tiberias. They said: He saw it, and the beasts of the sea and the land had scattered its parts. When the sea rose, the fish and the sea creatures came and ate from it, and what fell from it went into the sea. When the sea receded and withdrew, the predatory beasts came and ate from it, and what fell from it turned to dust. When the beasts had gone, the birds came and ate from it, and what fell from it the wind scattered into the air. When Abraham, peace be upon him, saw this, he marvelled at it and said: "My Lord, You know that You will gather it from the bellies of the beasts, the crops of the birds and the insides of the sea creatures. So show me how You give it life, that I may witness it and my certainty may increase." Then God, Exalted is He, rebuked him: ﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes"﴾ — O my Lord, I know and I believe. ﴿"But so that my heart may be at rest"﴾, that is, so that my heart may be tranquil through direct observation and witnessing. He wanted that the knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqin, knowledge by inference) become the certainty of sight (ʿayn al-yaqin, knowledge by direct witnessing), because hearsay is not like seeing.[[See: Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi, p. 79.]]

It was also said that the reason for this question from Abraham was that when he argued against Nimrod, saying ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ (2:258), Nimrod said: "I give life and cause death." He then killed one of the two men and released the other. Abraham said: "Indeed God, blessed and exalted, brings a dead body and gives it life." Nimrod said to him: "You have seen it." So he could not say "Yes," and he moved on to another argument. Then he asked his Lord to show him the giving of life to the dead.[[Al-Wahidi attributes this view to Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar. Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 80.]]

﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest"﴾ — by the strength of my argument. So if it is said to me, "You have seen it," I would say, "Yes, I have seen it."

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: When God took Abraham as a khalil (intimate friend), the Angel of Death asked his Lord for permission to give Abraham the good news of this. He was permitted, so he came to Abraham, who was not at home. He entered his house. Abraham, peace be upon him, was the most protective of people: whenever he went out, he locked his door. When he came back, he found a man in his house, and he rushed at him to seize him and said: "Who gave you permission to enter my house?" The man said: "The Lord of this house gave me permission." Abraham said: "You have spoken the truth," and he realised that he was an angel. He said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the Angel of Death. I have come to give you the good news that God, Exalted is He, has taken you as a khalil." So Abraham praised God, Mighty and Majestic is He, and said: "What is the sign of that?" He said: "That God will answer your supplication and will give life to the dead at your request." At that point Abraham said: ﴿"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest"﴾ — that You have taken me as a khalil and answer me when I call upon You.[[Asbab al-Nuzul, p. 81.]]

Al-Malihi informed us: ʿAbd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad informed us; al-Nuʿaymi informed us: Ahmad ibn ʿAbd Allah informed us; Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Ahmad ibn Salih informed us: Ibn Wahb informed us: Yunus informed us, from Ibn Shihab, from Abu Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham, when he said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.' And may God have mercy on Lot, for he used to take refuge in a strong pillar. Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph did, I would have answered the summoner."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari, in the Book of the Prophets, chapter: "The saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: 'And inform them about the guests of Abraham'" (6/410–411).]]

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj narrated this hadith from Harmalah ibn Yahya, from Wahb, with this same chain, similarly, and he said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham, when he said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.'"[[Narrated by Muslim, in the Book of Faith, chapter: "The increase of the heart's tranquillity through the convergence of evidences," no. 151 (1/133). The author also cites it in Sharh al-Sunnah (1/111).]]

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah reported from Abu Ibrahim Isma'il ibn Yahya al-Muzani that he said, concerning this hadith: The Prophet (ﷺ) did not doubt, nor did Abraham, that God is able to give life to the dead. They only doubted whether He would grant them what they asked for. Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: In his saying, "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," there is no admission of doubt on his own part or on Abraham's part. Rather, it negates doubt from both of them. He means: If I do not doubt God's power to give life to the dead, then Abraham is more entitled not to doubt. He said this out of humility and self-abasement. Likewise his saying, "Had I remained in prison as long as Joseph did, I would have answered the summoner." In it is the information that Abraham's request did not arise from doubt, but from a desire for increased knowledge through direct witnessing, for direct witnessing gives a knowledge and tranquillity that inference does not give. It was also said: When this verse was revealed, some people said, "Abraham doubted, but our Prophet did not." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said this statement out of humility, and to give precedence to Abraham over himself.

His words, ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ — its meaning is: "You have already believed, so why do you ask?" He testified to his faith, like the verse of Jarir:
"Are you not the best of those who mounted the mounts,
and the most generous of all the peoples in giving drink?"
He means: You are like that. But "so that my heart may be at rest" refers to an increase in certainty.

﴿He said, "Take four birds"﴾ — Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ and Ibn Jurayj said: He took a peacock, a rooster, a dove and a crow. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, that he also took an eagle in place of the dove.

ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani said: It was revealed to him: "Take a green duck, a black crow, a white dove and a red rooster." ﴿Then make them incline toward you﴾ — Abu Jaʿfar and Hamzah read ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ with a kasrah on the ṣad, meaning: cut them up and tear them apart. It is said ṣāra yaṣīru ṣayran when one cuts, and inṣāra al-shayʾ inṣiyāran when a thing is cut off.

Al-Farraʾ said: It is a metathesis (qalb) from ṣaraytu aṣrī ṣarʾan, when I cut. The others read ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ with a ḍammah on the ṣad, and its meaning is: incline them toward you and turn them to you. It is said ṣirtu al-shayʾ uṣawwiruhu when I inclined it. A man is aṣwar when his neck is inclined. ʿAtaʾ said: Its meaning is: gather them and draw them to you. It is said ṣāra yaṣūru ṣawran when they gathered, and from this the swarm of bees is called ṣawr. Whoever interprets it as "inclining" and "drawing toward" says that there is an ellipsis (idmar) here, whose meaning is: "So incline them toward you, then cut them," and he omitted it because of the saying ﴿Then place on every mountain a part of them﴾, since that indicates it. Abu ʿUbaydah said: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ also means "cut them up," and ṣawr means cutting.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then place on every mountain a part of them﴾ — ʿAsim, through the transmission of Abu Bakr, read ﴿juzʾan﴾ with the ʿayn pronounced with a heavier stress and with a hamzah (the reading of the heavier form). The others read it lightly, with a hamzah. Abu Jaʿfar read it with a doubled zay, without a hamzah, and meant by it some of the mountains.

Some exegetes said: God commanded Abraham to slaughter those birds, pluck their feathers, cut them up, and mix their feathers, their blood and their flesh with one another. He did so. Then He commanded him to place their pieces on the mountains.

They differed about the number of parts and mountains. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, and Qatadah said: He was commanded to make each bird into four parts and place them on four mountains, with a quarter of each bird on each mountain. It was also said: one mountain on the east side, one on the west side, one on the north side, and one on the south side.

Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi said: He divided them into seven parts and placed them on seven mountains, and he held their heads. Then he called them: "Come, by God's permission!" Each drop of a bird's blood flew to the other drop, each feather flew to the other feather, each bone went to the other bone, and each piece went to the other piece, while Abraham watched. Until every body met the others in the air without a head. Then they came toward their heads, running. Whenever a bird came, it inclined its head; if its head was near, it came close; if not, it fell back. Until each bird was joined with its head. This is the meaning of His words, ﴿Then call them, and they will come to you running﴾.

It is said the meaning of "running" (saʿy) is hastening and running. It is also said that it means walking rather than flying, as God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Then hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ (62:9), meaning: proceed. The wisdom in walking rather than flying is that it is further from suspicion, for if they had flown, someone might imagine that they were other birds, or that their legs were not sound. And God knows best. It is also said that saʿy means flying.

﴿And know that God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The Exalted said: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. There is an ellipsis here, and its implied sense is: "The likeness of the charity of those who spend their wealth." ﴿Is like a grain﴾ of a sower ﴿that grows﴾, meaning "that produces" ﴿seven ears﴾, the plural of sunbulah (ear of grain), ﴿in every ear a hundred grains﴾.

He meant by "the way of Allah" jihad, and it is said that it means all the avenues of good.

If it is asked: "We have not seen an ear with a hundred grains in it, so how is it that this is used as a likeness?" It is said: that is conceivable and not impossible, and what is not impossible may be used as a likeness even if it has not been found. Its meaning is: in every ear there are a hundred grains, so that what grows from the seed that was in it is multiplied by it. Al-Dahhak also interpreted it this way, saying: every ear produces a hundred grains.

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. It is said that its meaning is that He multiplies in this manner for whom He wills. It is also said: its meaning is that He multiplies upon this, and increases for whom He wills, from seven to seventy to seven hundred, and to whatever multiples Allah wills, of which none knows except Allah.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, Rich, who gives out of abundance, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the one who spends his wealth.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 262–264:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. Al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abd al-Rahman came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with four thousand dirhams as charity and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I had eight thousand, so I kept four thousand for myself and my dependants, and I lent four thousand to my Lord." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "May Allah bless what you kept for yourself and what you gave." As for Uthman, he equipped the army of the Muslims for the expedition of Tabuk with a thousand camels, with their saddles [[Plural of qatab, the pack-saddle fitted to the size of the camel's hump, so that one may ride or be loaded upon it.]] and their saddle-blankets [[Plural of hils, a cloth placed on the back of a camel beneath its saddle.]]. So this verse was revealed concerning them both.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura said: Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, came with a thousand dinars during the army of hardship (jaysh al-usra) [[The expedition of Tabuk, so called because of the hardship the Muslims faced in it.]], and poured them into the lap of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. I saw the Prophet ﷺ put his hand into them, turning them over, and saying: "Nothing that Ibn Affan does after today will harm him." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Manaqib, chapter 76, section 10, p. 193, who said: "A hasan gharib hadith from this route." Ahmad in his Musnad, 5/63, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura, and its isnad is hasan.]] Then Allah revealed: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, in obedience to Allah, ﴿then do not follow what they have spent with reminders (mann) of it﴾.

Mann is that one reminds the recipient of his gift, saying, "I gave you such-and-such," and enumerates his favours upon him, thereby spoiling them. ﴿Nor injury (adha)﴾ is that he reproaches him, saying, "How long will you keep asking, and how long will you keep hurting me?" It was also said that injury is that he mentions his giving in front of someone who does not like that the recipient be made known to them.

Sufyan said: ﴿Reminder and injury﴾ is that one says, "I have given you and given you, yet you have not thanked me." Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: My father used to say: "When you give a man something and you see that your greeting weighs heavily upon him, withhold your greeting from him." Allah forbade His servants to reproach for a favour and reserved it as an attribute of Himself, because for the servants it is a form of reproach and spoiling, whereas for Allah it is bounty and reminder.

﴿They will have their reward﴾, that is, their recompense, ﴿with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾.

﴿Kind words (qawl ma'ruf)﴾: that is, good speech and a gracious response to the one who asks. It was also said: a good promise. Al-Kalbi said: a righteous supplication, one praying for his brother in his absence. Al-Dahhak said: it was revealed concerning reconciliation between people (islah dhat al-bayn). ﴿And forgiveness﴾: that is, that one conceals his need and does not expose his concealment. Al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: by overlooking the one who wronged him. It was also said: that one overlooks the poor man when he behaves arrogantly towards him in refusing him. ﴿Better than a charity﴾ that one gives to him ﴿followed by injury﴾, that is, reminder and reproach to the beggar, or words that hurt him. ﴿And Allah is Self-Sufficient (ghani)﴾, that is, free of need for the charity of the servants, ﴿Forbearing (halim)﴾, not hastening to punish the one who reminds and hurts with his charity.
